News.title: Kyrenia ferry live: 8 dead as boat capsizes off northern Cyprus and crew arrested
News.content:
An ambulance arrives at the port of Kyrenia in the Turkish occupied northern part of Cyprus after a ferry overturned off the coast

Eight people have died after a passenger ferry carrying 267 people capsized off northern Cyprus, with a search underway for 18 missing people

Eight people have died and 18 are missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus - with the boat's captain and seven crew members arrested.

Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, confirmed the fatalities following the disaster off the port of Kyrenia, which sparked a major search effort and saw 249 people being rescued.

The vessel capsized early on Sunday afternoon after "taking in water" just 15 minutes into its journey to the Turkish port of Tasucu.

Mr Ustel said the ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began sinking off the coast of Diana beach before a call for help was made.

Turkish Cypriot and Turkish coastguard crews have been deployed, along with rescue helicopters and other vessels, as efforts continue.

News.title: 'My neighbour says I can’t run my car on driveway before moving off'
News.content:
'My neighbour says I can’t run my car on driveway before moving off'

Resident said neighour dashes out whenever he runs the car for more than 10 seconds

View Image A neighbour objected to diesel fumes from an idling car, a resident said (Image: Getty)

A resident says that when he starts up his car and he leaves it running for 30 seconds before driving off, a neighbour ‘runs over’ and tells him it’s illegal. Taking to Reddit the motorist said he likes to let to idle for a short while to make sure the engine isn’t damaged by moving off when it’s cold.

However, he said he wasn’t even given 10 seconds before the neighbour dashed out. He said: “I have a diesel car which I like to leave running for 30 seconds to a minute before driving just to allow the oil/metal to acclimatise and to not damage the car. I have just moved into a new property, and I had my car running for maybe 10 seconds at idle and a neighbour ran over and asked me not to leave my engine running and that idling is illegal and the exhaust ill go into their bedroom.

”I’ve just moved in and I really don’t want to be a d***, but I would like to know what the law would suggest surrounding this? I can’t seem to find anything online.”

People flagged up the rule about letting the engine idle ‘unnecessarily’ on a road. One said: “Public Roads: Rule 123 of the Highway Code states you must not leave an engine running unnecessarily while stationary on a public road.

“30 seconds doesn’t seem unreasonable though, not many people get in their car, start it and drive off instantly.”

And the resident replied that also: “It is also not a public road, it is my driveway.” One suggested not to get too worried about it: “Just smile, nod and carry on with your life. People moan about anything.”

One person suggested that it was pointless from a mechanical perspective: “Aside from the neighbour complaints you are wrong. Idling a car for 30 seconds to a minute doesn’t prevent damage. Cars are supposed to be warmed up whilst driving. While not under any load oil doesn’t reach all of the engine, meaning some of it is not lubricated for a while. To prevent wear, as is your intention, you should set off driving within 10 - 15 seconds of starting the engine.”

On the subject of engine idling the RAC said: “Idling, instead of turning your engine off while stationary, increases the amount of exhaust emissions in the air.

“These emissions contain a number of harmful gasses including carbon dioxide, which is bad for the environment and contributes towards climate change, as well as a range of other harmful gasses including nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons which are linked to asthma and other lung diseases.

“Diesel vehicles - older ones in particular - are thought to be one of the biggest contributors to the problem due to high levels of nitrogen oxide and particulates.

” Rule 123 of The Highway Code looks at ‘The Driver and the Environment’. It states that drivers must not leave a parked vehicle unattended with the engine running or leave a vehicle engine running unnecessarily while the vehicle is stationary on a public road.”

Article continues below

Some local authorities charge a £20 fixed penalty notice (FPN) for emission offences and stationary idling under The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) (England) Regulations 2002. There’s potential for the fine to increase to £801.

More information here.

News.title: Taxi driver who left mum 'terrified' with mystery passenger has licence removed
News.content:
Taxi driver who left mum 'terrified' with mystery passenger has licence removed

Laura Hegart, 50, was left terrified when the taxi driver turned up to take her home from a bar with a mystery man sitting in the front seat

View Image Laura Hegart, 50, said the incident left her scared (Image: Supplied)

A taxi driver who left a mum "absolutely terrified" has had his licence removed.

‌



Laura Hegart, 50, had been out for dinner and a couple of drinks with her daughter, 26, when she ordered the Renfrewshire Cabs taxi to take them home from Whisky Joe's Bar in Paisley, Scotland at around 9pm on January 27.

‌



However, as the private hire taxi appeared, she noticed two men within the vehicle - with the driver having turned up with a mystery man in the front seat.

‌



Initially thinking it may be for someone else, she phoned the driver who got out the car to tell her that it was hers. After approaching the vehicle, she confronted the pair and was informed by the passenger that he was 'training' the driver.

UK weather maps show heatwave conditions returning for 3 days as dates revealed READ MORE :

Officers died from head and neck injuries when car driving wrong way on A66 crashed READ MORE :

Laura told Glasgow Live: "I approached the car and opened the rear door and explained that there is never two males in any Renfrewshire cab. I was then told by the passenger 'I am trainer' to which I said absolutely not. I then informed them I would be calling the office.

"I called Paisley Cabs to inform them that two males were trying to pick up people, which is illegal and highly worrying. I was told by the office that this driver would be signed off immediately and this is not something that is allowed to happen. While I was on the phone, the two men started shouting at each other and tried to shut the door to leave.

‌



"I refused to get out of the way until my daughter got a photo of their licence plate. I'm scared that if it was just my daughter on her own she might not have questioned it.

"How many people would have challenged them if they had been out drinking. It felt sinister... When I got home, I was furious. It's absolutely terrifying."

Following the incident, Laura contacted Renfrewshire Cabs who said the driver was no longer employed by the company. In a statement, the firm said "Passenger safety is our absolute priority" and that the individual "was a newly registered driver" who joined just before the incident.

‌



Laura, who took her complaints to Renfrewshire Council, says the driver had his licence removed earlier this month. She said she was 'happy' with the result but was still 'furious' over the incident, which scared her and her daughter.

"I'm very surprised that the council took his licence off of him. It's been a long process to get here. I don't understand why eight months to get here," she explained.

"But I'm not going to have anyone frighten my child. I am so sick and fed up of seeing women being unsafe taking these sort of taxis.

Article continues below

"There was absolutely no reason for another man to have been there. My daughter hasn't got a taxi since the incident unless me or her father is with her.

"It was traumatising. She thought we were going to get attacked.

"There needs to be more checks on the people being issued these licences."

News.title: Emmerdale fans rumble Joe Tate twist after Dawn Taylor's death as new storyline 'sealed'
News.content:
Emmerdale fans rumble Joe Tate twist after Dawn Taylor's death as new storyline 'sealed'

Emmerdale fans are convinced they've worked out a new romance for Joe Tate following the sad death of his fiancé Dawn Taylor

View 3 Images Could Joe end up in another romance? (Image: ITV)

Emmerdale fans have rumbled a potential new storyline for Joe Tate following Dawn Taylor's death.

‌



Dawn sadly died in devastating scenes last night following the marquee accident, which also claimed the life of Jimmy King. Olivia Bromley has now departed the soap, waving goodbye to a character she has played for years.

‌



Speaking to The Mirror about her exit, she admitted: "It was the toughest storyline I've done during my time in the soap. I was surprised by how emotional I found it and it was way more emotional than I was expecting.

‌



"I did cry. It is very strange to kill off your character as an actor and in front of your colleagues. But that said, what a gift to be given. Often people leave and just slip off."

View 3 Images Dawn sadly died, leaving Joe alone

Now, fans are convinced they've worked out a brand new storyline - which could see a grieving Joe Tate end up with Gabby Thomas, who is also a solo parent to a Tate baby.

‌



One fan suggested: "Her leaving paves the way for Joe and Gabby. Gabby will help Joe with the baby, they will commiserate about being single parents to Tate babies and they’ll end up together until Graham susses out that Gabby was driving while lightheaded from her eating disorder and Jimmy swerving to avoid her caused the accident that killed Jimmy and Dawn."

Another added: "I don't know why, but I think there's the potential for one of those couples who shouldn't work, but do. The actors have enough chemistry to pull it off, and it would be believable as a slow burn.

View 3 Images Could Gabby end up with Joe?

‌



"She has impressively bad luck in men and he has a history of breaking women's hearts. I'm guessing an embarrassed one night stand at first, put behind them, then a slow emotional match before anything else physical. They would make a cute little family unit of their own as single parents of two boys relatively close in age."

Fans are convinced we could see Joe and Gabby get together, with one describing them as a "perfect" couple.

"When Dawn leaves, Joe & Gabby would be a perfect couple imo. I feel like Gabby would actually challenge Joe more than Dawn ever did. Gabby doesn't take shit at all, and I can't see her enabling any of Joe's behaviour, much like Dawn did, both last year, and earlier this year," they wrote.

Article continues below

"With a relationship, there needs to be balance. While Joe & Dawn are of course very cute and sweet together, a lot of it was Dawn turning a blind eye to his behaviour, until she decided to grow a conscience too little too late."

News.title: 'I was one of the first on Wegovy weight loss pill - the effects have been big'
News.content:
'I was one of the first on Wegovy weight loss pill - the effects have been big'

Lauren Carrigher says the pill was the only option for her as she is 'terrified of needles'

View 5 Images Lauren Carrigher, after taking the pills (Image: SWNS)

A woman who was among the first in the UK to try the Wegovy weight loss pill says she lost 12lbs in just six weeks - and has had no side effects. Lauren Carrigher, 35, signed up for the oral GLP-1 medication as soon as it became available after struggling to lose two stone she gained while taking medication for menopause symptoms and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

‌



The influencer, from Maldon, Essex, said she had tried healthy eating and regular exercise but found it impossible to shift the weight. Although she had considered injectable weight-loss medication such as Mounjaro, she was put off by a fear of needles and concerns that injections could interfere with the absorption of her other medication.

‌



When she heard an oral version was available, she decided to give it a try. The Wegovy pill has been approved for use in the UK and is now available at pharmacies such as Superdrug, ASDA, and MedExpress - although is not yet available on the NHS.

‌



ASDA pharmacy reported 7,000 orders for it on July 6 - the day it launched. Lauren said: "I feel like I have had no side effects, I feel great living my best life out with the kids.

"Losing the weight has boosted my confidence – losing those 12 pounds. I was really excited when I saw the pills had come out because I knew I could never do the injections.

"I'm terrified of needles, and I'd also read that injections can affect how your body absorbs tablets. Because I'm on menopause medication, that was something I was worried about."

‌



View 5 Images Lauren Carrigher, before taking the Wegovy pills (Image: Lauren Carrigher© SWNS)

She hopes her body mass index - which has dropped from 30 to 29 - will further drop to 24, helping her hit her goal weight of 12st. Lauren signed up through online weight management provider Voy, where she completed a health questionnaire before receiving the medication.

The first batch cost her £99 for a month - while the influencer also opted for some additional £20 vitamins to help her health while taking weight loss pills. Lauren first started taking her pills on July 11, and has so far taken one each morning.

‌



She said: "I'm always nervous about taking new tablets, so I researched everything properly first. Once I'd done that, I felt really confident about trying them and I was excited to see what would happen."

Lauren takes one tablet each morning on an empty stomach before eating. Just three days after starting the medication, she says she had already noticed significant changes.

She said: "I've only taken one and a half boxes and lost 12lbs. The biggest thing I noticed straight away was that I was getting full much quicker. I got about a quarter of the way through my dinner and I couldn't eat any more.

‌



"Normally I would eat the whole plate and then I'd still want something afterwards."

View 5 Images Lauren Carrigher says she lost 12lbs in just six weeks (Image: SWNS)

Lauren says she has not experienced any of the unpleasant side effects she had heard about from friends who used injectable weight-loss medication. She said: "I've had no side effects apart from feeling fuller more quickly.

‌



"My energy levels have been absolutely fine. I'm taking the nutritional support vitamins as well, so that could be helping, but overall I feel really healthy.

"I have been on it for six weeks no side effects. I feel happy and healthy. I plan to stay on it until I get to 12 stone. Right now I am 14st 7lbs – I was 15st 5lbs before.

"My family have noticed I have lost weight and think I look good and I think it's that confidence that I like as well."

‌



View 5 Images Lauren says she had tried healthy eating and regular exercise but found it impossible to shift the weight (Image: SWNS)

She has also noticed a reduction in bloating. Lauren said: "I always carry weight around my stomach and my hips. When I put weight on, my stomach sticks out and I feel really bloated. That's already started to improve, which has been lovely to see."

Standing 5ft 10in tall, Lauren said she weighed 15st 5lbs before starting the treatment and now weighs 14st 7lb. She hopes to continue taking the medication until she has lost another couple of stone.

‌



Lauren believes the tablet offers advantages over injectable treatments because it can be stopped immediately if it does not suit the user. She said: "For me, the pills are much better because if they don't agree with you, you just stop taking them.

"With injections, they're in your body for a month, so if you have complications you've got to deal with them for much longer."

She says several friends who opted for injections experienced sickness and stomach problems, something she has so far avoided. Lauren added: "I've got friends who were being sick and spending ages in the bathroom after having the injections, but I haven't had anything like that.

‌



"I know everyone reacts differently, but my experience has been really positive."

View 5 Images Lauren Carrigher's Wegovy pills (Image: SWNS)

While she acknowledges there has been plenty of debate surrounding GLP-1 weight-loss medication, Lauren hopes sharing her own experience will reassure others who may be considering the oral treatment.

Article continues below

She said: "There are so many stories online that can make you nervous because people often talk about the negatives. There are always going to be pros and cons, but for me it's worked brilliantly so far.

"I'm eating healthy, I'm eating less and, for the first time in a long time, I'm seeing the weight come off. I'm really excited to see what happens over the next few weeks."

News.title: Met Office maps show 72 UK areas face rain on bank holiday Monday – full list
News.content:
Met Office maps show 72 UK areas face rain on bank holiday Monday – full list

There are floods warnings and alerts in place across parts of the country after a soggy Sunday led to festival mudslides, delayed cricket matches, and a damp end to summer

View 4 Images The outlook for 7am on Monday, August 31

More than 70 areas could see showers on bank holiday Monday, but sunshine will still peak through the clouds for most.

The Met Office believes today should bring the best weather of the long weekend, after festival-goers braved the rain and mud in plastic ponchos on Saturday and Sunday.

It comes as Bradworthy Common in Devon saw 34.2mm of rain over 12 hours on Sunday, more than a third of the average for Devon for August. A flood warning was also in place for Spadesbourne Brook in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, on Sunday night, meaning flooding is expected, while 15 areas were covered by Environment Agency (EA) flood alerts, meaning floods are possible.

Met Office senior operational meteorologist Dan Stroud said: “It’s another day of sunny spells and showers, a generally bright but cloudy start with sunny spells in the east, we will have some showers from the get-go in the west and they will become a bit more heavy, the odd rumble of thunder is possible.

News.title: 'Andy Burnham is right to keep notorious killers inside jails and block their early release'
News.content:
'Andy Burnham is right to keep notorious killers inside jails and block their early release'

"Prison overcrowding is a real crisis - the answer is tougher management of the system, not letting dangerous offenders out before justice has been served."

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

There are crimes so grave that the public rightly expects the punishment to mean what it says.

‌



That is why Andy Burnham was right to step in and block some of Britain’s most notorious killers from being freed early. The prospect of those convicted of manslaughter in horrific cases benefiting from the government’s early release scheme caused revulsion. The Prime Minister has heard that anger and acted.

‌



He deserves credit for moving quickly, even though this was his own party’s policy. Governments are judged not just on the decisions they make, but on whether they have the courage to correct them when they are plainly wrong.

‌



The families of victims, though, should never have had to fight this battle. Mr Burnham is also right to promise more prison space by deporting foreign criminals who have no right to remain here. That should be accelerated.

Prison overcrowding is a real crisis. The answer is tougher management of the system, not letting dangerous offenders out before justice has been served.

Healthy move

A seven-minute finger-prick test at the local chemist could help save thousands of lives.

‌



That is the promise behind the NHS's plans to offer quick cholesterol checks to people aged 40 to 84 without the need for a GP appointment or a laboratory test. Almost half of adults have high cholesterol, yet many have no idea they are living with a condition that can lead to heart attacks and strokes.

Taking these checks onto the High Street makes sense, particularly in poorer communities where access to healthcare can be harder, and health inequalities remain stubbornly wide.

The NHS is under huge pressure. Smart prevention like this can ease that burden while catching problems before they become emergencies.

‌



If a simple test can spot a ticking time bomb in minutes, it should be available as widely as possible.

Spot on, Kylie

Kylie Minogue has spent four decades proving that perfect pop never goes out of fashion.

Now Can’t Get You Out Of My Head has passed one billion Spotify streams, more than 20 years after it conquered charts around the world.

Article continues below

La la la indeed.

News.title: Nurse in her scrubs killed in horrific hit-and-run crash as she crossed road in New York
News.content:
Nurse in her scrubs killed in horrific hit-and-run crash as she crossed road in New York

Footage has captured the terrifying moment a nurse, 28, was walking along a busy street when a black Cadillac sedan drove through a red light and hit her

View 3 Images A 28-year-old nurse has been killed in a high-speed hit-an-run (Image: News12)

A 28-year-old nurse has been killed in a high-speed hit-and-run after an overnight shift.

‌



Jiayi Zheng was wearing her scrubs while she walked along a busy road after her shift at a hospital in Brooklyn in New York on Saturday, August 29.

‌



Footage has captured the terrifying moment she was walking along 55th Street and Third Avenue when a black Cadillac sedan drove through a red light and hit her around 7.30am.

‌



Zheng was tossed in the air, just a block away from where she worked. The driver did not stop and drove away at speed.

View 3 Images Jiayi Zheng had just finished an overnight shift (Image: News12)

Medics rushed her to the same hospital where she succumbed to her head and neck injuries.

‌



"I heard the bang. Her bag was over here, and they left her there," witness Antonio Perez told News12 Brooklyn.

"The car just kept on, it never stopped for nothing at all."

The crash occurred on a perilous roadway, according to Senator Andrew Gounardes, who represents the neighbourhood.

‌



View 3 Images The driver never stopped (Image: News12)

A Department of Transportation redesign plan for the stretch of roadway was presented in 2023 but never went into effect.

Zheng is the ninth person killed by a hit-and-run driver in the last two weeks across New York City.

Article continues below

She is also the 11th killed while walking or biking the two-mile stretch of Third Avenue that runs under the Brooklyn Queens Expressway since 2014, according to advocacy group Transportation Alternatives.

As of Sunday afternoon, the driver has not been apprehended

News.title: Prisoners freed early are returning to jail at rapid rate, governors tell BBC
News.content:
Prisoners who were freed under the government's last early release scheme are returning to jail at a rapid rate, prison governors have told the BBC.

They say they are seeing the same inmates, who were let out as part of the 2024 early release scheme to ease overcrowding, coming back after reoffending - including for breaching their conditions.

"The churn is what stresses me out," said one governor in the Midlands, describing it as a "revolving door".

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the next early release scheme, starting in October, following outrage that the killers of PC Andrew Harper were among those eligible to be released.

On Sunday, Burnham announced that they will not be, telling the BBC that anyone convicted of unlawful killing will be excluded from the scheme.

He conceded that it means "hundreds" more people will stay in prison - as prisons in England and Wales reach breaking point at more than 97% full.

The government says there are plans to create more prison space by deporting foreign inmates and releasing some who are serving indefinite sentences, but they are unlikely to create much more space by the time the first batch of inmates are released in October.

BBC News spoke to three serving prison governors in England to gauge the state of correctional facilities and how staff are dealing with overcrowding. Prison staff are not supposed to speak to the media so their names and the prisons they govern will not be mentioned to protect their identity.

One governor from a prison in the north of England said the PM's plans to ease overcrowding "is all short-term solutions and we need space now".

"Providing additional cells in existing prisons will mean more prison staff needed to monitor that - it's not easy," they said, adding that staff shortages mean "prisoners are not living in a safe and decent environment".

The governor also said they were frustrated by the rate of prisoner recalls, saying: "We see the same people coming back after being released early and reoffending again, or breaking their [release] rules."

News.title: Patel to be replaced by Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary
News.content:
Dame Priti was appointed to Badenoch's shadow cabinet after finishing sixth in the leadership election, and previously held senior roles in successive Tory governments, including a three-year spell as home secretary under Boris Johnson.

Announcing her departure in a statement on X, she wrote: "It has been an honour to lead the Party's foreign affairs team in Parliament over the last two years.

"I'm pleased to continue supporting Kemi and the Conservative Party in a new role strengthening our relationships with fellow conservatives and centre right parties around the world."

She said she would continue to serve as the MP for Witham in Essex.

A Conservative reshuffle had already been expected in the coming weeks because of the shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho's upcoming maternity leave.

In recent weeks, people within the party have played down speculation that the shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride could also lose his job in the changes.

But some sources within the party still believe Badenoch could choose to replace him.

Many within the Conservative Party view Coutinho as a likely future shadow chancellor. The shadow energy secretary is said to have impressed colleagues with her performances in Parliament and the media.

But it is unlikely Badenoch will move to appoint her as shadow chancellor while she is on leave from the front bench.

The Conservative leader will also need to replace Sir James as her shadow housing secretary after he quit the front bench to focus on setting up a campaign to run for London mayor.

He has not yet been selected as the party's candidate for the May 2028 election, nor has he resigned as the MP for Braintree.

News.title: Djokovic in tears during US Open first-round exit
News.content:
Novak Djokovic broke down in tears during a US Open first-round defeat by Argentina's Mariano Navone which provided further evidence age is fast catching up with the 39-year-old great.

The 24-time Grand Slam champion was overcome by emotion in the deciding set of a dramatic match where he struggled physically throughout and had to vomit into a towel bin.

Djokovic, seeded fourth, showed the fight for which he has always been renowned before succumbing to a 7-6 (7-5) 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1 loss in a humid New York.

It was the first time the Serb had been beaten in the opening round at Flushing Meadows and the first time he had lost in the opening round of a Grand Slam tournament since 2006.

"I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me," Djokovic said.

"I don't want to take too much out of Mariano's win. Congrats to him, he's a nice guy and a fighter - but I didn't enjoy myself."

Djokovic managed to raise a smile as he congratulated 25-year-old Navone on what will rank as one of the biggest victories of the world number 49's career.

But, after showing grace and class while congratulating his opponent, a disconsolate Djokovic was unable to keep a brave face for long and appeared close to tears again as he trudged back to the locker room.

The defeat ended Djokovic's latest bid for a standalone record 25th Grand Slam singles title, which would move him clear of Australia's Margaret Court.

Chances are clearly running out for Djokovic. Many sensed this was another decent opportunity given world number one Jannik Sinner is missing through injury and defending champion Carlos Alcaraz is making his comeback from a long-term wrist injury.

News.title: This actor was told he had Alzheimer's, now he's performing a one-man show
News.content:
For four days running, Peter Marinker had arrived at rehearsals that were not even taking place. Dementia had muddled the dates in his mind.

Yet he is now preparing to do something most actors would find daunting even with perfect recall: performing a much-loved Samuel Beckett play alone on a London stage.

Marinker, 85, is best known for his voice work: from radio plays and video games to big-budget films like Labyrinth and Paddington in Peru.

On camera he was the adviser to the US president in Love Actually and one of the airline passengers in the drama United 93.

In 2023 he was playing Gandalf in a stage version of Lord of the Rings when he felt himself "switching off" and an understudy had to take over for the rest of the run.

MRI scans and other health checks followed. Then two years ago, he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease.

"I just had to accept it," he says. "It explained why I kept losing things and I started laughing at myself, at all the other silly things I do again and again."

News.title: The mystery of why so many black Britons still can't swim
News.content:
As I push through the doors, the smell of chlorine hits me. Instantly, I feel sick, and I remember why I don't go swimming. I'm getting ready for my first swimming lesson in over 10 years, trying to convince myself it won't be so bad.

Before I know it, I'm in the water.

I glance around the pool; I'm surrounded by other black women learning to swim, all at different levels. Some are confidently swimming lengths; others, like me, are learning how to feel at home in the water.

I'm learning to breathe properly, dunk my head under and let the water carry me, rather than fight against it. There are so many things to remember.

At the age of 27, I'm still unable to swim - and I'm far from alone.

Swimming ability is not spread evenly across the population; figures compiled by Swim England, swimming's governing body, based on a survey of 4,500 people suggest poorer people, for example, are much less likely to be able to swim, as well as Muslims, people of South Asian descent and children known to social care.

As a black woman, it's the figures for the black community that always jump out to me. Swim England's figures suggest that 67% of black women and 44% of black men in England cannot swim 25 metres unaided - far higher than the national average, and far higher than the numbers for white people (17% of white women and 12% of white men cannot swim 25 metres). Behind those figures, published in 2022, are very different stories.

News.title: Parents of seriously ill children should get paid leave, says commissioner
News.content:
Parents of children with serious illnesses or disabilities should be entitled to paid leave from work, the children's commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza has said.

She called on the government to introduce a legal right to 12 weeks of paid leave at 90% of normal pay in order to lift the "immense pressure" and lost earnings families face when a child develops a debilitating condition.

Her intervention came as the government continued to consult on how to financially support families and unpaid carers looking after ill children in England, Scotland and Wales.

She said: "Parents should not be forced to choose between being at their seriously ill child's bedside and keeping their job."

Dame Rachel said that parents have told her of the "impossible choices" they have made when "splitting time between caring for their seriously ill and disabled children and trying to hold down a job".

She has also backed a "right to return to work" following extended periods of leave, saying it could help "families whose children have complex or fluctuating needs to remain in employment while providing the care their children need".

Dame Rachel called unpaid carer's leave to be increased from five to 10 days a year, and for the introduction of a form of paid carer's leave.

It comes after campaigning by the parents of Hugh Menai-Davis, who died of cancer aged six in 2021.

His parents Frances and Ceri Menai-Davis have advocated for a change to employment law that would require employers to guarantee three months' salaries to parents whose child faces serious physical or mental illness.

"There's no specific right that allows the parents to legally be by the bedside of the child in hospital," Ceri Menai-Davis said in June.

"If you're a parent with a child, there is nowhere else you are going to be other than their bedside."

A consultation on reforms to the support available to families and carers is due to close on Monday.

Kate Dearden, minister for the future of work, said: "Serious childhood illness is a heartbreaking situation for families.

"I've been incredibly moved by the powerful stories we have heard, and we will move quickly to consider how we can strengthen support and employment rights for families facing serious childhood illness."

News.title: Jewish community in harder position than immediately after synagogue attack, says rabbi
News.content:
The Jewish community at a synagogue where two men were killed in 2025 feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack, its rabbi has said almost one year on.

Rabbi Daniel Walker said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation in Manchester â and British Jews more widely â feeling increasingly vulnerable as the anniversary of the attack approaches.

"I think we're actually almost in a harder position than we were even immediately after the attack," he said ahead of a memorial service for the victims and survivors which will take place later today.

"I think the sense of vulnerability has grown. It hasn't diminished."

Two men, Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby, were killed and three others were injured as they tried to defend their synagogue from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, on 2 October 2025.

A wave of worldwide attacks followed over subsequent months.

In Sydney, Australia, 15 people were killed in a shooting at a celebration for the festival of Chanukah on Bondi Beach.

In London, Jewish people and property were targeted in arson attacks, including in March on ambulances belonging to the Hatzola emergency medical service.

In April, two orthodox Jewish men were stabbed as they left morning prayers in Golders Green.

A BBC Freedom of Information request to police forces in England and Wales has found that across 33 forces, violent hate crimes targeting Jewish people â such as harassment and assault â have risen by nearly two thirds since 2022.

News.title: Russian strikes destroy 12 million books ahead of Ukraine's first week back at school
News.content:
Viktoria Haidai surveys the mangled remains of the printing press, which should have been busy churning out textbooks ready for the new school year.

The plant, on the edge of Kyiv, was hit during the night by a Russian missile, just as production was ramping up to deliver 1.3 million books â 10% of Ukraine's schoolbooks.

In the ashes there is a charred page from an English language textbook: "My name is William, I'm from the UK. My grandmother lives in Nottingham. It's a beautiful city."

Russia has hit printing presses and publishing houses across Ukraine in a series of recent attacks, destroying 12 million books and damaging other icons of Ukrainian history and culture. Local media report, external that Russia has destroyed one third of all the books printed in Ukraine this year.

Nothing is salvageable at this Kyiv printing press. Even the pages that survived the flames have succumbed to water damage, from firefighting or exposure to the elements from the collapsed roof.

"I believe it is deliberate on the part of the Russian Federation," says Haidai, commercial director of the Konvi publishing firm. "Over the past two months, some of the largest publishing houses have lost their logistics warehouses, where very large quantities of books were stored.

"The Russians are also destroying printing houses in an attempt to erase Ukraine as a nation. But frankly they will not succeed."

News.title: Emergency measures needed to stop teachers quitting, say Lib Dems
News.content:
Burnt out teachers urgently need better working hours and more support to stop them leaving the profession, the Liberal Democrats say, as the new term approaches.

Nearly half of the teachers surveyed by the party in England said they were planning to quit the classroom in the next five years, with many saying they felt overworked and stressed.

The Lib Dems are urging new Education Secretary Lucy Powell to fully fund teachers' pay, rather than raiding school budgets to cover increases, and to bring in limits on overtime.

The Department for Education said last year saw the lowest rate of teachers leaving the profession since 2010 but acknowledged there was "more to do".

The survey asked more than 900 teachers, headteachers and Special Educational Needs Coordinators (SENCOs) across England how long they planned to stay in teaching.

Almost half of those in post said they were considering leaving teaching in the next five years, while one in ten were planning to spend less than a year in the job.

More than three quarters of those surveyed, which included former teachers, said they had felt "frequently or constantly burnt out" while at work.

Respondents cited high workloads on marking, lesson preparation and other tasks, which they said gave them less time in the classroom.

The Liberal Democrats' schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said this pointed to a government that is "not listening" to the profession.

"We rely on teachers to educate our children, the least we can do is make sure they want to come back after the summer," she said.

Teacher retention is a challenge successive governments have had to grapple with.

The National Education Union (NEU) reported that 4 in 10 teachers were planning to quit over "huge workloads and excessive accountability" in 2019.

This latest survey was also conducted with the help of the NEU, as well as the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL).

"After over a decade of austerity and chronic underfunding in our schools the system is on its knees" said the NEU's general secretary Daniel Kebede.

"The new academic year is the perfect time for Andy Burnham to signal a fresh start for our schools" he added.

"That means fully funding the pay award and properly funding all our schools and colleges to stem the recruitment and retention crisis and give children the education they deserve."

"As Lucy Powell enters her first term as education secretary the Liberal Democrats are calling for her first act to be to introduce an emergency package of 'back to school' measures to face this crisis head on," Voaden said.

The Lib Dem proposals include the government fully funding teacher's pay, which will increase in England by 3.5% from September, with an additional 3% the year after.

Currently, half of the pay increase will come from existing school budgets.

The party is also calling for proper enforcement of teacher's legally mandated working hours, the introduction of reasonable limits on overtime, and for all schools to be required to introduce flexible working policies.

The party did not identify where funding might come from to pay for the policies.

An education department spokesperson said: "We know teachers do an incredible job and we're determined to make sure that dedication is matched with the right support.

"Last year saw one of the lowest rates of teachers leaving the profession since 2010, and a record number of teachers returning to the classroom, but we know there's more to do.

"We're taking action by announcing pay awards of almost 17% over two years, funding schools to improve maternity pay and offering targeted support to normalise flexible working and manageable workloads so that more teachers stay in our classrooms and thrive."

News.title: Hints of fiery finale for last ever episode of River City
News.content:
Johnny McKnight has written for River City for almost a decade so, when it was announced that the show was drawing to a close after 24 years, he asked if he could write the final episode.

"Those moments don't come up very often with long-running shows so I thought it might be cathartic and a nice way to say goodbye as a writer," he says.

Details of the episode, which will air on Monday, are a closely-guarded secret but images released showing a bloodied Lenny Murdoch amidst a dramatic fire scene suggest the show's arch-villain, played by Frank Gallagher, is at the centre of it.

He said he felt a huge responsibility to the show's fans to give them a satisfying ending.

He points to cult TV shows whose endings have divided fans - like The Sopranos, Dexter, Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Angel.

Gallagher says: "I'm just part of a massive collective team effort and I hope we've done the fans proud to the end."

He thinks the show has always managed to walk a fine line between comedy and drama.

"River City is what I think it is to be Scottish. Our punches have punchlines.

"We take our trauma and we find a way to tell it in a pub that makes it palatable, and the humour co-exists alongside the drama."

News.title: Samuel breaks more new ground with first win at a Slam
News.content:
British qualifier Toby Samuel broke more new ground with a dominant victory over Tomas Machac on his US Open main-draw debut.

The 23-year-old came from a set down in each of his three qualifying matches in New York this week to guarantee a third Grand Slam appearance of the year.

However, he had no such issues against former world number 20 Machac, wrapping up a 6-2 6-3 6-2 victory in just over 90 minutes to register his first win at a Grand Slam.

"It means everything to me. It's what I dreamt of as a kid watching these big tournaments," Samuel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Being able to win my first Grand Slam match is unbelievable."

Just two years ago, Samuel fell to almost 2,000th in the world rankings as bone bruising in his right arm ruled him out of much of the 2024 season.

He now sits inside the top 100 in the live ATP rankings, along with earning $140,000 (Â£103,000) in prize money in the biggest payday of his career so far.

Samuel won 36 of 39 matches on the ATP Challenger Tour to return to the top 300 last year, but has reached new heights in 2026.

The Winchester native came through qualifying to make his Grand Slam debut at the French Open, having never previously contested a single match on the ATP Tour.

He continued that momentum with a run to the semi-finals at Eastbourne, a Wimbledon wildcard, and a third Challenger crown of the year on Winnipeg's hard courts.

Samuel's new ranking would secure automatic qualification for next January's Australian Open, completing the set of major appearances a year after making his top-250 debut.

He is joined in the second round in New York by compatriot Katie Boulter, who battled past American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee 6-4 3-6 6-0.

News.title: UK raises case of British activist detained by settlers in West Bank with Israel
News.content:
The UK Foreign Office says it has raised the detention of a British national in the occupied West Bank with Israeli authorities.

Finn Joughin, a 22-year-old student activist, was arrested in Umm Al-Kheir on Saturday after he was forcibly detained by Israeli settlers who had advanced on the Palestinian village.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

All settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts are also illegal under Israeli law, although they are often supported by state services and funding.

The confrontation on Saturday took place in a town near Hebron that has been recently surrounded by settlers.

According to other activists who witnessed what happened, Palestinian children were playing football when children from settler families started intervening. They then ran to a house and started to dismantle a fence.

Footage posted online by both settlers and activists and seen by the BBC appears to show Joughin standing by the fence and trying to protect it using his body as a child pushes against him.

Settlers removed Joughin forcefully and took the London-based student to an outpost.

Israeli police said a foreign national was detained by security personnel of a settler community who suspected him of an indecent act against a minor.

In a later statement on Sunday, they said: "The suspect was transferred to the police for questioning, which included, among other things, taking statements that raised suspicion of an assault against a minor.

"Following his questioning, the suspect was taken into custody, and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing."

However, Joughin's family told the BBC he was due to be deported from Israel on Monday.

Activists who were with Joughin at the time deny there was any inappropriate behaviour.

"In every single instance, it was the settler kids who approached Finn," fellow activist Matthew, who declined to give his surname, told the BBC.

News.title: Fears over 'high risk' crossing after train crash death
News.content:
An investigation is continuing into how a delivery vehicle and a train collided on a crossing, killing a van driver.

The incident happened off Martin Lane and Whitehouse Lane in Burscough, West Lancashire, on Saturday at about 15:00 GMT, when a train from Southport to Manchester collided with what is understood to be a supermarket delivery vehicle.

People living in the area have told the BBC that it was not uncommon for the gate on the crossing to be left open at times by people using it.

The claims have been put to Network Rail, which, while not able to comment on the claims, said it was involved in an investigation alongside British Transport Police and the Rail Accident Investigation Board.

The train was travelling towards Burscough town centre when the collision happened. A woman who was on board the train described seeing the van travelling along Martin Lane before it collided with the Northern train.

The crossing where the crash took place is not a full level crossing, but one operated by people as and when they use it.

It has lights and makes warning noises when the gate is not shut.

News.title: British woman killed in stabbing at German railway station
News.content:
A British woman has died after being stabbed at a railway station in southern Germany in the early hours of Sunday morning, police have said.

The 31-year-old woman was attacked at the station in Rosenheim, Bavaria, shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00 BST). She was taken to hospital where she died as a result of "severe" injuries, the Bavarian Police said in a statement.

Officers arrested a 27-year-old German man at the scene immediately after the incident. The background and motive for the attack is under investigation, the statement added.

Police have asked anyone who may have witnessed "an argument or physical altercation" at the station late on Saturday or early on Sunday to contact them.

The suspect, from the FÃ¼rstenfeldbruck district, will be brought before magistrates later on Sunday, according to German news agency DPA.

It is unclear whether the two knew each other or what the woman was doing in Bavaria, DPA also reported.

Rosenheim is one of the largest cities in Upper Bavaria and is a busy rail hub for passengers travelling to Austrian cities including Vienna, Salzburg and Innsbruck.

The Rosenheimer Herbstfest - an event similar to the Oktoberfest beer festival - is currently taking place in the area.

Responding to the attack, Rosenheim Mayor Abuzar Erdogan said "there are no indications of a security threat in our city or of any link to our Herbstfest".

"The criminal investigation department is working closely with the public prosecutor's office to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the crime as a matter of urgency," he wrote in a statement.

A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities."

News.title: Church leads tributes for man killed at festival
News.content:
The man killed at a Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday has been named by his church as Robert Guanco, 41.

He was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.

Six other people were injured at the event by a falling sign at the Big Church Festival, near Steyning, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment.

In a statement, his church said: "Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love, and his service to God will never be forgotten."

On a fundraising page for Guanco's family, pastor Norman Ponce from Jesus the Living Water Worldwide Church, said he was a "faithful servant of God".

"What was meant to be a time of worship, fellowship, and celebration became an unimaginable tragedy," he added.

Ponce said Guanco was a "beloved son, cherished brother, loving husband" and "great father".

"He was also a good friend, mentor, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched," Ponce said.

"His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion, and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers, and encouragement, he touched many lives."

News.title: Sons of officer who died in A66 crash lead out Man Utd as mascots
News.content:
The two sons of a police officer killed in a crash on Teesside led out the Manchester United team as mascots for Sunday's Premier League match against Ipswich at Old Trafford.

PC Matthew Blades, described as a "proud Red" by United, was a regular at Old Trafford.

The club paid tribute to him in Sunday's match programme, while his widow attended the game with their children.

PC Blades and his colleague PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.

United said they learned of the deaths of the two officers "with great sadness".

"Matthew was a proud Red, a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others," said the club, in a tribute in the programme.

At Elland Road, match officials for Leeds United's Premier League fixture against Brentford on Sunday wore black armbands as referee Tony Harrington was a friend of PC Blades.

On Saturday, there was a minute's applause in memory of PC Blades and PC Clough before Middlesbrough's Championship encounter with West Brom at Riverside Stadium. Pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.

People also gathered to pay tribute at Seaton Carew FC's game against FC Hartlepool. PC Blades had been a junior football coach at both teams.

Earlier this week, 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash, bringing the total number of arrests to 24.

The occupants of the other vehicle, a Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, also died.

American Sofia Kenin ​beat 46-year-old compatriot Venus Williams 6-2 7-6(6) in a US Open first-round match that began at 12.13am on Monday, the latest start in women's tournament ⁠history.

Kenin, the 2020 Australian ‌Open champion, will next face ​top-ranked American Jessica Pegula.

The match at Arthur Ashe Stadium got underway after Novak Djokovic's five-set defeat by Mariano Navone, with a sizable contingent of fans staying on well past midnight for one more look at Williams, who was playing as a wild card in her 96th career Grand Slam main draw appearance.

Williams said afterwards: “It's not ideal. I would have preferred something else definitely. It wasn't great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best.

“I just don't know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there's room for improvement there. It's not easy to do in the first round. It's not easy to do it at 1:00 or 2:00 a.m. in the morning to try to find your rhythm and play your best, but I tried my best.”

Kenin broke serve in the opening game ⁠and never trailed in the first set, racing to ​a ⁠3-0 lead as both players ‌struggled to find their rhythm, combining for nine double faults.

Williams, cheered on by chants of “Let's go Venus”, broke back to love to trim the deficit to 3-1 but dropped serve again as Kenin pulled away to close out the set.

Kenin reeled off three straight games to lead 3-1 in ⁠the second set and while Williams showed flashes of the form that earned her seven Grand Slam titles she struggled to string points together, with her second serve proving especially costly.

Kenin saved four break points to level at 5-5, leaving Williams screaming in frustration at handing her opponent another game with unforced errors.

However, Williams still found a way to hold for 6-5 before Kenin forced a tiebreak. Williams appeared to ⁠have the upper hand in the tiebreak but could ⁠not convert any of her seven set points, as Kenin dug in ‌to close out ​the win.

Kenin will next face top-ranked American ​Jessica Pegula.

Reuters

Singer Lola Young has surprised fans with a secret set at Reading Festival a year after pulling out of the event due to scheduling conflicts

The 25-year-old, wearing a Vivienne Westwood bodysuit with her signature statement earrings, appeared on the main Grid stage on Sunday for a performance which was originally labelled for a “special guest”.

“I am backstage, the cat is out of the bag and I am going to be performing so see you at 14:15 at the Grid stage,” she posted on her Instagram story moments before.

“Can’t wait to see you there!”

The pop star also had to cancel a string of shows after she collapsed on stage in September 2025.

The incident took place while she was performing at the All Things Go music festival at Forest Hills Stadium in New York.

Festivalgoers during Reading Festival ( PA )

The pop star cancelled all upcoming performances and told fans she was “going away for a while” in order to “come back stronger”, making her return to the stage in February 2026.

During her set, she sang some of her top hits, including Messy, One Thing and Conceited.

Young wore green tracksuit culottes and a black top with long black acrylic nails and joined a star-studded Sunday line-up which includes Florence and the Machine, Loyle Carner, Role Model and Kneecap.

The set comes weeks after Young completed a brief six-date UK tour including shows in Manchester, Birmingham and Glasgow before finishing with two dates in London.

The singer rose to fame following the release of her number one song Messy.

Earlier this year, she took home her first Grammy award, winning Best Pop Solo Performance for her 2024 hit track and also took home the Brit Award for Breakthrough Act.

Also headlining the final day of the festival were drum and bass duo Chase & Status, known for hits such as 2023’s Baddadan and 2017’s All Goes Wrong.

London indie rock stalwarts Florence + The Machine also took to the main stage earlier in the evening, with singer Florence Welch serenading the crowd with songs such as Everybody Scream, Shake It Out and You Got The Love, with Idles’ Mark Bowen on guitar.

Closing their set, Kneecap performed THE RECAP, their 2025 track which confronts the media scrutiny and political backlash the band faced for their pro-Palestine stance and police investigations.

A search for two missing crew members has been called off after a French fishing boat sank in the English Channel, though three other people were safely rescued.

On Sunday night, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which had described the two remaining crew members as "unaccounted for", stated that search efforts were "suspended pending further information".

The three crew members who were saved and taken to hospital on Saturday are now in the process of travelling back to France.

An intensive search south-west of Eddystone Lighthouse, just off the coast of Plymouth, was launched after a distress call was broadcast from the vessel on Saturday evening.

French authorities confirmed the stricken fishing vessel was named The Maranello, adding that it had reached out to a second trawler, The Stradale, to report an issue with its fishing gear.

The Stradale managed to recover three of the five crew members before the Maranello sank, the French naval prefecture for the Atlantic added.

One of the rescued sailors was evacuated by helicopter and is being treated at Truro Hospital, while the others were taken to Plymouth for medical attention.

Earlier, an MCA spokesman said: “HM Coastguard maintained the intensive search during the night and it is continuing today with multiple assets sent to help with the search.

“Three people were rescued last evening from the French-registered fishing vessel which had made the call for help.

“They were taken to hospital for further care.”

The MCA also confirmed that “the vessel has sunk”.

A coastguard rescue helicopter, a fixed-wing aircraft plus RNLI lifeboats from Falmouth and Plymouth were among the vessels scrambled to the scene.

Local vessels have also been helping with the British-led search-and-rescue operation.

The MCA was alerted by a report about the vessel just after 6pm on Saturday.

The French Navy’s Falcon 50 was also deployed to assist.

Twisha Sharma flies internationally at least twice a year. But she never travels with Air India.

Her reluctance to use the airline only hardened after a London-bound Air India flight crashed shortly after take-off in Ahmedabad last summer and killed 260 people.

“Since the crash there have been a lot of news articles about how the airline continues to not uphold good safety standards,” Sharma tells The Independent. “Maybe because of extra scrutiny, and maybe these things happen with every airline, but the fear factor has kind of set in.”

Her concerns reflect a broader shift in passenger attitudes towards Air India on the India-UK route in particular, according to data shared exclusively with The Independent by Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

The data shows a sharp drop in Air India's performance on the route. The airline had posted strong year-on-year growth in passenger traffic in the first five months of 2025 but the crash reversed the trend.

Between January and May 2025, Air India flew 18 to 32 per cent more passengers on the India-UK route a month than in the corresponding months of 2024. While the numbers were still marginally higher year-on-year in July 2025, they fell every month from August to December.

open image in gallery The wreckage of an Air India aircraft that crashed in Ahmedabad, India, on 14 June 2025 ( AFP/Getty )

The decline was particularly pronounced between August and October. Air India carried 85,024 flyers on the route in August 2025, down from 96,576 a year earlier. In September, the number fell from 100,559 to 81,291, before dropping by 14 per cent in October. The figures suggest that the fall in demand was greater than the reduction in Air India's capacity on the route.

In August and September, the number of seats operated by Air India fell by 4 per cent year-on-year, while passenger numbers declined by 11 per cent and 19 per cent respectively.

In October, the contrast was starker. The airline operated slightly more seats than a year earlier but carried nearly 14,000 fewer passengers.

There were signs of a partial recovery during the winter season. The number of flyers rose to 107,568 in November 2025, leaving Air India only 0.7 per cent below the level recorded in the same month the previous year. In December, the number was 7 per cent lower year-on-year.

“That period is a heavy travel season – Christmas and holiday season – so the spike is noticed,” says Rajiv Mehra, general secretary of the Federation of Associations in Indian Tourism and Hospitality.

“This is normal, particularly for the India-UK sector. The Indigo issue may have contributed, but not much as Indigo doesn’t have a major presence on the route,” he says, referring to the cancellation of roughly 4,600 Indigo flights in December owing to problems with crew rostering and a transition to stricter pilot rest-time rules.

open image in gallery An Air India aircraft at the Mumbai airport in India on 8 December 2025 ( AFP/Getty )

For passengers such as Asha Raj, the Indigo disruption was indeed the reason to use Air India. Raj, who works in corporate communications, had been a loyal IndiGo customer but switched to the competitor in the wake of the disruption.

“I knew about the Air India crash but I think the Indigo strike probably turned me off more,” she says.

“I had friends who were gonna come in for a music festival and there were so many people who were stranded during that time. It was very difficult and there was a lot of uncertainty,” she continues.

“There was a lot of money lost. So after that I remember when I was travelling, I actively chose not to take Indigo.”

Why is she still choosing Air India? “One of the main reasons I do Air India is because of their pricing,” Raj says. “Even during the Indigo crisis, they kept it on time and didn’t really inflate the costs.”

In spite of a competitor’s troubles, Air India maintained a year-on-year passenger deficit in November and December. Fellow international carriers on the India-UK route, on the other hand, saw substantial growth. Their passenger numbers rose by 11.9 per cent year-on-year for both months, while capacity increased by 10.3 per cent and 10.99 per cent respectively.

The data for 2026 suggests Air India is yet to return to the pre-crash rapid growth. Passenger numbers were lower year-on-year in each of the first five months for which figures were made available.

The decline was relatively modest in January, February and March before widening sharply in April and May.

In April, Air India carried 77,822 passengers on the India-UK route, about 27 per cent fewer than in April 2025, despite reducing the number of seats by less than 10 per cent.

The pattern continued in May, when the number of passengers fell almost 25 per cent year-on-year, to 74,499, while capacity only dropped about 11 per cent.

open image in gallery IndiGo aircraft is displayed during the Wings India 2026 civil aviation show at the Begumpet airport in Hyderabad, India, on 29 January 2026 ( Reuters )

Mehra argues that the recent decline cannot be attributed to the crash alone, pointing to geopolitical tensions and restrictions on Indian carriers using Pakistani airspace. “Clearly the Iran-US war and the continued closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian carriers have contributed to this situation. Foreign airlines are not constrained by restrictions on use of Pakistani airspace, so they have been impacted much less.”

According to data released this month by India’s aviation regulator, DGCA, Air India's global passenger carriage plunged 36 per cent in the April-June quarter.

The Air India Group, comprising Air India and the low-cost carrier Air India Express, carried about 2.76 million international passengers to and from the country during the quarter, down from 4.33 million in the same period last year. In contrast, foreign airlines saw their passenger carriage to and from India rise by 7 per cent. Emirates carried 1.48 million passengers during the quarter as against 1.28 million the year before, while Lufthansa carried 370,000, up from 350,000. Etihad's traffic remained broadly stable at about 850,000 passengers.

“I know Air India will save me about six hours because my layover in Dubai is six hours, but I still choose Emirates because I am a very nervous flier and on top of that, sitting in an Air India plane does not help,” says Sharma.

Air India, unlike many of its more popular foreign rivals, offers direct flights between Delhi and London.

Namit Kabra, a consultant at Ernst and Young, preferred Air India for flights from India to London, or Birmingham before the crash because of its “price compatibility”. But, he says, he no longer trusts the airline since the crash.

“I don't think they have made anything significantly better so that their passengers can ease out on the anxiety. Apart from reducing prices after the crash, I do not feel there is any difference in how the staff treated you before and now,” he complains. “Other airlines are far better.”

Falling passenger traffic only increases the financial pressure as Air India attempts a sweeping overhaul of its operations.

The airline is reportedly seeking about $1.5bn in fresh equity from its owners, Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, months after posting a record annual loss.

Air India and Air India Express posted combined losses of $2.33bn in the financial year ended March, more than double the losses recorded the year before.

Responding to a detailed questionnaire from The Independent, a spokesperson for the airline said: "Air India continues to see encouraging customer response on its UK services as the airline's transformation programme delivers tangible improvements in customer experience. This progress has been achieved despite a challenging operating environment marked by prolonged Pakistan airspace restrictions, evolving competitive dynamics, and periodic geopolitical disruptions affecting international aviation markets.”

The airline said over “the past several years, Air India has invested significantly in upgrading its fleet, introducing new cabins and seats, enhancing onboard dining, expanding digital capabilities, and modernising customer service systems. These investments are translating into stronger customer sentiment.

“Across Air India's UK operations, Net Promoter Score (NPS) has improved from -46 in FY24 to +2 in FY26 and further to +13 in FY27 year-to-date. On London routes, NPS has improved by 66 points, from -45 in FY24 to +21 in FY27 year-to-date, reflecting the positive impact of the airline's product, service, and digital enhancements.Air India remains focused on delivering a consistently better experience for customers and further strengthening its position in the UK market."

N Chandrasekaran, the outgoing chair of Tata Sons, previously said that Air India's turnaround could take up to a decade, citing persistent supply-chain disruptions and the need to overhaul the carrier’s legacy systems, culture and fleet.

The airline nevertheless continues to invest heavily in expansion and fleet modernisation. It plans to add about 100 aircraft across the group in 2027 and 2028 and is retrofitting 16 Boeing Dreamliners.

“See, Indian aviation is growing and booming,” Mehra explains the expansion plans. “Yes, there are temporary blips, but long-term growth remains intact. That explains the order for the new aircraft.”

The United Arab Emirates’ air force intercepted an Iranian drone over its territorial waters Monday, the Defense Ministry said, an attack that comes after the U.S. and Iran exchanged fire on the weekend, the first significant military action in a month.

In a short statement, the Defense Ministry said it “dealt with” an Iranian drone that was detected over its waters approaching from Iran.

There were no immediate claims of responsibility from Tehran nor any reports of damage. The UAE Defense Ministry later issued a second statement denying the Al Menhad Air Base in Dubai had been targeted by Iranian missiles, as had been reported by Iranian media outlets.

The incident came after U.S. forces on Sunday struck Iranian rocket launchers on an Iranian island, breaking a lull in fighting in the war that has lasted more than six months.

Iran responded by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, which were intercepted.

Early Monday, Iran's Foreign Ministry said that Iran would “not hesitate to exercise the inherent right of legitimate defense and will respond decisively to any military aggression.”

Before heading to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization's summit in Kyrgyzstan with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who has favored a negotiated end to the conflict, stressed that Iran was not seeking war.

“But,” he said, “we will respond decisively to aggressors.”

The summit brings together a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence, and includes Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Pezeshkian was scheduled to meet with Putin on the sidelines on Tuesday.

Meantime, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was set to host meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in North Carolina on Monday and Tuesday, which come as Washington pressures other countries to help the U.S. economically isolate Iran to try and exact concessions out of its leaders to end the war.

The U.S. had been focusing on economic pressure in recent weeks but on Sunday, U.S. Central Command said it had struck Iranian launchers after observing forces with Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military said last week it had completed clearing sea mines from the waterway’s international shipping routes.

Semiofficial news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait and the Revolutionary Guard said there had been casualties.

U.S. military officials disputed Iran’s claim that the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a “limited, precise action” against what they said were minelaying forces.

Iranian state television later showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired at American bases in Jordan, and Jordan’s military said had intercepted eight that had entered its airspace.

A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted U.S. military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began on Feb. 28.

The last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, when it announced a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets including coastal surveillance and defense sites.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Aug. 1 he would order the military to hold off on new strikes at the urging of Gulf allies Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

When the Days of Thunder follow up film was announced Saturday by Tom Cruise and Anne Hathaway, many fans were thrilled — with one notable exception.

Randy Quaid, who starred with Cruise in the original 1990 Nascar film, ranted about Hathaway’s casting in a post on X.

“Anne Hathaway is a leftist, woke, horrible choice for DAYS OF THUNDER NASCAR audience who are MAGA,” Quaid began.

“The sexy older chick for Tom in this film needs to be Nicole,” he continued, likely referring to Nicole Kidman who starred in the original film.

“That’s the casting that would sell the idea. It’s interesting because when we made the first one there was also a rush to get it out; editors slept in the cutting room on shifts. This is a weird thing, like they want it to come out and tank.”

open image in gallery Randy Quaid has railed against the forthcoming ‘Days of Thunder’ film ( Randy Quaid/X )

In a separate post, Quaid again advocated for Kidman’s casting while railing against Hathaway and Cruise, writing: “We need Nicole back. Don’t be a p***y, @TomCruise. You need the original girl. It’s not personal; it’s filmmaking. Anne isn’t sexy, because and if you haven’t noticed, she’s pregnant.”

And in yet another post, he wrote: “If I were in control of production, a real sequel worth watching for DAYS OF THUNDER would be seeing Tom and Nicole together on screen again. We don’t need a new girl; we need a new race car!”

The Independent has contacted representatives for Cruise and Hathaway for comment.

Hathaway is one of the most in-demand stars in Hollywood, with four films out already this year and another — Verity, the latest film adaptation from author Colleen Hoover — slated for an October release.

open image in gallery Tom Cruise and Anne Hathaway are teaming up for a 'Days of Thunder' follow up film ( PA )

An Oscar winner for the 2012 film adaptation of Les Misérables, Hathaway is also pregnant with her third child. She confirmed in the announcement for the Days of Thunder sequel that she’ll give birth before filming commences.

Hathaway and Cruise will film the sequel nearly 40 years after the original movie was released. The new film is slated for a June 2028 release.

According to Variety, Cruise will reprise his role from the first film as Cole Trickle. Hathaway will play a racecar team owner and engineer. Jonathan Levine will direct, and Cruise will produce alongside Jerry Bruckheimer and Tommy Harper.

In addition to Cruise, the original Days of Thunder starred Kidman, Quaid, Robert Duvall and John C. Reilly. It is not yet clear whether any of the original cast will return for the follow up. Duvall died earlier this year.
