He accuses the trio of a "criminal conspiracy to commit false accusation... influence peddling... and aiding and abetting influence peddling".

World.title: Feroz Khan's health in spotlight ahead of Madlanga Commission appearance
World.content:
PRETORIA - The Madlanga Commission says it is aware of reports about Major-General Feroz Khan’s health.

However, it has not received anything official from his legal team, which has since indicated that it will provide a medical statement.

Khan was expected to appear before the Commission on 1 September after he was hospitalised following a shooting in Houghton.

He was treated for injuries sustained in the shooting. However, reports now indicate that he has been readmitted to a Johannesburg hospital, days before he was due to take the stand.

World.title: Tembisa Hospital tender fraud suspect to appear in court
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - A suspect linked to multimillion-rand tender fraud at Tembisa Hospital is expected to appear in court on Monday.

The 37-year-old doctor was arrested at OR Tambo International Airport after returning from abroad.

He is accused of colluding with officials from the Gauteng Health Department to manipulate the procurement process.

He faces charges of fraud, money laundering and corruption.

The Hawks say the investigation comprises seven legs, with the doctor’s arrest forming part of one of them.

The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: SA's Lloyd Harris powers into US Open second round
World.content:
NEW YORK - South Africa’s Lloyd Harris is through to the second round of the US Open, after earlier successfully negotiating three rounds of qualifying.

Harris beat American Jack Kennedy in straight sets in Round 1 on Sunday, winning 6-4, 6-2 and 6-2 in an hour and 43 minutes.

It’s a massive boost for SA men’s top-ranked star after he battled injuries and inconsistent form in recent seasons.

READ | Tennis SA president talks on the state of SA tennis

The big-serving Capetonian will take on the winner between Greece’s Stefanos Tsitsipas and 10th-seed Arthur Fils of France in Round 2.

Harris has previously enjoyed a memorable run at the tournament, reaching the quarterfinals in 2021, his best Grand Slam performance to date.

World.title: Ramaphosa vows to fix Hammanskraal’s water crisis
World.content:
HAMMANSKRAAL - President Cyril Ramaphosa has promised Hammanskraal residents safer communities and better services.

But in an area plagued by water shortages, where residents can go days without running water, those promises are wearing thin.

In 2023, a cholera outbreak in Hammanskraal claimed 30 lives.

Ramaphosa insists progress is being made and that the water crisis will be resolved.

He also says the ANC is changing how it selects candidates, calling for qualified people to run for mayor and council.

“Councillors must not be chosen in offices. They must be chosen by you, because you are the ones who know them,” he says.

The ANC has lost its outright majority in all three Gauteng metros and is trying to rebuild trust and regain support in some of its former strongholds.

World.title: Where is Sang? Key suspect remains missing as another cop linked to Dr Mutiso's murder seized in Uganda
World.content:
Dr Victoria Mutiso murder suspects from left Kevin Ngugi Kinuthia (motorcycle rider) , Daniel Mwangi Njoroge (Land cruiser Prado driver) and Elijah Kibelion Kimoi (alleged killer) at Milimani law courts for mentioning. The three suspects will be detained in police custody for 30 days pending investigations. [Collins Oduor Standard]

One of the police officers on the run and linked to the murder of Dr Victoria Nthunya Mutiso has been arrested while in hiding in Kampala, Uganda.

Police Constable Collins Kiplangat Bett was smoked out of Kyanja Heights flats in Nakawa suburbs of Kampala on Saturday by a special team from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) headquarters.

World.title: Trumpets of reforms blow louder as Kenya marks 16 years under 2010 Constitution
World.content:
The Constitution, Kenyan flag and the National anthem. [PCS]

On Thursday, August 27, a group of people largely composed of the youth gathered under some trees at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, carrying Kenyans flag, and banners and placards inscribed with "implement the constitution. Kenyans first" words.

These were in protests against what they believed is deliberate failure of those in authority to fully implement the 2010 Constitution.

World.title: Ruto allies hit back at Gachagua over IEBC tender concerns
World.content:
The Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kit. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto’s allies led by National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula have launched a scathing attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and the Opposition over their criticism of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), citing blackmail by the Opposition.

The leaders warned that attempts by politicians to dictate how the electoral agency procures technology and other election materials could undermine public confidence in the 2027 General Election.

World.title: IEBC rejects Gachagua's claims, defends 2027 polls preparations
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

IEBC dismissed Gachagua's claims of political interference, graft and voter suppression in 2027 polls.

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has dismissed allegations of political interference, corruption and voter suppression surrounding preparations for the 2027 General Election, terming the claims false, unsubstantiated and aimed at undermining public confidence in the electoral body.

In a statement issued on Thursday, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon said the allegations followed statements made by Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a press briefing on Wednesday.

The commission specifically rejected claims that politicians had purchased a house for its chairperson to influence him, saying the allegation had changed from an alleged Sh80 million property to one worth Sh200 million.

"The allegations that a house has been purchased for the Chairperson of IEBC by some politicians for purposes of influencing him are unfortunate, unfair and unsubstantiated to date," Ethekon stated.

The commission also challenged Gachagua to provide evidence, including the location of the property, sale and transfer documents, payment receipts and details of the parties involved, and submit them to the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission for investigation.

The electoral body also dismissed claims of improper staff changes, saying deployment and redeployment of employees was part of its normal administrative functions and was guided by its human resource policies and public service regulations.

"The Commission complies with its Human Resource policies, guidelines and other relevant instruments under the larger public service when engaging employees," the statement read in part.

It further denied allegations of malpractice against the chairperson and vice-chairperson, describing them as fabricated claims intended to damage the reputation of the commissioners and the commission.

Magarini by-election

On the Magarini by-election, IEBC said the poll was conducted in a free, fair and credible manner and was not challenged through an election petition. The commission added that it had successfully conducted several by-elections and was prepared to oversee the 2027 General Election.

At the same time, IEBC also defended its procurement process for election technology and ballot papers, saying all tenders were being conducted in accordance with Chapter 12 of the Constitution and the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015.

"Two key tenders, one for the Integrated Elections Management System, hardware and accessories, and another for ballot papers and other election materials, have temporarily been halted following a request for review filed before the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board," IEBC stated.

According to IEBC, documents for the technology tender were uploaded on its website and the Public Procurement Information Portal on August 11, 2026.

The commission said the technical specifications were generic and performance-based and open to all qualified suppliers. It stressed that the procurement process was still at its initial stages and that no company had been awarded the tender.

Voter register protected

The commission also dismissed claims that voter registration data could be manipulated or shared with external parties, insisting that the Register of Voters remained under its exclusive custody.

"Voter registration involves several stages, including in-person registration, verification of identity, collection of biometric and biographical data, transmission to a central database and automated biometric deduplication," IEBC added.

Flagged records are subjected to data cleaning, validation and adjudication before valid records are incorporated into the register.

The register will subsequently undergo a 30-day biometric verification exercise, followed by an independent audit before it is finalised and certified for use in an election.

IEBC said allegations of bribery, predetermined tender awards and voter suppression were false and potentially harmful to public confidence in the electoral process.

World.title: Ruto hands Sh2.6bn to Mau Forest evictees
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto also announced the lifting pf the caveat that had been placed on land bordering the Mau Forest. [PCS]

President William Ruto has announced the payment of Sh2.6 billion to 13,000 families evicted from the Mau Forest in Narok six years ago, marking what he described as the closure of a long chapter.

Each beneficiary received Sh200,000 through M-Pesa to help them resettle and rebuild their lives away from the water tower.

Speaking at Sogoo in Narok South Constituency on Wednesday, during the final day of his two-day tour of Narok County, Ruto said the Government had taken steps to address the longstanding Mau Forest resettlement problem.

He noted that in 2023, the Government gave Sh300,000 each to 2,000 families living in tents in the Mau Forest to enable them to leave the water tower and purchase land elsewhere.

“We are today officially closing the long and painful chapter of people who were removed from the Mau Forest, which the County Government of Narok will now manage,” Ruto said.

The President criticised politicians who, he said, had continued to politicise the Mau Forest issue without providing lasting solutions.

“Many politicians have talked of the Mau question, but I talked of the Mau answer. This is why we are here today closing this chapter,” he said.

Ruto also announced that the Government had purchased 5,800 acres of land to settle families who have been living as squatters on property previously owned by the family of former Provincial Commissioner Isaiah Cheluget.

“We are processing title deeds of the people living on the land after buying the Cheluget farm,” he said.

Construction of Johanna Ng'eno University

The President also announced the allocation of Sh1.2 billion for the construction of Johanna Ng’eno University in Emurua Dikirr Constituency.

Speaking during the laying of the foundation stone, Ruto said the institution would fulfil a pledge to residents while expanding access to higher education for students from across the country.

“You told me, as residents of Emurua Dikirr, that you want a university. Today, I have brought KSh1.2 billion to construct the university that will be named after our brother Johana Ng'eno,” he said.

He said the university would create employment opportunities and attract new investments to the region.

At the same time, Ruto maintained that his administration had fulfilled at least 80 per cent of the pledges contained in its 2022 campaign manifesto.

“Kenyans will elect leaders based on their development record. Sloganeering will not make Kenyans vote for them. They have a long way to go,” he said.

The President further launched the construction of the 18-kilometre Mogondo-Cheramgoi-Mogor-Soit road in Emurua Dikirr, saying the project would improve connectivity and unlock economic opportunities in the region.

“This new road will strengthen connectivity and unlock greater economic opportunities in the region,” Ruto said.

World.title: Gachagua to Duale: You don't own pastoralists
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua and delegates from Isiolo and Marsabit at Wamunyoro, Nyeri County on August 25, 2026. [Ali Abdi, Standard]

Democracy for Citizen Party (DCP) Leader Rigathi Gachagua has accused Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale of allegedly doing nothing for pastoralist communities in the country.

Mr Gachagua said Duale, while being the only CS from northern Kenya and claiming to be the spokesperson of the group, had instead been a liability to pastoralists.

“You, the Borana who are here, along with the Turkana and Somali, are all complaining like other Kenyans. You suffer from runaway insecurity and widespread underdevelopment. We must join hands to vote out this rogue government (in next year's general election),” the former Deputy President told a delegation of grassroots leaders and residents from Isiolo and Marsabit who paid him a courtesy call at his Wamunyoro rural home in Nyeri.

“Duale thinks that the pastoralists are his property, his children or servants. What has he done for the people of Isiolo and Marsabit? (He has) only rhetoric, shouting pastoralists everywhere, every day,” he said.

Gachagua questioned how Duale would be able to marshal ‘millions’ of votes for President Ruto in the 2027 General Elections while he (Duale) could only raise 7,000 votes for the UDA presidential candidate in the 2022 polls in his Garissa Township Constituency backyard.

Despite his little contribution to the Kenya Kwanza administration's victory, Gachagua said Duale was appointed as the only CS from northern Kenya but had ended up doing nothing for the region and pastoralist communities.

“He only gave him (Ruto) 7,000 votes in Garissa Township. It's Central Kenya that propelled this government,” Gachagua told the gathering.

“Duale was appointed CS and he has nothing to show apart from empty words, going round shouting (the name of) pastoralists, and you (the pastoralists) are suffering. If you love them, then why are their livestock stolen every day?” He asked the CS.

“These pastoralists are killed every day and their cows and goats stolen. What have you done for them and you are in the government?” Gachagua posed.

The Opposition leader claimed that the government was ill-prepared for the heavily forecasted El Niño rainfall, pointing out that those living in flood-prone areas like the Tana Delta and Garissa are exposed to danger.

“Now, going into El Niño, what plan has been put in place to save people from death as a result of floods and how livestock will survive?” he asked the State.

During the event, Gachagua revealed that Yusuf Huka Jillo from Isiolo would represent Upper Eastern at the DCP secretariat and serve as a member of the National Executive Committee (NEC) in an acting capacity.

Gachagua said the mountain was now complete, with Isiolo and Marsabit forming Mt Kenya North.

The locals alleged that the Health CS was interfering in Isiolo County politics, with elder Hussein Jama claiming that Duale and the Office of the DCI were shielding a section of leaders accused of corruption and criminal activities.

Speakers claimed that there was massive corruption at the local lands registry office, while Mr Jillo faulted the State for the slow pace of registration of community land in Isiolo.

Jama said Isiolo International Airport, which was constructed during the administration of President Kibaki to help in the export of miraa and horticultural goods from the Mt Kenya region and livestock products, mainly meat and hides, lies idle because the expansion of the runway from 1.5 metres to 3 metres had not been done.

In response, Gachagua said the airport was meant to create employment and wealth, but the Kenya Kwanza administration had instead left it in ruin deliberately, claiming the move was aimed at sabotaging the economy of Mt Kenya and pastoralists’ economies.

“What was the good about destroying the Imenti forest to construct an airstrip for an individual while there is an international airport meant partly to serve the entire region just a few kilometres from Meru town?” Asked the DCP leader.

World.title: Relief for schools as government releases Sh18.5b capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Education CS Julius Ogamba. [File, Standard]

The government has released Sh18.5 billion in capitation to support operations in public basic education institutions during the third term of 2026, as schools reopened across the country on Monday.

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba said the funds have already been released and will support learners in pre-primary, primary, junior and senior schools.

The allocation is intended to facilitate smooth school operations and ensure learning activities continue without disruption.

The Sh18.5 billion has been distributed across three major capitation programmes, with Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) allocated Sh10.963 billion, accounting for the biggest portion of the Term Three capitation.

The money will support operations in public day and secondary schools and comes as institutions prepare learners for a busy academic term.

Free Day Junior School Education has received Sh6.1 billion, to support learners in the second tier of basic education and help institutions meet operational requirements as the Competency-Based Education system continues to expand.

Meanwhile, Free Primary Education has been allocated Sh1.4 billion to support learning in public primary schools.

The funds come as a relief to school heads who had raised concerns on the insufficient funds disbursed to schools this year.

However, Ogamba said the disbursement demonstrates the Government's commitment to ensuring that learners have access to free and compulsory basic education as provided for under Article 53(1)(b) of the Constitution.

“The Government affirms its commitment to fulfil its duty to learners and educational institutions,” said the CS.

Ogamba also warned school heads and principals against misuse of the funds, directing them to ensure the money is spent prudently and for the benefit of learners.

School administrators have further been cautioned against imposing unauthorised levies on parents and learners.

Ogamba said the Ministry would take firm action against institutions found to have misappropriated public resources or imposed illegal charges.

“We will deal firmly with any verified cases of misappropriation of resources and the imposition of unauthorised levies,” he said.

The warning comes as schools reopen for the third term, a period that is expected to be particularly demanding for institutions and learners because of the academic activities and assessments scheduled for the school calendar.

The Ministry has maintained that capitation is meant to ease the financial burden on families and enable schools to provide essential services without passing prohibited costs to parents.

Ogamba reiterated that school administrators must remain accountable for the public funds entrusted to them, warning that verified cases of misuse will attract action from the Ministry.

The Government has also reaffirmed that every child is entitled to free and compulsory basic education, placing the responsibility on education officials and school managers to ensure capitation achieves its intended purpose.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro begins nationwide political mobilisation ahead of 2027
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro after attending service at Gathuki-ini ACK Church on August 23, 2026. [Boniface Gikandi, Standard]

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro has said he will take his campaign for national transformation across Kenya as he positions himself for the 2027 presidential race.

Ndindi said he was interested in leadership committed to addressing concerns in education, health, youth and unemployment, among other needs.

Nyoro, who is the People’s Party of Kenya leader, spoke at St Michael Gathuki-ini ACK Church in Kiharu on Sunday, where he called for respect and political maturity.

Addressing residents in Kiria-ini (Mathioya) and Gakira (Kangema), he urged politicians to engage in a responsible manner.

“I trust in God that after next year Kenya will be able to have leadership that will be responsible for improving citizens' standards of living,” he said.

He regretted that hundreds of university graduates in the area were yet to secure employment.

“I plead with Kenyans to support my course that is geared to transform the nation and ensure equality and transparency,” said the PPK leader.

Nyoro said that after engaging Murang'a residents, he will take his transformation campaigns to all parts of the country.

Speaking at Kiria-ini market, he said he would engage the people to seek their blessings.

“All along had been feeling the urge to lead the country, thus the need to come out in the open and fight for position,” he said.

On Monday, the MP announced his exit from the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA), declaring that he will join the opposition ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Nyoro, an economist serving his second term as Kiharu MP, said he will work with opposition leaders to push for what he termed real change in Kenya.

The legislator said all opposition presidential aspirants are welcome at rallies organised by the PPK.

His move marks a significant political shift as parties and leaders begin positioning themselves ahead of the 2027 polls.

World.title: Trump remains vague on sanctions plan for Iran’s partners
World.content:
President Donald Trump remained vague Friday when asked about his campaign to choke off Iran’s economy, refusing to say whether he planned to sanction Chinese banks or if he’d discussed the matter with foreign counterparts.

The administration announced earlier this week Operation Economic Outcast, which threatened tough new sanctions on Iran’s trading partners if they didn’t cut off ties to Tehran.

But the administration stopped short of putting in place any new measures, and so far hasn’t listed any major financial institutions from China — Iran’s largest trading partner — as being subject to US sanctions.

Trump bristled when asked why he wasn’t applying new sanctions on Chinese banks doing business with Tehran.

“Who said I’m not? You don’t know if I’m doing it,” he said. “I don’t have to announce everything, do I?”

Later, asked which world leaders he’d discussed the pressure campaign with, Trump suggested it wasn’t on his agenda, even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday that Trump was placing calls to foreign counterparts “with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime.”

“There’s not a lot to speak to. We don’t want to speak to them,” Trump said Thursday. “We’re not looking to meet or anything.”

World.title: Iceland rejects EU membership plan in referendum held under the shadow of Trump’s Greenland threats
World.content:
Reuters —

Icelanders have voted to stay out of the European Union, broadcaster RUV reported on Sunday, rejecting a government push to reopen membership talks and siding with those who said Iceland’s fishing waters were too important to risk.

Some votes from one constituency are pending but these were not expected to change the outcome, RUV said.

A ‘no’ vote will disappoint Brussels, as some officials had cast the island nation of 40,000 as a low-risk case that could help ease scepticism toward EU enlargement and strategically strengthen the bloc when Arctic security is in focus.

The government has framed membership as a shield against trade wars and Arctic rivalry and presented ​the referendum as a “now or never” moment, with Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadóttir warning that a “no” would put the membership ⁠question aside.

The government is due to hold a press conference at 1 p.m. (1300 GMT).

Decades of membership debate

Iceland first applied to join the EU in ​2009 when a financial crisis hit the country’s small, exposed economy. A Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.

Geopolitical turmoil, including war in the Middle East and US ​import tariffs, has brought urgency to an issue Icelanders have debated on and off for decades.

People with Icelandic flags attend an “Afram Island”, “Forward, Iceland”, rally, opposing the resumption of European Union accession talks at Austurvollur in Reykjavik, Iceland, on August 27, 2026. Marco Di Marco/AP

“Yes” campaigners have said joining the bloc could help to lower interest rates and offer more security in a world unsettled by the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about annexing another Arctic island, Greenland.

“No” campaigners said EU membership would threaten the island’s sovereignty and fishing waters.

The referendum campaign has fueled debate about Iceland’s place in the world, Frostadóttir told reporters after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.

“This is a great day. We’ve been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote,” Frostadóttir said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.

Interest rates and the cost of living

Debates inside Iceland have focused on interest rates, fishing rights and the cost of living rather than on security.

Iceland has grappled with high inflation and interest rates that have made mortgages expensive. Supporters of a “yes” vote have said EU membership, and possibly adopting the euro, could bring relief. Iceland’s central bank interest rate is 8%, compared with 2.25% at the European Central Bank.

The Central Bank of Iceland headquarters in Reykjavik, Iceland, on Saturday, May 30, 2026. Laura Zapata/Bloomberg/Getty Images

“It would ​not solve Iceland’s structural faults, but ​it could become a catalyst ⁠to a more healthy economy,” said chief economist Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson at Viska, one of Iceland’s largest labour unions.

Opposition leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, who has led the “no” campaign, said the economic case is overstated. “These are not problems that Brussels ​will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve,” she said.

Voter Ragnhildur Skarphedinsdottir, 70, said ​Iceland was managing ⁠well on its own and that she was voting “no.”

“By staying independent as we are, we look brightly to the future,” she said before casting her ballot in Reykjavik.

Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based on historical fishing patterns, among other factors. Some Icelandic officials have said Iceland would therefore retain control of ⁠its waters, ​since no EU country has fished there for decades.

Hafsteinsdottir disputes that. “I know that the European ​Union will come up with some promises of some flexibility, especially in the beginning, but we know that it will not be for good,” she said.

This story had been updated.

World.title: Here’s what Meta’s $18 billion multistate settlement could mean for kids — and for its bottom line
World.content:
New York — Meta on Wednesday agreed to make sweeping changes to its platforms as part of an Meta on Wednesday agreed to make sweeping changes to its platforms as part of an $18 billion settlement with dozens of states over claims its platforms contributed to a youth mental health crisis.

Regulators and online safety advocates called it a watershed moment, and both Meta and state attorneys general called on TikTok and YouTube to make similar changes.

But whether the settlement fundamentally alters the business of one of the world’s most powerful tech giants remains an open question.

The $18 billion agreement is a drop in the bucket for the nearly $1.5 trillion company (META) and a fraction of what states were seeking at trial, although Meta still faces hundreds of other similar cases. The litigation so far has revealed internal documents suggesting that Meta knew of the risks its platforms posed to young people, despite public statements about its commitments to safety.

Still, some online safety advocates say they wish the deal went further to upend Meta’s core, ad-based business model. And many are now calling on Congress to codify the changes in industry-wide federal legislation.

What is clear: Meta will no longer be able to grade its own homework on youth safety. An independent auditor will review its implementation of the required changes — a crucial step that parents and advocates have been demanding for years.

“It’s transformational,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNN’s Richard Quest on Wednesday. “There’s a real, durable enforcement mechanism here and safeguard in place now.”

Meta did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement.

“The framework we’ve negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement Wednesday, adding that the changes “set the right path forward for our whole industry.”

Changes to protect kids

Among the changes for users aged 13 to 17 are a two-hour daily time limit across Facebook and Instagram, a “night mode” making the apps unavailable from midnight to 6 am and a “school mode” limiting notifications during school hours. Only parents will be able to adjust those settings.

Meta will also turn off “like” counts by default on teens’ content and “extreme makeup” beauty filters.

Teens will have the option to turn off autoplay, so videos don’t start automatically when they open the apps, and select a feed not based on algorithmic recommendations.

Meta will have six months to implement the changes.

For Lori Schott, a founding member of the online safety parent advocacy group Parents RISE!, the changes are a “movement in the right direction.” But she said she wishes Meta had made them earlier, without litigation.

Schott says her daughter, Annalee, died by suicide at 18 in 2020 after Meta’s platforms repeatedly served her harmful content.

“For this, the mental health aspects are really important to me — the aspects of no beautification filters and the like buttons that are going to be removed — that impact so many little girls,” Schott, whose own individual lawsuit against Meta is pending, told CNN.

Lori Schott holds a picture of her daughter, Annalee Schott, during a press conference held by parents of young people whose deaths were allegedly related to social media use, outside of a federal courthouse where Meta was facing a landmark trial over claims from 29 states that the company designed its social media platforms to keep young users hooked, in Oakland, California, on August 18, 2026. Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters/File

But while the settlement includes some “meaningful” changes, others don’t go far enough, said Sebastian Mahal, co-chair of the youth online safety organization Design It For Us. For example, while teens can opt-in to a non-algorithmic feed, the default remains a personalized version that’s better for Meta’s business, Mahal said.

“They’re really allowing users a semblance of a different experience,” Mahal said. “But we would rather see that these safest experiences be switched on automatically for users.”

The settlement also includes several carve-outs. “Night Mode,” for example, will still allow access to messaging on Instagram and Facebook when the apps are otherwise blocked for teens, according to court documents.

The effectiveness of many of the changes will largely depend on whether Meta can accurately detect teen users.

The settlement requires Meta to implement age verification software, either its own or from a third party. Meta said it is “investing in even stronger technology” to catch teens who misrepresent their age and keep users under 13 off the apps, but it also argues that app stores should bear some responsibility for verifying users’ ages.

Meta has previously backed legislative proposals to require app store age verification, something Google and Apple have pushed back on.

“Ideally, Meta will decide that the required design changes in this settlement would be beneficial to all users, not just children, but it is very possible that this will not be what happens given the profit Meta receives from locking in its adult users,” Syracuse University communications professor Alexis Shore Ingber said in emailed commentary.

Hitting Meta’s bottom line?

Wednesday’s settlement is a “home run for (Meta CEO) Mark Zuckerberg” financially, said Michael Coffey, a defense litigator and founding partner of Coffey Modica LLC, who was not involved in the Meta case.

It’s a small percentage of what Meta could have been forced to pay — up to more than $1 trillion, the company had estimated — if it lost in the trial with just four of the state attorneys general. And Meta will pay out the $18 billion settlement in annual tranches over ten years, which will go toward state youth mental health and online safety training programs.

Meta has also said it will pay out only 70% of the settlement unless TikTok and YouTube agree to pay around $6 billion each and make similar changes.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who helped lead a federal trial against Meta that ended in an $18 billion settlement, says he will seek platform changes from TikTok and YouTube as well. Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

Bonta said the states are willing to take those companies to court if needed to get them on board with the deal. TikTok and YouTube did not respond to a request for comment.

The bigger question for Meta is what happens if it loses in the hundreds of cases from individuals, school districts and other states that remain. The company acknowledged in its most recent earnings report that the youth safety-related trials posed a risk of “material loss.”

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Wednesday that his state didn’t join the settlement because the “payouts are peanuts compared to the profound harms Meta’s profit-driven addictive features inflicted on kids.” He added, “We’ll see them at trial.”

If teens spend less time on Meta apps because of the changes, that could dent the company’s bottom line. Forrester Principal Analyst Kate Winick said research indicates that the company earns around $11 billion annually from minors, although she added that “Meta is a very big business with lots of ways to make up that revenue.”

William Blair analyst Ralph Schackart said the deal largely removes uncertainty around what could have been an even higher penalty. Meta shares (META) ended Wednesday up just over 1%.

Especially as Meta pivots more to artificial intelligence, investors will likely now “place a greater focus on the company’s fundamentals … which remain strong,” Schackart wrote in a research note.

World.title: No, Iran is not winning: In Act IV of the war, it’s losing its leverage in Hormuz
World.content:
A conventional wisdom has begun to settle over the war with Iran: Iran won.

The argument is straightforward. The US and Israel bombed Iran for weeks, inflicted enormous damage, and demanded major concessions. Iran refused to surrender. Its government remains in power. Its missiles remain a threat across the region. And most important, Tehran still has the ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, imposing higher energy costs on the US and much of the world. Over the summer, Trump warned of a global depression if the Strait remained shut.

That’s a strong argument. But it may have proved premature.

Wars are contests of leverage and endurance. And the contest now looks very different from even a few months ago.

The fourth act

The arc of this six-month conflict has proceeded in four acts. Act One began with intensive airstrikes on February 28 and lasted through six weeks of high-intensity military operations. Act Two began with the April 7 ceasefire and negotiations, culminating with the June 17 MOU signed by Trump and Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian. Act Three began weeks later when Iran chose once again to target commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, leading to another tit-for-tat military exchange.

A drone view shows vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 28, 2026. Stringer/Reuters

That was the moment calls rose for the US effectively to give up and cede control of the Strait to Iran. The United States appeared to be out of options.

Not so fast.

Since mid-July, the US has reimposed its military blockade on Iranian ports and sanctions on Iran’s oil trade. In parallel, the U.S. military has worked tirelessly to clear shipping lanes and help protect commercial ships transiting the Strait. The result has been an effective blockade on Iranian oil shipments, with global shipments recovering and energy prices remaining remarkably stable. Bloomberg reported this week that oil flows through the Strait have recovered to 2/3 of pre-war levels.

That means pressure is now compounding on Iran, and not the US. And if Iran loses its ability to hold the Strait hostage, its leverage dissipates rapidly.

A better US strategy

Iran entered the war weakened by years of sanctions and economic mismanagement. Its position today is considerably worse.

According to the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s economy is expected to contract by more than 5% this year, with inflation approaching 70%. The value of Iran’s currency has fallen sharply. Prices for basic goods have soared. An Iranian Labor Ministry official recently estimated that more than one million jobs disappeared during the first three months of the war alone.

A salesman counts Iranian Rials at a local market in Bandar Abbas, Iran, August 25, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/Wana News Agency/Reuters

These statistics matter because Iran’s ability to sustain the conflict ultimately depends on more than its remaining missile arsenal. Before the war, the Iranian regime confronted unprecedented public pressure against its repressive rule and failing economy. Thousands of Iranians were reportedly killed in the streets.

A better American strategy from the start may have been an economic campaign to support the Iranian people demanding change. The first act of the war — removing most of Iran’s leaders — resulted in consolidation by the Revolutionary Guards and further crackdowns against the majority of Iranians that oppose their rule.

But the Guards require resources to rule by force, and this new fourth act — a military embargo — is something that Iran has never confronted before. Indeed, this is the first time since the 1979 Revolution that Iran has faced a quarantine on its economic lifeline through Hormuz.

Their way out is to stop threatening ships in the Strait and abandon what’s left of its mostly destroyed enrichment program. That’s a deal Trump would accept. Doing either, however, from the vantage point of the Guards would show weakness and threaten their rule.

Iran’s cards

Tehran may seek to fight its way out of this noose. Its strategy through the first three acts was clear: threaten commerce in the Strait, raise energy prices globally and gasoline prices in the US, increase global economic pressure and ultimately force Trump to back down, particularly with midterm elections approaching.

Iran has also targeted the energy infrastructure of the Gulf states and could do so again. Its proxy force in Yemen, the Houthis, have threatened to shut down commerce through the Red Sea with Iranian missiles and drones.

Smoke rising from the direction of a major UAE energy installation on March 14, 2026 in what appeared to be the latest strike targeting the Gulf’s petroleum facilities hours after the US struck Iran’s Kharg Island. AFP/Getty Images

All that would mean resorting to the same tactics from the early acts of the war. Strategically, it has not worked for Iran. The Gulf states are not happy with the war, but most do not support giving in to Iran’s extortionist demands in the Strait. Iran’s attempts to close the Strait with drones and mines are also now — for the first time — failing.

So, I would not discount the risk of an Iranian escalation as the economic pressure builds. But it may not be enough at this stage to reduce that pressure. Trump appears far more committed than Iranian leaders apparently presumed.

Breaking point

Iranian leaders and many Western analysts project immunity to pressure. Iran will never surrender its nuclear program or the Strait of Hormuz. Or its terrorist proxies around the region.

That’s something we all must accept as a fact of life in the Middle East, according to Tehran.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi attends a ceremony where Iran’s Foreign Ministry and Health Ministry sign a memorandum of understanding on cooperation in rebuilding infrastructure damaged during the war in Tehran, Iran, Aug. 11, 2026. Shadati/Xinhua/Getty Images

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi argued last week that the blockade and sanctions pressure are “bound to fail” just as all other campaigns, he said, had failed to change Iranian policy.

I used to hear the same thing from experts about ISIS, when I was leading the campaign to defeat the group. And Hamas, when negotiating to free the hostages held in Gaza.

In fact, everyone has a breaking point. Iran thought it had found Trump’s. Trump may yet find theirs. It’s too early to call.

Not the last act

This contest in some form may last through the end of Trump’s presidency and beyond. It’s been ongoing for nearly five decades.

Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Thomas Hudner (DDG 116) fires a Tomahawk land attack missile in support of Operation Epic Fury, on March 1, 2026. U.S. Navy/Getty Images

The earlier acts in this war were mired from the US side by shifting and ill-defined objectives, widely careening positions, and inconsistent statements.

But Act Four seems different. The US military has a clear objective as outlined this week by the commander of CENTCOM, Admiral Brad Cooper. It is enforcing the blockade on Iran and facilitating the movement of commercial traffic.

The objective for the US should be similarly well-defined. Iran must abandon claims on the Strait and give up the nuclear enrichment program. Until then, this will be the new status quo.

And that status quo — perhaps for the first time since the war began — now favors Washington, not Tehran.

World.title: Transport Minister inspects high-speed rail project ahead of trial operations
World.content:
Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir inspected work on Sunday, August 30, 2026, along the first line of Egypt’s high-speed electric rail network, which runs from Ain Sokhna to Alamein and Matrouh, as preparations continue for trial operations on part of the line.

The first line stretches 660 km from Ain Sokhna on the Red Sea to Matrouh on the Mediterranean. al-Wazir inspected the section between Ain Sokhna station and the Central Capital station as part of efforts to meet President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi’s directives to complete mass-transit projects within their scheduled timelines, the transport ministry said.

al-Wazir was accompanied by the head of the National Authority for Tunnels, Tarek Gewily, and project consultants.

The minister first inspected a roughly 6-km rail connection between Ain Sokhna station and Ain Sokhna Port, designed to link the port to the high-speed rail line and facilitate freight transport to and from the port.

He then inspected Ain Sokhna and Central Capital stations, reviewing final finishing work, passenger flows from entrances to ticket halls and platforms, and plans to make the best administrative and commercial use of station space.

al-Wazir also reviewed work on service roads running alongside the track, ahead of the installation of ballast, sleepers and rails, as well as plans to use external roads to serve nearby residential areas, and he ordered work to be completed on access roads serving the stations from all traffic directions to facilitate passengers’ arrival.

al-Wazir also inspected a maintenance facility covering about 259,000 square meters near the Central Capital station and the main workshop for the first line, which covers 578 feddans (about 243 hectares) and will serve all three lines by operating the trains, carrying out major and minor overhauls, and storing up to 50 trains and locomotives.

He reviewed sections of the track handed over to the Siemens-Orascom Construction-Arab Contractors consortium for the installation of ballast and rails and overhead catenary poles, as well as electromechanical works and other systems.

Trial operations without passengers are expected to begin on one section of the first line in the coming months, with further non-passenger trials to follow according to the project’s timetable, the ministry said.

The minister also inspected completed bridges and other structures, including Wadi Hagoul Bridge, the June 30 Bridge, the new Quarries Bridge, Al-Khor Bridge, and Autostrade Bridge. He reviewed construction of bridges east of the Nile, the Nile bridge, and bridges west of the river, and called for the completion of rail and road bridges and flood culverts east of the Nile.

al-Wazir praised the work carried out by Egyptian workers and engineers, highlighting Al-Khor Bridge over Wadi Degla — 600 meters long, 90 meters high and 14 meters wide — as well as bridges south of Helwan and east of the Nile.

The high-speed rail network will connect different parts of Egypt, and the first line will provide a land link between the Red Sea and Mediterranean, which al-Wazir described as a “new Suez Canal on rails.”

The project extends beyond transportation, supporting industry, tourism, urban development and agriculture, attracting domestic and foreign investment, creating direct and indirect jobs, and reducing travel and transport costs, he said.

It will also connect newly developed areas with existing cities and strengthen Egypt’s position as a regional transport, logistics and transit-trade hub, he said.

The ministry said the stations had been designed to interchange with airports located near the network’s routes, facilitating travel between airports and destinations across Egypt and connecting the high-speed network with other public transport systems.

Construction is progressing simultaneously across the project’s various sections, with the overall completion date determined by the last activity to be completed, al-Wazir said.

Civil works, bridges and other structures, including tunnels, have been carried out domestically and paid for in Egyptian pounds from the budget of the National Authority for Tunnels; the same applies to construction, architectural and track works, including ballast, sleepers, poles and rails, he said.

Trains and signaling and control systems were initially imported, he said, adding that the government was working to localize transport industries, including rolling stock, components and systems.

The localization program includes factories operated by the National Egyptian Railways Industries Company (NERIC), Alstom and Coloway, as well as plants producing rails and sleepers, he said.

The minister also met engineers and workers on the project and conveyed President Sisi’s congratulations to them on the anniversary of the Prophet Muhammad’s birth, according to the ministry.

He said the ministry would allow engineers who wished to work abroad to take unpaid leave after five years of service with the ministry or its affiliated bodies and companies. It would also grant mandatory leave in certain circumstances, including leave to accompany a spouse, as well as childcare leave for female engineers, and regular, emergency and sick leave in accordance with government regulations.

Egypt’s high-speed electric rail network is planned to comprise four lines totaling 2,250 km, with the first three lines, covering about 2,000 km, currently under construction.

The first line, running from Ain Sokhna to Alamein and Matrouh, will include 21 stations, a control center, 15 high-speed trains, 34 regional trains and 14 freight locomotives.

The line will interchange with the Light Rail Transit (LRT) at the Central Capital station, the planned sixth metro line at Ahmed Omar Hashem station, the Cairo-Aswan diesel railway at Giza station, the West Nile Monorail at October station, and the second high-speed rail line at Hadayek October station.

Hadayek October station will also connect to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system on Cairo’s Ring Road via a planned shuttle bus service. The first line will also connect with the Alexandria Metro at Borg El Arab station.

World.title: Labor Minister: Egypt prioritizes training to prepare workers for Arab, European markets
World.content:
Labor Minister Hassan Raddad said on Sunday, August 30, 2026, that the ministry is working to remove obstacles and empower young people to enter the labor market, stressing that training is a top priority aimed at enhancing the skills of Egyptian workers and preparing them for employment in Arab and European markets.

In statements to the Nile News Channel, Raddad said the state is keen to empower Egyptian workers and provide them with the highest level of training in line with labor market needs. He added that the state has achieved major progress, most notably in reducing the unemployment rate, which stood at more than 13 percent in 2013-2014, compared with about eight percent today.

Turning to investment incentives, he added that the state has also introduced a package of measures to support investors and facilitate the resolution of any obstacles they may face, noting that a committee has been established at the ministry’s headquarters to provide support to investors.

Asked about the launch of general rules governing labor regulations in private-sector companies, Raddad said the new rules are part of the government’s program to promote greater stability in the work environment, encourage investment and enhance workers’ job security through unified labor regulations for both small and large establishments.

The labor minister added that establishments employing 10 or more workers are required to issue labor regulations and have them approved by labor offices, while establishments with fewer than 10 workers may adopt simplified regulations covering working hours and weekly rest periods.

World.title: Egypt’s Handball team reaches Mediterranean Games final after defeating Algeria
World.content:
Egypt’s handball team reached the final of the Taranto 2026 Mediterranean Games after securing a hard-fought 27-25 victory over Algeria in a highly competitive Arab semifinal.

The Pharaohs delivered a strong performance against Algeria, handling the intense pressure throughout the match and maintaining their composure to secure a place in the final and remain in contention for the gold medal.

With the victory, Egypt secured a new medal at the Mediterranean Games by advancing to the final, leaving the team one step away from claiming the gold medal and adding another achievement to Egypt’s record at the tournament.

Egypt will face the winner of the semifinal between Greece and Portugal in the final, as the Pharaohs look to complete their successful campaign by winning the gold medal and securing a place at the top of the podium.

World.title: Egypt’s Dar Al-Ifta joins Al-Azhar’s annual Quran Recitation Day
World.content:
Egypt’s Dar Al-Ifta on Sunday, August 30, 2026, joined Al-Azhar in the annual “Quran Recitation Day,” a global event organized by Al-Azhar that brings Muslims from around the world together to recite the Quran simultaneously in a single day.

The event aims to highlight the importance of the Quran to Muslims and reflect the unity of the Muslim community through recitation and contemplation of its verses, Dar Al-Ifta said.

Dar Al-Ifta’s participation underscores its commitment to the Quran and its support for initiatives that strengthen people’s connection with the holy book and encourage reflection on and adherence to its teachings, it said.

The institution also seeks to use digital platforms to promote sound religious awareness and make religious content available to a wide audience in Egypt and abroad.

Dar Al-Ifta is broadcasting the “Quran Recitation Day” on its official Facebook page, with several of its scholars taking part in the recitation, allowing audiences around the world to listen to the complete recitation and take part remotely.

World.title: Liberia: A Nation Finally Writes its Own Story
World.content:
The Historical Society of Liberia has launched a 24-volume Presidents Biography Series — one book for every Liberian head of state since 1848. The first volume, on Edwin Barclay, is out now, with a dozen more presidents already assigned to Liberian authors and manuscripts due through 2028.



BOOK REVIEW: The Presidents Biography Series (Historical Society of Liberia)

Volume One: Edwin Barclay, by Anthony Barclay

Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – For a country that has produced twenty-four heads of state since 1848 — more, by the Historical Society of Liberia’s own reckoning, than any other African nation can claim — it is a strange fact that so few of them have ever had a book written about their lives. That gap is now being closed, one volume at a time, and the opening entry in the new Presidents Biography Series suggests the wait may have been worth it.



The series, launched by the Historical Society of Liberia, aims for twenty-four volumes in all, one for every president from Joseph Jenkins Roberts to the present day. Five biographies and their authors have already been announced, and a dozen more writers have signed on to cover another thirteen presidents, with manuscripts due through 2028. Every author on the list is Liberian — a deliberate choice, and the right one.

Volume One takes up Edwin Barclay, president from 1930 to 1944, a leader whose historical footprint has long been, in author Anthony Barclay’s own assessment, “generally sketchy and devoid of robust analysis.” The board’s foreword makes a broader claim on the same theme: that for all of Liberia’s presidents, book-length studies remain “remarkably scarce.” Reading the opening volume, one senses the series is less interested in monument-building than in the harder, more useful work of filling in blanks — treating its subject as a man to be understood rather than a name to be honored.



That instinct runs through the project’s guiding philosophy. Liberian historiography has too often been flattened into a single fault line — settler descendants versus indigenous populations — and the Society says it wants this series to resist “simplistic binaries and enduring stereotypes.” It is an ambitious ask of any single book, let alone twenty-four written by twelve-plus different hands. But if the first volume is a fair indication, the series is aiming for complexity over convenience, which is exactly what a body of work this overdue should be doing.



Two names carry particular weight behind the project. D. Elwood Dunn, a director on the Society’s board, planted the seed for this series fifteen years ago, when his three-volume 2011 collection of Liberian presidential addresses closed with a complaint that no one had yet written the biographies to go with the speeches. The Rev. Kedrick Brown, at work on a life of Joseph James Cheeseman, brings his own thread back into the story: he is the son of Mary Antoinette Brown Sherman, the first woman to head a university in Africa, to whom Dunn dedicated his 2011 volumes — a dedication Brown discovered only recently, on a library shelf at Princeton.



Whether the full series can sustain the standard set by its opening volume remains to be seen; a project spread across a dozen authors and several years will inevitably vary in voice and rigor. But the ambition itself is the story here. As Dunn puts it, the completed series “will constitute a significant contribution to the country’s historical and cultural heritage.” On the evidence of Volume One, that is not overstatement — it is overdue.

About the Author

D. Elwood Dunn is the scholar whose long-standing argument set this series in motion. A former Liberian government official, he served between 1974 and 1980 as assistant minister of foreign affairs and later as Minister of State for Presidential Affairs and chief of staff to President William R. Tolbert, Jr. He was traveling with an advance team when the April 1980 coup ended that government, and he relocated to the United States shortly after.



Dunn holds a bachelor’s degree from Cuttington College and Divinity School and a master’s and doctorate from The American University in Washington. Over a 35-year academic career, he taught at the University of Liberia, Cuttington, Seton Hall, and Fordham’s Lincoln Center campus, before spending three decades at Sewanee: The University of the South, where he now holds the title of Alfred Walter Negley Professor of Political Science Emeritus. He edited the Liberian Studies Journal from 1985 to 1995 and retired from teaching in 2012.



His published work includes the 2011 three-volume collection of Liberian State of the Nation addresses, the Historical Dictionary of Liberia, and History of the Episcopal Church of Liberia Since 1980: A Sequel, along with decades of journal articles. In 2012, Liberia named him National Orator for its 165th independence anniversary. He told his own story in the 2022 memoir A Liberian Life, published by Brill. He now lives in Silver Spring, Maryland, sits on the board of the Historical Society of Liberia, and continues to consult privately on Liberian and African affairs.

World.title: Gongloe Calls for National Relief Fund for Victims of Liberia’s Brutal Civil Wars
World.content:
Monrovia — Renowned human rights lawyer and former presidential candidate Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has called for the establishment of a National War Victims Relief Fund to provide medical, economic and welfare assistance to Liberians still suffering from the physical, emotional and economic consequences of the country’s 14-year civil conflict.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Gongloe, in a commentary titled “We Must Not Forget the Victims of Liberia’s Civil War,” said that although Liberia’s civil war ended years ago, many victims continue to live with bullets and fragments in their bodies, lost limbs, impaired vision, chronic pain and emotional trauma.

Others, he noted, remain trapped in poverty after losing homes, farms, businesses and family members during the conflict.

“Many feel abandoned and forgotten by the country for whose conflict they paid such a terrible price,” Gongloe said.

He argued that Liberia has a moral obligation to address what he described as a historic imbalance in post-war assistance.

The Liberian civil wars (from 1989 to 1997, and from 1999 to 2003) became notorious for extreme brutality against civilians, including widespread massacres, torture and systemic sexual violence. Factions widely used and forcibly recruited children, often giving them drugs and arming them with cheap, accessible automatic weapons. About 250,000 people lost their lives, and hundreds of thousands were displaced.

According to Gongloe, former combatants received organized disarmament and demobilization packages, including financial assistance, vocational training and other support aimed at facilitating their reintegration into civilian life.

While acknowledging that such assistance was necessary to secure peace, Gongloe said many civilians who were injured, widowed, displaced or economically devastated by the war received little or no comparable support.

“Liberia must correct this historic injustice,” he declared.

Proposed Five-Year Relief Fund

Gongloe proposed that the National War Victims Relief Fund initially operate for five years, financed through contributions from Liberians and a substantial government counterpart contribution.

Under his proposal, every unemployed adult Liberian who is able to contribute would pay L$100 annually, while every employed Liberian would contribute US$1 per year.

Liberians living abroad, he added, should also be encouraged to contribute at least US$1 annually.

The Liberian Government would then match national contributions at a ratio of US$5 for every US$1 contributed under the scheme.

Gongloe said the fund should prioritize victims with severe disabilities and provide assistance including medical treatment, medication, prosthetic devices and modest welfare support.

It should also provide interest-free microloans to victims capable of engaging in farming, petty trading and other small businesses.

He said the objective should not simply be financial assistance, but to help victims regain independence and restore hope.

Separate Victims’ Relief From War Crimes Court

The Liberian Government is in an advanced stage in establishing a war and economic crimes court. Currently, two draft legislations are before the Legislature for passage.

Gongloe stressed that the proposed relief fund must remain completely separate from the establishment of Liberia’s War and Economic Crimes Court.

He said the two initiatives would serve different purposes: the court would address accountability for crimes committed during the civil conflict, while the relief fund would respond to the immediate needs of victims still suffering today.

“A wounded victim who needs medicine should not have to wait for a prosecution, and a widow living in poverty should not have to wait for the creation of a court before receiving assistance,” he said.

According to Gongloe, Liberia can simultaneously pursue accountability for wartime atrocities and provide practical support to victims.

Calls for Transparency

Gongloe also warned that the proposed fund must be insulated from political interference and managed transparently.

He called for the establishment of a credible national registry of qualified war victims and annual audits by the General Auditing Commission.

He further proposed that administrative costs—including salaries, offices and operational expenses—not be deducted from money intended for victims.

Instead, he said such expenses should be financed through a separate appropriation in the national budget.

“Why Now?”

Anticipating questions over why such a fund should be created decades after the war, Gongloe said the passage of time has not erased the suffering of victims.

“Delay is not a reason for continued neglect; it is a reason to act now,” he argued.

For Gongloe, the proposal goes beyond providing financial assistance.

He described it as a national declaration that Liberia remembers those who suffered during the conflict, recognizes their continuing hardships and accepts responsibility for helping them rebuild their lives.

World.title: Liberia: Supreme Court Clears Way for Enforcement of Judgment in Urban Marketing–Tubman Estate Dispute
World.content:
Monrovia— The Supreme Court of Liberia has dismissed an appeal in the long-running legal dispute involving Urban Marketing Group, through its Chief Executive Officer Allen R. Brown, and the interests of the late John Hilary Tubman, clearing the way for the lower court to resume jurisdiction and enforce its November 28, 2025 judgment.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In a judgment handed down on Friday, August 28, the Supreme Court ruled that the respondents failed to take mandatory steps required to perfect their appeal, including filing the required appeal bond and serving and filing a notice of completion of appeal.

The Court consequently granted the motion to dismiss the appeal and ordered that the matter be returned to the court below for enforcement.

The ruling was handed down during the Court’s March Term 2026, with Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, Sr., and Associate Justices Jamesetta H. Wolokolie, Yussif D. Kaba, Caineh D. Clinton-Johnson, and Boakai N. Kanneh participating.

According to the judgment, Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law provides for dismissal of an appeal when an appellant fails to comply with mandatory requirements governing appeals.

The Court emphasized that once a bill of exceptions has been signed, the case is removed from the trial court’s jurisdiction, except for limited ministerial matters such as approving an appeal bond or entertaining a challenge.

However, the Court found that the respondents failed to file the required appeal bond and did not serve and file the notice of completion of appeal.

The failure, the Court ruled, constituted sufficient legal grounds to dismiss the appeal.

“Wherefore, and in view of the foregoing, the motion to dismiss the respondent’s appeal is granted, and the appeal is ordered dismissed as a matter of law,” the Court ruled.

The Clerk of the Supreme Court was subsequently ordered to issue a mandate to the court below, directing the presiding judge to resume jurisdiction and give effect to the judgment.

Costs were also ruled against the respondents.

A Procedural Victory for Brown

For Brown and Urban Marketing Group, the ruling removes the latest appellate obstacle to enforcement of the lower court’s judgment.

Importantly, the Supreme Court’s latest decision was procedural. The Court did not reconsider the underlying merits of the November 28, 2025 judgment or rule that the lower court’s decision was erroneous.

Instead, the Court determined that the appeal could not proceed because the parties seeking appellate review failed to satisfy mandatory requirements for perfecting the appeal.

The consequence is that the lower court’s judgment remains standing and the matter can now proceed to the enforcement stage.

The dispute has its roots in a Joint Venture Agreement between Urban Marketing Group and the interests of the late John Hilary Tubman.

The disagreement eventually proceeded to arbitration, where an arbitral tribunal ruled in favor of Tubman. The trial court subsequently confirmed the arbitration award.

Urban Marketing challenged the arbitration outcome, arguing, among other things, that the arbitral tribunal had exceeded its authority.

The dispute eventually reached the Supreme Court, turning the case into a significant test of the enforceability of arbitration agreements and awards in Liberia.

Supreme Court’s Earlier Ruling

In a February 2024 decision, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court’s action and found that Urban Marketing had failed to meet the legal threshold required to vacate the arbitration award under Section 64.11(1) of the Civil Procedure Law.

The Court’s earlier decision also underscored the principle of contractual sanctity, with the Judiciary emphasizing the constitutional protection afforded to contractual obligations under Article 25 of the Liberian Constitution.

The Supreme Court has described the sanctity of contracts as important to legal and economic stability, predictability, and confidence in commercial transactions.

The 2024 ruling, however, did not bring the dispute to an immediate end.

Urban Marketing later sought re-argument before the Supreme Court. The petition was heard on March 25, 2025, but the Court rejected the effort in May 2025.

With the substantive arbitration challenge having already received consideration at the highest level of Liberia’s judicial system, subsequent proceedings increasingly focused on enforcement, possession, property interests, and procedural questions surrounding the parties’ competing claims.

Dispute Escalates

The legal battle became more contentious in 2025, when representatives of the Tubman Estate initiated separate criminal proceedings against Brown and others over alleged conduct involving property in Sinkor.

A writ of arrest was issued in September 2025, with allegations reportedly including criminal trespass, criminal mischief, felonious restraint, criminal conspiracy, and criminal facilitation.

Those allegations were contested and remain distinct from the civil and commercial proceedings addressed in the Supreme Court’s latest ruling.

In January 2026, a separate criminal case involving Brown was dismissed with prejudice by the Monrovia City Magisterial Court.

Judge L. Ben Barco, in dismissing the charges, reportedly cautioned that the court should not be used to harass a defendant under the guise of seeking justice.

The separate criminal proceedings should not, however, be conflated with the Supreme Court appeal decided on August 28.

What the Ruling Means

The immediate effect of the Supreme Court’s decision is to return the case to the trial court.

With the appeal dismissed, the lower court is no longer constrained by the pending appellate proceeding and has been expressly instructed by the Supreme Court to resume jurisdiction and give effect to its November 28, 2025 judgment.

The ruling does not constitute a new finding of criminal liability against Brown, nor does it independently resolve every property or commercial dispute between Urban Marketing and the Tubman interests.

Rather, it removes a procedural barrier that had prevented enforcement of the lower court’s judgment.

The Supreme Court’s mandate now shifts responsibility back to the trial court, where implementation of the judgment is expected to proceed.

For Brown and Urban Marketing, the latest development therefore changes the legal landscape significantly. The question is no longer whether the particular appeal will be heard, but how the judgment already entered by the lower court will be implemented.

The precise consequences will depend on the terms of the November 28, 2025 judgment and the property, assets, rights, or obligations covered by that decision.

Still, the latest ruling marks another significant chapter in a dispute that has traversed commercial negotiations, arbitration, trial-court proceedings, Supreme Court litigation, property-related confrontations, and separate criminal proceedings.

For now, the Supreme Court has closed the latest appellate route—not by overturning the lower court’s judgment, but by ruling that the appeal was not properly perfected under Liberian law.

The mandate now returns the matter to the trial court for enforcement.

World.title: Liberia: AML Honors Four Rail Workers for Preventing Potential Safety Incident
World.content:
BUCHANAN, GRAND BASSA COUNTY — ArcelorMittal Liberia has honored four members of its Rail Department for demonstrating exceptional vigilance, professionalism, and courage during a critical operational event along the company’s main railway line.

Train Drivers Norman Chidarikire and Rynier McCabe, along with Train Assistants Stanley Mulbah and Horace S. Neppy, received special recognition during an Incident Prevention Safety Award Ceremony held in Buchanan.

The four railway professionals were celebrated for their swift and decisive response after identifying a potential hazard during operations on the mainline. Their timely actions prevented what could have developed into a serious safety incident, protected lives, and safeguarded important railway infrastructure.

The recognition reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s commitment to building a workplace where employees are encouraged to remain vigilant, follow safety procedures, communicate openly, and take responsible action whenever a potential risk is detected.

During the ceremony, management praised the crew for maintaining composure under pressure and applying their training and professional judgment when it mattered most.

According to the company, the team demonstrated exceptional situational awareness by recognizing the developing danger and responding before the situation could escalate. Their actions showed how employee alertness and sound decision-making remain essential components of safe railway operations.

Felipe Lage, Rail General Manager at ArcelorMittal Liberia, described the incident as a powerful demonstration of the alertness, skill, and dedication of the company’s railway workforce.

“This event is a testament to the alertness, skill, and dedication of our railway team,” Lage said. “Even under immense pressure, they kept their composure, followed proper procedures, and made the critical decisions that kept the situation under control.”

He explained that procedures, operational systems, and safety equipment provide important layers of protection across the railway. However, he emphasized that trained and responsible employees remain vital to preventing incidents when other protective measures may not be sufficient.

“Procedures, systems, and safety equipment provide essential layers of protection, an architecture we must continuously strengthen as a whole,” Lage said. “But it’s equally important to pause and recognize moments like this one, when our people step up and become the decisive layer that stops a potential incident where others weren’t enough.”

ArcelorMittal Liberia operates the railway connecting its mining operations in Yekepa, Nimba County, to the Port of Buchanan in Grand Bassa County. The corridor passes through several towns and communities and is central to the movement of iron ore and other operational materials.

Because the railway interacts with communities, road crossings, workers, equipment, and other infrastructure, maintaining the highest safety standards remains a major responsibility. The actions of the four employees therefore went beyond protecting company operations. Their response also helped protect members of the public who live and travel along the railway corridor.

Togar Carter, Buchanan Health and Safety Manager, emphasized the wider importance of the team’s intervention.

“They didn’t just help ArcelorMittal. They helped keep Liberian citizens alive and ensured they could return home safely to their families,” Carter said.

His statement highlighted the human value of workplace safety and the responsibility railway employees carry during every journey. Each safety decision can have consequences not only for employees and company assets, but also for families and communities along the Yekepa to Buchanan rail corridor.

The award ceremony also provided an opportunity for the honorees to encourage their colleagues to remain alert and honest about their physical and mental readiness for work.

Train Assistant Horace S. Neppy called on railway employees to respect fit-for-duty requirements and communicate openly whenever they are not prepared to safely perform their assigned responsibilities.

“Always stay alert, and speak up if you’re not fit to work,” Neppy said.

His message reinforced the importance of personal responsibility in preventing incidents. Fitness for duty includes being physically rested, mentally alert, properly prepared, and capable of responding appropriately to changing conditions during railway operations.

Fatigue is an important safety concern in railway operations, particularly during extended shifts and long-distance travel. Recognizing this challenge, ArcelorMittal Liberia’s Rail Department is strengthening its fatigue-management protocols.

Among the measures being introduced is the integration of in-locomotive driver alert systems. These systems are intended to help monitor and support driver alertness during extended operations on the mainline, adding another layer of protection for employees, communities, railway equipment, and company infrastructure.

The investment forms part of AML’s broader approach to safety, which combines technology, training, established procedures, employee responsibility, and continuous operational improvement.

The recognition of Chidarikire, McCabe, Mulbah, and Neppy also sends an important message across the company: proactive safety behavior will be acknowledged and celebrated.

By honoring employees who identify risks and act responsibly, ArcelorMittal Liberia is encouraging others to speak up, follow procedures, report hazards, and take immediate action when safety is threatened. This approach supports a workplace culture in which preventing incidents is a shared responsibility at every level of the organization.

The ceremony concluded with management reaffirming its commitment to continuous engagement with employees, further investment in safety systems, and ongoing improvements to railway procedures.

AML management also pledged to maintain a working environment where professional judgment, vigilance, open communication, and proactive safety actions are actively supported.

Through their conduct, the four railway employees demonstrated that safety is more than a set of written rules. It is a daily commitment expressed through alertness, discipline, teamwork, and the courage to act when potential danger emerges.

Their recognition stands as an example of how properly trained and dedicated employees can make a decisive difference, preventing harm, protecting infrastructure, and ensuring that both workers and community members return safely to their families.

World.title: Liberia: CMC Rejects CDC Invite To Attend Roundtable For Opposition Leaders
World.content:
Monrovia – The opposition Citizens Movement for Change (CMC) has rejected an invitation from the former ruling Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) to attend a roundtable for opposition political leaders on the grounds that the CDC has predetermined a leadership for the opposition ahead of the 2029 presidential and legislative elections in Liberia.

By Obediah Johnson

CDC invited various opposition political parties, including the CMC, to participate in an Opposition Leaders’ Roundtable scheduled for September 5, 2026, at the Jamaica Resort, outside Monrovia.

But in a letter dated August 28 and addressed to CDC Chairman Atty. Janga A. Kowo under the signature of CMC Political Leader Musa Bility, the CMC says it appreciates the effort to promote dialogue and cooperation among Liberia’s opposition political parties, but it would not attend the gathering for multiple reasons.

Predetermined

The party observed that the scheduled meeting has already predetermined a leadership of the opposition and other arrangements.

“We believe that opposition unity is necessary, and we remain prepared to work with every responsible opposition institution committed to building a credible alternative for the Liberian people. However, opposition unity must be negotiated among equals. It cannot begin with predetermined leadership, authority, or organizational arrangements.”

CMC observed that the invitation from the CDC that the invitation from the CDC goes beyond convening an initial dialogue.

It added that the invitation designates a presiding leader, establishes a National Convening Secretariat, and places that Secretariat under the authority of an already appointed “Lead and Coordinator” of the Opposition Leaders’ Roundtable.

The party noted that these arrangements create the impression that a collective opposition structure and its leadership have already been established before the invited political parties have met, discussed, or agreed to such a framework.

The CMC disclosed that it does not accept this approach.

Agreed process

The party emphasized that it recognizes and respects George Weah as a former President of Liberia and Political Leader of the CDC, and he or the CDC may invite the CMC and other opposition political parties to an exploratory dialogue.

It added that the convening of the first discussion does not confer leadership or coordinating authority over the collective opposition.
