World.title: Are you sure that Kimmel clip was real? Late-night AI deepfakes are spreading online
World.content:
Are you sure that Kimmel clip was real? Late-night AI deepfakes are spreading online

toggle caption ALAMIN_TUBE /Screenshot by NPR

Jimmy Kimmel is currently out on summer break from his late-night talk show on ABC. But the casual fan might be forgiven for thinking the host hasn't left the building. Social media videos appear to show him commenting on everything from President Trump falling asleep in the middle of a meeting, to the president's attacks on Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Fake videos showing Kimmel and other late-night TV talk show hosts are mushrooming on social media. These videos, made using generative AI, are in some ways easier to create than deepfakes of other types of celebrity — and could potentially be more disruptive.

Sponsor Message

Why people are easily duped

Jed Rosenzweig, the founder and editor of the online publication LateNighter.com, has been investigating the rise of these deepfakes. He said late-night TV talk show hosts are especially vulnerable to having their likenesses transformed into video simulations on social media because of the ease with which audiences accept the context in which they are presented.

"Jimmy Kimmel really does go on television and talk about politics all the time, and these clips really do get posted on social media every day," Rosenzweig said. "So if you see a Kimmel thumbnail tied to something Trump did yesterday, there's a built-in context and trust there that gives [it] a kind of camouflage. It just has to look like one more Jimmy Kimmel clip in a feed that's already filled with Jimmy Kimmel clips."

Rosenzweig said there are telltale signs that these monologues are not authentic.

"The gestures are odd. The writing doesn't really sound like a live monologue. And after about 10 seconds, Kimmel disappears and the cloned voice just runs over news footage," he said.

Yet some of these videos rack up hundreds of thousands of views and elicit comments that suggest at least some people think the content is real. One viewer commented on a YouTube video: "Thank you Jimmy for speaking the truth."

Sponsor Message

Threats to free speech

Rosenzweig said while other hosts like Jon Stewart are also victims of these AI simulations, the Jimmy Kimmel Live! deepfakes are of particular concern because of the host's especially contentious relationship with the Trump administration.

President Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel to be fired. Rosenzweig said the fake videos, many of which make fun of or criticize Trump, could strengthen his administration's resolve at a time when the Federal Communications Commission and ABC are in a legal battle over free speech rights. "ABC are being scrutinized on a nightly basis for what Jimmy Kimmel is saying," Rosenzweig said.

ABC did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

Easy to create

These AI-generated talk show hosts as a genre in some ways pose a bigger threat than other kinds of celebrity deepfakes, such as of singers and actors: They are usually easier to create because these hosts typically just stand or sit in one place and talk to the camera, and there are plentiful high-quality audio recordings of their speaking voices available online to clone.

"In many cases, I can take a single image from a late show host and just animate it," said Dartmouth College computer science professor Hany Farid, who specializes in analyzing deepfakes. "Here's a voice, fifteen seconds. Here's a script. Go."

Also, Farid said, late-night TV is where many Americans get their news and validate their opinions.

"The deepfakes we are seeing, it's essentially disinformation campaigns that now seem to be coming out of the [voices] of those very people that we're used to listening to," Farid said. "So they're quite effective."

The allure of Late Night … online

Even though the audience is in decline, roughly a quarter of Americans still watch late-night talk shows regularly. According to a 2025 survey from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, the majority of these viewers are Democrats, and more of them are watching clips online than the full shows on regular linear TV. Farid and Rosenzweig both said this may explain why it's harder to find AI deepfake monologues from right-leaning talk show hosts on social media.

Sponsor Message

"The things I've seen are more on the side of scams and fraud," Farid said. "It's like, 'Sean Hannity says you should buy this cryptocurrency!'"

Representatives for hosts including Jimmy Kimmel, Jon Stewart, Sean Hannity and Greg Gutfeld declined or did not respond to NPR's requests for comment.

The handful of creators who produce talk show host deepfakes did not respond to NPR's questions about their motives.

Farid said they could be doing it for ideological reasons — or to make money.

"It's pure clickbait. Get eyeballs. Get ads. That's it," Farid said.

Platforms respond

The platforms that host this AI slop are trying to police it. TikTok, along with Google, which owns YouTube, and Meta, which owns Instagram, all sent statements to NPR saying they require creators of deepfake content to label it as being made with AI. They said they use likeness detection and moderation technologies to find unauthorized deepfakes as well as provide ways for victims of these simulations to request takedowns themselves.

"We tackle low-quality or deceptive AI content using systems we've developed over years to fight spam and clickbait," said the statement from Google, of which YouTube is a subsidiary. "As this technology advances, we've developed industry-first tools to protect the likenesses of public figures and civic leaders, and we automatically apply labels to realistic AI content for viewer transparency."

"We require people to disclose, using our AI-disclosure tool, whenever they post organic content with photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio that was digitally created or altered, and we may apply penalties if they fail to do so," said the statement from Instagram and Facebook parent company, Meta. (Meta required NPR to submit an example of a late-night talk show deepfake video from Instagram or Facebook in order to respond to questions. The company confirmed that it took the page, which featured Kimmel, down – after being notified by NPR.)

Sponsor Message

"TikTok's policy is to remove harmful deepfakes, and separately, to require labels on realistic AI content that is not otherwise violative," said the statement from TikTok.

But the sheer speed and volume with which these videos pop up means many slip through.

One Jon Stewart deepfake about Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has been up on TikTok for more than two months. It does not have a visible AI label. Similarly, a video on YouTube featuring a deepfake Kimmel talking about Trump boasting about his prowess on the golf course was still up online at the time of publication — three weeks after being posted. It has more than 230,000 views.

Laws lag behind

Besides the platforms' whack-a-mole attempts to get rid of the deepfakes, there are currently few legal remedies to counteract the issue.

"The issue of deepfakes for things like late-night TV hosts falls into a space that is a little bit of a gap in the law right now," said Louis Tompros, an intellectual property litigator who handles artificial intelligence cases.

Tompros says existing copyright law only combats unauthorized uses of creative works, not unauthorized synthetic doubles of creative people. However, a few states such as California and Tennessee do provide protections against AI-generated voice clones and video deepfakes. A growing number of states have enacted guardrails or now require disclosures for deepfakes used in political ads; the federal TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed into law last year, criminalizes the non-consensual publication of intimate deepfakes. But that doesn't cover deepfakes of non-sexual content, like talk show hosts' commentary.

Meanwhile, several late-night hosts, such as John Oliver, have spoken out about the dangers of deepfakes on their shows. The technological downsides also provide fodder for comedy.

"There are some real downsides to the unchecked growth of all of this, some of which admittedly are pretty minor," said John Oliver in a 2025 Last Week Tonight segment on the topic. "Like the fact that lots of us are now having to explain to our parents that the unbelievable thing they saw on Facebook is not real."

World.title: 'A glorious dawn launch': NASA's newest space telescope has left the Earth
World.content:
'A glorious dawn launch': NASA's newest space telescope has left the Earth

toggle caption John Kraus/NASA

A new NASA space telescope launched Sunday from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida that will help scientists probe the nature of dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is about the size of a tour bus, lifted off at 7:26 a.m. ET on SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket. The 18,000-pound spacecraft is now on a million-mile journey that will take it to its new home in space.

"What a glorious dawn launch," NASA's Jackie Townsend, Roman telescope project manager, said at a press briefing soon after liftoff. "The ride was magnificent. It put us right where we wanted to be."

More good news came shortly after launch as the telescope began deploying its solar panels and other instruments. "Ground controllers at NASA Goddard have been receiving telemetry data from Roman, and apparently all systems are nominal," said NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

The journey to Roman's new home

Roman has an unusual origin story: Initially designed as a spy telescope for the National Reconnaissance Office, the spacecraft was donated to NASA instead. The new telescope is named for Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer who was known as the 'Mother of Hubble' for her championing of the iconic Hubble Space Telescope. Her namesake observatory will have the sharpness of Hubble but a field of view that is at least 100 times larger, allowing it to image huge swaths of the sky at once.

Sponsor Message

Before it can do that, the Roman Space Telescope will have to get to its new home in the sky about a million miles away. Roman will live at the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point known as L2. There, the competing gravitational pulls of the Earth and the Sun help the telescope keep a steady orbit while using minimal fuel. The James Webb Space Telescope orbits at this point, which gives the spacecraft an unobstructed view of the sky.

"It takes us a good three-plus months to get out there, and we're spending that time checking everything out and doing a whole bunch of calibrations and making sure everything is working the way we know it can," said NASA's Jeremy Perkins, an integration and test scientist on the mission. "It's basically like our time to kick the tires and just make sure that the focus is right, the pointing is right."

Uncovering cosmic mysteries

Roman is on a kind of ghost hunt, searching for more evidence of dark matter — mysterious, invisible stuff whose gravitational influence appears to hold galaxies together and define the overarching structure of the cosmos. Roman will study how gravity subtly affects the path of light along great distances throughout a massive survey of the sky. By doing this, the telescope will help map both normal and dark matter, giving scientists a better understanding of just what this elusive substance might be.

Sponsor Message

Astronomers will also use Roman's observations to uncover dark energy, the strange force that is believed to drive the expansion of the universe. Scientists' understanding of dark energy comes from observations of a kind of exploding star known as a Type Ia supernova. These supernovas appear to shine at known and predictable brightness throughout the cosmos, giving them the nickname of 'standard candles'. By cataloguing even more of these supernovas, scientists hope to develop a better understanding of how dark energy works, which could fundamentally change the way astronomers view the universe.

Roman will also search for planets outside our solar system. Since astronomers confirmed their existence in the 1990s, more than 6,000 exoplanets have been identified. With Roman, NASA expects to identify more than 100,000 of them by identifying dips in starlight caused by a planet passing in front of its own star. The telescope also hopes to find some 1,000 through microlensing — a technique that searches for tiny changes in background starlight caused by the gravity of a far-off planet.

"Why do we care so much about exoplanets? Because one of our main goals at NASA is answering the question: Are we alone in the universe," Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator of the science mission directive, said at the Sunday morning briefing.

The spacecraft is poised to bring scientists a step closer to answering that question: It will demonstrate technology that can take a picture of a planet by selectively blocking out the light from its home star.

"We are going to make this giant leap forward with the coronagraph technology that is going to allow us to look at these distant worlds and start to really resolve the atmosphere around them to let us know if they could be habitable," she said.

A deluge of data

The telescope will beam back 1.4 terabytes of raw science data each day, using a refrigerator-sized high-gain antenna. The data will be available immediately to scientists and the public.

Sponsor Message

"Roman's database at the end of its prime mission after five years is going to be bigger than your standard music streaming platform," Perkins said.

Because of the massive amounts of data, NASA is making it available to anyone through a cloud-based system called Roman Nexus. For Perkins, that's what makes this mission unique — anyone can look at the raw data and find new discoveries.

"It's all the things that we are not expecting to see," he said. "It's all these one-in-a-million things that we're going to be able to see with Roman that really excites me."

World.title: Lake America replaces Lake Ontario on multiple Canadian websites after Google Maps update
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Some Canadian websites, including for the federal government, displayed maps with Lake Ontario renamed as Lake America on Sunday, a day after Google Maps announced the change to align with an executive order by U.S. President Donald Trump. The search giant said in a Saturday post on its corporate website that it made the change because the U.S. government's geographic names database has formally renamed the lake. Google said the change would only affect U.S. users, but a number of websites for Ontario and Canadian entities appeared to display Lake America on maps. Among them were Hydro One's outage map, the Liquor Control Board of Ontario's (LCBO's) store locator, GO Transit's station finder and the federal government's housing and infrastructure map. "We are aware that Lake Ontario is being incorrectly labeled on our outage map," a spokesperson told CBC News in an email, adding that Hydro One regrets the "error." A screenshot of the Liquor Control Board of Ontario's website on Sunday afternoon shows Lake Ontario labelled as Lake America. The map has since reverted to the Lake Ontario name. (CBC) "The issue originates from a third-party mapping service," the utility said. "We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference." Metrolinx, an Ontario government agency that owns GO Transit, said in a separate email to CBC News that it is aware of the issue. "We are actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario," Metrolinx said. "We are in the process of disabling the map function on the GO stations' page where this occurred." By late afternoon on Sunday, the GO Transit map in question had been disabled, and the LCBO map had been changed to again show Lake Ontario. MapQuest, a U.S. online mapping service, has posted on social media that it would not change the lake's name, while Apple has not publicly commented on the matter. In a statement Sunday night, Google said website developers who embed Google Maps on their sites can select a region to localize the map. That determines how place names are displayed on sites, the company said. "'Lake Ontario' will show when developers have set their region to Canada," the statement said. APIs behind the confusion: tech expert Tech analyst and journalist Carmi Levy said although websites like Ontario Hydro's and the LCBO's are Canadian, their maps are likely powered by Google's application programming interface (API). APIs are not location-aware, so all maps powered by Google API have switched to Lake America. "Even if it's a government website or a government app or government digital service, it will show as Lake America in Canada because we're stuck using an American technology to power it under the surface," Levy told CBC News. Companies and government organizations use third-party APIs rather than developing their own mapping software. Google Maps itself provides results based on a user's location, so people within Canada's borders should still see Lake Ontario — even if they type Lake America. Levy said Google has updated its search index globally, "so that Lake America is now searchable no matter where you live." On Sunday evening, Google's pin — a red, teardrop-shaped marker — was showing up as Lake America in at least some Canadian searches when either name was typed in the search bar. Zoomed in closer, however, the map still said Lake Ontario. The name change highlights the cost of Canada not having its own Google Maps equivalent or mapping APIs, Levy said, leaving a huge portion of online activity powered and collected by American companies. WATCH | How the trade war could turn on Trump: Where Trump’s trade war with Canada could backfire | About That | Duration 2:47 Avneet Dhillon explains how Canada is targeting imports from specific U.S. states with its dollar-for-dollar retaliation against President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs, and how the counter-tariffs could have an impact in key battleground states ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images) "In many cases, that data is sitting on an American server. I'm screwed if the government decides to put limits on that or starts to scrape that data for whatever purpose, wants to use it against me the next time I decide to cross the border," Levy said. "The fact that we aren't more digitally sovereign, we are today seeing a very high-profile example of what that costs us as Canadians." Stephen Crawford, Ontario's minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, acknowledged the issue on social media and said the provincial government is "actively reviewing our websites" to make sure they identify Lake Ontario as such. Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps. Following recent changes by Google, we're actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario

As Ontarians, we will always stand up for… —stcrawford2 Ford slams name change Appearing on ABC's This Week program on Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the name change won't stick, despite Trump signing the executive order on Thursday. "It was like something out of Saturday Night Live when [Trump] signed a document saying change it to Lake America," Ford said. "No one's going to call it Lake of America. It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario." On Saturday, Ford unveiled a large sign in Winona, Ont., a small community in the eastern part of Hamilton, that says, "Lake Ontario Now and Always." WATCH | Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveils new sign: 'Lake Ontario Now and Always': Ford unveils new sign | Duration 0:56 Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a new 'Lake Ontario' sign Saturday in Winona, a small lakeside community on the outskirts of Hamilton. This comes after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change the name of the body of water to 'Lake America.' Also on Saturday, Trump posted a video rendered by artificial intelligence where he replaces a Lake Ontario sign with another that reads "Welcome to Lake America," then dances to the YCMA song by the Village People. Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump's bid to rename the lake in a social media post on Thursday. Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, "then, now and always." Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said after Trump signed his order that her state won't call it Lake America. Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade talks fell apart on Aug. 21. Both countries have accused each other of implementing last-minute changes to a proposed interim trade deal. On Tuesday, the federal government unveiled upwards of $27 billion in retaliatory measures, set to kick in on Sept. 8, in response to new U.S. tariffs. WATCH | Ford softens trade war message on American TV: Doug Ford softens trade war message on U.S. TV | Duration 2:04 A day after hurling insults at U.S. President Donald Trump, Ontario Premier Doug Ford took a more measured approach while discussing the trade war during appearances on American TV. Meanwhile, Canadian officials rebuffed Trump’s threat to change Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America. Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario's premier. Ford had called the president a "bully" and a "loser" on Aug. 24, while Trump said the premier was a "less charismatic" and less "intelligent" version of his late brother Rob Ford. The premier said during his ABC appearance on Sunday that things "got heated" between Trump and himself, but "you've eventually got to stand up to someone who just continuously attacks our country and insults our country." "It's unfortunate that he stoops down to that level and unfortunately I did that day," Ford said, adding he wants to see both sides return their focus to advancing a mutually beneficial free-trade deal. Trump signed a similar executive order last year to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The orders apply only to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services have since called it the Gulf of America. Most major news organizations in the U.S. and internationally continue to call it the Gulf of Mexico.

World.title: On the road with pro-independence Albertans, one small town at a time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Alberta inches closer to answering a referendum question on independence, CBC's Joel Dryden joins a group of separatism supporters in the Let's Talk Alberta motorhome. They spent the day traveling around southern Alberta, mostly visiting smaller towns.

We hit the road with separatists as they meet supporters in rural Alberta

Chris Scott sat in the driver’s seat of his 2001 Monaco Dynasty motorhome last week, bumping along the network of rural highways in southern Alberta.

The vehicle creaked a bit. Some leather-covered furniture was cracking, and some cabinet drawer latches didn’t work anymore.

It’s like Alberta, Scott said: you can ignore problems and let them get worse, or you can pay attention to them and fix them.

“I see there's a lot of things going on with Alberta that need some care and attention,” said Scott.

The restaurant owner, who gained prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, has hit the road this summer to talk independence, travelling with a group of people who also support the idea of Alberta becoming its own nation.

Chris Scott is with the group Let’s Talk Alberta. Last week, they toured around southern Alberta, handing out lawn signs and talking to residents about independence. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

CBC News recently spent a day aboard the “Let’s Talk Alberta” bus, speaking with passengers about what motivates them at a time when Albertans are weighing their vote in an Oct. 19 referendum.

Earlier this summer, CBC spent time with volunteers helping the pro-Canada group Forever Canadian, talking to them about their efforts and why they wouldn’t be voting to have a future referendum on whether Alberta should stay in the country.

Federalist and separatist groups have been a common sight this summer, fundraising and shaking hands with voters at events like the Calgary Stampede. Voter mobilization efforts are expected to ramp up considerably with less than two months to go to the referendum.

On the bus

On a recent weekday in August, Scott’s bus hit the road for a 10-stop tour through the southern part of the province.

Scott’s passengers included Jasper Smit, a friend from the Netherlands who runs a social media channel called CommonSense TV.

Leaning on a countertop in the back of the motorhome, Smit studied the packaging of a snack purchased from a highway gas station. He read it aloud: roasted grilled pepperoni cheesesteak.

“Mystery meat!” called out another rider.

The wrapping on the bus’ exterior was less ambiguous.

The vehicle is emblazoned with the “Let’s Talk Alberta” decal, framed by provincial viewscapes: the hoodoos of Drumheller flowing into sweeping mountains and rivers, topped by an expansive prairie sky. It was an Alberta postcard, designed with artificial intelligence and then smoothed out by a designer.

On the back of the vehicle, a Bible verse printed in script: Jeremiah 29:7 — "Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile. Pray to the Lord for it, because if it prospers, you too will prosper."

The back of the Let's Talk Alberta bus, displaying a Bible verse. (Joel Dryden/CBC)

It was Scott who procured the motorhome to criss-cross the province.

With a full standup shower and decent-sized bed in the back, Scott could spend days on the bus if he needed to.

Increasingly, he has been, as he’s travelled to all corners of the province with the clock running down to voting day.

He carries with him his experiences from the pandemic.

He was charged and later acquitted for breaching public health restrictions during COVID-19 related to his Whistle Stop Cafe in east-central Alberta.

Scott was highly critical of politicians that he viewed as allowing laws that " strip our fundamental rights and freedoms away ." His reputation has made him something of a folk hero amongst those who share his views in these small towns.

“I just learned that if there's something that's wrong, you need to stand up for yourself,” Scott said of his experience.

Chris Scott, right, talks with pro-independence Albertans who came out to a stop in Bassano, Alta., last week. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

When the bus pulls into a town, it’s often greeted with supporters. Some caught word of the trip on social media.

In Rosemary, Alta., with a population of little more than 350, a lone man who came out to get a lawn sign said he heard news of the trip on a Facebook group entitled, “Bassano Bitching or Bragging.”

“The whole thing is really not about separation, in my opinion,” said Bassano resident Tom Schaffer.

“It's about making the government wake up and go, hey, these guys might want to separate. Maybe we should actually do something and listen to them?”

Tanya Clemens, co-leader of a separate Alberta independence group, Let Alberta Decide, was on the bus too, as was John Bolton, a former Calgary radio host who now provides emcee services at various independence events, and Patti Vold, a mother of nine and a grandmother of 15.

There was also Sandy Duguay, who was born and raised in Montreal, where she lived through two referendums as an English speaker. Duguay also spent 26 years in Victoria, where her husband was a chaplain at a prison on Vancouver Island.

Jasper Smit, left, and Sandy Duguay sit aboard the Let’s Talk Alberta bus as it moves from town to town in southern Alberta last week. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Duguay was never involved in politics before, but was motivated to become political after the COVID-19 pandemic hit, which evolved into helping the Alberta independence signature drive. She’s now travelling full-time on the bus.

“I feel very close to these people,” Duguay said, who turns 72 in a few weeks.

As the bus weaved its way along the route, the conversation snaked through the group’s motivating complaints with the federal government. Some, like frustration with the federal equalization program or Ottawa’s approach to firearms, have been kindling for alienation for years.

The cultural divide at play quickly came into focus, too. Certain federal bills, perhaps less familiar to the broader Canadian public, are viewed by this group as threats to religious freedom.

“Bill C-9 especially,” Duguay said, referring to the Combatting Hate Act, which amends the Criminal Code to strengthen penalties for hate crimes. The Liberals received support from the Bloc Québécois after including a clause to remove a religious exemption from the country's hate speech laws.

The Conservatives have argued that amounts to an “assault” on religious freedoms, while Justice Minister Sean Fraser has said the new law won’t “criminalize faith.”

“Look what’s happened to Europe,” Duguay said, turning to Smit. “You were founded on Judeo-Christian principles. And you guys were the first to get rid of them."

Wearing a Let’s Talk Alberta shirt and a Whistle Stop hat, Smit, the visitor from the Netherlands, didn’t entirely agree. He said he's “not religious at all" and that embedding Christian principles into governance would set a precedent that would require adopting other religious laws whenever demographics shifted in the future.

“In all fairness, you should bring that [into] politics,” he said.

Patti Vold is helping on the Let’s Talk Alberta bus tour. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Vold, the grandmother of 15, feels Christian values have been fading from public life, which is pushing society towards moral decline.

“For many, many years, the idea was you shouldn't mix church and state, right? I disagree,” Vold said. “The state should not be in the church, but people of faith should be in the state. They should be helping to guide the country.”

Soon after this conversation, the bus arrived in Strathmore and pulled near Kinsmen Park. Scott and Smit exited. Talk of faith continued, until suddenly, Smit ran back up the bus stairs.

“The police are here.”

A heated confrontation

Outside the bus, a crowd had formed in the parking lot.

Various supporters of the independence movement who had arrived to greet the bus gathered around Scott as he was engaged in an argument. On the other side was a town official, flanked by a peace officer.

“So anyway, we'll be here for about an hour,” Scott said.

“I’m asking you to leave,” the official responded. The group was free to express its opinions, the man said, but not on the town’s property.

“But I can,” Scott responded. “It’s public property.”

An official for the Town of Strathmore spoke to Let’s Talk Alberta leader Chris Scott during a bus tour last week. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

The crowd grew increasingly frustrated. Scott was told that if he did not move the vehicle, the RCMP would be called.

“Well, I mean, it’s not the first time I’ve been arrested,” Scott said.

Minutes passed. Separatist influencers began to livestream from the scene. Eventually, word came that the bus was allowed to stay.

“The town respects individuals' right to peacefully express their views and participate in democratic processes,” a town spokesperson later said in an email to CBC News. “The group was able to continue gathering and expressing its views.”

The bus moved on to an Airdrie pizza place that’s become a gathering spot for the separatist movement.

Supporters of Alberta independence gather at Pauls Pizza in Airdrie, Alta., as part of a bus tour hosted by Let’s Talk Alberta. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Behind schedule and with three stops still to go, the Let’s Talk Alberta crew sat down and scarfed down slices, with a Toronto Blue Jays game playing on the screens above and curious onlookers surrounding the crowd of blue shirts.

One man asked what the group was doing there.

“It’s an Alberta independence bus tour,” he was told.

The man grimaced.

Polling suggests that support for independence is stronger in the rural regions, and Let’s Talk Alberta’s tour last week to smaller locales was largely met by receptive crowds.

But to win in October, the group understands it needs to make gains in the cities, where it hasn't received as friendly a welcome as it has in rural Alberta. That’s where they're headed next.

“September, October will be all cities,” Duguay said. “The cities, different cultures, different mindsets … we’ve covered just about every little town. But now, the cities.”

World.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guard retaliates after U.S. bombs targets in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. forces struck Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday in the first military action in a month, prompting an Iranian response and breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.

Forces with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military movements.

The U.S. military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes.

Semi-official news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak Island on the strait.

Later, Iranian state television showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired by Iran at U.S. bases in Jordan in response to the American strikes. Jordan's armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that penetrated the country's airspace early Monday in the Mideast.

U.S. military officials disputed Iran's claim that the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a "limited, precise action" against what they said were minelaying forces.

"In essence, Iran created the threat and the U.S. military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce," U.S. Central Command said in a statement late Sunday.

A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted U.S. military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began on Feb. 28.

The last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, when it announced a "heavy wave of strikes" on dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets, including coastal surveillance and defence sites. On Aug. 1, U.S. President Donald Trump said he would order the military to hold off on new strikes at the urging of Gulf allies Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Economic war

The fighting comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure — rather than military action — to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centres on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran.

The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine U.S. military readiness in other parts of the globe.

As the conflict grinds on, Trump's talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he's "not in a hurry" to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic's leadership is on the ropes.

Trump has consistently emphasized that the campaign against Iran by the U.S. and Israel has been devastating for Iran's navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered $270 billion US in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government's leadership structure.

But Iran has found leverage through its own strikes in the critical Strait of Hormuz, where relatively few vessels carrying oil and liquefied natural gas are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the vital energy waterway, through which 20 per cent of the world's oil normally flows, effectively controlling much of the traffic in the strait.

Trump has repeatedly declared that the "Strait of Hormuz is open," saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that's a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that traversed the vital waterway daily before the war began.

Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the U.S. navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at "reduced levels." And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said the ship had been moving inbound and no casualties or environmental impact had been reported. It cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.

A major flash flood at Arizona's Grand Canyon forced the evacuation of dozens of people and swept large boulders, metal structures and other debris into the Colorado River that runs through it, the U.S. National Park Service said.

Flash flooding also knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents at the national park, the park said late Sunday. Starting Monday, tourists won't be able to stay overnight at lodges and hotels within Grand Canyon National Park. The park is also asking residents who live there year-round to conserve water.

The flooding in Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, happened Saturday afternoon and has left the park service seeking information about 15 people who may be missing or unaccounted for.

Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and significantly altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and creating what appeared to be a new river rapid.

As the park service tries to account for everyone in the area, it is asking asked anyone with details about people hiking or camping there to get in touch. It said it was working with the Arizona Department of Public Safety to continue evacuations on Sunday.

"This is a reminder of what a dynamic and active landscape Grand Canyon is," said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University.

Popular tourist spots including the Bright Angel Campground, Phantom Ranch and parts of the North Kaibab trail remained closed on Sunday while park officials surveyed the damage, the park said. Rafting trips on the Colorado River have also been halted for now.

Bright Angel Creek near the Phantom Ranger Station in the Grand Canyon in Arizona is seen after flash flooding from storms on Saturday. (Parth Desai/The Associated Press)

More than 60 people were evacuated from Phantom Ranch, which has a historic canteen and dorms, and is a common spot for rafters to get off and on the river. More evacuations were planned on Sunday, the park said. No injuries have been reported.

Erica Viola said she was at Bright Angel campground when the rain started Saturday afternoon, and she and about 50 other hikers watched the creek rise and then debris start to flow by, including what looked like a bunkhouse.

The group was taken by helicopter to safety, ending her adventure two days early, Viola said.

'Up, up, up, up!'

Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with a group of fellow physicians and a park ranger when the downpour started.

"We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere," he said.

Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted "Up, up, up, up!" as a one-metre debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said. They were finally rescued by helicopter that evening after making it to the Phantom Ranch area, he said.

About 1.2 to 2.5 centimetres of rain fell within about 30 minutes in the rocky area where there's a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Justin Johndrow in Flagstaff.

"Most of it ran off instantly," Johndrow said.

He said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping about 1,830 metres.

More rain and thunderstorms were possible for the area into Monday.

World.title: Sask. woman crowned Mrs. Canada Universe after 26 years away from the stage
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Earlier this summer, Jasmin Esquivel flew from Saskatchewan to British Columbia, unaware that her life was about to change.

Just a few days later, Esquivel was crowned Mrs. Canada Universe 2026 at the Bell Performing Arts Centre in Surrey, B.C.

“I didn't expect it, after many years, after having five kids,” Esquivel told CBC Saskatchewan.

“I realize that one day your dream is going to come true.”

Esquivel was 17 when she competed in her last pageant. When the opportunity arose to be part of this contest at 43 years old, something inside her sparked, she said.

“I think it's a memory, like it's in my blood."

43-year-old Jasmin Esquivel from Prince Albert was crowned Mrs. Canada Universe 2026 in Surrey, BC. (Submitted by Jasmin Esquivel)

Esquivel lives in Prince Albert, Sask., with her children. She said they've supported her and inspired her all the way, in spite of her own doubts about entering the competition.

“We were shocked at first,” said her eldest daughter, Brianna Balajonda.

“But then looking at her through preparing and training, it really amazed us and inspired us too.”

Esquivel said her kids are the reason she wears the national crown today. Not only are they her motivation, but they have been with her behind the curtains throughout the pageant.

Jasmin Esquivel and her children are part of a committee for kids' sports in Prince Albert. (Submitted by Jasmin Esquivel)

“They are my reason why — why am I here and why am I wearing this gown,” she said. “They are on the back of this pageant.”

A great part of the process is about the things contestants can do for their communities, and she's happy and thankful to have such a large one, she said.

Esquival and her family started volunteering in care homes and at multiple sports events, even organizing their own fun runs, in the lead-up to the pageant.

Jasmin Esquivel and her children started a fun run in their hometown of Prince Albert, Sask. (Submitted by Jasmin Esquivel)

Her goal is to remind every woman and mother that there’s always space in life for your own dreams, she said.

“There's always a perfect time for you. So after having this crown and this title, I just realized that you can still continue your dreams,” she said.

“Having kids doesn't mean we will stop.”

WATCH | Sask. woman crowned Mrs. Canada Universe wants other moms to dream big too: Sask. woman crowned Mrs. Canada Universe wants other moms to dream big too | Duration 1:43 Mrs. Canada Universe reigns from Prince Albert, and her name is Jasmin Esquivel. The mom of five returned to pageantry after decades away, won the national competition in July, and wants to set an example.

Balajonda said she’s grateful to have been right beside her mom through the process.

“She inspires me as a woman, that even though you're still a mother, you can still pursue your dreams. Even though you have five children, you can still do what you love.”

Jasmin Esquivel says her eldest daughter, Brianna Balajonda, has been her biggest supporter. (Submitted by Jasmin Esquivel)

Esquivel will head to Sri Lanka in October for Mrs. Universe 2026, representing Canada and her hometown.

Her children said they can’t wait to root for her on the next stage.

“We're here for you and we're cheering for you and we love you so much.”

World.title: Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the Trump administration's promise to impose more tariffs on us in January, many Canadians are asking: What leverage should we use to get them to change course?

The question suggests that there are actually real things we can do to change U.S. President Donald Trump's mind — that if Canada hits back hard enough, or demonstrates its willingness to suffer enough, we will get that policy change.

Christopher Ragan, the founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy and former chair of Canada’s Ecofiscal Commission put it this way: "Canada is in a set of negotiations with a party that appears to be unpredictable, volatile, so I don't think anybody really knows what's going to work here."

Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, said if Canadians are willing to suffer the consequences, there are plenty of ways to punch back at the U.S.

WATCH | Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’: Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’ | Duration 0:38 Prime Minister Mark Carney called U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs a 'miscalculation' because Canadians are united and 'masters of our destiny.'

"You first strike the things they've said are the most important to them," Drummond said. "They made it painfully clear that the only thing they want or need from Canada is oil, and maybe for a while electricity.

"We've had an export tax on oil and natural gas before and we could introduce that. We could also introduce quotas," he said.

Canada's leverage is significant when it comes to energy and fertilizer. In 2025 Canadian comodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81.3 per cent of imported electricity, almost 100 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.

A number of non-tariff options

And while there's still a long way to go before Canada fully develops its critical mineral reserves, Drummond says we could notify the U.S. that they won't get preferential access when those reserves come online.

"We could also restrict American access to Canada," Drummond said. "In the extreme we could require a visa and we could be very stingy with them."

Canada could also refuse to buy the F-35 fighter jets from the U.S. and choose instead to go with the Gripen from Sweden, he said.

Canadian banks, governments, pension funds and others currently hold about $459.6 billion US in U.S. treasury bonds.

"Given that the U.S. is tormented at the moment trying to get their long-term bond yields down, if we said we were going to divest ourselves of those, or at least not buy any more, that would tick them off," Drummond said.

Drummond also said that Canada's CPP fund could divest itself of all U.S. assets (51 per cent of the $864-billion fund is invested in the U.S., compared to just 12 per cent in Canada), but that would open the door to using Canadians' retirement as a political tool and placing retirees at risk — a step he said the country should avoid taking.

"You could put back the digital services tax, for example. Why the hell did we give it away? We got absolutely nothing for giving it away," Drummond said.

He says we could also eliminate the Canadian Film or Video Production Tax Credit, which he says results in lost tax revenue of about $500 million annually, with little economic benefit for Canada.

"So it could be fairly broad-based, it could be export restrictions or export taxes, it could be any number of things," Drummond said.

Some economists warn that while employing these non-tariff measures might feel good and would certainly harm the U.S. economy, they would hurt Canada's economy more.

Long-term, short-term pain

"I think emotions are pretty high and there's just a desire to lash out, but cooler heads require us to take a moment to think about what it is we're trying to achieve," said Trevor Tombe, director of fiscal and economic policy at the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy.

Tombe says the 50 per cent tariffs on about $27 billion of Canadian goods represent a hit to Canadian GDP of about 0.4 or 0.5 per cent, and taking retaliatory action that costs Canada more than that doesn't make economic sense unless it changes U.S. behaviour.

"That's a lot easier said than done," Tombe said. "And if we do things that increase costs in the United States, that might very well play into the hands of the U.S. administration by allowing them to blame Canada."

Beyond hurting Canada's economy in the short term, there's another negative side effect: hurting it in the long term.

WATCH | Canada won't accept being 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Carney: Canada won't accept being 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Carney | Duration 0:57 When asked by the Globe and Mail when Ottawa will come back to the table to hammer out a trade deal with Washington, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his delegation won’t accept attitudes that see Canada as a 'subsidiary' of the U.S. Carney's comments come after U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada would come back to the table due to its dependence on the U.S. for security.

"Maybe we have a lot of leverage, a lot of ability to impose pain, but it comes at a huge cost for us because we are both losing revenue and we are potentially severing relationships with our best customer," said Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa.

What if, for example, the U.S. replaced all Canadian oil with Venezuelan oil in a decade?

By way of example, Alschner says, China's export controls on critical minerals have prompted the U.S. to try to strike new deals, find new customers and build new critical mineral supply chains. Perhaps the best example of this is Canada's push to diversify in the face of the Trump administration's trade war.

"Even if you do it for a short period of time, you're sending a signal that this can be turned on and off. And so maybe the United States will not have time to mitigate that particular disruption at that moment, but it will then put measures in place to mitigate it in the future," he said.

Alschner also said bringing back concessions such as reimposing the Digital Services Tax or cancelling tax credits would be a direct provocation with an unclear dividend.

Sometimes there is only the fight

Ragan from McGill University says the U.S. would likely react strongly to export controls or taxes that drive up U.S. gas prices. That would risk turning energy scarcity caused by Canada into something that unites Americans against this country.

"That move escalates the trade war a few notches at once," Ragan said. "I say this half jokingly, but I wonder if you restricted electricity sales or oil sales or natural gas sales, whether that would lead Donald Trump to calling the troops. I'm not so sure."

Some economists say that rather than take actions that cost the Canadian economy in the short and long term, Canada should focus on how it can make up the difference with trade expansion and diversification abroad while building at home.

"Another way to think about the U.S. right now that I find kind of helpful is that they are flailing around in increasingly irrational ways and we are getting hit in the face," Tombe said.

"To the extent that their moves are crazy and not grounded in economic rationale, the best option might be to step back, try to weather the storm, and hopefully they work out their own issues domestically."

Tombe says that aside from the broader move to diversify our exports, sign new trade deals and build at home, Canada still hasn't liberalized internal trade, an opportunity he calls low-hanging fruit.

He says that by simply recognizing credentials across the country, Canada could boost productivity enough to offset a 25 per cent across-the-board tariff.

Alschner says the advantage Canada has right now is that the EU and other global trading partners are locked in similar trade disputes with the United States, which means they may be highly motivated to work with Canada.

"We should really use this as an opportunity to forcibly substitute U.S. imports with strategically selected non-U.S. imports," Alschner said. "We should say to the European Union, 'All right, what are the things that you can sell to us that the United States used to sell to us?'"

WATCH | Canada hits back at U.S. with $28B worth of retaliatory tariffs: Canada hits back at U.S. with $28B worth of retaliatory tariffs | Duration 1:42:33 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly tells Power & Politics that Canada is 'fighting back' against U.S. tariffs by introducing retaliatory tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of U.S. goods. Economist Trevor Tombe lays out how these tariffs could affect Canadians. And NDP Leader Avi Lewis shares details about his recent meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Tombe notes that while there are plenty of economic reasons to avoid employing non-tariff retaliatory measures in this trade fight, Canada's battle with the U.S. isn't entirely economic.

The U.S., as Prime Minister Mark Carney has said, wants to break us so it can own us, and some say a threat to our sovereignty requires an un-economic response.

"I'm getting a little tired, mainly, with fellow economists who point out that it's harmful to Canada to retaliate. I think that's pretty narrow-minded," Drummond said.

"I'd like to give that advice to the kid in the schoolyard who's getting bullied, [because] it's not much more complicated than that: If you want to stop a bully you have to be prepared to get your nose bloodied. It just eggs them on otherwise."

World.title: Nepal warns of possible fresh flooding as communities grapple with devastation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, which killed at least 800 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The Chinese state news agency Xinhua, citing the country's Ministry of Water Resources, said a new lake that formed after Wednesday's floods high in the mountains had largely drained.

But Xinhua said the ministry warned that a crater located 5.6 kilometres upstream, which held an estimated 1.4 million cubic metres of water, still posed some risk and required close monitoring.

Nepal's disaster agency said on Sunday the death toll had climbed to 788 with 2,502 missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing on the Chinese side of the border.

The missing include hundreds of people from more than a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over 100 Nepalis and others from around the world.

WATCH | Rescuers in Nepal search tunnels for possible flood survivors: Hundreds feared trapped in tunnels after Nepal flash floods | Duration 2:50 Thousands of people are still missing after devastating flooding in Nepal and searchers are turning to tunnels at some hydropower sites, where hundreds are feared trapped. The number of confirmed dead has risen to about 800.

Canada's foreign affairs minister, Anita Anand, said on social media Saturday that a Canadian who was previously missing had been found safe.

Anand said 31 Canadians are still unaccounted for, noting the figure could still "fluctuate" as information becomes available.

Families in Canada seek government's help

Seema Rawla's brother, Sumit Rawla, is among those missing. The Canadian permanent resident from the Vancouver area was visiting Nepal when he stopped picking up the phone immediately after the flooding, Rawla said.

"I'm sitting miles away We don't know what's going on. Is my brother dying, lying dead somewhere?" she said from Toronto.

The pain comes in waves, she said. So does the anger — the feeling that Canada should be doing more to help families like hers.

Rawla said she's been reaching out non-stop to the prime minister's office, to local MPs and to Anand, trying to get help.

"There's a generic message I just get back from them, that we will pass along your message," she said. "I was told two times that they will get in touch with you when they're ready to get in touch with you."

Rawla — along with other Canadian families whose loved ones are missing — shared a letter on Saturday, asking the federal government to share resources, like thermal and infrared cameras, with the government of Nepal.

They're also asking Ottawa to set up a point of contact for each family — some of whom have travelled to Nepal in the aftermath.

But the federal government has not responded yet, Rawla said, other than to say it will share some information at a virtual meeting Monday morning. Anand's office did not respond to CBC's request for comment on Sunday.

WATCH | 31 Canadians are still unaccounted for: Families of Canadians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood cling to hope | Duration 1:55 Families of Canadians missing after the Nepal-Tibet flash flood disaster are desperate for any news of their loved ones, with some planning to travel to join the search efforts. Of the 32 Canadians reported missing, none have yet been confirmed dead.

Rescue operations are underway at five hydroelectric projects, including a major effort at the Upper Trishuli complex, where authorities said on Friday they received information that about 350 people could be trapped inside a tunnel.

About 10,000 Nepali troops have been deployed for tunnel rescue operations alongside specialists from China and India, said Uprety, of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

A team of rescuers and soldiers worked through the night at Upper Trishuli, Nepali Prime Minister Balen Shah's office said on Sunday, posting video on social media showing a helicopter carrying heavy machinery to the area.

Some returning to what remained of their homes

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what could be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.

"Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home," Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.

At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves more than 20,000 people across four districts.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick grey-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Prithivi Highway is a crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

Residents look at the swollen Trishuli River on Sunday. (Niranjan Shrestha/The Associated Press)

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Uprety.

But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

"Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain," said Govind Shreshta, a resident. "It's really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It's going on like this for those who are still alive."

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

"Those who are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It's going to be very difficult," said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday's floods came.

Nepalis are victims of climate change: minister

Wednesday's flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region.

Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

A young boy is helped by a woman to put up a photo of her missing relative on a wall alongside photos of missing and deceased people, outside a hospital in Kathmandu on Sunday. (Dar Yasin/The Associated Press)

Nepal's foreign affairs minister called for a global response to climate change, saying Nepal was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.

"Despite having only 0.1 per cent contribution to the global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change," Shisir Khanal said Saturday.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday's catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth's temperature rises because of human activities such as burning oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase — especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
