World.title: From the archive: Learning Spanish? Don’t be shy or afraid of making mistakes
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article, for example — originally published in November 2019 — explores the leap of faith required when learning Mexican Spanish.

When I first arrived in Mexico, I had two years of college-level Spanish under my belt. While I was an enthusiastic learner, I was also a very self-conscious speaker, terrified of making embarrassing mistakes and generally sounding like a 2-year-old.

I did, in fact, sound like a 2-year-old at first, as there’s simply no way around being a “baby” when one is first learning. Happily, I survived that stage and now speak at least as well as a know-it-all 13-year-old.

Part of my apprehension with the language was the sense that Mexico’s love-hate relationship with the United States would lead to some situations in which I’d be mocked for my accent or mistakes that I would inevitably make.

After all, most people here know very well how Latinos are treated by certain segments of the U.S. population when they’re on the other side of the border, so I’d imagined that the temptation to dish some out to us collectively would be at least a little irresistible.

For the most part, that didn’t happen. It’s also possible that I simply didn’t realize it was happening, but I think most of us humans have a pretty good sense of when others are laughing at us.

Once in a while someone will have a longish conversation with me (in Spanish) and then say something like, “So, you don’t speak Spanish, eh?” or they’ll point out that they “could tell right away that I was American because of my accent” which always makes me bristle, as I’m pretty sure my accent is, while definitely existent, not obviously American.

(My Mexican friends may disagree with me on that one; I’d ask them, but the answer might be too painful for me to hear.)

There’s some sting in it, but I do my best to chalk up any unflattering comments about my Spanish to cosmic justice and not take it too personally.

In the part of Mexico where I live, English is not considered an essential skill the same way it is in the north or in tourist areas. Because of this, most foreigners in my area do their best with the language: they take classes, they practice, they work hard to get better.

Learning a language is sign of respect

They understand, above all, that learning the language of your hosts, if you are able, is a matter of respect.

When I traveled to Los Cabos recently to visit a friend, I saw how different things were in a town that depends on tourism from their English-speaking neighbors: I was addressed in English at all times, and if I answered in Spanish it almost seemed to startle people, as if they’d come into contact with a dog that had learned to produce human sounds.

For the most part, Mexicans are charmed when we non-native speakers at least try. They’re patient and encouraging, and try their best to be helpful. Mexico really is an ideal place to learn Spanish, as I can’t imagine another place in which more impromptu and consistent support among the general population would be given.

That said, I know many of my compatriots are shy about learning — and especially about using — the Spanish that they know already. I completely understand: there’s nothing that makes us feel quite as vulnerable as not being able to “prove” that we are smart, complex, discerning individuals.

There’s no way around sounding like a simpleton when we’re on that long uphill trajectory, and simply put, it can be a humiliating experience.

But again: at least attempting to learn the local language, if one is able, is a matter of respect. “Well then, what about all the people in the U.S. that haven’t bothered to learn English? I bet you don’t go around preaching to them about respect, do you?”

The short answer is that no, indeed I do not. Because here’s the difference: most people who go to the U.S. without already speaking English are in survival mode, just trying to make it from one day to the next, often working a dizzying number of hours both to both survive, and likely to send money back home.

Most Americans and Canadians, however, come to Mexico either in vacation or retirement mode. Some, sadly, come because their spouses or loved ones have been deported and they want to keep the family together.

If one is on vacation, of course, learning the language won’t be expected. But if you settle here, an effort must be made.

Find a school, or find a teacher. Find someone to sit and help you practice. Spend time just listening to people with no intention of adding to the conversation. One of the best pieces of advice I’ve ever received for learning a language is literally to pretend to be a baby: listen to the sounds, watch people, let whole social situations piece themselves together and come into focus slowly.

Babies, after all, spend at least a couple of years listening and observing before they try to string together a sentence with more than four words in it.

On my first plane ride into Mexico, my nervousness increased with each sentence given in Spanish by the flight attendants: the more they spoke, the more I realized I wasn’t catching anything at all that they were saying.

Since then, I’ve made about a million mistakes, linguistically embarrassed myself in every way imaginable, and surely sounded much less sophisticated than I imagine myself to be.

But I’ve gained the ability to talk to most people on this side of the world and have developed some of the closest relationships of my lifetime in this language.

Hands down, totally worth it.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: A governor takes a U-turn, CJNG loses more ground and business booms
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 24 in Mexico began on awkward footing following a Morena party faux pas in Sinaloa. Rubén Rocha Moya, currently under investigation in the United States for alleged collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel, briefly reclaimed the Sinaloa governorship after months on leave, only to retreat again two days later. Meanwhile, several storm systems dumped rain on most of the country, and an investigation into fuel theft in Tamaulipas turned up a startling menagerie of exotic animals.

Also this week, President Sheinbaum revealed new reforms and a US $6M windfall for Guerrero schools as she prepares to soon give her second annual report to the nation.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum weighs in on Rocha’s status in Sinaloa

President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the week fielding questions about the fallout from Rocha Moya’s brief return to the Sinaloa governorship from Aug. 21–23 and the future of Sinaloa’s leadership.

At Monday’s mañanera, as Sonora’s cattle trade with the U.S. reopened, she addressed the episode directly for the first time, saying she learned of Rocha’s Friday return through his social media post and had no prior knowledge of his plans. “I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” she said, later calling the decision “imprudent.” She credited Rocha’s renewed leave request — approved unanimously by Sinaloa’s Congress that Sunday — as “the best thing for Sinaloa,” and dismissed rumors that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador had encouraged Rocha’s return as “political fiction.”

Sheinbaum extended the same standard to other Morena officials swept up in the same U.S. indictment. Asked on Tuesday about Senator Enrique Inzunza — one of 10 Sinaloa-linked officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking ties, who had signaled he might return to the Senate — she said the same principle applied. “Yesterday I gave my opinion on the case of the governor of Sinaloa, who is now on leave. I feel the same way about all 10 cases under investigation by the Attorney General’s Office,” she said. Inzunza subsequently separated from Morena’s Senate caucus on Wednesday, though he remains in office as senator.

Multiple CJNG busts across three states

Security forces delivered a string of blows against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) this week. A coordinated operation across Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán from Aug. 21–23 resulted in 20 arrests and the seizure of weapons, drugs and exotic animals tied to the cartel, with authorities raiding 36 properties and confiscating firearms, fentanyl, methamphetamine, 113 vehicles and a drone jammer.

That action followed a separate military-led operation in Michoacán targeting alleged CJNG leader Heraclio “El Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez last week, which produced roughly a dozen more arrests, including relatives of the suspect. Combined, the two operations brought the week’s tally of alleged CJNG detentions to 32, part of what Security Minister Omar García Harfuch described as an effort to systematically dismantle the group’s operational and financial capacity rather than simply rack up arrests.

Confusion and concern in Mexicali

A U.S. security alert warning of a possible “August 25 threat” in Mexicali created a tense but ultimately murky standoff between caution and normalcy. The alert prompted the U.S. Mission to suspend official travel and activity in the border city, reportedly linked to fears that the crime gang Los Rusos might retaliate after a 120-kilogram fentanyl seizure — roughly 4 million doses — from a property connected to the group.

Mexican officials responded by increasing patrols around public buildings, but as Tuesday came and went without a major incident, the federal security cabinet said it had found no evidence of a specific or imminent threat to the public. Residents described a largely normal day, and the Mexicali-Calexico border crossing remained open throughout, leaving the alert’s basis and its practical necessity still unclear.

Economic data: Record highs alongside warning signs

Revised GDP figures showed the economy grew in the second quarter but contracted in June, with the primary sector contributing the steadiest growth. Foreign direct investment in Mexico yielded US $34.968 billion in FDI in the first half of 2026, its highest semester total ever recorded, up 2.1% year over year, even though the second quarter alone saw a 3.5% annual decline. Manufacturing captured 38.6% of that investment, and the United States remained the dominant source at $16.871 billion.

Trade data added to the good news: July exports hit a record US $81.4 billion, up 43.7% annually, driven by a 134% surge in electrical and electronic equipment shipments tied to U.S. demand for AI and data-center infrastructure inputs. At her Wednesday press conference, Sheinbaum cheered the numbers as proof of a “strong” economy, pointing to record FDI, 60 million people employed and a firm peso, and argued that years of minimum-wage increases had not triggered the inflation or capital flight critics once predicted.

That optimism gained further support when Mexico placed among the OECD’s fastest-growing economies, ranking sixth with 1.4% quarterly growth against an OECD average of 0.5%. But the jobs report complicated the picture: Mexico posted its best monthly job gain of 2026 in July, yet the increase was driven entirely by informal employment, with more than 1.08 million informal jobs added while over 412,000 formal positions vanished. Informality climbed to 56.2%, its highest level since December 2021 — a reminder that headline growth figures can mask deteriorating job quality.

This week’s investment announcements

Schneider Electric announced a major expansion of its operations in Querétaro, reinforcing the state’s role as an industrial and technology hub. Danish firms unveiled a US $510 million renewables project set to boost Campeche’s clean energy supply, adding to the country’s growing green energy portfolio. And Jalisco is set to host Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant, a facility in Ciudad Guzmán capable of recovering up to 95% of materials from the roughly 1.6 million panels already installed statewide.

A fresh framework for environmental protection

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena presented a bill to put environmental justice at the center of Mexican law, proposing reforms to the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection. The initiative would require more forward-looking assessment of major projects, close loopholes that let developers split projects to dodge full environmental review, strengthen restoration and remediation requirements and add specific protections for environmental defenders and Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, rural and urban communities.

Foreign Minister strengthens ties in South Korea and Washington

Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco kept a packed international schedule this week. In Seoul, he met with South Korean officials and executives from Samsung, Hyundai, LG and Posco to promote investment in technology, semiconductors and education, part of groundwork for a 2026–30 bilateral action plan ahead of a planned visit by South Korea’s president. He then traveled to Washington, where he held his first face-to-face meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both sides publicly stressed cooperation against drug and arms trafficking, Bloomberg reported that Washington privately pressed Mexico to do more to stop its own citizens from crossing into the U.S.

Aura farming battles debut in Mexico

A new social-media-driven trend reached Mexican public squares this week: aura farming battles, in which participants strike poses, dance and reference memes to project confidence and style while crowds judge who accumulates the most “aura.” Events popped up at Mexico City landmarks as well as in Xalapa and Torreón, though at least one Veracruz municipality banned the contests in public parks on administrative grounds.

Sheinbaum proposes dual-citizenship ban

Sheinbaum also unveiled a constitutional amendment that would bar dual nationals from running for president, governor or Mexico City mayor unless they renounce their other citizenship before registering as candidates. The government argues current constitutional language contains a loophole and that the country’s highest offices should be held only by people with unambiguous national allegiance — a proposal likely to draw scrutiny over its impact on Mexican-born citizens with binational ties.

Mexican athletes shine internationally

Cyclist Isaac del Toro won the Tour of Germany, becoming the first Latin American rider to capture the race, finishing 53 seconds ahead of France’s Louis Barré.

Mexico won two gold medals and a bronze at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam: Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez took gold in women’s lightweight double sculls, Kenia Lechuga won gold in lightweight single sculls, and Alexis López earned bronze in men’s lightweight single sculls.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test whether this week’s political and security cracks widen further. In Sinaloa, the ongoing conflict between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos remains unresolved, complicating the search for a permanent successor. Pressure is also unlikely to ease on other Morena-aligned officials named in the same U.S. indictment, amid broader questions about the party’s exposure to organized crime in states beyond Sinaloa. With Sheinbaum’s second annual report to the nation approaching, how she navigates these overlapping crises could shape both her security narrative and her party’s credibility heading into the fall.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Activists rally to stop luxury project on Yucatán dunes
World.content:
A proposed luxury real estate development along a protected beach community in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula has sparked protests and backlash online. It’s the latest in a string of projects that activists have sought to stop, saying the developments will have detrimental impacts on their communities.

Las Dunas tourist complex is a planned luxury real estate and tourism venture that aims to encompass 92,000 square meters (more than 22 acres) of virgin beach area less than an hour’s drive from Mérida, the state capital of Yucatán, including more than 70 apartments spread across six towers.

Given its size and scope, activists say the project will have a significant economic and environmental impact on the small beach town, and that it ignores pressing issues that need to be addressed.

“In Chuburná, there are real needs – problems stemming from a lack of basic infrastructure and systematic neglect by the authorities,” Salvemos las Dunas, a local environmental activist group, told Mexico News Daily. “They want to foster the false belief that megaprojects bring economic benefits, but the question is: benefits for whom?”

‘A crime against biodiversity’

It’s not just Salvemos las Dunas that’s sounding the alarm.

Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) denied the project’s initial proposal in December 2023, as the site was deemed highly vulnerable. However, in April 2025, after adjustments were made to the proposal, the project was federally approved.

As the Las Dunas development began to take shape, the outcry from community members and activists was swift. Salvemos las Dunas launched a petition calling for a halt to the project and an official review of the proposed plan.

“[A]bove all, this area is not just a stretch of sand; it’s the history and identity of the people who already live there,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

Their concerns were supported by a three-day inspection led by the Federal Prosecutor’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) in late July. That report detailed multiple violations of federal regulations, some of which could carry criminal charges.

“Omissions, non-compliance and subsequent damage to species of wild flora and fauna protected by Official Mexican Standards may transcend the administrative scope and constitute a crime against biodiversity,” Profepa wrote in a statement shared with Mexico News Daily.

Profepa and the government of Yucatán have since paused the project while they verify its compliance. During a press conference in early August, Gov. Joaquín Díaz Mena said that the “protection of Yucatán’s natural heritage will prevail over any particular project.”

Meanwhile, Salvemos las Dunas’ petition to protect the dunes has garnered more than 140,000 signatures. A protest was also held at the Monumento a La Patria in nearby Mérida in late July.

The public opposition to the project appears to be working.

“Given the concern of citizens, the State Government formally requested, since last July 25, Semarnat and the Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) to verify the timely compliance with the project authorizations and delivered all the technical information it has,” Yucatán’s government wrote in a statement.

Designia Desarrollos, the development firm behind Las Dunas, declined to comment on the ongoing proceedings.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said. “The lack of regulation and the ease with which permits are granted to real estate developers have hijacked the state.”

How important are the Chuburná Dunes?

The Chuburná Dunes are an integral part of the coastal ecosystem, recognized as one of the most well-preserved in Yucatán. Hosting various endangered wildlife species, including some that are endemic to Yucatán, as well as a nesting ground for a tortoise species on the brink of global extinction, the current ecosystem is both fragile and consequential.

Among the animals that call the dunes home are the Mexican sheartail hummingbird (doricha eliza) and the Yucateca wren (campylorhynchus yucatanicus), both of which have been granted a protective status, as well as the hawksbill sea turtle (eretmochelys imbricata) and the green sea turtle (chelonia mydas).

The dunes also serve as a natural protector against wind, tides, hurricanes, erosion and other storm systems that frequently batter the area, meaning any damage to them could prove irreversible.

“We believe that progress can be achieved consciously, hand in hand with environmental protection and citizen participation, but above all, by safeguarding the interests of the people, not just a few families in Mérida,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

A stalled Royal Caribbean project

The Las Dunas tourist complex is just the latest in a string of recent developments that didn’t sit well with local activists and conservationists.

Earlier this year, a Royal Caribbean megaproject in Quintana Roo came to a halt after citizens and activists expressed concerns.

The project, known as “Perfect Day,” is a proposed amusement park in the municipality of Othón P. Blanco, in the small fishing village of Mahahual. The famous cruise line had purchased the property, located close to the port of Costa Maya, which Royal Caribbean also owns, for $292 million.

An online petition against the development has garnered more than 5 million signatures to date.

Royal Caribbean officially withdrew its environmental assessment application in May, citing Semarnat’s intentions to deny the project. The company said it was “disappointed” in Semarnat’s decision and would “respect the role of Mexico’s environmental authorities,” but stopped short of saying “Perfect Day” would be scrapped entirely.

“We continue to believe in Mexico, and are optimistic in the potential to advance our investment responsibly,” the company wrote in a statement at the time. “Over the coming weeks, we will re-engage stakeholders to move forward in a way that delivers shared prosperity through the development of essential environmental infrastructure, the creation of thousands of local jobs, and community programs that support the people of Mexico.”

Tren Maya’s 900-mile development

The activism surrounding both Las Dunas and Perfect Day is set against the backdrop of the Tren Maya megaproject, which was completed in 2024 under then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

So far, the 900-mile train route spread across five states in Mexico’s southeast has failed to realize its promised financial benefits for local communities, while also understating its overall environmental impact.

Tren Maya carried its first passengers in December 2023. Since then, 42 trains have been inaugurated, traveling more than 900 miles of track across Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

According to an August 2023 report by CartoCrítica, Tren Maya’s construction spans more than 26,000 acres, requiring deforestation efforts in 61% of the surrounding jungle. The report alleges that 87% of the deforestation was done without the necessary permits.

This, despite López Obrador’s assertions in a 2018 interview that “Not a single tree” would be cut down. Semarnat similarly released a statement in January 2023, saying that “More than 64,000 plants have been rescued with 85% survival.”

However, Priscila Alaniz Uribe, the general director for the Sélvame nonprofit, has a different take.

“About 12 million trees have been cut down, and around 125 cenotes have been damaged,” Alaniz Uribe told Sierra Club in July. “There are 15,000 piles of concrete poisoning the water in underground rivers – water we humans, animals, and plants use to live here.”

Such concerns define the environmental activism that has taken place around the Yucatán Peninsula in recent years.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said of the project they’re working to stop. “If this area is cleared, it will leave the residents who have cared for their city for years unprotected; not to mention that it is home to endemic species of the area that are in danger of extinction.”

Jesse Foley-Tapia is a writer and photographer living in the Yucatán Peninsula, where he has dedicated his time and energy to shedding light on issues affecting Indigenous communities. His biggest journalistic accomplishment is interviewing Kendrick Lamar in 2010. His work has appeared in The Sun Magazine and BreakThrough News.

World.title: Chile: Kast Approval Rebounds to 33.8 Percent as His Coalition Pushes Him to Negotiate
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

CHILE · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: President José Antonio Kast’s approval rose to 33.8 percent in August, with 54.4 percent of Chileans disapproving. —The trend: Pulso Ciudadano shows a recovery from July’s record low of 28.9 percent, his worst reading in office. —The real story: Kast’s own coalition is pressing him to negotiate his stalled security reform with the opposition. —The catch: Even after the rebound, more than half the country disapproves of how the president is governing. —The economy: Santiago announced tax credits for greenfield mining exploration while household arrears keep spreading. —Who is hurting: One in four Chileans with a previously clean credit record now reports overdue debt.

The Kast approval number is climbing off its floor, but the presidency remains underwater with voters. Meanwhile Santiago is buying growth with mining tax breaks, and Chilean households are falling behind on their debts.

A rebound from the floor

The August edition of Pulso Ciudadano, produced by Activa Research, puts Kast approval at 33.8 percent. Disapproval stands at 54.4 percent, and 11.8 percent did not answer.

The recovery is real but modest. July delivered 28.9 percent, the lowest Kast approval reading since he took office in March.

The series tells the story of a difficult first semester. Kast approval was 34.7 percent in March, 29.1 in April, 31.0 in May and 30.1 in June.

The president keeps 63.4 percent support among right-wing identifiers. Among independents, the figure collapses to about one in five.

Crime remains Chileans’ top national concern at 46.4 percent, according to the poll. Unemployment rose to 32.7 percent, its highest level this year.

His own coalition wants negotiation, not confrontation

The poll recovery lands in the middle of a legislative siege. Kast’s flagship security reform is stuck in Congress, and his own allies want him to bargain.

We documented how the coalition split over the bill and how Kast retreated after a cross-party revolt last week.

Inside Renovación Nacional, the largest government party, the pressure is now explicit. Party leaders have spent weeks asking for dialogue instead of a defeated vote.

Andrés Balladares, an RN deputy, summed up the mood in early August. He asked the government to focus on employment and security and warned against distractions, Publimicro reported.

Senate president Paulina Núñez, also from the coalition, has become the public face of that pressure. Her message is consistent: negotiate the reform instead of losing it.

Tax breaks to restart mining exploration

On the economic front, the government moved to wake up its strongest industry. Daniel Mas, who holds both the Economy and Mining portfolios, announced a plan of tax benefits for mining exploration.

The target is greenfield exploration, the search for entirely new deposits. The package includes direct tax credits and regulatory simplification to unblock projects, Radio Interamericana reported on 30 August.

The logic is jobs. Chile’s economy was flat in the second quarter, joint-weakest in the OECD, and employment is slowing.

Núñez welcomed the plan but asked the government to look beyond large projects. Small and medium miners, entrepreneurs and the state promotion agencies Sercotec and Corfo need attention too, she said.

The quiet deterioration in household credit

The most uncomfortable number of the week comes from Destácame, a Chilean financial platform. Its Financial Wellbeing Thermometer shows arrears reaching households that used to pay on time.

Among consumers with a positive commercial record, 24.5 percent now report some overdue debt. In the first quarter, that share was 16 percent.

The broader measure is worse. Some 53.2 percent of respondents report at least one debt in arrears, up from 44.8 percent in the previous reading.

Destácame’s Financial Wellbeing Index fell from 36.5 to 33.5 points in the second quarter. The company classifies that level as low-critical.

The survey covered 512 platform users in June, so treat the exact percentages with care. The direction, however, matches the consumer protection agency Conadecus, which counts more than four million adults with unpaid debts.

What to watch from here

First, the security reform. Whether Kast accepts a negotiated text will decide if his first big law survives the spring.

A durable Kast approval rebound depends on it.

Second, September’s budget. The government is preparing what local media describe as an austere first budget, due in Congress within weeks.

Third, the mining package. Watch whether the tax credits reach small explorers or stay a tool for the big projects.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kast’s approval rating in August 2026? Pulso Ciudadano puts Kast approval at 33.8 percent in August, with 54.4 percent disapproving. That is a recovery from July’s record low of 28.9 percent. Why is Kast’s coalition pressing him? His security reform is stalled in Congress after a cross-party revolt. Allies in Renovación Nacional, including Senate president Paulina Núñez, want a negotiated text instead of a lost vote. What did Chile announce for mining? Economy and Mining Minister Daniel Mas announced tax credits and regulatory simplification to reactivate greenfield exploration, the search for entirely new mineral deposits. How bad is Chile’s household debt problem? Destácame finds 24.5 percent of consumers with a previously positive credit record now report overdue debt, up from 16 percent in the first quarter. Overall, 53.2 percent report at least one debt in arrears. What worries Chileans most? Crime leads at 46.4 percent in Pulso Ciudadano, followed by unemployment at 32.7 percent and inflation at 25.4 percent.

World.title: Colombia: Reconstruction Begins After the Earthquake as the Puracé Volcano Rumbles
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

COLOMBIA · DISASTER

Key Facts —What happened: Three weeks after the 10 August earthquake, the Colombia reconstruction phase is formally under way, led by the Housing Ministry and private builders. —How big: The magnitude 7.4 quake killed more than 300 people and affected nearly 45,000 families, with damage estimated above US$9.5 billion. —What is new: Valle del Cauca starts a pilot in Buenaventura to rebuild 90 stilt houses, paying local residents for the work. —The catch: The money is not settled; Colombia is still arguing over which taxes will pay for a rebuild that could take six years. —A second worry: The Geological Service recorded 58 tremors near the Puracé volcano on Sunday, already on orange alert. —What comes next: Teams now assess buildings plot by plot to decide which homes are repaired and which are rebuilt from zero.

“We are going to get back up” has become Colombia’s unofficial motto since the earthquake. This week the phrase turned into machinery, as the Colombia reconstruction effort shifted from rescue to rebuilding while the Puracé volcano added a fresh scare.

From rescue to reconstruction

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake of Monday 10 August tore through western Colombia, hitting Cali, Pereira and Manizales hardest. The death toll passed 300, with the AFP news agency reporting 321 victims as funerals continued into late August.

The damage count explains the scale of the Colombia reconstruction task. Nearly 45,000 families were affected, and early loss estimates started above US$9.5 billion, concentrated in the western departments of Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas and Chocó.

President Abelardo De La Espriella set the national plan in motion on 13 August, sitting down with the country’s biggest construction companies at the San Carlos palace. The response, he said, cannot fall on the state alone.

Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán now leads the effort. Its first tools are rental subsidies for homeless families, relief on utility bills, machinery for rubble removal and a materials bank to supply the damaged regions directly.

The Valle del Cauca pilot: rebuild, repair, reanimate

The most concrete new step comes from Valle del Cauca, the department around Cali. Governor Dilian Francisca Toro announced a three-track programme she summarised as rebuild, repair and reanimate, the last one meaning psychological and spiritual support for survivors.

The pilot project will rebuild 90 stilt houses, the traditional waterfront dwellings known as palafitos, in the Pacific port of Buenaventura. Residents themselves will join the work crews and be paid daily wages, turning reconstruction into temporary income.

Toro was explicit that the emergency phase is over. Colombia cannot stay in humanitarian-aid mode, she said, and must start rebuilding while aid continues for as long as needed.

Technical teams are now going plot by plot across the damaged zone. Their job is to separate homes that need structural repair from those that must be demolished and rebuilt entirely.

Who pays for the Colombia reconstruction, and how long it takes

Former finance minister Juan Camilo Restrepo, who managed the coffee-region rebuild after the 1999 Armenia earthquake, has called for a home-grown Marshall Plan. He puts the bill at 20 to 40 trillion pesos (US$6.3 billion to US$12.6 billion) and wants it written into the 2026-2030 development plan.

That money fight is unresolved. As we reported in our coverage of the reconstruction finance debate, the government is leaning on subsidised mortgages and frozen student debt while Congress argues over taxes.

The honest timetable for the Colombia reconstruction is long. Our earlier estimate put full reconstruction at up to six years, and the government itself says this tragedy will not be overcome by the state alone.

Cali’s mayor, Alejandro Eder, supplied the phrase of the week after the last body was found in his city. “We caleños are going to get back up,” he said, “as a rebuilt city.”

A fresh scare from the Puracé volcano

As if one disaster were not enough, the Colombian Geological Service, known by its Spanish initials SGC, issued an extraordinary bulletin on Sunday. It recorded 58 tremors about 11 kilometres north-east of the Puracé volcano’s main crater, at an average depth of nine kilometres.

The strongest, magnitude 4.1, struck at 6:18 p.m. in the San Rafael valley and was felt in Puracé, Totoró and the city of Popayán. Three more quakes of magnitudes 3.9, 3.1 and 2.8 followed.

The SGC said the swarm is volcano-tectonic, caused by rock fracturing inside the volcanic structure, and that other monitoring parameters have not changed. Puracé has been on orange alert since late July, and we covered the 3,250-metre ash column last week.

Authorities asked residents to stay calm and follow only official channels. For a region already living through the Colombia reconstruction, the tremors were an unwelcome reminder that the ground has not finished moving.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Colombia’s earthquake reconstruction formally begun? Yes. The national plan led by the Housing Ministry with private construction companies began on 13 August 2026, and Valle del Cauca has started a pilot to rebuild 90 stilt houses in Buenaventura with paid local labour. How bad was the 10 August earthquake in Colombia? The magnitude 7.4 quake killed more than 300 people, with AFP reporting 321 deaths, and affected nearly 45,000 families. Damage was estimated at more than US$9.5 billion, concentrated in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and the Pacific coast. What happened at the Puracé volcano? The Colombian Geological Service recorded 58 tremors near the crater on Sunday, the strongest of magnitude 4.1, felt in Puracé, Totoró and Popayán. The volcano has been on orange alert since late July, but other monitoring parameters are unchanged. How much will rebuilding cost and who pays? Former finance minister Juan Camilo Restrepo estimates 20 to 40 trillion pesos (US$6.3 billion to US$12.6 billion). The government plans rental subsidies, cheap mortgages and private-sector help, while Congress still debates the tax funding.

World.title: Honduras Returns to the World Bank’s Arbitration Court With an Eye on Investors
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

HONDURAS · ECONOMY

Key Facts —What happened: Honduras has been a full member of the World Bank’s arbitration court again since 16 August. —Why it matters: Analysts read the Honduras ICSID return as a clear message that the country is open for business. —The catch: The state still faces a US$1.63 billion claim from the Próspera charter-city investors at that same court. —Next vote: Congress could pass the energy reform splitting the state utility ENEE into three companies next week. —The squeeze: The lempira has broken 27 per dollar for the first time, pushing up import and fuel prices. —The handshake: Presidents Asfura and Abinader agreed a new cooperation stage on trade, security, air links and Haiti.

The Honduras ICSID return puts the country back inside the World Bank’s arbitration system after 18 months outside it. The government of Nasry Asfura calls it the foundation of an investment push that next week could carry an energy reform through Congress.

Back at the World Bank’s court

ICSID is the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, the World Bank body where foreign investors can sue states. Honduras had belonged to it for 35 years.

The previous president, Xiomara Castro, pulled the country out in February 2024, calling the system biased toward corporations. The withdrawal took effect on 25 August that year.

Asfura reversed the decision in his first weeks in office. He signed the convention in Washington on 6 March, Honduras deposited its ratification on 17 July, and Honduras ICSID membership took effect on 16 August.

World Bank president Ajay Banga called the move a clear signal that Honduras is open for business. Lawyers and analysts have echoed that reading; more than 50 civil-society groups instead called it a “signal of submission” to foreign capital.

The claim that hangs over the return

The Honduras ICSID return comes with baggage. The investors behind Próspera, a charter city on the island of Roatán, are still pursuing the state in arbitration.

The claim originally reached US$10.775 billion, close to 40% of the Honduran economy. The investors cut it to US$1.63 billion last October, and the case has run for more than three years without a ruling on the merits.

The dispute began when Castro’s government repealed the special economic zones known as ZEDEs. For potential investors, how Honduras handles this case will prove what the Honduras ICSID membership is worth.

The energy reform’s decisive week

Congress will concentrate next week on the energy bill Asfura sent in late May, and it could pass. The reform rewrites 12 articles of the 2013 electricity industry law.

Its centrepiece is the split of the state utility ENEE into three state-owned companies, for generation, transmission and distribution, under ENEE as the parent. An independent operator would run the grid and the wholesale market.

The case for it is financial. ENEE loses around US$600 million a year; in the first quarter of 2026 alone the hole was 4,049 million lempiras (about US$151 million), and Asfura puts monthly losses at 1,200 to 1,500 million lempiras (US$45 to 56 million).

The US State Department publicly backed the reform in June. The opposition Libre party calls it privatisation by instalments, and the ENEE workers’ union wants guarantees written into the text.

A double currency shock at the wrong moment

The politics would be easier if households were not squeezed. The dollar has broken through 27 lempiras for the first time, as we reported on Sunday, and a globally strong dollar compounds the slide.

Honduras imports its fuel and much of its food, so a weaker lempira lands directly in shop prices. The government is spending around 49 million lempiras (about US$1.8 million) a week on a temporary fuel subsidy to soften the blow.

The cushion is remittances, which bring in roughly US$7.7 billion a year from Hondurans abroad. That inflow supports the peso-poor, dollar-rich households that dominate the countryside.

The Dominican handshake

Asfura has also been building regional alliances. He met Dominican president Luis Abinader in Cali on 7 August, at Colombia’s presidential inauguration.

The two agreed to open a new stage of cooperation covering trade, security, air connectivity and coordination on the Haiti crisis, according to official statements. Asfura also asked for Dominican backing for Honduras’s 2029 Central American and Caribbean Games.

For a government selling stability to foreign capital, friends matter. The Dominican Republic is the region’s growth star, and a direct line to Santo Domingo fits the same investor-facing strategy as the Honduras ICSID return.

What to watch from here

The first test is the energy vote itself. The bill has already survived one debate and a long negotiation; passage next week would be Asfura’s biggest legislative win.

The second is the lempira. If the currency keeps sliding, the fuel subsidy bill grows, and the fiscal room for the investment agenda shrinks with it.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did the Honduras ICSID return take effect? President Nasry Asfura signed the convention on 6 March 2026, Honduras deposited its ratification on 17 July, and membership took effect on 16 August 2026. The country had left in August 2024. What is ICSID? ICSID is the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, part of the World Bank Group. It runs the arbitration and conciliation system where foreign investors and states resolve investment disputes. What is in Honduras’s energy reform? The bill splits the state utility ENEE into three state-owned companies for generation, transmission and distribution, and creates an independent grid and market operator. ENEE loses around US$600 million a year. Why is the Honduran lempira under pressure? The dollar has broken 27 lempiras for the first time, driven by global dollar strength and local demand for hard currency. Because Honduras imports fuel and food, the slide feeds directly into consumer prices. What did Honduras and the Dominican Republic agree? Presidents Nasry Asfura and Luis Abinader agreed a new stage of cooperation covering trade, security, air connectivity and the Haiti crisis. They met in Cali, Colombia, on 7 August 2026.

Sources: World Bank / ICSID press release of 6 March 2026; Forbes Centroamérica / EFE; Diario La Prensa; Criterio.hn; Centroamerica360; Ecosystema Startup. Exchange rates as of 31 August 2026.

World.title: Colombia’s Guaviare Bombing Killed Three Minors — the Offensive That Replaced ‘Total Peace’
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Key Facts —What happened: Three minors were among the dead in last week’s Guaviare bombing of a FARC dissident camp, Colombian media report. —The operation: President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered Operation AMON in El Retorno, against the faction of commander “Calarcá”. —The catch: The dead children were forcibly recruited, which under international law still obliges the state to protect them. —A second blow: Days later the military killed a dissident commander known as “Arcadio” in Valle del Cauca. —The policy shift: Colombia’s new government has closed the “total peace” chapter and put the United States back at the centre. —What comes next: The US Southern Command chief was in Bogotá as the bombing unfolded, deepening joint operations on both borders.

Three minors are confirmed among the dead from the Guaviare bombing of a FARC dissident camp, days after the new government formally turned the page on “total peace”. The offensive is expanding, and Washington is back in the frame.

The Guaviare bombing’s youngest victims

The numbers from El Retorno keep getting worse. Three minors died in the Guaviare bombing of the dissident camp, the Bogotá radio network La FM reported on Monday, as forensic identification of the bodies advances.

President Abelardo de la Espriella had announced a preliminary toll of eight “terrorists neutralised” in what he called a precision bombing followed by a commando raid. Later counts, including ours, put the figure at eleven.

The operation, named AMON, targeted the faction of Alexander Díaz, better known as “Calarcá”. His group is one of the FARC dissident structures that rejected the 2016 peace accord and now fight over coca territory in Colombia’s south-east.

The presence of minors is the recurring wound in this strategy. A bombing in Calamar, Guaviare, last November killed seven children, and forensic examiners later counted 15 minors across four operations in late 2025.

Colombia’s ombudsman has repeated the same warning each time. Children forced into armed groups keep their reinforced legal protection, and the state must take every feasible precaution before striking.

From total peace to total offensive

The Guaviare bombing is the first major strike of a new era. De la Espriella took office this month after campaigning against his predecessor Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” policy of negotiating with armed groups.

He had promised to treat guerrillas who refused to demobilise as military targets. Within weeks he replaced the military high command and ordered a territorial push, and the remaining talks with the dissidents were formally closed.

“Colombia must know that we are going on the offensive,” he wrote on X as Operation AMON unfolded. The major ringleaders, he said, would have no sanctuary anywhere in the country.

A second blow in Valle del Cauca

The Guaviare bombing was not the only blow. Days later, the president announced that soldiers had killed a dissident commander known as “Felipe” or “Arcadio” in Valle del Cauca, on the Pacific side of the country.

He called the death a “crushing blow” to the dissident network, the Associated Press reported. Valle del Cauca has become a battleground as the factions push toward the port corridors used to move cocaine out by sea.

Washington back in the frame

The timing was not subtle. As the bombing unfolded, the head of the US Southern Command, Francis Donovan, arrived in Colombia to meet Defence Minister Jorge Mora.

The stated agenda was intelligence sharing and capabilities against “narco-terrorist organisations” under the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. It follows the expansion of joint operations with Ecuador along the shared border, which we reported yesterday.

The hardware is already moving. Colombia signed a 16.5-trillion-peso order (US$5.2 billion) for 17 Swedish-made Saab fighter jets last year, aircraft suited to precisely the kind of strike flown in Guaviare.

What to watch from here

The first test is legal. Prosecutors and the ombudsman will examine whether the El Retorno strike met the duty to protect forcibly recruited children, the same question that haunted Petro last November.

The second is retaliation. After last year’s Calamar bombing, dissident leader Iván Mordisco promised “revolutionary trials” against those responsible, and his faction is now fighting Calarcá’s men and the army at once.

The third is the border. Joint operations with the United States and Ecuador put pressure on the same groups from three sides, which historically pushes violence somewhere else rather than ending it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in the Guaviare bombing in August 2026? Colombian forces bombed a FARC dissident camp in El Retorno, Guaviare, in Operation AMON, ordered by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Three minors are among the confirmed dead, and the total toll is around eleven. Why were minors in a guerrilla camp? FARC dissident factions forcibly recruit children in Colombia’s poor jungle regions. Rights monitors say the state must still take all feasible precautions to protect them during military operations. What was “total peace” and is it over? It was former president Gustavo Petro’s policy of negotiating simultaneously with all armed groups. The new government of Abelardo de la Espriella has formally closed the remaining talks and returned to a military offensive. Who was the commander killed in Valle del Cauca? The president announced that soldiers killed a dissident leader known as “Felipe” or “Arcadio”, calling his death a “crushing blow” to the faction. The Associated Press reported the announcement on 31 August. What role is the United States playing? The head of the US Southern Command visited Bogotá during the operation to deepen intelligence sharing and counter-cartel cooperation. Washington is also expanding joint operations with Colombia and Ecuador along their shared border.

Sources La FM (Bogotá), Xinhua, the Associated Press, El Colombiano, Colombia Reports, statements by the Colombian presidency and the Defence Ministry, and prior Rio Times coverage.

World.title: Cuba Tourism Hits Bottom With 73 Percent of Hotels Closed as Havana Says It Is Opening Up
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

CUBA · TOURISM

Key Facts —What happened: Cuba’s government admits that 73 percent of the country’s hotel facilities are closed. —How deep: Foreign visitors fell 60.7 percent in the first half of 2026, to just 387,591. —The exits: Seven international chains have left, including Meliá, Iberostar and Barceló. —The catch: In the same week, Havana enacted private-sector reforms and told USA Today that Cuba is opening up. —Who pays: Some 25,000 hotel workers are furloughed, and Spanish chains have up to €100 million (US$116 million) trapped. —What comes next: Private firms will soon trade directly with foreign partners, and all 176 reforms should be law by year-end.

Cuba tourism has hit bottom, with 73 percent of hotels closed and seven international chains gone. In the very same week, Havana passed private-sector reforms and its deputy trade minister told USA Today that Cuba is opening up.

The numbers from the government’s own mouth

This is not an opposition estimate. Prime Minister Manuel Marrero Cruz told the National Assembly on 29 July that 73 percent of hotel facilities remain closed.

He also confirmed that seven international chains had ceased operating on the island. Those chains ran 46 percent of the rooms managed under foreign brands.

Around 25,000 hotel workers are now in disponibilidad, the Cuban term for being sent home without work. State news agency Prensa Latina returned to the crisis in two articles on 27 and 28 August.

The agency blames United States sanctions and pressure on foreign companies. The figures themselves come from the government and its statistics office, the ONEI.

Who left, and what they left behind

The biggest blow to Cuba tourism was Meliá, which once managed 34 Cuban hotels. It told Spain’s stock market regulator on 21 July that it would stop all services on the island.

The exit took effect on 24 July 2026. Iberostar closed 12 of its 18 hotels on 1 June and then abandoned the remaining six.

Barceló rescinded its contracts for two hotels in Varadero. The departures gutted the core of Cuba tourism in a single summer.

News agency EFE also lists Canada’s Blue Diamond, Indonesia’s Archipelago International and Turkey’s ATG among the departures. Minor Hotels had already pulled its two NH hotels out of Havana in February.

The money tells its own story. Spanish chains had between €80 and €100 million (US$93 to 116 million) trapped in the Cuban banking system, funds they could not repatriate.

Head offices had already written those sums off. Total Spanish investment in Cuba from 1993 to 2024 came to €465 million (US$539 million).

Most of that money went into accommodation, according to the Spanish trade agency ICEX. Much of it now sits in buildings that do not open.

A visitor count that has collapsed

Cuba received 387,591 international visitors between January and June 2026. The same period of 2025 brought 985,606, so the fall is 60.7 percent in one year.

Canada, historically the biggest source market, fell hardest. It went from 428,118 visitors in the first half of 2025 to 126,937 this year, a drop of 70.3 percent.

In February, Air Canada, WestJet and Air Transat suspended flights because Cuban airports lacked aviation fuel. In March, just 511 visitors arrived from Canada, against almost 99,000 a year earlier.

Hotel occupancy in the first quarter ran at 12.9 percent. A year earlier it was 23.7 percent, itself a weak figure.

The government is now seeking new operators for the empty infrastructure. It highlights the Italian chain Domina, which runs one Varadero hotel and projects two more in Havana.

The electricity system behind the empty rooms

Cuba tourism is collapsing on top of a failing power grid. On 2 August the entire national electricity system disconnected, leaving the island dark.

Through August, generation deficits ran between roughly 1,700 and 2,400 megawatts a day against demand of around 3,300. Provinces such as Holguín reported more than 18 hours without power in a single day.

Hundreds of millions of euros sit sunk into hotels that do not operate. A hotel without electricity or guests is a building, not a business.

The same week, Havana says it is opening up

Against this backdrop, Cuba enacted private-sector reforms this week. Deputy Minister of Foreign Trade and Foreign Investment Carlos Luis Jorge Méndez gave USA Today an exclusive interview in Havana.

“This reinforces the idea that Cuba is opening up,” Méndez said. “This is a real process; this is for real. This isn’t a ploy.”

Three measures are expected to become law within days. Private Cuban companies will import and export directly without a state agency.

Foreign investors will no longer hire workers through the state. Foreigners will also gain broader rights to develop real estate on the island.

The changes belong to a package of 176 economic reforms approved in June. Méndez said all of them should be law by the end of the year.

John Kavulich of the US-Cuba Trade and Economic Council called the trajectory good. But he warned the constitution would need amending to make the changes permanent.

Reforms from the Obama-era thaw were later rolled back. That history is why outside analysts stay cautious.

The opening comes under maximum American pressure. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a new round of sanctions on 20 August, and direct talks between the two countries are stalled.

What to watch from here

First, watch whether the three trade and investment measures actually become law this week. An announcement is not a statute.

Second, watch the winter season. Canada decides whether Cuba tourism survives, and the Canadian carriers have not restored their February schedules.

Third, watch the grid. Until the blackouts end, every hotel reopening rests on a diesel generator and a prayer.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many hotels are closed in Cuba? Prime Minister Manuel Marrero Cruz told the National Assembly that 73 percent of hotel facilities are closed. Around 25,000 hotel workers have been sent home without work. Which hotel chains have left Cuba? Seven international chains have ceased operations, including Meliá, Iberostar, Barceló, Blue Diamond, Archipelago International and ATG. Minor Hotels left earlier, in February. How many tourists is Cuba receiving in 2026? Cuba received 387,591 international visitors from January to June 2026, down 60.7 percent on the same period of 2025. Canadian arrivals fell 70.3 percent. What did Cuba’s deputy trade minister tell USA Today? Carlos Luis Jorge Méndez said Cuba is opening up and called the reforms a real process, not a ploy. He said all 176 measures approved in June should be law by the end of the year. What do the new Cuban private-sector reforms do? Private companies will trade directly with foreign partners, foreign investors will hire workers without a state agency, and foreigners gain broader rights to develop real estate. The first measures are expected to become law this week.

04 Copom and the macro backdrop

The Selic benchmark was 14.00% on 28 August 2026, and the B3 Copom options dashboard is the cleanest market-implied gauge of where the central bank goes in the August meeting. Traders use those options to bet on the size and direction of the next policy decision.

Today’s data changes the arithmetic. If gross debt-to-GDP prints at or above the 82% consensus and GDP lands at just 0.2% quarterly growth, the Copom would face a slowdown that coincides with stretched public finances.

The BCB Focus Market Readout, due at 11:30 BRT, will also show whether economists are shifting their Selic projections for the coming meetings. That survey feeds directly into the options market’s pricing.

For foreign investors, the message is straightforward: Brazilian assets at the open are a bet on how much slack the central bank must create, and every basis point of implied easing moves both the Bovespa and the real.

Locaweb Serviços de Internet pays an annual dividend of BRL 0.0427 per share today, though the stock traded ex-dividend on 19 August, meaning the cash goes to investors who held shares two weeks ago rather than to new buyers today.

World.title: Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro Wants Gangs Declared Terrorists and a Security Ministry
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ELECTION 2026

Key Facts —What happened: Flávio Bolsonaro met El Salvador’s justice minister Gustavo Villatoro in São Paulo on 30 August and called it inspiring. —The plan: A dedicated public security ministry would run the crime fight alongside state forces and municipal police. —The label: He would declare criminal organisations and militias terrorist groups if elected president in October. —The numbers: Brazil has too few prisoners and should have more, the senator told reporters after the meeting. —The catch: El Salvador’s model cut homicides by 97%, but rests on mass incarceration and suspended constitutional guarantees. —What comes next: The platform feeds his October duel with Lula, who has promised a security ministry of his own.

Flávio Bolsonaro has sketched the hardest-edged public security platform of Brazil’s 2026 campaign. Fresh from meeting El Salvador’s justice minister in São Paulo, the senator promised a terrorist label for gangs and more prisoners.

The São Paulo meeting with Bukele’s minister

The meeting happened on Sunday 30 August, as first reported by Poder360. Gustavo Villatoro is El Salvador’s minister of justice and public security and a right hand of President Nayib Bukele.

Bolsonaro said the encounter left him inspired to build a firm anti-crime plan. The aim, he said, is to defend citizens and victims, not criminals, as he claims the current government does.

Villatoro told him the Salvadoran result could be repeated in Brazil. El Salvador is small and poor, Bolsonaro recounted, while Brazil is large and rich, so gang control of territory has no excuse.

The guest list doubled as a campaign photo. Alongside Bolsonaro sat his running mate Alfredo Gaspar, former judge Sérgio Moro, and Senate candidates Guilherme Derrite and André do Prado.

A public security ministry built with the states

The institutional centrepiece is a dedicated public security ministry. It would manage the fight against organised crime together with state forces and municipal police, Bolsonaro said.

In Brazil, policing sits mainly with the 26 states and the federal district. A federal ministry would coordinate rather than command, offering money, organisation and intelligence sharing.

Bolsonaro called himself a strongly municipalist president in waiting. He promised support across all levels of government, from financing to the exchange of intelligence between forces.

The idea is not his alone. President Lula promised his own public security ministry at a Rio de Janeiro campaign event on 22 August. Both frontrunners now sell the same institution.

Terrorists, not just criminals

The sharpest pledge is the label. Bolsonaro said he would declare Brazil’s criminal organisations and militias terrorist groups if elected, Valor Econômico reported on 31 August.

He has named the targets before. In March he said the PCC and the Comando Vermelho would be classed as terrorists under his government. They are Brazil’s two biggest prison-born gangs.

The proposal tracks a United States policy pushed by President Donald Trump. Washington has weighed the same designation for both gangs, and the Lula government treats the idea as a sovereignty risk.

A terrorist label changes the legal toolkit. It can unlock asset freezes, travel bans and deeper international cooperation against anyone tied to the named groups.

“There are too few prisoners in Brazil”

After the meeting, Bolsonaro defended incarceration as policy. Brazil has few prisoners and should have more, he told reporters, in remarks carried by the G1 news portal.

Brazil already holds one of the world’s largest prison populations, and its jails are chronically overcrowded. The senator’s answer is capacity built in the Salvadoran style.

That model is the catch in the whole platform. Since 2022, Bukele’s government has run a state of exception that suspends constitutional guarantees and jails people without normal due process.

The results explain the appeal. Official figures show homicides fell from 3,346 in 2018 to 114 in 2024, a drop of 97%. Bukele was re-elected in 2024 with 84.65% of the vote.

Human-rights groups document mass arbitrary arrests under the same policy. Asked about that record, Bolsonaro brushed the criticism aside, G1 reported.

The political frame around the platform

Bolsonaro is the eldest son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is barred from running. The son inherited the family’s voters and now trails only Lula in the polls.

Security is the theme where he polls strongest, and he has built it out for months. We covered the first version in how his security plan mirrors the Bukele model.

The economic half of the platform is in our report on his economic team. The legal war around his candidacy is in Brazil’s election moves into the courts.

What to watch from here

The first marker is the written government plan. The terrorism label and the ministry both need congressional approval, and the detail will show the legal path.

The second is the American track. A United States designation of the PCC or Comando Vermelho would hand Bolsonaro’s argument a tailwind, whoever wins in October.

The third is whether Lula’s rival ministry proposal steals the theme. Two frontrunners selling the same institution is how a campaign idea becomes a mandate.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Flávio Bolsonaro’s public security platform? He would create a dedicated public security ministry working with state forces and municipal police. He would also declare gangs and militias terrorist groups and expand imprisonment. He presented the ideas after meeting El Salvador’s justice minister on 30 August 2026. Who did Bolsonaro meet from El Salvador? Gustavo Villatoro, El Salvador’s minister of justice and public security and a close ally of President Nayib Bukele. The meeting took place in São Paulo, and Bolsonaro said it left him inspired. Which gangs would be declared terrorist groups? Bolsonaro has named the PCC and the Comando Vermelho, Brazil’s largest criminal organisations, and now includes militias. The designation mirrors a policy pushed by US President Donald Trump. What is the criticism of the Bukele model? El Salvador’s crackdown runs under a state of exception that suspends constitutional guarantees, and rights groups document mass arbitrary arrests. Official figures show homicides fell 97% between 2018 and 2024. Does Lula also promise a security ministry? Yes. Lula promised to create a public security ministry at a campaign event in Rio de Janeiro on 22 August 2026. Both frontrunners now propose versions of the same institution.

World.title: Eluide Miller defeats Allan Pollard to win PUP Belize City mayoral nomination; ‘El Toxico’ leads all candidates in voting with 564 votes
World.content:
Eluide Miller defeats Allan Pollard to win PUP Belize City mayoral nomination; ‘El Toxico’ leads all candidates in voting with 564 votes

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Deputy Mayor Eluide Miller has won the People’s United Party’s Belize City mayoral convention, defeating fellow City Councillor Allan Pollard Jr. in a closely watched internal contest to lead the party into the 2027 municipal elections.

PUP Chairman Henry Charles Usher announced the results Sunday night following voting at the ITVET compound. All 787 delegates reportedly participated in the convention, with one spoiled ballot leaving 786 valid votes in the mayoral race. Miller received 445 votes, while Pollard received 341.

The result makes Miller the PUP’s mayoral candidate to succeed his father-in-law, outgoing Belize City Mayor Bernard Wagner, who is not seeking another term. Miller currently serves as Deputy Mayor and was unanimously re-elected to that position by the City Council earlier this year.

The convention also determined the PUP’s ten councillor candidates from a field of 19 aspirants. Social media personality Kristian “El Toxico” Alpuche, a newcomer to electoral politics, topped the councillor poll with 564 votes. The successful slate also includes a mixture of incumbent councillors and newcomers who will campaign alongside Miller.

Following his victory, Miller thanked the delegates and described the campaign as an exhausting but rewarding several weeks. He rejected suggestions that his candidacy was based on entitlement and said he had asked delegates to decide who they trusted to lead Belize City.

Miller also extended an olive branch to Pollard, saying politics should never become personal.

“There is absolutely no contention between Allan Pollard and I,” Miller said, adding that he looks forward to working “side by side” with Pollard to complete the current council’s term and prepare for the municipal election.

The mayoral contest had attracted significant attention in recent months, with Pollard, a three-term councillor and former Deputy Mayor, facing Miller, who entered City Hall as an intern in 2019 before becoming an employee, councillor and eventually Deputy Mayor.

Miller said the new slate combines youthful leadership and new ideas with experience and maturity, while urging unsuccessful candidates and current councillors who did not make the slate to remain involved.

The PUP will now turn its attention to the March 3, 2027 municipal election, where it will seek to retain control of Belize City Hall.

World.title: 787 votes cast as PUP Belize City convention heads into counting
World.content:
787 votes cast as PUP Belize City convention heads into counting

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The People’s United Party’s Belize City municipal convention recorded 787 votes cast on Sunday.

According to official figures provided by a party official, 787 delegates and 50 alternates were eligible to vote.

Of the 787 votes cast, seven came from alternates. One vote was spoilt.

The last alternate delegate voted around 4:05pm, with counting beginning thereafter.

The convention was held at the ITVET compound on Freetown Road to determine the party’s mayoral candidate and ten councillor candidates for Belize City.

Party Chairman Henry Charles Usher had said ahead of the convention that hundreds of delegates were expected, describing the Belize City municipal convention as larger than the UDP’s national convention.

The PUP is aiming to have all nine municipal slates in place by September 29, the party’s birthday, before turning full attention to the campaign for the March 2027 municipal elections.

World.title: Double Murder in Santa Elena – Gil ‘Flaco’ Pineda, mechanic and friend of Rasheed Hyde, succumbs to gunshot injuries
World.content:
Double Murder in Santa Elena – Gil ‘Flaco’ Pineda, mechanic and friend of Rasheed Hyde, succumbs to gunshot injuries

By Jose Luis Cruz: 36-year old mechanic Gil Pineda, a friend of Rasheed Hyde and more commonly known as Flaco, succumbed to his injuries late this morning.

Hyde and Pineda were both shot early on Saturday afternoon on George Price Avenue in Santa Elena. Following the shooting, both victims were rushed to the San Ignacio Hospital where Hyde was pronounced dead on arrival. Pineda arrived in a critical condition and was transferred to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Breaking Belize News has confirmed that Pineda died late this morning while receiving treatment.

Investigations into this latest shooting incident, now classified as a double murder, is ongoing.

World.title: Put the books in school, not on their backs – A simple policy idea that could lighten the load on Belizean children
World.content:
Put the books in school, not on their backs – A simple policy idea that could lighten the load on Belizean children

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News

By Nuri Mohammad: For years I advocated for tablets in our schools. One reason was simple: I watched our children going to school every day lugging heavy backpacks filled with textbooks. Why carry all those books when they could be stored on one lightweight tablet? I have now changed my position.

Recent research has caused me to reconsider replacing books with screens. While the evidence is not absolute, there is good reason to believe that, for some kinds of learning, children comprehend and retain information better from printed material. Research published in recent years, including a 2018 meta-analysis in Educational Research Review, has found that students often perform better when reading longer or more demanding texts in print rather than on digital screens. The evidence is not a rejection of technology, but it does suggest that printed books remain valuable learning tools.

Maybe the problem was never the books. The problem was making our children carry them back and forth every day.

Belize is a warm country. Unlike children in colder regions, our students do not need to carry heavy coats, winter clothing, or other bulky items simply to stay warm during the school day. Yet many are now being required to carry increasingly heavy schoolbooks and supplies. That makes the weight of their backpacks even more unnecessary.

My policy suggestion is simple: retrofit our secondary schools with lockers.

This is standard practice in many schools elsewhere. Students can keep books and other supplies at school and take home only what they need for homework.

There is also a physical wellbeing issue. We don’t need to exaggerate the medical evidence to recognize that some of those bags are unnecessarily heavy, particularly for smaller students. Why should a child carry six or seven books when only two are needed at home that evening?

Government could start with a few secondary schools as a pilot. Install simple, secure lockers—possibly manufactured locally—work out the cost and practical problems, and then gradually expand the program across the country.

Yes, it will require a change in school culture. Teachers and students will have to plan which books go home and which stay at school. But I suspect the children will happily adjust to leaving that unnecessary weight behind.

Technology still has an important place in education. But sometimes progress doesn’t require another electronic device.

Sometimes the solution is much simpler.

Keep the books—but put them in school, not on our children’s backs.

World.title: Belize stays hot and mostly dry this Sunday
World.content:
Belize stays hot and mostly dry this Sunday

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Warm and relatively dry conditions prevail over Belize today, according to the National Meteorological Service.

Expect sunny skies with a few cloudy intervals through the day and partly cloudy skies tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with a low chance of a few more over southern Toledo tonight.

Inland temperatures will reach 95 degrees Fahrenheit before dropping to 74 overnight. The coast reaches 90 with a low of 82, while the hills stay at 82 and fall to 68.

World.title: You will be dead much longer than you will be tired, the Sunday arithmetic
World.content:
You will be dead much longer than you will be tired, the Sunday arithmetic

By Horace Palacio:

A line has been circulating this week, dressed in the name of Alexander the Great.

You will be dead much longer than you will be tired.

Did Alexander actually say it? Honesty first, as always in this column. No ancient historian records the sentence, and it carries the fingerprints of the internet, which loves to lend its best lines to famous corpses. But for once, the internet mailed the quote to the correct address. Because whether or not the words are his, no life in recorded history argues them harder.

Consider the record. A young man inherits a small kingdom at twenty. By thirty two he has marched an army more than twenty thousand miles, from Greece to the edge of India, never once losing a battle, founding cities from Egypt to Afghanistan that carry his name to this day. He fought at the front, not the rear. At one siege in India an arrow went through his chest into his lung, and the man got up and kept campaigning. Plutarch records that Alexander said it was sleep that reminded him he was mortal. Tiredness, to him, was weather. You do not negotiate with weather. You march through it.

Now sit with the sentence itself, because it is really a piece of arithmetic, and arithmetic is this column’s love language.

How long will you be tired? Tonight, perhaps. This season, maybe. Tiredness is a visitor. It arrives, it sits heavily, and it always, always leaves, usually by morning, sometimes by Monday, occasionally by next year.

How long will you be dead? Forever. Not a long time. Forever. Every year that has ever passed and every year that will ever come, stacked end to end, and then eternity after that. Death is not a visitor. Death is the address.

So the sentence is simply asking you to compare the two durations before you make any permanent decision based on the temporary one. And yet, look around Belize, and listen to the national anthem we actually sing daily. Mi tired.

Let me be careful here, because this column has spent a year honoring Belizean tiredness, and I will not insult it now. The mother working the hotel shift and the market stall, whose month is longer than her money, she is not the target of this sermon. She is its proof. She wakes exhausted every single morning and rises anyway. She has been living Alexander’s arithmetic her whole life without a meme to tell her so. Salute her.

No, the sentence aims at something else entirely. It aims at the dreams we execute with fatigue as the weapon. The business never registered, because mi tired. The course abandoned at module three. The field never planted. The application never sent. The apology never made, the book never opened, the savings circle never started. Ask the honest question, Belize. How many of our unlived lives were cancelled not by failure, not by enemies, not by lack of talent, but by a feeling that would have passed by Thursday?

We keep signing permanent resignations with temporary ink.

Now, the double edge, because this column never sells half a story, and Alexander’s own life carries the correction inside it.

Two facts about the undefeated general. First, the only force that ever beat him was tiredness itself, just not his own. At a river in India called the Hyphasis, his soldiers, eight years and twenty thousand miles from home, refused to take another step. The man who had conquered the known world stood before his own exhausted army, and lost. The mutiny of the weary turned him around. And second, he was dead at thirty two, burned through, feverish in Babylon, a torch that consumed itself entirely.

So hold both truths, because together they make the whole lesson. Tiredness must never cancel your purpose. And unmanaged fire consumes the torch. The sentence was never an instruction to skip sleep. Even Alexander slept, he simply never stopped. The instruction is finer than that. Rest, fully, nightly, guiltlessly, and never once resign. Rest is a pit stop. Quitting is a destination. The tragedy is not the Belizean who takes Sunday off. The tragedy is the one who mistook a Sunday feeling for a final answer.

Which gives us the practical tool, in the tradition of this column’s tests. Call it the tired-or-done test, and run it any night the towel feels ready to be thrown. Ask one question. Am I tired, or am I done? Tired needs a bed. Done needs a decision. And here is the iron rule that comes with the test. Decisions are never to be signed by fatigue. Never quit at night. Sleep first, and let the morning cast the deciding vote, because the morning has never once agreed with midnight.

And remember the ledger this column opened months ago, the one about your forty seconds on the radio. In the grave, understand, you will finally receive every hour of rest you ever skipped, refunded in full, with interest, and eternity added. Death is scrupulously fair about rest. It repays all of it. What death never refunds, not one, is a chance. The naps come back. The openings do not.

One last widening of the lens, because you know this column never leaves the nation out. Belize itself is tired. Tired of blackouts, tired of prices, tired of the same arguments in new jerseys. Fine. A tired country is entitled to sigh. It is not entitled to resign. Everything on this year’s blueprint, the scorecards, the megawatts, the classrooms, the ledgers, waits on the far side of a nation that decides its exhaustion is a visitor and not an address.

So here is your Sunday arithmetic, Belize, whoever first did the math.

Tonight, you will be tired for perhaps eight hours.

You will be dead for the rest of eternity, and eternity keeps no office hours and grants no appeals.

The tomb has already reserved your eternal rest, fully paid, no booking required.

Until it calls, there is light left, and work worth doing in it.

Sleep well tonight.

Rise anyway tomorrow.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.
