World.title: Ten bags of suspected cocaine lead to intent to supply charge in Orange Walk
World.content:
Ten bags of suspected cocaine lead to intent to supply charge in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 39 year old construction worker of Staines Alley has been charged with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply following a foot patrol in Orange Walk Town.

Police say the Quick Response Team was on foot patrol along Staines Alley around 4pm on Friday when officers noticed a man exiting a well known drug base.

An officer approached, identified himself and informed the man that a search would be conducted for illegal drugs, firearms or ammunition.

During the search, the officer observed that the man was holding something in his right hand. When instructed to show what he had, he produced a transparent bag containing several small blue and transparent ziplock bags holding a white powdery substance.

He was placed under arrest, cautioned and escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

The bags were counted and weighed in his presence. Ten ziplock bags were recorded with a gross weight of 3.61 grams of suspected cocaine.

Hilton Lopez was charged with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply. He chose to remain silent.

World.title: 10 subjects we think Jamaican schools must add
World.content:
The curriculum in Jamaica is filled with helpful subjects curated to help young people not only navigate their prospective careers, but also become well-rounded citizens. However, there is always room for improvement. With the 2026/2027 academic year about to start, Observer Online has compiled a list of 10 subjects we believe should be added to the educational experience in the country.

Civics

This one needs to make a widespread reappearance on the curriculum. Students should understand how Jamaica’s Government works, their rights and responsibilities as citizens, how elections work and the importance of participating in civic life. While some aspects of this may be covered in subjects like Social Studies and History we are seeing many Jamaican adults who are unaware of the systems that govern them and how they play a part in it.

Sign Language

Learning sign language would help to create a more inclusive society. Introducing it in schools could allow students to communicate with members of the deaf community while making inclusion a normal part of everyday life. The reality is that just like we learn other languages to communicate with foreigners we should know how to communicate with those who are deaf and live amongst us.

African History

Jamaican students learn about aspects of African history, but there is room for a deeper exploration of the continent and its contribution to world history. A stronger focus could help students better understand Jamaica’s African heritage, culture and identity. As Marcus Garvey said “A people without knowledge of their past history, origin and culture is like a tree without roots.”

Financial Literacy

Knowing how to manage money is a life skill. Students should be taught budgeting, saving, investing, credit, taxes, loans and responsible spending before they enter adulthood. Understanding money early could help young people make better financial decisions later in life. Whether they go on to become employees or employers this will be beneficial in the long run.

Sexual Health

Young people need accurate, age-appropriate information about their bodies, relationships, consent, contraception, sexually transmitted infections and reproductive health. A comprehensive sexual health subject could help students make informed and responsible decisions. This ultimately will benefit us as a country that has seen rising numbers of sexually transmitted diseases over the past few years. Far too many adults know very little to nothing about how to effectively use contraception, the warning signs that they have contracted a sexually transmitted disease and how to take care of their private areas. This is an essential life skill.

Swimming

Some schools offer swimming lessons in Physical Education class but too many local students go through the system without learning this skill. We believe that swimming is more than a recreational activity; in fact, it is a lifesaving skill. With Jamaica being an island surrounded by water, basic swimming and water-safety lessons could equip students with skills that may one day save their lives or someone else’s.

Driving

We are aware that some sixth form programmes offer driving lessons and instructions but this one should be compulsory because whether students start driving early or not they will always benefit from being aware of basic road code. Lessons could cover road signs, the rules of the road, responsible driving, pedestrian safety, the dangers of speeding and driving under the influence. In a day and age where we see so much recklessness on the road and road fatalities this would benefit all Jamaicans who traverse the roads.

Mind Matters

Students should be given the tools to understand their emotions, manage stress, recognise when they or someone else may need support and know where to seek help. Making mental health education part of the curriculum could also help reduce stigma around asking for assistance. This is especially necessary where we see more of our youths resorting to violence as a way to solve their disputes.

First Aid and Emergency Response

Every student should have basic knowledge of what to do when someone is injured or experiencing an emergency. First-aid training could cover CPR, bleeding, burns, choking and other common emergencies, giving young people practical skills that can be used inside and outside the classroom.

Entrepreneurship (mandatory)

Many schools have subjects like Principle of Accounts, Principle of Business and some do delve into how to operate a business but we believe that it should be compulsory that our students know how to create a livelihood for themselves. Students should learn how to turn ideas into opportunities. Entrepreneurship education could cover starting and managing a small business, marketing, customer service, innovation and basic business planning giving young people practical skills whether they eventually become business owners or employees.

World.title: Top class!
World.content:
Highly rated United States teacher recruitment agency is stepping up its search for Jamaican educators, citing their strong classroom management skills, curriculum knowledge, and positive energy as qualities that set them apart from their peers.

A J-1 designated teacher sponsor recognised by the United States Department of State in Washington, DC, the Foreign Academic & Cultural Exchange Services (FACES) recruits educators from around the world and places them in classrooms in South Carolina for periods ranging from three to five years under a cultural exchange programme.

The programme allows participants to bring their professional expertise, academic qualifications, and cultural experiences into American classrooms, while exposing students to the traditions and practices of other countries.

At the same time, teachers gain certifications, professional development, and skills that they can take back to their home countries when they return at the end of the allotted period.

FACES has recruited more than 2,000 teachers over its 27 years of operation. However, Aleksandra Patrascu, communication director at the agency, said Jamaican educators have distinguished themselves and are frequently sought after by schools participating in the programme.

“We’ve found great success with Jamaican teachers due to the great English that they speak. For them, there’s not a lot of language barrier when they get to South Carolina, as opposed to teachers from other parts of the world where the language might be a little bit strange. Jamaican teachers are strongly trained in the curriculum… We’ve had a lot of very successful English teachers from Jamaica,” said Patrascu.

“They are trained in the British curriculum, which is something that was very popular here in South Carolina and that schools loved a lot,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“Jamaican teachers have very strong classroom management. I’ve had the honour to observe Jamaican teachers in their elementary school classroom and in their Spanish classroom, and you can see that there was a presence in that classroom… I know how hard it can be to be in a classroom with 30 students that you’re trying to mould and model, and Jamaican teachers have done a tremendous job in doing that,” Patrascu

added.

In addition to the Jamaicans’ skills training, she said the island’s proximity to the United States is a bonus because it is easier for the educators to travel home for special events and celebrations to see their family. She added that Jamaicans are also familiar with American culture, making it easier for them to adapt and face less culture shock.

Above all, Patrascu said the positive attitude of Jamaicans is contagious.

“I think it’s something in the air in Jamaica because our Jamaican teachers are very happy. They’re very positive people… They have sunshine in their heart. They’re just happy people. We see that with a lot of the teachers that come from the Caribbean, and we joke that it’s just the sun in the island and the sea air that make people just be a happy individual. They’re happy to be in the classroom, they’re happy with their career, and they’re proud of their career. We’ve experienced nothing but success with Jamaican teachers in our programme,” she told the Sunday Observer.

According to Patrascu, FACES recruited 12 Jamaican teachers this year, while approximately 60 Jamaican educators have participated in the programme over the past 27 years, with some returning to the United States for more than one exchange period.

With continued demand for educators, she said FACES is hoping to recruit even more Jamaican teachers to participate in the programme in a wide range of areas, including elementary education, English, Spanish, physical education, special education, and science.

She boasted that many Jamaican educators have been recognised for their success on the programme, walking away with awards for teacher of the week, month, and year.

Among them is Jermaine Howell, who taught grade five at Golden Spring Primary in St Andrew before joining the programme. He was named teacher of the year at Cedar Fork Elementary School in Morrisville, North Carolina. Camilla Walsh-Reynolds, a Spanish Town educator with 26 years’ experience and a background as a school principal, also serves as international teacher lead at JW Coon Elementary in Cumberland County.

Additionally, Tamar Blair-Robinson, a May Pen, Clarendon native, was honoured as teacher of the month, international teacher of the year, and adviser of the month at Lillington Shawtown Elementary School.

“For an international teacher to be honoured or to be recognised as teacher of the year at their school, that means they did something to stand out from all of the other American and international teachers in that school, and that is huge,” said Patrascu in congratulating the educators.

“That’s why if there’s a chance that we see Jamaican teachers apply, we get super excited and super giddy because we know that there’s other sponsors recruiting from the island and there’s only so many teachers in Jamaica, but they know our programme, they trust us, and we welcome them,” she told the Sunday Observer.

She invited interested individuals to visit the agency’s website facesinc.org to apply to the programme, noting that the application process is free. Once applications are received, an interview will be conducted to assess the educators’ goals and reason for joining the programme. Individuals are also screened, after which their teaching profile will be posted on the company’s website for school districts to assess and select their desired candidate.

Patrascu said FACES covers the air fare for successful candidates, providing them with assistance to secure housing, transportation, and a cellphone with a monthly plan. She stresses that international teachers receive the same benefits as local teachers and are compensated on the same scale.

World.title: Let’s do more business
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WITH Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago appearing to have moved beyond the trade tensions that once strained their commercial relationship, the twin island republic’s High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix wants to build on that progress by creating stronger business connections, encouraging investment, and opening up more opportunities for companies to enter each other’s markets.

Thomas-Felix said, as Trinidad and Tobago’s high commissioner to Jamaica, her role is to identify opportunities on both sides and bring businesses and other stakeholders together, with the aim of turning both states’ improving relationship into greater commercial activity.

“One of the things I want is to — and I spoke to your Government about it — I want us to have more trade missions. We have a very strong relationship and I want to continue strengthening that relationship, not only in trade and culture and everything, [but] the mark that I leave should be a mark of strengthening and building the relationship that we have,” she said while speaking during a Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters.

Her comments come against a history of difficult trade relations between the two Caribbean countries, including complaints from Jamaican exporters about access to the Trinidad and Tobago market and a significant imbalance in merchandise trade. The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in August 2022 establishing a Trade Complaints Mechanism intended to provide a channel for resolving trade-related problems.

More recently, however, both sides have been emphasising deeper commercial ties. In July 2025, Trinidad and Tobago’s Government said increasing private sector links between the countries were helping to strengthen bilateral and intra-regional trade, while officials committed to further deepening the partnership.

Thomas-Felix said the shift is reflected in Jamaica’s growing presence in the Trinidad and Tobago market. Figures provided to her, she said, showed a substantial increase in Jamaica’s reach between 2019 and 2025.

“From 2019 — the figures from 2019 to 2025 — it seemed to show a 170 per cent increase, particularly in 2025 in terms of Jamaica’s reach into the market. So I would say that some of the issues before would not be issues now,” she said.

The diplomat said Jamaica’s changing economic profile also creates room for the relationship to evolve beyond the traditional movement of manufactured goods.

Thomas-Felix also acknowledged Jamaica’s growing strength in financial and professional services, digital and technology services, and tourism, which she noted is earning the country greater recognition in Trinidad and Tobago and other international markets.

Therefore, she wants greater emphasis placed on helping businesses identify where their strengths can complement those of companies in other countries.

“So not only in Jamaica, throughout the Caribbean and parts of the world, we supply and export manufacturing and energy products…I think that is why there would be an imbalance because, over the years, Trinidad has significantly had a very large manufacturing and energy sector,” she said.

Rather than treating the imbalance as a problem that leaves one country winning and the other losing, Thomas-Felix said both countries should be looking at how they can expand their economic footprint together.

“I don’t think we should ever look at it as one having more and one having less, but how do we help each other to be out there and be large or big in trade. And that’s the way I look at it,” she added.

The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge. Thomas-Felix said Jamaica exported approximately US$36.6 million in merchandise to Trinidad and Tobago in 2024, compared with about US$249.7 million in merchandise flowing in the opposite direction.

But she also pointed to Jamaica’s strength in services, saying the country exported approximately US$5.6 billion in services globally, against imports of about US$3.46 billion, giving it a services trade surplus of roughly US$1.8 billion. She said that strength should form part of the conversation about how Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago can expand their commercial relationship.

That approach is already being reflected in trade missions. A Trinidad and Tobago Manufacturers’ Association trade mission to Jamaica in May 2025 was aimed at expanding market opportunities and identifying investment prospects, with the association describing Jamaica as a significant market for Trinidadian products while also encouraging Jamaican manufacturers to target the Trinidad and Tobago market.

A Jamaican trade mission to Trinidad and Tobago in September 2024 was similarly described as a step towards deepening economic ties by officials there who highlighted opportunities in food, beverages, manufacturing, and investment.

However, Thomas-Felix wants to create relationships that continue after the missions end by putting entrepreneurs, investors, and private sector organisations in contact with one another.

She also wants, when her tenure ends, to leave the bilateral relationship stronger than she found it, with trade forming only one part of a wider network of links between the two countries.

She noted that the relationship cannot be measured solely by government agreements or trade figures. Trinidadians have established lives and careers in Jamaica, while Jamaicans have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago, creating links that run through families, workplaces, education, and culture.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds and to make sure that if I can spot connections, opportunities, et cetera, that I share it with people in Trinidad and Tobago, because I’m here to advance the interests of Trinidad and Tobago and also share it to the people in Jamaica,” she said.

World.title: More than beauty: Lu Sierra says Jamaican models bring their ‘hunger’ to international markets
World.content:
Lu Sierra.

There is no shortage of beautiful women in the world. But after decades spent strutting across international runways and preparing beauty queens for some of pageantry’s biggest stages, former model and renowned runway coach Lu Sierra believes Jamaican women possess something beauty alone cannot provide — hunger.

For Sierra, who was recently in the island as an international headliner for the inaugural Jamaica Beauty, Fashion & Wellness Week at AC Hotel Kingston, that hunger may very well be Jamaica’s secret weapon.

“The cheekbones, the jawlines and, most importantly, the hunger. I’m telling you right now that in this business, you’ve got to be hungry,” she said. “Modelling is not just something you show up to and say, ‘I thought I could do this because I’m tall.’ Your women come with a sense of ‘I’m hungry’,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“They want it, and they get that from a generational kind of thing that if you want something, you’ve got to work for it. It won’t be handed to you. Your ladies come knowing that they’ve got to show up, look good, network, and ask questions. They come with a hunger as well as beauty.”

It is high praise from a woman whose career has afforded her a front-row seat to the international fashion and pageant industries.

Known as Runway Lu, Sierra has modelled for the likes of Bill Blass, Escada, Byron Lars, Bob Mackie, B Michael, Cesar Galindo, and Yves Saint Laurent. She has also worked as a muse fit model for fashion houses and designers including Oscar de la Renta, Givenchy, and Patrick Kelly.

Her career eventually expanded beyond walking the runway to teaching other women how to command it. Named Best Coach by the Global Beauty Awards, Sierra has become a runway expert, confidence mentor, and pageant coach whose work has extended to both the Miss USA and Miss Universe competitions.

It is against that international backdrop that Sierra has developed an appreciation for what Jamaican models bring to the table.

“Let’s face it, there are beautiful women everywhere in the world — Ukraine, Russia, Brazil — but Jamaica gives us some beautiful women who are hungry,” she said.

Long before becoming the coach helping other women navigate rejection, Sierra had to manoeuvre her own struggles. She recalled arriving in New York only to have modelling agents repeatedly point out the things they believed she needed to change.

“When I moved to New York, every agent rejected me. They told me, ‘Clear up your skin, lose weight, fix your teeth,’ and all that stuff,” she recalled.

Those experiences helped shape a philosophy she now passes on to the women she mentors: Rejection does not necessarily mean someone does not belong in the industry.

“You have to love what you do,” Sierra stressed. “There has to be something in you that says rejection doesn’t bother me and the word ‘no’ is not an option.”

Sierra’s own experience with rejection has also informed the way she defines beauty. There isn’t, she insists, a single formula as beauty is indeed in the eyes of the beholder.

“In one day I was told I was too skinny, too tall by one designer, not tall enough by another, too black by one designer, and too Puerto Rican by the other. Too pretty by one client and not pretty enough by the other,” she recalled.

For each client, she explained, their assessment was based on what they needed at that particular moment rather than an objective measure of her beauty or worth.

“There is no one thing. As I always tell girls, don’t get upset if they don’t want you, just find someone that does. Get up every day and do that. But that takes a special mentality to get up after rejection and say, ‘Today is a new day, and I’m going in,’ instead of starting to self-medicate.”

Sierra jetted off the island following the conclusion of the Miss Universe Jamaica pageant on Sunday, but not before dropping a few pointers on how pageant organisers can nab a few more titles internationally. For Sierra, the question isn’t whether Jamaica has women capable of competing with the world’s best, it’s a matter of support from the entire industry, especially local designers.

“Jamaica sends us some of the most beautiful women there is, and body — oh Lord!” she exclaimed. “I personally think it’s wardrobe and practising interviews more.”

After getting a first-hand look at local creativity during Jamaica Beauty, Fashion & Wellness Week, Sierra issued a direct challenge to Jamaican designers: Become more involved in outfitting the country’s representatives for the international stage.

“I’m looking forward to seeing what your local designers have to offer the world, and so I hope Jamaica makes this into something that can grow because Miss Jamaica Universe needs some of you designers to dress her,” she said. “When we go to Universe, the girls are dressed to the T. Some of the countries give these girls an outfit to wear. They walk into rehearsals and we’re like, ‘Oh my God!’ They have hand-painted boots, floral jackets that have been painted and things like that.”

“So I’m challenging the Jamaican designers to step up and have Miss Jamaica Universe go there and rock with her own countrymen’s outfit,” she continued.

But Sierra believes clothes are only part of the equation. If Jamaica wants to add more international crowns to its pageant résumé, she believes contestants must also become more comfortable with selling themselves when it matters.

“Your ladies come with a sweetness, kindness, and an island mentality that everyone is family,” she observed. You can be kind, but there has to be a certain sense of business with your answer.”

We teach our ladies in the island not to be boastful,” she continued. “But let me just say to the ladies, conceit is talking about yourself when no one asks. An interview is telling everyone the reason why you should win. It’s like a résumé. Please remember that. We need boss ladies.”

World.title: Not stealing Jamaican teachers
World.content:
Teacher recruitment agency Foreign Academic and Cultural Exchange Services allows participating teachers to stay up to five years on the cultural exchange programme before returning to their home country.

A United States teacher recruitment agency is making it known that, unlike its counterparts, it is not in the business of draining the Jamaican education system of its finest educators, even as the island struggles to keep teachers in its classrooms.

Foreign Academic and Cultural Exchange Services (FACES), a J-1 cultural exchange programme based in South Carolina, said instead its mission is to give the educators international exposure, new teaching techniques and technology-driven skills they can implement when they return to their home country after three to five years.

The agency’s position comes at a time when Jamaican schools are grappling with teacher shortages and migration, particularly in specialised subject areas.

Recent data from the Ministry of Education revealed that 1,185 teachers resigned between September 2024 and August 2025. The figures reflect a decline in teacher resignations compared to 1,517 the previous year. The staffing challenge mainly arises from global demand for teachers.

While some programmes create the opportunity for teachers to reside permanently in their host country, FACES Communication Director Alexandra Patrascu said it is not in the business of stealing teachers.

“We’ve heard of this interpretation, and we’ve heard of these types of programmes that, to be honest with you, they’re hurting us as sponsors as well. There are many ways that a teacher can stay here [in the United States] after the five years, but it’s not through our programme. Our cultural exchange programme that we sponsor clearly states that a teacher can stay up to five years, and they need to return for at least two years to their country and then they can come back for five years,” said Patrascu.

“There are other programmes that sponsor more pathways towards being a citizen and being here permanently. Those programmes hurt our programme, because the whole purpose of the cultural exchange is not there anymore if somebody’s coming here to stay. Our programme, our J-1 programme, the goal behind it is to bring back the teachers in Jamaica with the US experience, with more technology experience, and with a global teaching experience. The goal is not to steal teachers from Jamaica. We want, and we demand that our Jamaican teachers return to their country because if they don’t, they’re hurting our programme,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Patrascu said since its establishment in 1987, the agency has recruited more than 2,000 educators from across the globe. Of that number, approximately 60 teachers have been from Jamaica. She said the agency particularly loves to work with Jamaican teachers because of their ability to control a classroom, their knowledge of the curriculum and their positive spirits, but more than anything, they want the educators to go back and apply what they learned in the local education system.

She pointed to a Jamaican Spanish teacher who did just that, as proof that the programme is effective in building the local education system.

“I had this amazing Spanish teacher join our programme that I was training, and she went back to Jamaica, and now she works in her school. I keep in touch with her from now and then, and she keeps on saying, ‘I can’t believe how much I’ve learned from the programme in the United States. I was able to make my classroom so much better when I returned due to the things that I’ve learned in South Carolina.’ That makes my heart very proud,” said Patrascu.

She added that she is grateful to every participant who came on the programme and applied what they learned in their local schools, stressing the need to protect and enrich education systems across the country.

“If they [educators] don’t go back, they hurt us, they hurt the Jamaican population, and they hurt the Jamaican Government. That’s not something that we want,” said Patrascu, urging educators to give back to their country.

World.title: LATTIMORE’S LEGACY
World.content:
Late former national footballer Keith Lattimore

Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has paid tribute to former national player, coach, and administrator Keith Lattimore, describing him as someone who remained deeply committed to football even in his later years.

Lattimore, who died at age 75 on Saturday, was a national player in the 1970s and went on to make significant contributions to the sport at the club and national levels.

“It’s always sad when you hear of the passing of a sports icon. I remember Lattimore well; in fact, the last time I saw him it was in the Spanish Town area, and we had a brief conversation and he told me that he’s trying to resuscitate a football club in a community where he lives, and even though he was getting on in years he still had the love, the passion, and the commitment to ensuring that young men get an opportunity to play football,” said Ricketts.

“So I am just deeply saddened at the passing of someone whom I would have known well and someone who would significantly have contributed to the sport of football, not just at the club level, but certainly at the national level,” Ricketts said.

“May his soul rest in peace as we sincerely offer our condolences to his family members and close friends,” he said.

Lattimore was one of the prominent footballers of his generation, alongside his brother Arthur Lattimore. He played for Liguanea FC, YMCA, FC Nascimento, and Electro Cap in St Thomas.

A talented striker, Lattimore was also known for his long throws, which fans likened to corners.

He later ventured into coaching and led Portmore Strikers to the Sherwin Williams Women’s Premier League title in 2002. He also played for RJR 720 Kickers, winning the Tourers Masters League.

Lattimore worked as a sports officer at the Institute of Sports (InSports) until his retirement, and was instrumental in the development of the Primary Schools Athletics Championships.

His career spanned playing, coaching, and administration, with his contribution to Jamaican sport extending well beyond the football field.

World.title: We Love House Jamaica
World.content:
Establishing shotDrazen Zigic

Another exciting chapter in Jamaica’s rich cultural legacy will be written with the launch of the island’s first international house music experience on October 17, 2026 at Pineapple Beach, Montego Bay. This landmark event will introduce an elegant new entertainment experience, bringing together internationally acclaimed DJs, discerning music lovers, and visitors from around the world for an unforgettable celebration beneath the Caribbean sky. Before the beats drop, the Style Observer explores the history of house music in Jamaica.

History of House

For decades, Jamaica has been synonymous with rhythm — reggae, ska, rocksteady and dancehall have carried the island’s musical identity far beyond its shores. Yet beneath the familiar basslines and riddims, another sound has been quietly developing, finding its own place within Jamaica’s extraordinary musical landscape. House music, born from the underground clubs of Chicago and New York and later embraced across Europe, has been present in Jamaica for decades. Its journey from subculture to an increasingly visible part of the island’s nightlife owes much to a generation of Jamaican DJs and promoters who were willing to look beyond the established sound while never losing touch with the instincts of a Jamaican dancefloor.

The roots of that movement reach back to the 1980s. Boyd James began DJing in 1984, while Alric Anglin started in 1988, both developing their craft within Kingston’s vibrant club culture. James’s formative years in New York exposed him to the city’s underground dance culture and legendary clubs such as the Tunnel and Palladium, while back home Mixmaster Marvin’s Upper Room Sessions were helping forward-thinking Jamaican DJs experiment with house, hip-hop and dancehall through cutting, scratching and blending. When Alric & Boyd joined forces in 1992, they brought a distinctly open-minded approach to the turntables. Their sets could move through house, techno, jungle, drum & bass and hip-hop without apology, while still responding to the energy of a Jamaican crowd. By the mid-1990s, their FAME FM programme, The Edge, was taking house, progressive house, jungle, techno and speed garage into Jamaican homes and introducing listeners to sounds then transforming dance floors in London and Ibiza.

Then came the parties. In 1996, Alric & Boyd staged what their biography describes as Jamaica’s first rave, the Hill House Jam, where approximately 500 people danced through the night until 10:00 am. What followed was a remarkable period of underground experimentation: Free after-hours sessions at Mingles, the Harry’s Bar event that introduced glowsticks to Jamaica, and the legendary Monday-night raves at Club Asylum. There, in a setting better known for Jamaica’s dominant dancehall culture, house music was given its own theatrical world of lasers, themes and immersive production. The response demonstrated something important: Jamaican youth were not abandoning their musical heritage; they were expanding it. The same instinct that draws Jamaicans to a powerful bassline, a hypnotic rhythm and the communal release of dancing could find expression in the four-on-the-floor pulse of house.

That openness is perhaps the secret to house music’s growing appeal among Jamaica’s younger generation. House has always been unusually inclusive — less concerned with who you are, where you come from or what musical tribe you belong to than with what happens when the music takes over. Its deep bass, percussion, soulful vocals and emphasis on the collective dance floor have striking cultural overlaps with Jamaican music. Alric & Boyd’s own production history reflects this meeting of worlds, spanning reggae, dancehall, hip-hop and house, including collaborations with artistes such as Sly & Robbie, Jill Scott, Sean Paul and Beenie Man, alongside international electronic figures. Their philosophy has been to respect each genre in its true form while understanding the demands of the crowd.

That tradition is now being reinforced by a new generation of Jamaican house advocates. Charles Lazarus has emerged as an innovative and established force within Jamaica’s house music landscape, bringing his own creative identity and understanding of the local dance floor to a movement that continues to evolve. Alongside him, the international experience being brought back to Jamaica by Errol Rennalls adds another extraordinary dimension. Rennalls is co-founder of Peppermint Jam, one of the world’s leading house music imprints, and was formerly CEO of SPV, one of Europe’s leading independent music companies. His career includes co-writing 12 European Top 10 hits, as well as the worldwide hits Horny and Sexbomb, the latter famously recorded by the legendary Tom Jones. His involvement gives Jamaica’s emerging house scene a direct connection to the international music business, its networks, its history and its creative possibilities.

Mr Mike brings another layer of international credibility. His career stretches from the UK and Belgium to Switzerland and five continents, and includes platinum success in the Benelux, influential radio work, the We Love House movement and record labels including MAP Dance and Vertige Records. Booker T brings more than four decades of experience spanning reggae, rare groove, hip-hop, R&B and house, including his distinction as the first British producer signed to the legendary New York label Strictly Rhythm and a Grammy nomination for Best Remix. And Tony Humphries — the legendary KISS FM Mastermixer, Zanzibar resident and one of the defining figures in the development of soulful, eclectic house — represents a tradition in which musical boundaries were never meant to be rigid. His New York sound was famously built around the idea that everything could be intertwined.

The significance of this international connection should not be underestimated. House music has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to transform places into global cultural destinations. Ibiza is perhaps the most powerful example: Its rise as one of the world’s great music-tourism hubs is inseparable from the history of house and electronic music and the international crowds drawn to its clubs and DJs. Jamaica already possesses many of the ingredients that made Ibiza successful — a globally recognised musical identity, an instinctive relationship with rhythm, an extraordinary tourism industry and an international audience hungry for authentic cultural experiences.

What is happening now, therefore, is not simply the arrival of another imported musical genre. It is the continuation of a Jamaican tradition of taking outside influences, absorbing them, reshaping them and eventually making them part of the island’s own cultural vocabulary. From the pioneering work of Alric & Boyd to the creativity of Charles Lazarus, and from the international networks of Mr Mike, Booker T and Tony Humphries to the deep music-industry experience of Errol Rennalls, the foundations are being laid for something potentially much bigger. Jamaica’s house movement is creating a new space where generations, cultures and musical histories can meet — and where young Jamaicans can express themselves through dance without having to choose between their heritage and the wider world. The house is no longer underground. In Jamaica, its doors are opening.

We Love House Jamaica

Headlining this historic occasion is New York’s legendary Tony Humphries, widely recognised as one of the true architects and Godfathers of House Music. Joining him are internationally respected house music icons Booker T from London and Mr Mike from Switzerland. Proudly representing Jamaica will be Alrick & Boyd, Mix Master Marvin, Charles Lazarus and Jamaica-based Italian DJ Pietro, whose passion and artistry reflect the island’s rapidly growing appreciation for authentic house music and its place within the global dance music community.

More than a concert, this is a premium lifestyle experience where world-class music meets Jamaican elegance and hospitality. Guests will enjoy expertly crafted cocktails, exceptional cuisine, a sophisticated open-air setting, beautiful people, and an atmosphere defined by positive energy, connection, and the timeless rhythms of house music. As the genre continues to captivate audiences across Jamaica, this event celebrates the island’s openness to new cultural experiences while honoring its enduring reputation as one of the world’s great musical destinations. Already attracting visitors from Europe, North America, and across the Caribbean, with many having secured flights and accommodations well in advance, this inaugural event marks the beginning of what is envisioned as a prestigious annual series of international house music experiences.

Photos courtesy of We Love House, Thierry Galeuchet and Hakeem Hunter

World.title: Youth Praise to raise funds for community initiatives
World.content:
Gospel artiste Johnmark Wiggan (right) performs at last year’s staging of Youth Praise.

Gospel artistes Prince Saj, Orville Sutherland, Treze-Gaye Smith, Donielle Anderson, and youth ministers from Church of the United Missions (COTUM); Christian Fellowship World Outreach; Union Baptist Church from Pennsylvania, USA; and Waltham Park Road New Testament Church Of God are scheduled to perform at the fourth staging of Youth Praise on October 2.

The event, which seeks to raise funds for the COTUM Youth Ministry, will take place at the Waltham Park New Testament Church of God. According to organisers, it provides a safe and spiritually sound platform for young people to express their faith and talent as well as immerse themselves in worship irrespective of church affiliation.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer, Youth praise director and youth leader, Kay-Ann Swaby, spoke about the initiative and its growth since its first staging in 2023.

“COTUM Youth Ministry has been impacting many young lives, especially young males who are considered “at-risk” youths. We currently have a 17:4 male-to-female ratio and Youth Praise is our main fund-raiser to fund the youth initiatives and programmes to help impact these youths and help us to reach more young men. Through Youth Praise we offer full sponsorship to youths from different communities to attend Christian Youth Camps we have seen the impact: educational support — community youths now go to school five days per week instead of two or three days, scholarships and grants; social exposure — engaging them in spaces that cultivate good values and purpose-driven activities; sports programmes; youth development workshops. Our goal is to maintain an active presence and an influential voice that overshadows the negative influences in the lives of the youths,” Swaby explained.

She added, “We also use this initiative to share the gospel with the youths through the arts and music because Youth Praise is a youth-targeted event reaching youths from all over.”

Swaby states that the event has grown since its first staging three years ago.

“Our first event was well supported. At that time, it was our first youth concert in probably over two decades. The event was planned and executed in less than six weeks, no social media promotion — just word of mouth and a voice-over recording circulating to a few contacts — and we had over 400 people in attendance. The church was full to capacity, and we even had people standing outside. And now, entering our fourth consecutive staging, Youth Praise has grown on a significantly wider scale — from a local church initiative into a transformative community event. We have youth ministries reaching out to have their young people minister at Youth Praise; we also have gospel artistes requesting to be on the line-up. The trajectory has accelerated impressively,” Swaby disclosed.

“The high point over the period has been the energy each year, which is unmatched,” said Swaby. “Experiencing the youths channelling their energy into purpose and creativity as they honour the Lord with their talent/gift, worship together, and enjoy the presence of God whilst ministering and supporting each other. The realness of the artistes — over the years in the midst of their ministry they have shared their personal stories (testimonies), level and relate with the youths whilst encouraging them to stay with God or give their lives to Jesus Christ.”

DJ Tarik Pryce will provide recorded music prior to the performance of the gospel acts, and radio personality Ava-Gay Black Blair is the host.

Said Swaby, “You can expect to be richly blessed by the youths! Expect a euphoric evening of praise and worship from beginning to end. Be ready for the move of God; Expect prizes and surprises.”

World.title: Les think tanks musclent leur jeu en vue de 2027
World.content:
Qu’en sera-t-il pour le cru 2027, dans le contexte d’un débat champ médiatique et politique très polarisé ?

Bataille culturelle

Une chose est sûre : les laboratoires d’idées conservateurs ou d’extrême droite occupent une place grandissante. Le cercle Orion voit d’ailleurs dans la campagne l’occasion de “rouvrir la guerre des idées” dans son premier document, tout comme l’Institut de l’espérance “d’inspiration chrétienne”, fondé il y a un an par Vincent Bolloré, qui achève avec un peu de retard son manifeste pour le début de l’automne.

L’Observatoire de l’immigration et de la démographie, qui accumule les reprises dans les médias plutôt classés à droite, a préparé un projet de révision constitutionnelle. L’Institut Thomas-More, un franco-belge, a déjà dressé son inventaire des “50 décisions qui ont coulé la France” ces cinq dernières décennies. C’est aussi l’angle retenu par les nouveaux venus Hexagone ou Hémisphère droite, tous les deux de tendance conservatrice. Ces structures sont financées par Périclès, l’organe d’influence du milliardaire Pierre-Edouard Stérin, décrit comme une “pépinière d’initiatives métapolitiques” par son directeur général Arnaud Rérolle.

Face à la prégnance des thèmes imposés par le Rassemblement national et La France insoumise, la fabrique des idées se double donc d’une bataille culturelle. Mais les modérés ne sont pas en reste : ce printemps déjà, plusieurs think tanks se sont attelés à une rare tribune collective pour se dresser comme un “outil primordial de stabilité et de modération”, alors que le “débat public s’électrise de plus en plus”, nourri aussi par “les nouveaux diktats de la communication politique”. L’Institut Montaigne, l’Institut Terram, la Fabrique de l’Industrie ou encore la fondation Robert-Schuman étaient signataires.

Thierry Pech, qui dirige le progressiste Terra Nova, explique par exemple que des textes “de riposte” seront préparés sur les “propositions les plus contestables” du Rassemblement national, comme prochainement l’analyse des votes de leurs eurodéputés. Il aborde toutefois cette campagne inquiet : “La campagne va se dérouler dans un climat dégradé avec un contexte géopolitique assez stressant.” “Les producteurs d’idées sont soit tétanisés, soit à court d’idées ou totalement idéologisés dans une forme de radicalité”, déplore encore le libéral Dominique Reynié, qui entame sa quatrième campagne présidentielle à la tête de la Fondation pour l’innovation politique. Celle-ci creusera tout de même plusieurs sillons sur la fiscalité, l’énergie, la productivité ou l’éducation.

La floraison d’écrits qui s’annonce est aussi à l’image d’un paysage contrasté, à l’influence diffuse aussi, loin de l’assise des think tanks en Allemagne, au Royaume-Uni ou aux Etats-Unis où ces organisations sont plus installées et financées. Le risque : une multiplication de structures, toutes couleurs politiques confondues, à l’image de la fragmentation de l’offre politique. “Si vous avez des propositions et des chiffres dans tous les sens, vous ne retenez plus rien”, estime le cadre d’un labo d’idées qui a requis l’anonymat.

World.title: The Trump-shaped problems awaiting Andy Burnham, ranked
World.content:
Burnham has played down the jeopardy, but he also promised to “say what I feel.” He has the advantage of having seen his predecessor Keir Starmer try to please Trump, only to be hectored relentlessly on Truth Social. Like Italy’s Giorgia Meloni or Canada’s Mark Carney, Burnham may sense a political advantage in not kissing the ring.

A visit will still tie him up in diplomacy, however; tricky for a man who wants to keep his focus at home rather than engaging in the geopolitical wrangling for which voters gave Starmer little credit. It will also come days before his first Labour conference as leader, where some of his party faithful oppose oil and gas drilling and want him to take a harder line against Israeli settlements.

POLITICO runs through a few of the Trump-shaped headaches awaiting Burnham, informed by conversations with more than a dozen U.K. government political aides, civil servants and ministers who were all granted anonymity to speak frankly.

Oil and gas drilling

The U.K. is inching closer to a politically fraught decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in two of the North Sea’s last major untapped fields.

An oil rig is seen through the mist on the Cromarty Firth on the north-east coast of Scotland on April 24, 2026. | Andy Buchanan/AFP via Getty Images

The Jackdaw gas field received initial approval in 2022, while the Rosebank oil field was green-lit in 2023. Further consultation due to a legal tussle over their environmental impacts ended in mid-August and Whitehall and industry officials expect a final decision in September. Jackdaw operator Adura has claimed gas could start flowing from Oct. 1.

Burnham — who pledged to give voters “breathing space” on the cost of living, yet is watching unrest in the Middle East push up energy bills — has spent his summer dropping positive hints about the projects, painting North Sea drilling as a “bridge to a renewable future.” He indicated similarly to Trump, who has repeatedly urged Britain to get drilling.

World.title: How Greeks conquered the Brussels coffee bubble
World.content:
Before walking off with her iced sugar-free order, the customer falls into a back-and-forth with the staff. The chitchat has the polite familiarity of old friends bumping into each other while running errands on a Saturday afternoon. Heads preen toward the counter, as several French-speaking suits in the queue appear equal parts impatient and fascinated — perhaps even a bit jealous to not be part of the in-crowd.

I smile to myself, knowing the customer is at home — and so am I. Born and raised in Athens, I feel most comfortable at an establishment where the coffee is iced, the staff is warm and the pastries are savoury.

To Meli opened in 2019 in the heart of the mundane grid of concrete and power that connects the headquarters of the European Commission, Council and Parliament. Its name means “honey.”

An iced greek coffee, also known as freddo cappuccino. | iStock

Greek coffee houses have quietly conquered the Brussels bubble, offering a daily respite from the hustle and bustle of the corridors of power, beating local Belgian cafés, generic American chains and even the Italian barista masters on their turf.

Many of the cafés driving the Greek coffee coup — beyond To Meli, there’s Papillon, Caffeine and Cherry, to name the most popular ones — were born out of the debt crisis of the 2010s, when the country faced an economic collapse that saw unemployment top 27 percent.

The owners of To Meli originally moved to Belgium in 2013 in search of better opportunities before opening their first location six years later. Many of the staff members similarly arrived in Brussels during the crisis to find jobs. In typical Mediterranean fashion, many were spurred by family or friends who were already working in the cafés.

World.title: Germany is poised to enter one of its most dangerous moments yet
World.content:
The strategy clearly backfired. Siegmund’s allies bought up as many copies of the magazine as they could, so he could sign them in front of adoring crowds. But the underlying sentiment was not wrong — what happens in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 will affect all of Germany, Europe and the wider world.

Polling at 42 percent in Saxony-Anhalt, that the AfD will emerge as the strongest force in this regional election is now beyond doubt — that’s around double the support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU). The Left party, another insurgent group, comes in third in the polling, while Merz’s coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), barely sit above the 5-percent threshold originally intended to keep out extremists, and the Greens are hovering perilously around that limit.

Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), campaigns prior to state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on August 19, 2026 in Dessau-Rosslau. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

The arithmetic is convoluted but crucial. If the SPD and the Greens make the cut, the various mainstream parties could cobble together enough seats to run the state. But if they don’t, the AfD will be able to govern either on its own or possibly with the support of the far-left social conservative grouping Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht, which is also hovering right below the 5-percent threshold.

The latter outcome would precipitate a political crisis across Germany not seen in decades.

But it doesn’t end there. Two weeks after Saxony-Anhalt, voters will head to the polls in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and in the once reliably leftist city-region of Berlin, which is showing strong AfD support as well.

This means that in the coming weeks or months, Germany could be faced with a collapsing government and even an ousted or replaced Merz — a move with little precedent in recent German history. And stuck with its stuttering economy, the country that prizes stability above all else is preparing to panic.

World.title: Iceland’s parliament will ‘discuss’ withdrawing EU bid after failed referendum
World.content:
Frostadóttir reiterated, however, that the referendum outcome will be respected, that no further accession negotiations with the EU will be undertaken under the current government, and that EU accessions will likely be a theme in the next general election.

“It’s crucial right now that we take stock; we make a decision on what we do with … the application,” she said. The prime minister did not say when the matter would be put to parliament.

Iceland first started talks to join the EU in 2009, but those collapsed in 2013. Its membership application, however, was never formally withdrawn.

Frostadóttir said the result would not impact her role as prime minister because the referendum “was not a party political matter” — despite her support for restarting talks.

Eiríkur Bergmann, a professor of politics at Bifröst University in Iceland, called the vote a “heavy blow” for the government.

“The coalition will emerge significantly weakened domestically, having staked considerable political capital on securing a mandate to reopen these negotiations,” he said. “However, the government will probably still survive the loss.”

World.title: 6 issues that will shape Ursula von der Leyen’s legacy
World.content:
In the Commission’s Berlaymont HQ, von der Leyen and her team are feverishly working on her State of the EU speech, to be delivered on Sept. 16. It’s when she will set out her plan for the years to come. After that, she’ll have to deliver.

“Speeches are important. But it’s the actions that create legacy,” said Martin Hojsík, a vice president of the European Parliament from the Renew Europe group.

“Europe has become more vulnerable economically, competitiveness remains a major challenge, social and regional inequalities persist, and too often her Commission has reacted to crises rather than anticipated them,” said Victor Negrescu, a Parliament vice president from the Socialists and Democrats group. “I expect her to use this moment to defend her record, but also to explain how Europe can deliver more on growth, investment, social cohesion and strategic autonomy. For me, the real question is not how her legacy is presented, but what concrete results Europeans will see by the end of this mandate.”

Here are six potential headaches likely to define von der Leyen’s remaining time in office.

1. Reversing Europe’s decline

Will von der Leyen be able to stem the Continent’s economic decline … or oversee the death of its industrial heartlands?

It was von der Leyen who asked former Italian PM and European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi to draw up a report into the continent’s competitiveness. He was brutal in his assessment, saying that “without action, we will have to either compromise our welfare, our environment or our freedom.” He called on Europe to invest an additional €800 billion a year to drag itself out of a trough of low productivity and feeble growth that’s pushing it behind the U.S. and China in the international pecking order.
