World.title: Debrecen stabbing tragedy: 23-year-old man dies after being stabbed in the heart
World.content:
A 23-year-old man has died after being stabbed in the heart during an attack in Debrecen in the early hours of Saturday morning. According to eyewitness accounts cited by RTL Híradó, the two young men had confronted the alleged attacker after seeing him assaulting a woman in the street.

As previously reported, two young men were stabbed by a 64-year-old man on Múzeum Street in Debrecen at around 3 AM on 30 August. Police said the attack was preceded by a verbal altercation, after which the man pulled out a knife and stabbed both victims.

Both men were taken to hospital by paramedics. Police arrested the suspect approximately two hours after the incident.

Young man stabbed in the heart dies

The 23-year-old victim from Létavértes was stabbed in the heart and suffered life-threatening injuries. RTL Híradó has now reported that he died from his injuries despite efforts to save his life.

His 24-year-old friend was stabbed in the abdomen. He also suffered serious injuries but was able to reach a nearby tobacconist’s shop and ask for help. His condition is reportedly stable.

A third member of the group escaped the attack unharmed. According to the report, he tried to stop the bleeding from his friend’s chest wound with both hands while waiting for help to arrive.

The injured 23-year-old was still able to communicate at the scene, but paramedics were unable to save his life.

Young men allegedly confronted attacker over woman

RTL Híradó reported, citing eyewitnesses, that the incident began after the 64-year-old man allegedly assaulted a woman while shouting at her in the street.

The two young men reportedly approached him and told him to stop and leave the woman alone. The man allegedly then pulled out a knife and approached the two victims, who were sitting on a bench. The precise circumstances of the confrontation are still being investigated.

Police previously said that the 64-year-old suspect was arrested after officers searched the surrounding streets for approximately two hours. He was questioned as a suspect, taken into custody, and prosecutors were asked to order his detention.

The Hajdú-Bihar County Police Headquarters’ Criminal Directorate is investigating the case on suspicion of causing life-threatening bodily harm. Following the victim’s death, the legal classification of the alleged offence may now be subject to change.

World.title: 64-year-old man stabs two young men in Debrecen, Hungary – UPDATE: younger victim dies
World.content:
A 64-year-old man has been arrested after allegedly stabbing two young men during an altercation in Debrecen in the early hours of Saturday morning, Hungarian police said.

Stabbing in Debrecen

Two young men taken to hospital

Paramedics took the two injured men to hospital, while police officers began searching for the suspect based on a description provided by witnesses.

According to police, officers searched the surrounding streets and located the 64-year-old man approximately two hours after the incident. He was handcuffed and taken to police headquarters for questioning. Investigators subsequently questioned him as a suspect, placed him under arrest and initiated proceedings for his detention.

One victim suffered life-threatening injuries

Based on the information available so far, the man became involved in a verbal altercation with the two young men before allegedly pulling out a knife and stabbing both of them. Police later established that one of the victims, a 23-year-old man, suffered life-threatening injuries, while his 24-year-old friend sustained serious injuries.

The Hajdú-Bihar County Police Headquarters’ Criminal Directorate is investigating the Budapest resident on suspicion of causing life-threatening bodily harm. The investigation is ongoing, and further details about the circumstances leading up to the confrontation have not yet been released.

World.title: World’s most liveable cities ranking is out: here’s how Budapest performed
World.content:
Budapest has slipped four places in the latest Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) Global Liveability Index, ranking 36th out of 173 cities. While Copenhagen remains at the top, Asia is gaining ground and several Middle Eastern cities have suffered sharp falls amid worsening security conditions.

Copenhagen remains the world’s most liveable city

The overall picture of global liveability has not changed dramatically in 2026, but significant shifts are taking place beneath the surface. The EIU assessed 173 cities across 30 indicators, grouped into five broad categories: stability, healthcare, culture and environment, education and infrastructure. The resulting score is measured on a 100-point scale.

The average score this year was 76.1 points, unchanged from 2025.

However, individual categories moved in different directions. The average stability score fell by another 0.5 points, while culture and environment also deteriorated slightly. Healthcare, meanwhile, improved by an average of 0.7 points, with smaller gains also recorded in education and infrastructure.

At the top of the ranking, Copenhagen retained first place, followed by Vienna and Melbourne.

The top 10 remains dominated by cities in wealthy, developed countries, with Australia, Canada, Japan and Switzerland all represented.

Asia is catching up with Europe

Western Europe remains the strongest-performing region overall, but it has stopped extending its lead. The region’s average liveability score remained broadly unchanged, while Asian cities continued to improve. As a result, nine Asian cities and seven European cities now feature among the world’s 20 most liveable cities.

The EIU attributed some of the progress made by Chinese cities to improvements in healthcare indicators. New York also recorded a stronger stability score, helped by declining crime figures in recent years and a lower perceived risk of a major terrorist attack, Pénzcentrum writes.

If you missed it: Budapest lifts energy restrictions as normal operations return on 1 September

Budapest falls four places

Budapest ranked 36th out of 173 cities, with a liveability score of 91 points. That represents a four-place drop compared with last year, while the Hungarian capital’s overall score declined by one point.

Budapest was therefore among the cities experiencing one of the more noticeable falls in the ranking. Its four-place drop was the same as those recorded by Luxembourg, Portland, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Saipan, although their starting positions and scores differed considerably.

Despite the setback, 91 points remains a strong result.

Photo: Anadolu Agency

For comparison, Zurich scored 96 points and ranked fifth, while Auckland and Luxembourg both scored 95 points, placing 12th and 15th respectively. Athens, meanwhile, ranked 88th with 78 points, meaning Budapest’s absolute liveability score remains considerably higher than that of the Greek capital.

The ranking does not simply measure how enjoyable a city is to live in. It also considers its stability, healthcare and education systems, cultural and environmental conditions and the quality of its infrastructure.

Middle Eastern cities suffer major setbacks

The most dramatic deterioration in this year’s ranking was recorded in the Middle East. In previous years, stability scores had been particularly affected in Europe by the war in Ukraine, terrorist attacks and protests. In 2026, however, the focus shifted towards the Middle East.

According to the EIU, the war involving Iran that began in February, Israeli and US strikes on Iran and subsequent regional responses significantly damaged perceptions of security across the region. The 18 Middle Eastern and North African cities included in the index fell by more than three places on average.

Muscat experienced the sharpest decline, falling 14 places to 123rd, with a score of 68. Kuwait City dropped 12 places, Amman 11 and Manama 10. Doha fell seven places, while Tehran entered the 10 least liveable cities in the world.

For Budapest, the four-place fall is a setback, but the Hungarian capital remains firmly within the upper tier of the global rankings, despite losing ground compared with last year.

World.title: Cold front to sweep across Hungary as September begins: but summer is not over yet
World.content:
A cold front will reach Hungary on Monday, bringing a slight drop in temperatures as September begins. However, forecasters say genuinely autumnal weather is still some way off, while the country’s drought is unlikely to ease significantly.

Cold front arrives on Monday

Hungary will see a change in the weather on the final day of August, as a cold front reaches the country on Monday, 31 August, according to HungaroMet.

The front will bring somewhat fresher mornings in early September, but temperatures will remain relatively high. In the afternoons, temperatures could still approach 30°C in many parts of the country. So while the calendar is about to turn to autumn, the weather will not be making a dramatic seasonal switch just yet.

Rain may finally reach a wider area

The cold front could also bring the most widespread rainfall of the week. Current forecasts suggest that rain could fall in several parts of Hungary by Tuesday morning. However, HungaroMet warned that there remains considerable uncertainty in the forecasts, with some models still pointing towards a considerably drier scenario.

This means that although the front could provide some much-needed rainfall, it is unlikely to deliver a major breakthrough in the country’s persistent precipitation deficit.

Drought set to continue

HungaroMet’s weekly precipitation outlook indicates that the drought is unlikely to ease significantly during the coming week. The lack of rainfall has remained a major concern after an exceptionally hot and dry summer, and the start of meteorological autumn is not expected to bring a substantial change in conditions.

The coming days will therefore bring a combination of fresher mornings and relatively warm afternoons, rather than the sustained cool weather many people associate with September.

No real autumn just yet

For those already looking forward to autumn, there is still a little longer to wait. The cold front will lower temperatures by a few degrees, but HungaroMet says genuinely autumnal weather is not yet on the horizon.

Instead, September will begin with moderately warm conditions, while the rainfall situation is uncertain and the country’s drought could persist. In other words, summer may be taking a small step back, but it is certainly not ready to disappear just yet.

World.title: Tisza government takes back EUR 276 million in state assets as KEKVA system is dismantled
World.content:
The liquidation of Hungary’s public interest asset management foundations has been completed, with assets previously transferred to the foundations returning to the state. Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy says four foundations alone have returned around HUF 100 billion (EUR 276 million) in state assets to the budget.

HUF 100 billion returned to the state

The liquidation of Hungary’s public interest asset management foundations (KEKVAs) was completed at the end of August, meaning assets previously transferred to the foundations have now returned to state ownership.

Dávid Vitézy, Minister for Transport and Investment, said the process had been carried out over the past two months by liquidators appointed by the government. The ministries concerned will now take over the management of the assets and the functions previously performed by the foundations.

In the case of the Transport and Investment Ministry, four foundations were involved:

the Millenáris Scientific Cultural Foundation,

the Central European Foundation for the Preservation of Built Heritage,

the Hauszmann Foundation, and

the Central European Education Foundation.

According to Vitézy, taking over these four foundations has brought around HUF 100 billion worth of assets back under state control.

Government says public services will not suffer

Vitézy stressed that the restructuring would not negatively affect the day-to-day operation of the institutions or the services they provide. He argued that the new system would eliminate unnecessary positions while making the use of significant amounts of state property more transparent and subject to public oversight.

“There will be no public task or service whose quality will deteriorate under the new system,” Vitézy said, adding that numerous positions he described as unnecessary “pay-outs” had been eliminated.

The minister also portrayed the move as a major change in how public assets are managed, saying assets originating from public funds were now returning to the state.

KEKVA system was a long-running EU dispute

The foundations were originally established under the previous Fidesz government, but Vitézy has strongly criticised the system, arguing that it allowed state assets and public funds to be managed in an insufficiently transparent manner.

He claimed that the governing boards of the foundations were largely made up of Fidesz politicians and that the system was designed to keep control of the assets in the hands of people linked to the former governing party even after a possible change of government.

The KEKVA system has also been at the centre of a long-running dispute between Hungary and the European Commission. The Commission had criticised the presence of politicians on the foundations’ governing boards and their management of state assets, with reforms to the system becoming one of the conditions linked to the release of EU funding.

Vitézy argued that the previous government had refused to dismantle the system despite the consequences for Hungary’s access to EU funds.

He described the completion of the process as a major achievement for the new Tisza government, which took office earlier this year.

World.title: Romanian athletes make history at World Rowing Championships with three gold medals
World.content:
Romanian rowers Simona Radiş and Adriana Adam won their third gold medal over the weekend, becoming the first athletes in the history of the World Rowing Championships to win three gold medals at the same edition of the competition.

On Sunday, August 30, Romania’s mixed 8+1 boat secured the third gold medal for Romania at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam. The team consisted of Cristina Drugă, Amalia Chelaru, Adriana Adam, Florin Lehaci, Cosmin Iulian Pleşescu, Ciprian Tudosă, Ştefan Berariu, Simona Radiş and Victoria Petreanu.

The time recorded by the Romanian crew was 05:35.75. The British rowing team came in second, and the one from the United States in third.

During the same competition, Simona Radiş and Adriana Adam also won gold in the double sculls, as well as in the women's 8+1, alongside Cristina Drugă, Geanina Juncanariu, Ancuţa Bodnar, Maria Lehaci, Magdalena Rusu, Amalia Chelaru and Victoria Petreanu.

Romania finished the Championships in fourth in the medals ranking, behind the Netherlands, Germany, and the US.

Interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan congratulated the Romanian athletes for their achievement.

"The girls in Romania's 8+1 crew became world champions at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, setting a new record. Romania also won gold in the mixed 8+1 event, in the final race of the competition," the interim prime minister wrote on Facebook.

He pointed out that "behind these few extraordinary minutes are years of work, discipline, sacrifices and trust in one another, a true team, in which each one pulls for all the others."

World.title: Romania’s far-right AUR calls for faster route to early elections in case of political deadlock
World.content:
Romania’s far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) will promote in the coming period a draft amendment to the Constitution that would introduce clear deadlines for resolving government crises and “prevent the repetition of the situation” Romania is currently facing. The decision was made at a meeting of the National Leadership Council convened in Mehedinți County, according to Digi24.

Under the Romanian Constitution, an initiative to amend the Constitution can be launched by one-quarter of the lawmakers in either of the two chambers of Parliament. However, final approval by Parliament requires a two-thirds majority in each chamber and is followed by a public referendum.

“The Constitution must offer solutions when state institutions and representatives are no longer capable of producing them. Romania cannot remain for months with a dismissed Government, while the president calculates which prime minister suits him, what majority he can build and how he can avoid early elections,” the party’s statement reads.

Under the proposed amendments, the president would be compelled to make a second PM designation within a strict timetable, failing which he would lose his seat, while Parliament would be dissolved by default after two failed attempts to appoint a prime minister within 60 days of the first attempt. At present, the Constitution does not set mandatory deadlines for the president to designate PM candidates, and the dissolution of Parliament after two failed nomination votes depends on the president’s decision.

Romania has been without a full-fledged government since May 5. Parliament rejected a prime ministerial candidate, and 60 days have passed since that failed attempt, but president Nicușor Dan has not made another designation.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/George Calin)

World.title: Romania’s Liberal Party opts for reformist alliance’s PM candidate or early elections
World.content:
Romania’s interim prime minister and president of the Liberal Party (PNL), Ilie Bolojan, confirmed that his party will not vote for a government with Social Democratic Party (PSD) ministers and warned that if negotiations on a new government remain deadlocked, Romania may head towards early elections. However, he added that the odds of early elections are rather slim.

Speaking to Prima TV, Bolojan recalled that his party had already nominated MEP Siegfried Mureșan, backed by a reformist alliance of PNL, USR and UDMR, for the post of prime minister, and that no other option had been discussed since, G4media.ro reported.

Ilie Bolojan rejected the possibility of supporting a cabinet with Social Democratic ministers only to later join the opposition and support the government’s policies on a case-by-case basis. There is no guarantee that PSD will change the attitude it demonstrated during the negotiations on the Wage Law, he explained.

However, Bolojan said that the party’s position could be revisited after official consultations resume. President Nicușor Dan announced that such consultations would take place this week.

“When the consultations resume, we will clarify the position after a discussion with our PNL colleagues,” he added.

The PNL president said that there had been informal discussions recently, but that the negotiations had not produced a concrete formula for the future government.

He described the situation in recent weeks as one in which the parties had failed to reach an agreement on the composition of the government.

“But no formula was reached this summer,” Bolojan said.

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

World.title: Romanian president and Social Democrats reportedly resume attempts to build new ruling majority
World.content:
A new ruling-majority scenario with the Social Democratic Party (PSD) at its core is being promoted by the Presidency, according to sources familiar with the negotiations consulted by G4Media and Digi24. Most ministers would be appointed by PSD, except for the Foreign Affairs and Defence portfolios, which are claimed by president Nicușor Dan, while the prime minister would be a technocrat.

The planned calendar envisages the nomination during next weekend, followed by the vote in Parliament several days later.

The plan assumes the support of the Hungarian party UDMR, a dissident faction within the Liberal Party (PNL), and most representatives of the ethnic minorities, but also envisages support from a substantial number of lawmakers who have (or will) split from the far-right parties POT, SOS Romania, and AUR. The plan's weak point may be UDMR's reluctance to cohabit with far-right lawmakers, despite the party's declared commitment to contributing to a stable ruling majority through cooperation with any centrist party, including PSD.

The candidates for the post of prime minister are not new: the list includes President's adviser Eugen Tomac and interim Finance Minister Alexandru Nazare.

According to G4Media's calculations, the planned ruling majority (at least 233 MPs) would include the 127 MPs of PSD, the 31 MPs from UDMR, plus the 17 Liberal (PNL) MPs who supported the candidacy of former PM-designate Adrian Veștea. Based on the vote in Parliament on Adrian Veștea's cabinet - a project not much different from president Dan's current attempt - G4Media assumes that 15 of the 17 ethnic-minority MPs would also vote for the new majority. On these assumptions, the would-be majority would still need 44 votes to reach the 233-vote threshold. The caucus of former PSD president Victor Ponta could provide 18 votes without excessively diluting the centrist orientation of the majority. The remaining 26 votes would have to come from MPs who have split from SOS Romania, POT and other small far-right parties. Based on the political gesture of AUR MP Mohammad Murad, G4Media speculates that a faction of AUR could support the PSD-led majority.

Forming a fragile majority around PSD therefore emerges as a possible scenario, but only if UDMR and president Dan accept the compromise of relying on significant support from MPs with far-right views. Such MPs, representing various extremist orientations, would account for more than 10% of the ruling coalition and could demand a government portfolio.

Splitting a larger part of the PNL parliamentary group, either before or after the vote on the new government in Parliament, may be a follow-up plan aimed at addressing the concerns of various stakeholders - investors, the electorate and the European Commission - about including far-right MPs in the ruling coalition.

The odds of a major split within PNL may have increased as public support for acting PM and PNL president Ilie Bolojan appears to be dissipating, alongside a growing reformist fatigue amplified by the lack of results. Still, the magnitude of the PNL share needed by PSD to replace the far-right MPs is considerable.

The implications of a PSD-centred government for fiscal policy are moderately negative in the short term - Romania will not be downgraded or have EU funds frozen - and negative in the medium to long term, as the 2028 budget may deviate from the consolidation plan ahead of the elections.

Such a cabinet, particularly if headed by Alexandru Nazare, may keep fiscal consolidation broadly in line with the plans for 2027 even without a Wage Law in place. The payroll can be credibly capped through other means; the main role of the Wage Law is to ensure that the payroll envelope is shared equitably among employees. While it should be a key reform for the Romanian state and society, it may not be of primary importance for the investors as long as the fiscal consolidation is secured. We do not expect a Wage Law to be agreed and approved by the end of the year.

The Social Democrats understand the need to preserve financial flows from the EU and foreign investors, while inflation supports moderate nominal indexation of pensions and wages without generating significant fiscal slippage. Furthermore, the fiscal effort planned for 2027 is moderate under the Excessive Deficit Procedure plan.

The lack of reforms will, however, accumulate into a more significant problem in 2028, when PSD is likely to be inclined to boost expenditure ahead of the parliamentary elections expected in the autumn.

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

World.title: Romania cuts excise duty on diesel by 25% for two weeks
World.content:
The Finance Ministry in Romania announced that it will cut the excise duty on diesel by 25% for the following two-week period, under the dynamic excise regime introduced for situations when diesel prices rise above certain benchmarks. The new excise duty rate applies for the period September 1-15, after a 20% cut in the excise duty was in force during the second half of August.

Under the special regime, the excise duty is calculated every two weeks depending on international diesel quotations.

The new adjustment represents a decrease of RON 701 per 1,000 litres. Thus, between September 1 and 15, 2026, the effective excise duty level for standard diesel on the domestic market will be RON 2,103 per 1,000 litres.

“The mechanism provided for by Law no. 162/2026 operates gradually, depending on developments in the international market. In the context of the pressures of the last two weeks, the level of excise duty reduction on diesel has increased from 20% to 25%. It is a temporary and calibrated intervention, intended to reduce part of the fiscal pressure on the price, within the limits within which it can be absorbed by the market and transmitted further into the economy,” specified Alexandru Nazare, minister of finance, as reported by Economedia.ro.

The updated support level for the first half of September reflects recent market dynamics, with the variation in Platts diesel fuel (VPM) quotations of +45.65% and the variation in the standard average price (VM) of +25.45%.

The intervention aims to limit the chain-propagation effect of fuel costs, especially in the transport and logistics sector, with a direct impact on consumer-goods prices. The mechanism established by Law no. 162/2026 operates dynamically, through periodic reassessments every two weeks, the press release states.

“The Ministry of Finance will continuously monitor market indicators and will recalibrate the excise duty level depending on the evolution of international quotations and pump prices,” the Ministry of Finance concluded.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/George Calin)

World.title: EC confirms WWF CEE objected to works on Danube that would have helped Cernavodă NPP
World.content:
The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) in Central and Eastern Europe CEE filed an environmental complaint in June 2024, in the context of preparations for hydrotechnical development works on the Bala branch of the Danube. According to EC representatives, the complaint procedure is still open “until sufficient progress is made in addressing the concerns expressed,” according to Digi24.

The project challenged by WWF CEE would have secured the safe functioning of the Cernavodă nuclear power plant (NPP) during periods of lower water levels on the Danube. Former transport minister Sorin Grindeanu (PSD) previously blamed WWF CEE and Greenpeace for having blocked the project amid a controversy with current environment minister Diana Buzoianu (USR), who accused him of delaying the necessary works on the Danube.

At a press conference held on August 13, 2026, PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu, former minister of transport between 2020 and 2025, blamed two environmental organisations for blocking the Bala project.

“On September 5, 2024, that is, two years ago, a decision was published in the Official Gazette approving the implementation of these works. We had one billion euros in European funds allocated for this. Immediately, but immediately after the publication, the hassles began. There were two NGOs. One of them, Greenpeace, and the other, the World Wide Fund for Nature, denounced this project in court and simultaneously filed complaints with the European Commission,” Grindeanu declared.

According to him, the impact on the sturgeon habitat was the main reason cited by WWF representatives.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/Ovidiu Micsik)

World.title: Romania prolongs state of crisis in energy sector for another month
World.content:
The government of Romania approved the prolongation by one month, until September 30, 2026, of the energy crisis regime, given that the low level of the Danube has not yet improved sufficiently to allow the restart of at least one reactor at the Cernavodă nuclear power plant (NPP). Furthermore, the production forecast for wind and photovoltaic capacities indicates a lower contribution, while electricity consumption during peak hours is expected to be higher, according to a government note cited by Cursdeguvernare.ro.

Inter alia, the Russian military reportedly preparing a large-scale offensive against Ukrainian energy infrastructure may cause an energy crisis in a region that already faces scarce supply and relies on Ukraine as a supplier.

At the end of July, interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan announced that he had discussed with the deputy prime minister of Ukraine the possibility of supporting Romania with production from one of Ukraine’s nuclear power plants, Economedia.ro reported.

A few days later, Nuclearelectrica announced that it had begun purchasing electricity from Ukraine, through the company Energocom in the Republic of Moldova, to compensate for the production deficit caused by the shutdown of Unit 1 of the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant. At that time, Unit 2 had not yet been shut down.

“The extension is justified by the continued severe hydrological deficit on the Danube, the forecast of high temperatures and increased electricity consumption during peak hours, as well as the forecasted reduced production from wind and photovoltaic sources. At the same time, there is a risk of limiting import possibilities in the event of a possible regional energy crisis,” the government said in an official statement.

The government pointed out that restricting the consumption of large industrial consumers, one of the preventive measures under the special regime, will most likely not be applied, but it was established to ensure that the necessary levers are available under any scenario.

The measures provided for under the energy crisis regime include increasing the technological reserves of production units that can operate on alternative fuel, starting up groups in technical reserve, reducing or cancelling the available interconnection capacity and notified exchanges in the export direction. As a measure of last resort, the transmission system operator Transelectrica can restrict the consumption of some industrial consumers under a mechanism agreed in advance.

iulian@romania-insider.com

World.title: Moody’s warns failed Wage Law will result in a loss of EU funds and increase fiscal risks
World.content:
The political impasse that hindered the adoption of a Wage Law for the budgetary sector may complicate the drafting of a credible 2027 budget in line with the medium-term fiscal consolidation plan set under the Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP), which would significantly deteriorate the country’s credibility among foreign investors, according to Moody’s rating agency. Although the rating agency does not mention downgrade risk in its note, weaker political support for further deficit reduction was associated in its August 7 update with such risks.

“In our opinion, the failure to adopt the public sector payroll law is a signal that a political consensus in favour of implementing and maintaining a large fiscal effort, which structurally controls the growth of expenditures, may no longer exist, despite the very substantial reduction in the deficit that we expect to see this year,” according to Moody’s note cited by Profit.ro.

Moody’s on August 7 affirmed Romania’s Baa3 sovereign rating, the lowest in the investment-grade region, and maintained its negative outlook, warning that high implementation risks surrounding the country’s multi-year fiscal consolidation programme could lead to a downgrade if political support for further deficit reduction weakens. The rating agency now interprets the failure to adopt the Wage Law as a sign of weak political support for further deficit reduction - implicitly a first step towards a downgrade decision. We expect the formation of a new ruling majority may provide further insights about the political commitment to budgetary discipline.

Moody’s estimates that Romania’s deficit will significantly decrease in 2026, after exceeding expectations in 2025, to reach 5.8% of GDP, equivalent to a reduction of more than two percentage points in a single year, amid spending restrictions and the maintenance of revenues, despite difficult macroeconomic conditions.

“However, given the failure to adopt this law, it remains to be seen whether this progress is sustainable or whether fiscal consolidation will lose momentum in the current fragmented political environment,” the agency noted.

Because public-sector wages account for over 20% of total spending and are a significant source of upward pressure on expenditure, the likelihood that spending growth will remain under control from 2027 onwards has decreased, according to Moody’s.

Moreover, the political impasse that ultimately prevented the passage of this legislation will make it more difficult to control borrowing costs, which remain sensitive to fiscal and political developments.

“This is important because Romania’s interest burden is still rising. Our current baseline assumption is that interest on public debt will rise to 3.3% of GDP in 2028, up from 2.8% in 2025,” according to the rating agency.

iulian@romania-insider.com

World.title: Warsaw’s Political Fight with Kyiv Is Being Settled on Polish Streets
World.content:
Anti-Ukrainian card

In June, Polish-Ukrainian relations made international headlines after President Volodymyr Zelensky was stripped of Poland’s highest order, and returned it by post. But the hostility did not begin with a single political dispute.

Last year, BIRN documented how during Poland’s presidential race candidates across the political spectrum reached for the “anti-Ukrainian card”, pushing the boundaries of what is acceptable to say in public.

“The campaign was the real turning point, because that was when Ukrainians living in Poland – and, more broadly, Ukraine and support for it – became a domestic political issue,” says Iwaniuk.

It was much easier to blame “failing public services” on Ukrainian ‘privileges’ than to fix the system itself, she says: “Populists need an enemy, and after other groups, including the LGBTQ community, it became the Ukrainians’ turn – because there were enough of them to turn resentment into political capital.”

Ideas that had once largely been confined to the political right moved into the mainstream. After taking office, President Karol Nawrocki vetoed an extension of the Ukrainian assistance law, arguing that the 800+ child benefit should be reserved for Ukrainians working in Poland. Revised legislation tied access to some benefits more closely to employment and school attendance. In March, Poland also began winding down much of the exceptional system created after the invasion.

For Bartlomiej Pejo, an MP from the right-wing Confederation party, measures limiting exceptional treatment are not evidence of hostility but a correction to policies he believes privileged Ukrainians over other foreigners. “The Polish state should treat all foreigners equally, without granting special privileges,” he tells BIRN.

Pejo condemns attacks against Ukrainians but rejects the idea that Poland is experiencing an extraordinary wave of hostility. He argues that crimes by Ukrainian citizens against Poles receive less attention, and that Polish anger over Ukrainian attitudes to the massacres committed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA, during World War II is too readily dismissed as prejudice.

That historical dispute has become impossible to separate from the deterioration in relations.

The latest escalation began in May, when President Zelensky granted a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title of “Heroes of the UPA”. The UPA tis celebrated by many Ukrainians for fighting for Ukrainian independence during World War II, but its members were also responsible for wartime massacres of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia. Responding to Zelensky’s decision, President Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest state decoration in June, which Zelensky famously returned by courier.

By July, for the first time since this question was asked in polling, 52 per cent of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian refugees, against 42 per cent who supported it.

“In Poland, the feeling was roughly: ‘We helped them so much, we opened our homes to them, and in return they honour people responsible for the genocide of Poles’,” Dr Adamski explains. “In Ukraine, it was: ‘For four and a half years we’ve been fighting, suffering and, in doing so, defending Poland too from Russian aggression – and now they’re trying to tell us who we can and cannot regard as our national heroes.’

Russia has inevitably sought to amplify those tensions. An analysis by the Polish Institute of International Affairs found that between May 26 and July 13 the number of Polish-language social-media posts containing extreme anti-Ukrainian hate speech rose by 171 per cent, while engagement with them increased by 345 per cent. Russian fingerprints were visible throughout the surge: VKontakte (VK), Russia’s largest social network, was the most prominent forum, while coordinated pro-Kremlin networks such as Operation Pravda also featured prominently. The institute concluded that, while Moscow did not create the crisis, Russia has become its main beneficiary.

The deeper problem, Adamski argues, is cumulative. Older prejudices met Russian disinformation, social media and a coarsening political debate, while journalists and intellectuals lost some of their traditional role as gatekeepers. Resentments that might once have been moderated increasingly reach voters directly – and can be rewarded politically.

But carelessness has not been one-sided.

History itself is understood very differently in the two societies. Growing up in Kyiv, Iwaniuk says she was barely taught about Volhynia: “Poles are immersed in history. They talk about history in magazines, on television, at the dinner table.” In Soviet and post-Soviet Ukraine, by contrast, people were taught not to ask too many questions about the past. She remembers asking her father about the UPA and Volhynia when she was still a schoolgirl. He answered: “I don’t know – I think they were the ones who fought against everyone.”

That gap, she argues, helped produce remarkably hapless political gestures. For example, the former Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko knelt at a memorial to Polish victims of Volhynia a day after Kyiv renamed Moscow Avenue after UPA leader Stepan Bandera; Ukraine’s parliament recognised UPA members as independence fighters on the same day that former Polish president Bronislaw Komorowski was visiting Kyiv.

“President Zelensky certainly knew that Poland had a different view of the UPA than Ukraine, but I doubt the decision to name one of the units after the ‘Heroes of the UPA’ was meant as a deliberate provocation,” Adamski says. “My impression is that no one in Kyiv fully anticipated the fallout.”

There is also an economic asymmetry.

“Poland’s post-Communist transformation succeeded, while Ukraine is still fighting for survival as a state,” Iwanuk argues. “While Poles have the luxury of looking back and debating the past, for Ukrainians the reaction is often: ‘Are you kidding? You want to talk about this now, when we don’t even know if our country will exist?’”

That does not make anti-Ukrainian violence an inevitable or legitimate consequence. But it helps explain how a relationship built on extraordinary solidarity became politically combustible.

The distinction is visible in another paradox that Iwaniuk points to: Ukrainians are becoming more integrated into Polish society just as the imagined collective “Ukrainian” is becoming more threatening in political discourse.

“They are your neighbour, the father of your child’s classmate, a colleague, the woman working in the local shop, someone running a business down the street,” she says. Yet the abstract Ukrainian is increasingly portrayed as a criminal, competitor or security threat.

Vladimir Medvedev, a Belarusian-born Polish citizen who founded the Glos Migranta (The Migrant’s Voice) initiative this summer, encountered another consequence when organising a recent migrants’ rights demonstration: people with legal status worried about far-right activists, provocations and deportation. Even a German acquaintance of his, married to a Polish woman and fluent in Polish, had been told to “fuck off to Ukraine” after somebody heard his accent.

Both governments now appear to understand the danger. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk has publicly urged Warsaw and Kyiv to de-escalate, and recent bilateral talks have stressed the importance of “responsible communication” and a balanced tone in public debate.

On August 24, Warsaw hosted an event marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s declaration of independence at Castle Square, where blue and yellow flags flew next to the white and red ones.

But the political temperature does not fall on command. On August 14, a 14-year-old Ukrainian girl and her 12-year-old brother were allegedly abused and physically attacked near the railway station in Bydgoszcz after speaking Ukrainian. A woman was later charged with insulting them and violating their bodily integrity because of their nationality. She has denied the allegations.

World.title: Author Lea Ypi Explores Albanians’ Struggles for Dignity Under Communism
World.content:
Throughout her childhood, Lea Ypi knew her parents were “talking in secret”.

“My childhood was full of mysteries about my family,” she recalled.

Ypi, author of the acclaimed 2021 memoir Free: Coming of Age at the End of History and, more recently, Indignity: A Life Reimagined, was 11 when communism in Albania crumbled and only later came to learn of the suffering her grandparents endured under the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha.

“I grew up as a girl in a communist system, a child who believed in the truths of that system, while I understood that there was something in my family that was not exactly the way I saw it,” Ypi said in an interview with BIRN during a visit to Pristina as a guest lecturer at the annual International Seminar on Albanian Language, Literature, and Culture.

World.title: From Zvornik to Visegrad, Bosnian Serbs Keep Cult of Mladic Alive
World.content:
Hundreds of people marched through the streets of the eastern Bosnian city of Zvornik on Thursday night, clapping and chanting the name of the man convicted of some of the worst atrocities in Europe since World War II, glorifying his name as they paid tribute after his death in custody.

“Ratko Mladic!” they shouted in unison. “Ratko Mladic!”

In the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity, the cult of Mladic lives on. Significantly, many of the participants in the Zvornik march were young men who may not have even been born when the Bosnian Serb Army chief waged his bloody campaigns during the 1992-95 war.

“This is Zvornik, the city of the mass graves of my people,” Bosniak politician Camil Durakovic, vice president of Republika Srpska, wrote in a shocked reaction to the video footage.

World.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.

“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.

He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.

On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.

Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.

“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.

“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.

Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.

Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

World.title: Montenegro President Summons Security Council Over ‘Destabilisation Threats’
World.content:
President Jakov Milatovic’s office said on Friday that he has called the heads of the country’s security sector Defence and Security Council after allegations by Prime Minister Milojko Spajic that the country faces “hybrid threats” from two of its neighbours.

Spajic claimed that officials from at least two countries in the region are involved in coordinated activity aimed at destabilising Montenegro and undermining its path towards European Union membership.

Milatovic’s office said the security chiefs will be asked to provide precise information on Spajic’s allegations, as well as a comprehensive assessment of the country’s security situation.

Spajic said on Thursday that Montenegro had “serious operational security information” that threats would accompany the country’s expected progress in opening new EU negotiating chapters. Montenegro is currently seen as the frontrunner among Balkan states to become the next EU member.

“According to our information, such activities are aimed at destabilising Montenegro, with the expected support of certain political actors and part of the media scene in our country,” Spajic posted on X.

On Friday, Montenegrin newspaper Vijesti reported that Serbia and Albania are the two countries referred to by Spajic.

Vijesti quoted an unnamed source who said that some key players in the region were unhappy with Montenegro’s rapid progress toward European integration and wanted to slow it down.

Another anonymous source quoted by the newspaper claimed that a senior government official was vulnerable because of compromising information that could be used by foreign powers. The source suggested that the official’s political party might leave the ruling coalition as a result.

Milatovic’s office said that the president was concerned by the reports, and that “the public has the right to know which official this is”. But it added that serious security issues should not be used to score political points.

“Issues concerning the security and stability of the state must be addressed responsibly, based on facts and through the institutions of the system,” it said.

The warning did not stop some prominent figures connecting the security issue to responses to the death on Thursday of the Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic.

After parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic stated that he had sent condolences to the former general’s family, the head of Montenegro’s Islamic Community, Rifat Fejzic, asked if politicians who “mourn war criminals [are] in collusion with this hybrid war?”

Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha has rejected the suggestion that his country was part of any “destabilising scenario” in Montenegro. Posting on X, Hoxha insisted that the allegations could not “artificially create problems between our two countries”.

“Although no formal accusations have been articulated against Albania, I wish to state clearly and strongly that Albania is not, and cannot be, part of any destabilising scenario, whether in Montenegro – a neighbour, friend, partner, and NATO ally with whom we share the same EU membership goal – or anywhere else,” he wrote.

World.title: Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
World.content:
The question of who owns Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state property is a major point of dispute and an unresolved issue on the country’s path away from supervision by the Office of the High Representative and towards membership of the EU. Not surprising, perhaps, in a country where the core issue of sovereignty is contested.

Intractable though the issue may seem, might there be movement towards resolving it? Washington’s newly-discovered interest in energy, mining and infrastructure projects in the country is putting the spotlight on this issue. Now the question is whether Bosnia will solve the issue of state property on Washington’s terms or its own.

World.title: Mladic is Dead, and My Serb Grandfather Was Right About His Fate
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

“You will answer for this disgrace and make the entire Serbian people bear the blame,” my grandfather said, punctuating the sentence with a curse as he walked out of the house to calm himself down in the yard. On the television screen, Ratko Mladic was handing out sweets to children gathered in Srebrenica as cameras from the wartime Serb television station SRNA filmed him.

I could not quite understand what the problem was. I had just turned 15. I had grown up in a Serb family and a predominantly Serb community. Mladic was a hero and a liberator. A source of national pride. Fortunately, I had grown up with a grandfather for whom truth and facts mattered more than any other identity. Especially the national one.

At the beginning of the war, my grandfather was subject to military conscription. He did everything he could to avoid taking part in the aggression. We lived in the hills above Sarajevo, and every day and every night we watched shells falling on the city.

My grandfather kept repeating that they would be held to account. I did not give it much thought. Not until I turned 20, returned to Sarajevo, enrolled at the Media Plan School of Journalism and saw footage of Eduard Limonov, the Russian poet, and Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, firing a machine gun from Zlatiste, near Mount Trebevic. During pauses, they passed a bottle of rakija from hand to hand, sharing it with the soldiers and taking swigs.

World.title: Tribute Gatherings for Ratko Mladic Held Across Bosnia’s Republika Srpska
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik (C) attending a church service for Mladic in Banja Luka. Photo: SNSD/Facebook.

Crowds of Serbs gathered in towns and cities across Republika Srpska on Thursday evening to pay tribute to convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic after his death, with hundreds marching through Zvornik chanting his name and senior entity officials attending a memorial service in Banja Luka.

Mladic, the former commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, died on Thursday aged 84 at the UN Detention Centre in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The gatherings were attended by members of the public, war veterans and government officials, while some of the events featured open glorification of Mladic and his wartime role.

In Republika Srpska’s administrative centre, Banja Luka, Milorad Dodik, the president of the ruling Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, and Republika Srpska prime minister Savo Minic attended a memorial service at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, where they lit candles for Mladic.

The service was also attended by representatives of the entity authorities, veterans’ organisations and many members of the public.

Dodik said Mladic had and demonstrated “how to defend one’s people” in what he described as “an unstable, difficult period”.

“Some want this [Serb] people not to remember him, but people have feelings. You cannot ban them, you cannot erase feelings,” Dodik said.

Similar gatherings were held in Trebinje, Bijeljina, Prijedor, Srbac, East Ilidza and elsewhere. In Trebinje, former Bosnian Serb Army members, families of deceased soldiers and local officials lit candles in front of the town’s memorial room and monument to its defenders.

In Bijeljina, Bosnian Serb Army veterans, veterans’ organisations and members of the public gathered, while a memorial service was held in Prijedor.

The head of East Ilidza municipality, Marinko Bozovic, Banja Luka mayor Drasko Stanivukovic, Republika Srpska National Assembly MP Jelena Trivic and Bosnian Serb delegate to the House of Peoples of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina Zelimir Nes­kovic attended a memorial service for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic at the Monastery of St Nicholas on Mount Ozren.

In a social media post, Bozovic wrote of the convicted war criminal: “Eternal remembrance, General, and may you enter the Kingdom of Heaven.”

The memorial service was attended by a significant number of local residents, as well as Branko Blanusa, president of the opposition Serb Democratic Party.

The attendance of ruling party and opposition politicians marked a shared approach between them to commemorating Mladic, despite his convictions for wartime atrocities.

However, scenes from Zvornik in eastern Bosnia drew particular attention. Several hundred people, including a large number of young people, gathered and marched through the town chanting Mladic’s name. According to footage circulating online, participants also carried flags and symbols associated with the Army of Republika Srpska.

Republika Srpska vice president Camil Durakovic condemned the gathering, recalling that Zvornik was the site of mass persecution and killings of Bosniaks during the war.

“This is Zvornik – this is the town where Mladic’s dogs of war carried out his orders. This is the town of mass graves of my people. This is the town from which tens of thousands of Bosniaks were expelled,” Durakovic said.

He questioned whether state institutions existed that would respond to such scenes, warning that, in his words, this represented the “final stage of genocide”.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the public glorification of convicted war criminals is prohibited under the state-level Criminal Code, following amendments imposed in 2021 by then-High Representative Valentin Inzko after domestic authorities failed to adopt legislation addressing genocide denial and the glorification of war criminals.

Mladic was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2021 under a final verdict, as the UN war crimes court upheld his responsibility for genocide in Srebrenica, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, forcible transfer and terrorising civilians during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

World.title: Kucel – The Sandy Oasis Less Than an Hour from Zagreb
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – You’ll likely have never heard of it, but Kucel is a sandy oasis less than an hour from the heart of Zagreb, but it seems as if it couldn’t possibly be further away.

There’s a rather unknown touch of the tropics in a completely unexpected place not far from Zagreb, more specifically Lijevi Dubrovčak near Ivanić-Grad. Putni kofer writes that the beach is called Kucel Beach, and it’s worth discovering.

a surprise on the sava’s banks

Kucel Beach is nothing like a small accumulation of sand mixed with gravel. Instead, it’s an expansive stretch of shoreline made of the finest sand, which is quite a surprise compared to the gravel banks most are used to seeing. Almost perfect sand, together with the beautiful nature, are its main assets. The beauty of this beach also lies in its peace. You’re likely to have Kucel Beach entirely to yourself. Navigation will easily take you to this area, and it’s no more than an hour’s drive from Zagreb at most. There is no infrastructure on this beach, meaning that wild and natural is precisely what you’ll get. Nevertheless, various events are sometimes held on the beach. Kucel Beach isn’t an organised bathing area, nor is swimming actually intended on the beach. Because of the currents of the Sava, it’s safe only in the shallows, so it’s recommended only to dip your feet in and paddle. Dogs are also freely allowed on the beach.

an area for walks, bike rides and unwinding

Kucel Beach, if you don’t mind the sand, can indeed be an excellent option for a picnic and a starting point for exploring the rest of the area. In the latter case, it is enough simply to stay in the embrace of the Sava and follow its course. As you follow it you will notice that a number of places there have a left and a right version, depending on which bank of the Sava they are on. Lijevi Dubrovčak, home to the Posavina Corn Maze which we also visited that day, is just one such example. There is also Desni Dubrovčak.

The wider area is made for a relaxed road trip, cycling or walks. The region is peaceful, the fields are expansive, and although the road is quite narrow there is still room for two cars to pass. On one side of the fence there is often the steep bank of the Sava, hidden behind dense bushes and trees; on the other side it drops a few metres towards the fields. You can also “switch” sides of the Sava: you can cross the river by ferry or via the 160-metre-long bridge in Martinska Ves.

World.title: Martelovo Jezero: Meet The Strange Cave Deep Below a Town in Istria
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – Martelovo jezero lies inside a strange cave deep below a town in Istria. It is the name of an even stranger lake that lies inside it. Very strict rules apply if you want to pay it a visit…

Croatia’s main “event” is certainly the coast, but there are plenty of incredible lakes to enjoy up and down the country. From the world-famous Plitvice Lakes to the “colourful” ones near Imotski, they all share one thing regardless of their shapes, sizes and depths: supernatural beauty. Putni kofer writes that some of them hide from our view, forcing us to make a little effort and look deeper into the secrets of the earth. One such lake is found in the very heart of Istria and its administrative centre, the town of Pazin. Martelovo jezero, or Martel’s lake, is a real gem of the darkness.

pazin’s most striking feature

Martelovo jezero is located deep within the Pazin Cave. As one of Pazin’s most distinctive features, the cave dominates the town: Pazin’s buildings cluster above this abyss, which has been protected since 1964. The protected area covers the canyon and sinkhole of the little river Pazinčica, about 500 metres long and around 100 metres deep, as well as the 300-metre-long speleological object known as the Pazin Cave, in which this largest Istrian sinking river disappears. It is precisely this cave that is home to Martel’s Lake.

the cave is named after a frenchman

But let’s start from the beginning, from the very entrance to the cave. It is called Dante’s Vestibule and is a huge, rock-vaulted fissure more than 20 metres high and 30 to 50 metres wide. The fissure continues into the darkness in a south-westerly direction, first narrowing to a width of only 10 metres and then widening again. At a distance of 100 metres from the entrance begins an expansion that essentially grows into an 80-metre-long and about 20-metre-wide terminal hall. In it lies the siphon lake named Martel’s Lake. The lake is widest at the very end of the hall, where water swirling can sometimes be observed. On average it is 10 metres deep. The lake owes its name to the French speleologist Édouard-Alfred Martel, who at the end of the 19th century began exploring the Pazin Cave in cooperation with Wilhelm Putick, a forestry expert from Ljubljana. The two of them also made the first detailed plan of the cave, and it was Martel who recorded the greatest flood that has so far occurred in the cave: in 1896 the water in the cave rose to 30 metres below the walls of the Castle that stands above it. Major floods were also recorded in 1964 and 1993.

adventure deep below the surface…

Martelovo jezero itself is located in the “terminal” hall of the Pazin Cave, but it is not the only lake the cave hides. It is connected by a siphon to another lake. That second, smaller lake is called Mitar’s Lake and was discovered in 1975, when Pazin speleologist divers dove into the terminal siphon and discovered a 70-metre-long continuation of the sinkhole. The diver responsible for that discovery was Mitar Marinović, and the smaller lake bears his name. Although Martelovo jezero is at first glance hidden from view, it is still possible to enjoy the sight of it as part of a guided speleo-adventure lasting two and a half hours, with equipment provided. As part of it, visitors also get a small zipline with which they cross over to the gravel bank of the underground lake.

a descent into the bowels of the earth…

“Physically, what awaits you is a somewhat more demanding walk that is accessible to all healthy people. It is not accessible to children without parental supervision or to people with physical motor impairments. It is necessary to bring sturdy sports footwear and a change of clothes; light long sleeves are recommended because of the cooler interior (around 15°C). The minimum age for children is 8 years,” state the pages of the Tourist Board of Central Istria.

If you aren’t up for this adventurous option, the Pazin Cave can also be enjoyed in other ways. For example, on the large zipline above the canyon itself, at a height of about 100 metres. There is also the possibility of walking along an educational trail or simply enjoying the view of the Pazin Cave from the Vršić Bridge or from below the terrace of the Hotel Lovac. These two locations are considered the best viewpoints overlooking the Pazin Cave.

diving is exceptionally dangerous…

But let us return briefly, at the end, to an activity in the Pazin Cave that will truly remain beyond the reach of ordinary mortals, and that is diving, which is left to experts. And even for them it is demanding and dangerous.

“Diving in the Pazin Cave is one of the more demanding cave dives because of the poor visibility (only 0.5–1 metre), which makes orientation and exploration of new space difficult. In addition, large quantities of branches and tree trunks are packed into the lake in front of the siphon, and in the siphon itself they are jammed between the rocks. This has caused cave divers to get tangled in the branches as well as the safety line being pulled under tree trunks, which made the return from the siphon difficult in already poor visibility. On top of that, the rocks in the siphon are very smooth and compact, which prevented cave divers from attaching the safety line,” states, for example, a document on the subject of the Pazin Cave.

World.title: Serbian Influencer Detained in Split Over Chetnik Tattoos Faces Deportation
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – A Serbian so-called influencer has been arrested and detained in Split for publicly displaying his Chetnik tattoos and now faces deportation and a 5-year ban from entering Croatia.

Split police arrested a 31-year-old Serbian citizen who publicly displayed tattoos of Chetnik leaders Draža Mihailović and Momčilo Đujić, as well as a Chetnik emblem, on Žnjan and then posted the photo on Instagram. Index reports that the court ordered him held for 15 days, and after the misdemeanour proceedings are completed he will be expelled from Croatia and banned from entering the country for five years. According to earlier media reports, this is Serbian influencer Marko Stojković, who has around 90,000 followers on Instagram. Nacional reported that Stojković had been photographed in a hospitality establishment on Split’s Žnjan, where a large tattoo of Draža Mihailović was clearly visible.

multiple people reported the man

Police revealed that the incident occurred on Thursday around 18:15 on the outdoor terrace of a hospitality establishment on Šetalište Ivana Pavla II. They say the 31-year-old publicly displayed on visible parts of his body a tattoo of Draža Mihailović, a tattoo of Momčilo Đujić, and an emblem featuring a double-headed spread eagle, a skull and crossed swords. Next to the symbol were Cyrillic inscriptions reading “with faith in God” and “freedom or death”. Police note that such insignia was used by Chetnik forces. About ten minutes later the man posted the photograph taken at that location on his public Instagram profile. “The post caused unrest and outrage among the public in Croatia,” police stated, adding that they subsequently received multiple reports from distressed members of the public.

the police discovered him in a car in split

Police launched a criminal investigation and yesterday established his identity and location. Around 14:00 they found and arrested him in a vehicle in the Split area. The criminal investigation, police say, established a well-founded suspicion that by publicly displaying the tattoos he disturbed public order and peace and that, “with the aim of causing fear and creating a hostile and humiliating environment,” he violated dignity and caused public disturbance. Police are also charging him with a misdemeanour under the Law on Combating Discrimination. He was brought before the competent court today, and police requested a 30-day prison sentence and a fine of 2,000 euros. The court has so far ordered him held in custody for 15 days, while the verdict will be delivered later.

he will face a 5-year ban from croatia

Police announced that after the misdemeanour proceedings are completed he will be issued an expulsion order from Croatia and a five-year ban on entering the country. Measures were also taken against a 56-year-old Serbian citizen who was in his company. His stay in Croatia was cancelled under the Law on Foreigners. Police state that by participating in the activities he promoted behaviour which he “knew or must have known” was contrary to Croatian regulations and public order.

who were the people his tattoos are depicting?

Draža Mihailović was the organiser and commander of the Chetnik movement during the Second World War. The Croatian Encyclopaedia states that from the autumn of 1941 he openly collaborated with the Germans and their allies, and that his forces committed numerous crimes and carried out ethnic cleansing of the non-Serb population in the territories of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the war he was convicted as a war criminal, sentenced to death and executed by firing squad in 1946.

Momčilo Đujić was a Chetnik vojvoda from the Knin area and commander of Chetnik formations in Dalmatia. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon states that he collaborated with the Italian occupation authorities and, after Italy’s capitulation, with German forces. Units under his command committed numerous crimes against the Croatian population, as well as against Serbs who did not accept Chetnik ideology.

this isn’t the first such incident…

A similar case occurred back in 2004. Croatia at that time banned the entry of Serbian basketball player Milan Gurović, who had a tattoo of Draža Mihailović on his upper arm and did not intend to cover it during a Partizan vs Cibona match in Zagreb. The Ministry of the Interior explained at the time that publicly displaying such insignia expresses or incites hatred or violence on racial, national or religious grounds.

World.title: One of Largest Railway Accidents in Europe Happened in Zagreb 50 Years Ago Today
World.content:
August the 30th, 2026 – One of the largest railway accidents in all of Europe occurred in Zagreb 50 years ago today. It tragically ended the lives of 167 passengers.

Turning the clock back 50 years, to this day in 1974, one of the largest railway accidents in Europe occurred in Zagreb. As Index recalls, a train arriving at the station overturned, tragically killing 167 passengers. All nine passenger carriages overturned, and the cause of the accident was the train entering the station too quickly; it then derailed on a curve and overturned. The train, travelling from Athens to Dortmund, was called the Direct Orient. That August it was mainly carrying guest workers returning from their annual holiday to Germany.

167 people died from smoke inhalation or catastrophic injuries

HRT/Screenshot

One of them left his compartment just before the Zagreb station to light a cigarette with a colleague. Then the carriage suddenly began to sway, only to overturn a few seconds later. The carriage continued sliding across the ground, and soon screams could be heard from the compartments. When the carriage finally stopped, the trapped passengers began to suffocate from the smoke. The compartment doors could not be opened, so they smashed the windows to save themselves. Around forty passengers could not be identified because of their severe injuries and were buried together at Mirogoj cemetery. The rescue operation involved the police as well as the army, which quickly appeared at the scene of the accident.

exhausted workers were blamed for the tragedy

HRT/Screenshot

The accident was caused by the driver and his assistant. On the way from Vinkovci to Zagreb they stopped only in Slavonski Brod, so the journey did not involve many duties. Fatigue then overcame them and both fell asleep. They woke up only when they had already arrived in Zagreb, and by then they could no longer slow the train, which was racing at a little over 100 km/h, although trains normally slow to 50 km/h before the station. Later investigations revealed that the train could have derailed on the curve between Ludina and Novoselec, but they had been lucky then.

It was also established that the driver and his assistant had been working continuously for 45 hours at that moment. After this accident, working-time legislation was regulated, stipulating that such work could not be performed for more than 6 hours without a break. The driver was sentenced to 15 years in prison, and his assistant to eight. The Direct Orient tragedy remains the largest railway accident on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and today it is still among the five largest in Europe.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport No Longer Requires Liquid and Electronics Removal
World.content:
August the 30th, 2026 – Dubrovnik Airport no longer requires liquid and electronic removal from hand luggage, making the security process much more smooth.

Dubrovnik Airport has begun introducing a new generation of technology for the security screening of passengers and hand luggage. These are devices that enable a three-dimensional display of luggage contents and a simpler, faster passage through the security screening process. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the southernmost Croatian airport is currently the only one in the country using this advanced technology. The new security screening equipment includes six devices for screening hand luggage and six scanners for passenger security screening.

3d imaging

The first device is already in operation, and the remaining five will be installed by the beginning of December. Once all devices are installed, the entire passenger and hand luggage security screening system at Ruđer Bošković Airport will be equipped with the new generation of technical equipment. “By introducing this technology, we want to further improve and raise the level of aviation security protection and elevate the level of service and the overall passenger experience. The new devices enable higher-quality luggage screening, and for passengers they bring a simpler procedure because they will no longer need to remove liquids and electronic devices from their hand luggage. Together with the passenger security scanners, the entire process will be faster, more efficient and with less physical contact,” explained Viktor Šober, Director of Dubrovnik Airport.

faster security processing

This brand new equipment enables more effective detection of prohibited and dangerous items, while bringing passengers a faster passage through screening. The new C3 EDS CB technology brings concrete changes for passengers. With these scanners, it is no longer necessary to remove liquids, nor laptops, tablets, mobile phones and other larger electronic devices from hand luggage. Unlike conventional X-ray machines, C3 EDS CB devices create a three-dimensional image of the luggage contents and enable a more detailed inspection and more effective recognition of prohibited and dangerous items. This simultaneously speeds up passage through control and reduces passenger delays.

Part of the modernisation also includes new scanners for passenger security screening. During screening, the passenger stands in the device for a few seconds, and the system automatically alerts security staff if it detects an area that requires additional checking. The operator sees a generic outline of a human silhouette with any marked areas that need further inspection. The new equipment enables more effective detection of prohibited and dangerous items, while bringing passengers a faster passage through the security screening process, less waiting and less need to remove items from hand luggage. With this modernisation, Ruđer Bošković Airport is raising security screening standards and introducing technology used in the most modern European and world airports.

dubrovnik airport’s passenger numbers are very healthy

Back in June, Dubrovnik Airport ranked second in traffic among Croatian airports, behind Split, with 462 thousand passengers, which is also an increase of 3.3 percent on a monthly basis, while a slightly higher growth of 4.6 percent was recorded in the first half of the year, with 1.2 million passengers. In July, it served just over 558.5 thousand passengers, almost 18 thousand more than in the same month of 2025. The airport recently completed its Master Plan for the period from 2025 to 2045, which sets the framework for the next two decades of infrastructure development and capacity growth.

In general, they are satisfied with the tourist season thus far down in Dubrovnik. This year’s three-millionth overnight stay in the Dubrovnik area was recorded on 22 August, one day earlier than in 2025, reported the Tourist Board of the City of Dubrovnik. “This confirms stable tourism results and the continuous recognition of Dubrovnik on the international tourism market,” they stated from the Dubrovnik Tourist Board. According to data from the eVisitor system, more than 25 thousand guests are currently visiting Dubrovnik. From the 1st of January to the 22nd of August, a total of 931,660 tourists stayed in Dubrovnik, who achieved 3,000,099 overnight stays.

World.title: Speleologists Explore Biokovo Cave, Discover Evidence of Forgotten Craft
World.content:
August the 30th, 2026 – Speleologists have explored a deep Biokovo cave that has never been archived and discovered evidence of an almost entirely forgotten craft.

Croatia’s many rugged and imposing mountains hide many secrets of which we’re often not even aware while we admire them from afar or climb them. Putni kofer writes that a very large part of those secrets is hidden underground. On the Dalmatian giant Biokovo, high above Makarska, over 400 caves and pits have been explored. They continue to be explored, so members of the Speleological Section of HPD Biokovo recently descended into a pit near the mountain hut below Sveti Jure, which they themselves described as one from their series “it’s not in the archives.”

vertical walls in a 25-metre-deep pit

As Rikardo Škorlić from the speleological society revealed, the cave in question is called Kašogijeva jama, which was first explored back in 1987. “The pit is 25 metres deep and is located 120 metres east of the mountain hut,” he explained. Not unlike other Dalmatian caves, it is a typical karst pit, with almost vertical walls and narrow passages into which only a little daylight penetrates.

evidence of ice harvesting was discovered

What the speleologists found inside this Biokovo cave surprised them, as the pit hid many traces of an old craft that was important for decades on Biokovo. It seems that it was an ice house.

“This pit, quite like many other pits on Biokovo, was still full of ice about 30 years ago and once served the local population as a source of water in the dry summer months for watering livestock, and with the advent of tourism the ice was used for storing food and cooling drinks in Makarska. Today, due to climate change, there’s no more ice left, but traces of ice harvesting remain in the pit, including the remains of beams that the ice harvesters used to descend into the pit and extract the ice,” Rikardo Škorlić revealed.

harvesting ice on biokovo was a dangerous task

The ice houses on Biokovo are natural underground pits in which, due to the specific climate and cold air, eternal snow and ice are retained. In the past, local people called ice harvesters or cutters entered the dangerous pits. They broke off pieces of ice weighing up to 30 kilograms and then transported them on donkeys down to the foot of the mountain for cooling food and drinks in the Makarska area.

Fishermen, butchers and wealthier residents all came and bought it, and for many families, the sale of ice represented an important, for some even the main source of income. Before the appearance of electric refrigerators, what is everyday life for us today was a commodity that literally had to be extracted from the belly of the mountain. These old ice houses are also the subject of the international scientific project called IceLink, within which research of the Dusa and Crna ledenica pits in the area of Nature Park Biokovo was carried out this year.
