They had just brutally suppressed the Zviadists in Samegrelo, gaining extensive experience in illegal detentions, arrests, and crackdowns. They were well-practiced in these methods, and naturally, such behavior came seamlessly to them.

For the residents of Abkhazia, it was an absolute shock—not only for the Abkhaz, but for local Georgians as well. They could not believe their own countrymen were capable of such actions, given the notorious criminal background of the leaders driving the entire process and the figures actively carrying it out.

Of course, as a conflict expands and intensifies, violations inevitably occur on all sides. It would be naive to imagine that the Abkhaz are the kind of people to turn the other cheek in such a situation; it is a completely different reality, and that must be understood.

Crimes were committed on both sides, but the fundamental responsibility for initiating the process rests with the party that started it.

As for their methods… why stick our heads in the sand? Those methods are well known, not just from what happened in Abkhazia, but from what took place within Georgia proper.

It is clear that due to current domestic political issues in Georgia, they prefer to sweep this topic under the rug. I see virtually no public discussion about what transpired in Western Georgia on the eve of the Georgian-Abkhazian conflict. A taboo has been placed on that topic for obvious reasons—nobody wants to reopen those raw wounds when society already faces so many problems. Nevertheless, it must be taken into account.

Sooner or later, history always resurfaces in its darker manifestations if we attempt to study it in a sanitized form. We must know this history in its entirety. As for that… I suppose that is everything I wanted to say on the matter. Yes.

We are operating against a very heavy historical backdrop, yet there are occasional glimmers showing that people are attempting to look at the problem from a different angle. This is even happening within government circles.

Take, for example, the statements made by Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze. We certainly do not expect him to tell us how wonderful we are or that they intend to recognize Abkhazia’s independence, but he did mention the restoration of confidence-building measures. That is a very important step. Occasionally, articles appear offering a relatively objective look at the history of our relations since ancient times. Furthermore, some Georgian writers are even addressing the notorious pseudo-scientific theory of Ingorokva, which has poisoned the minds of multiple generations. Granted, such pieces are rare amid the vast sea of opposing literature, but they do appear.

In that sense, there are small glimmers of hope that genuine realization will come.

We also need to draw conclusions regarding our own policies—for instance, concerning the Gali district. That is something we will inevitably need to address.

However, given the current lack of trust, any step forward is easily misinterpreted as granting unfair advantages to the other side. For that reason, I do not believe in grand, immediate solutions, nor do I think it is productive to debate overarching political questions right now. Instead, targeted measures—focusing on transport, communication, humanitarian concerns, and the movement of people and goods across the border—are precisely what would help establish the foundational conditions needed for genuine dialogue.

Inal Khashig: Let’s move on to another topic: the de-isolation of Abkhazia. In Turkey, a campaign to de-isolate Abkhazia is gaining momentum. On the one hand, it includes the recognition of Abkhaz passports as valid travel documents; on the other, it seeks to restore direct communication—specifically maritime links—between Turkey and Abkhazia that existed immediately after the war. For a time, those connections operated, people could travel, and passenger boats ran. Although that was later cut off, a campaign to revive it is unfolding now.

At first, this was an initiative driven by private individuals within the Abkhazian and Adyghe civil sector. It then expanded to the point where eight political parties represented in the Turkish parliament formed a united front, declaring that Abkhazia must be de-isolated. Initially, our Confederation of Abkhaz Communities in Turkey (Abkhazfed) reacted with a certain degree of possessiveness, arguing that the movement had no right to take the lead and that Abkhazfed should have authored the idea. It was a completely unnecessary friction. However, after Abkhazian society here voiced strong support and our Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement, a course correction took place. Representatives from both the initiative group and Abkhazfed met and reached a consensus that a consolidated movement for de-isolation is essential.

How do you view this prospect overall? On the one hand, these eight political parties belong to the opposition, spanning a varied spectrum from left to right. How viable is this initiative, and to what extent might it simply be an element of internal Turkish political maneuvering to capture votes—specifically from the Abkhaz and Adyghe diaspora, who by various estimates number up to four million—ahead of upcoming parliamentary and early presidential elections?

In your view, is this driven purely by domestic politics, or is there a real opportunity here to translate this into a broader movement originating from the civil sector and picked up by the opposition? Could Ankara actually take concrete steps such as de-isolating Abkhazia, recognizing Abkhaz passports, and reopening maritime transport?

Astamur Tania: Naturally, I supported this initiative—as did you and many others. It would be foolish not to support it. Indeed, many on our side did.

At the same time, we must recognize that over the last few decades, there has been an obvious degradation in our expert and public outreach across all fronts, including the Turkish direction.

I carefully read what Elchin Adzinba wrote. Fortunately, we have experts of such high caliber who understand the inner workings of Turkish politics. We must take his insights into account in our work, as there are bound to be hidden undercurrents. But in politics, nothing is ever entirely positive or entirely negative; it is a constant struggle. He called for expanding the circle of people with whom we engage because decisions on such a significant issue—whether made behind the scenes or officially voiced—are ultimately crafted in government corridors. This strategy ensures the effort does not look like a mere pawn in Turkey’s internal political competition. He specifically warned about this, and we must keep it in mind.

Returning to the reaction of our own society: it often resembles a sparkler. Something reactive happens, everyone flares up instantly, and then all at once it goes out, gets forgotten, and passes. In six months, no one will even remember it. That is the tragedy.

We still have public organizations and specialized institutions that operate on state funding. Previously, we periodically held conferences, including on legal issues, where our situation was discussed from the perspective of international law—specifically how our rights are restricted regarding freedom of movement, education, and other matters.

In international politics, only that which exists in the information space actually exists. If we say nothing ourselves—well, thank God Turkish Abkhazians stepped up to raise this topic. But the initial momentum ought to stem from here, as they do not face direct isolation problems themselves; they hold passports that allow free movement worldwide. Yet no initiative originated from our side.

As a proposal, we could hold a scientific conference—one with real public resonance. Rather than merely recounting history, it should analyze how this tightening of constraints came about, which norms of international law it violates, and what consequences it brings. Even if we set aside the Georgian side’s internal political confrontation, the de-isolation of Abkhazia does not contradict their interests either.

Obstacles are always created from that side. For instance, after the armed conflict, we conducted negotiations and signed documents on the non-use of force, peacekeeping forces, and refugee return procedures. Then they claimed it did not suit them because the return was too slow. Now they make empty claims about 300,000 refugees, even though that many people never lived in Abkhazia to begin with. Meanwhile, we returned about 50,000 refugees to the Gal district—which apparently was still not enough for their narrative.

Later, we held negotiations on confederate relations and union structures—using various terminologies from 1997 to 1998, up until the May events. Domestic political circumstances intervened again. In the end, who won? Neither the refugees nor Georgian society. The exact same logic applies to this issue.

Honestly, I would consider it rational if the Georgian side did not obstruct Abkhazia’s de-isolation, as it could easily be included in a package of measures to build mutual trust.

As for Ankara, everyone understands that if the Georgian side stated it had no objections, the matter would be resolved much more easily. Otherwise, it is difficult to predict how long it will take or whether it will yield concrete results.

However, the fact that both our society and our diaspora are actively engaged around this vital issue is a result in itself. Regardless of whether our passports are ultimately recognized in Turkey, it demonstrates that society is thinking about its prospects and modeling its future. It shows a living society.

And this is not our only challenge; we have plenty of other problems. Sometimes one recalls how dynamic things were in the 1990s and early 2000s—the proactive responses, the strong stances taken by different individuals and organizations. Now, it feels like a stagnant swamp, with only the occasional outburst. You cannot achieve results in such a state. We must work on all fronts and in all directions. Some efforts will succeed, others won’t—but it can be said with certainty that if you do nothing, nothing will happen.

Life recently forced us to deal with pressing issues like fuel supplies. We will face many more such challenges, and we will have to manage them. If you claim to be an independent state, you have to act like one. Independence is not just a collection of legislative acts and political declarations; it requires active work to fill those structures with real substance. It is a creative process.

If a nation lacks that creative drive, it begins to fade and dull. Unfortunately, we are observing this trend. You and I spoke about the Abkhaz language earlier—it is good that there is activity, though whether it will yield results remains to be seen. But above all, society must show signs of life. Nobody will look out for us if we don’t stand up for ourselves. That is what I wanted to say.

Inal Khashig: In any case, during our turbulent times—and not only in turbulent times, but in any period, whether peaceful or turbulent—there must be clear plans for the future. Moreover, there should be multiple options across all directions, including a Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C, along with continuous modeling of potential scenarios.

I am basing this once again on the recent gasoline crisis, when under Aslan Bzhania, a sudden decision was made to hand the entire fuel market over to a single pair of hands. One ought to have considered the consequences beforehand and anticipated how all of this would play out—not just focusing on how beautiful and well-maintained our gas stations would look, but realizing that the primary problem arises when there is no gasoline at those stations in the first place. That situation highlights a lack of deep analysis and the absence of a pragmatic, truly calculated strategy.

Astamur Tania: Well, you understand that we aren’t experts in all fields of government, right?

Inal Khashig: No, of course not.

Astamur Tania: On gasoline, I’m definitely not an expert, nor on these monopolies. One simply needs to involve the expert community where we do not understand. Give public resonance to the problem. I see many things being done, but they lack competent public coverage.

Inal Khashig: Astamur, say you have money, right? No level-headed businessman will tell you that all your money needs to be placed in one specific bank. He spreads it across different banks.

What I’m getting at is that when we have no oil of our own—oil might be lying around somewhere, but there is neither refining, nor extraction, nothing—and we buy this gasoline… When you buy this gasoline, there must be different sources.

Astamur Tania: Now you and I are going in circles. I agree with you, which is why we spoke about diversification.

Inal Khashig: On that note, we will actually conclude our conversation: with the fact that Astamur agrees.

Astamur Tania: To each his own sore point. As for me, I don’t drive.

Inal Khashig: I drive. It somehow turned out that not only I, but probably the majority of Abkhazian drivers go to sleep in the evening with the thought of where to refuel tomorrow, where to find this gasoline. And in the morning they wake up with the same thought. And I think that for the state, this should be the very last problem in reality—when for its citizens, their main thought consists of how to get gasoline. In short, so that we don’t have such problems, I will wrap up. Astamur, thank you very much.

Astamur Tania: Thank you. All the best.

Inal Khashig: Let there be light. Goodbye.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: Reaching level of alliance in Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan relations is gratifying - President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. It is gratifying that relations between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan, rooted in traditional ties of friendship and brotherhood, have developed year by year, reaching the level of alliance and acquiring new substance, President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev said in a congratulatory letter addressed to President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Zhaparov on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of his country’s independence.

“My recent state visit to your hospitable country demonstrated our nations’ determination to pursue close partnership and an extensive agenda of cooperation, laying the foundation for a new chapter in the history of Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan relations,” President Ilham Aliyev emphasized in his letter.

The head of state expressed confidence that Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan ties and the alliance between the two countries will continue to develop and strengthen along an upward trajectory through their joint efforts and in accordance with the interests of the two countries’ peoples.

World.title: Iran's Foreign Ministry condemns U.S. attack on Larak Island
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. Iran’s Foreign Ministry has strongly condemned a U.S. military attack on Iran’s Larak Island, saying it resulted in an apparent violation of provisions of the U.N. Charter.

The ministry made the remarks in a statement.

“Iran’s Foreign Ministry calls on the U.N. secretary-general and the U.N. Security Council to fulfill their responsibilities in maintaining international peace and security,” the statement said.

The ministry said several military personnel and civilians were killed and wounded in the U.S. military attack on Larak Island overnight, while public property was also damaged.

“Iran reminds the U.N. secretary-general, the president of the Security Council and all states that have expressed concern over continued instability in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz that the only factor destabilizing maritime routes in the region is the illegal actions of the United States and Israel. This attack began on Feb. 28, 2026, and over the past six months has continued in various forms, including a naval blockade and other provocative actions,” the statement said.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry added that the country’s armed forces have no doubt about taking lawful defensive measures and will respond decisively and appropriately to military attacks.

“It is clear that the United States and those parties cooperating with Washington in these illegal actions bear responsibility for any new U.S. steps, the continuation of the naval blockade and the economic war against Iran,” the statement said.

The U.S. military has reportedly destroyed two missile systems on Iran’s Larak Island in the south of the country. Two people were reportedly killed and two others wounded in the airstrikes.

World.title: Kazakh FlyArystan to resume direct Aktau-Istanbul flights in October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. Kazakhstan's low-cost airline FlyArystan will resume direct flights between Aktau and Istanbul, with the first flight scheduled for October 22, 2026, the airline said.

Starting October 27, flights on the route will operate twice a week, on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

"Under the regular schedule, the flight from Aktau will depart at 08:40 on Tuesdays and arrive in Istanbul at 10:35. The return flight will depart Istanbul at 11:40 and arrive in Aktau at 17:05. On Saturdays, the flight from Aktau will depart at 08:35 and arrive in Istanbul at 10:30. The return flight from Istanbul is scheduled to depart at 11:15 and arrive in Aktau at 16:40 local time," the airline said.

The resumption of Istanbul flights is part of FlyArystan's continued expansion of its international network from Aktau.

Earlier, the airline also announced the resumption of direct flights between Aktau and Yerevan. Flights to the Armenian capital will resume on December 16, 2026, and will operate twice a week, on Wednesdays and Fridays.

FlyArystan's current international route network from Aktau includes Kutaisi, Baku, Dubai, Batumi and Urumqi.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev congratulates President of Kyrgyzstan on Independence Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has sent a congratulatory letter to President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Japarov.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear Sadyr Nurgozhoevich,

On my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Azerbaijan, I extend my most sincere congratulations and best wishes to you and, through you, to the entire people of the brotherly Kyrgyz Republic on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of its independence.

Today, under your leadership, Kyrgyzstan has achieved significant milestones in strengthening its statehood, advancing socio-economic development, and implementing large-scale construction projects, earning great prestige on the international stage. As a brotherly country, we rejoice in Kyrgyzstan’s successes as our own.

It is gratifying that relations between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan, rooted in traditional ties of friendship and brotherhood, have developed year by year, reaching the level of alliance and acquiring new substance. My recent state visit to your hospitable country demonstrated our nations’ determination to pursue close partnership and an extensive agenda of cooperation, laying the foundation for a new chapter in the history of Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan relations.

I am confident that Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan ties and the alliance between our countries will continue to develop and strengthen along an upward trajectory through our joint efforts and in accordance with the interests of our peoples.

On this festive day, I wish you robust health, happiness, and success in your high state activities, and the brotherly Kyrgyz Republic lasting peace and prosperity," the letter reads.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev extends condolences to President of Northern Cyprus
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev sent a letter to Tufan Erhürman, President of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear Mr. President,

We were deeply shocked by the news of the loss of life resulting from the capsizing of a boat near Kyrenia.

In the wake of this tragedy, on my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Azerbaijan, I extend my deepest condolences to you, the families and relatives of those who lost their lives, and your brotherly people, and wish a speedy recovery to the injured.

May Allah rest the souls of those who lost their lives in peace!" the letter reads.

World.title: UAE Air Force intercepts UAV approaching from Iran
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. The United Arab Emirates Air Force took measures against an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) detected over the country’s territorial waters. The UAV was approaching from the direction of Iran.

The UAE Ministry of Defence announced this on August 31.

“The Armed Forces remain on a high state of readiness to address any potential threats, while air defence systems continue to monitor and safeguard the country’s airspace around the clock,” the ministry said in a statement.

The Ministry of Defence urged the public to rely exclusively on official sources of information and refrain from spreading rumours or unverified reports.

On the same day, the Iranian military said it had carried out a drone strike on Al Minhad Air Base, located south of Dubai. According to Tehran, the attack targeted facilities hosting US military personnel and helicopters. Iran said the strike was a response to a US attack on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz carried out the previous day. As of publication, the UAE had not issued a separate comment specifically regarding Iran’s statement about the alleged attack on Al Minhad.

Earlier in August, UAE air defence systems detected launches of ballistic missiles from Iran; both projectiles fell into the sea, with one landing within UAE territorial waters and the other outside them. Following those incidents, the UAE suspended all trade, commercial exchanges, and financial operations with Iran.

World.title: Uzbekistan, China's Tencent plan roadmap for cross-border QR payments
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. Uzbekistan’s Central Bank and Chinese technology company Tencent discussed plans to integrate Uzbekistan’s Unified QR payment system with international payment ecosystems, potentially expanding cross-border cashless payment options for consumers and visitors.

This was reflected in the statement by the Central Bank of Uzbekistan, following discussions within the framework of the 2026 “Silk Road: Finance and Technology” Forum.

The meeting focused on opportunities to connect Uzbekistan’s Unified QR payment system with foreign payment networks and make digital payment services more convenient for Uzbek citizens and international visitors.

Under the potential integration, foreign visitors to Uzbekistan could use their existing payment applications to make cashless payments by scanning QR codes, while Uzbek citizens could gain broader access to QR-based payment services when traveling abroad.

The Central Bank and Tencent agreed to draw on the Chinese company’s experience in integrating national QR payment infrastructures with international payment ecosystems, according to the statement.

Moreover, the sides agreed to hold a series of technical meetings to determine the requirements for integration, coordinate further steps and develop a clear roadmap for cooperation.

The initiative could strengthen the interoperability of Uzbekistan’s domestic payment infrastructure with international digital payment systems, potentially supporting tourism, trade and broader financial connectivity.

For Uzbekistan, expanding cross-border QR payments would also complement the country’s broader shift toward cashless transactions and digital financial services, while giving local consumers and businesses greater access to international payment ecosystems.

The planned technical discussions are expected to determine the practical framework and timeline for advancing cooperation between the Central Bank and Tencent.

World.title: Iran's military says it struck U.S. base in UAE
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. Iran’s military said it targeted the U.S. military’s Al Minhad Air Base in the United Arab Emirates with kamikaze drones.

The claim was made in a statement released by Iran’s military.

“In response to last night’s U.S. military attacks on Larak Island, which killed innocent civilians and members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iranian forces targeted locations at Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE where U.S. forces and helicopters are stationed, using dozens of kamikaze drones,” the statement said.

The Iranian military said the air base is one of the key hubs for providing air support and transporting foreign forces.

Iran’s military said its forces are ready to protect the country’s territorial integrity, ensure its security and respond to any attacks.

The statement follows reports that the U.S. military destroyed two missile systems on Iran’s Larak Island in the south of the country. Two people were reportedly killed and two others wounded in the airstrikes.

World.title: Government not planning import ban for smart glasses, attorney-general says
World.content:
The federal government is not currently considering an import ban on smart glasses but has signalled the devices could be restricted by local councils, as it unveils a draft of sweeping new privacy laws including the "right to erasure".

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland on Monday released draft legislation designed to bolster privacy protections, as well as address risks related to artificial intelligence and wearable tech such as smart glasses.

She also announced a new initiative, IDLock, to allow individuals to have more control over how their personal documents were being used for verification online.

Ms Rowland acknowledged community concerns about potential harmful use of smart glasses but said the government was not currently planning an import ban, despite calls from the Greens and independents to halt imports for 12 months until privacy laws are strengthened.

"We are not specifically, in this consultation, consulting on an import ban," she told reporters on Monday.

"The Privacy Act consultation does not go to issues of import restrictions, however, we are not ruling anything out in terms of other measures we can take."

The government's consultation paper, released alongside the draft legislation, highlights the laws are designed to be technology-neutral to apply to potential privacy breaches from emerging technologies, including smart glasses.

Last week, Brisbane City Council banned people from secretly filming with AI smart glasses and other wearable recording devices at public pools.

"I would like other councils to consider what kind of public areas they have in their sphere of influence where this could apply," Ms Rowland said, citing council-run childcare centres as an example.

Education Minister Jason Clare's office told the ABC smart glasses were already covered by the ban put in place, saying any personal device capable of taking, storing or transmitting an image is not allowed in childcare centres.

The devices, worn as eyewear with a small computer embedded in them, have been labelled "pervert glasses" by critics because they can covertly record and live stream interactions.

Smart glasses can be used for secret filming, but can also be useful for people with disabilities. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

But the eSafety commissioner has pointed out they can also be used to improve accessibility for people with disabilities, such as live speech-to-text for deaf users or providing descriptions for those with low vision.

In an industry report circulated on Monday, the eSafety commissioner urged companies to automatically blur people's faces, delay live streaming and ensure there were clear visual indicators when recording audio or video.

While earlier versions of the product cost around $500, newer versions are available for under $100.

The attorney-general wrote to the privacy commissioner earlier this month, asking them to look into the growing uptake of smart glasses as a matter of urgency.

Ms Rowland said councils and businesses, such as retail shops with change rooms, could restrict the use of smart glasses as they saw fit.

"This is not the final piece of wearable information processing technology that will be developed," she said.

"I acknowledge there are deep concerns about this, but the notion that this is somehow a quick and uncomplex mechanism to impose an import ban is not correct.

"Right now we need to look at the harms that are being caused … and be proportionate in that response."

Push for import ban on 'pervert' smart glasses Support is growing for a ban on the import of so-called “smart glasses”.

Greens senator David Shoebridge said the draft laws were a modest step forward but they needed to be extended to cover the use of smart glasses and reiterated calls for an import ban.

"There is still no requirement for a prominent light, a recognisable sound, or any outward sign that a pair of glasses is recording or searching online about people the wearer is seeing," he said.

"A right to erasure that is limited only to platforms with $500 million or more in revenue, or 2.5 million monthly users, leaves out every small app and every emerging glasses startup building exactly this kind of surveillance product."

Right to erasure

The attorney-general said the draft legislation outlined a "right to erasure" which would allow people to request their personal information be removed and destroyed from social media platforms and search engines.

She said large digital platforms were already required to do this in the European Union and signalled there could be harsh penalties for those that failed to comply.

"Breaches of privacy can be tens of millions of dollars, and they can also be calculated as a percentage of revenues or turnovers as well," she said.

"We are not shy in terms of having high penalties, because what we are talking about here is damage to people."

Milica Stilinovic, an expert on digital cultures and technological harms at the University of Sydney, told ABC News the proposal was a good step forward but challenges remained.

"Is big tech actually going to come to the table and allow this type of erasure to occur, and on a permanent basis? I think the jury is still out on one," Dr Stilinovic said.

The draft legislation, part of a second tranche of privacy reforms from the Albanese government, also outlines a "fair and reasonable" test.

That is "so companies can no longer justify collecting more information than they need, or using it for purposes that Australians would never expect", Ms Rowland said.

Social media companies would be required to delete a user's personal data if requested.

The draft legislation also addresses meaningful consent from users about the information they share, and measures to prevent businesses from trading in personal information without permission, "so shopping habits, online interests or location data cannot be bought and sold behind Australians' backs".

"We know that Australians are increasingly concerned about how their data is being collected, used and shared, particularly as AI and other emerging technologies such as smart glasses become more accessible," she said.

"People should not have to choose between protecting their privacy and participating in the digital economy."

IDLock

The government also announced a new service allowing individuals to block and monitor how their identification documents are being used online.

The service, called IDLock, will be available through myGov from next year and will be released to a small number of users for testing later this year.

It will allow people "to block, unblock and monitor" how their identity documents, such as their passport or driver's licence, are being used through the government's document verification service.

For example, a person could block their documents to prevent scams or fraud, but if they were applying for a credit card, they could temporarily unblock them for a short period of time to allow the bank to verify their identity.

"As we know, we often have to share our personal identification, our personal data, whether that is to set up electricity, or open an account, or check into our tax file number," Dr Stilinovic said.

"What this does is essentially take the power back to individuals to provide certain agency to remove that very sensitive data from third parties."

World.title: Former massage therapist jailed for assaulting clients
World.content:
A former massage therapist has been sent to prison for sexually touching two clients in regional Victoria.

Warning: This article includes descriptions of sexual abuse.

Tomey Mathew, 33, had no qualifications for his role as a massage therapist and was learning on the job at a business in Mildura, north-west Victoria, in 2025.

His former employer told the Mildura Magistrates' Court that, during his training, Mathew had been told that touching women in private places was not permitted.

The court heard that, during his time in the industry, Mathew estimated he massaged five women.

Three of these women might have been staff.

The two that were not colleagues went to police after their massages to lodge sexual assault claims against him.

Touching 'not accidental'

The first victim went to Massage Borneo 1 in Langtree Mall on March 13, 2025 for a 45-minute oil massage.

Mathew was called, took payment and began the massage.

Tomey Mathew massaged five women during his five months at the business. (Supplied: Facebook)

The court heard everything seemed normal as he massaged the woman's legs, arms, feet, shoulders and head.

The victim then recalled being unable to speak and freezing in fear as Mathew reached under a towel covering her breasts and grabbed at her.

The court heard he was asked to stop but repeated the act soon after as he leaned over her from behind her head.

The second victim had booked a 30-minute neck massage which lasted close to an hour on April 5, 2025.

Tomey Mathew no longer works at Massage Borneo 1, where the offending took place. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

She was also touched under the towel by Mathew, who circled her breasts twice before he was told to stop and left the room.

Mathew denied touching the breasts of either woman, either intentionally or accidentally.

The court heard that, due to the manner of the touching and the duration, the conduct could not be explained as an accident.

Profound and far-reaching impact

Victim impact statements from both women were read in court.

The first victim said, since the incident, she had become hyper-aware of consent and boundaries and had experienced anxiety attacks.

She said she experienced ghost sensations and flashbacks of the incident.

The second victim said intimacy felt different and unsettling and she could not avoid a persistent uneasy feeling.

Defence lawyer Robert Thyssen argued there was no evidence of sexual gratification by Mathew in either act.

He said the offences were "of fleeting nature" due to Mathew's minimal experience and training.

Magistrate Greg Thomas said he didn't agree with the word fleeting, as Mathew knew he wasn't supposed to touch the women's breasts.

"The women were in a very vulnerable position. There is an element of breach of trust," he said.

Prosecutors push for jail term

Police prosecutor Leading Senior Constable Jackie Lowe argued that anything less than imprisonment would be manifestly inadequate.

She said the victims had expressed lifelong implications from the offending and were exposed to more trauma by giving evidence in court.

She also argued that Mathew was not remorseful, as he contested the charges, and said "regret post-conviction and remorse are two different things".

Tomey Mathew will spend the next five months behind bars. (Supplied: Facebook)

Mr Thyssen said the complainants were not at risk of being victims of reoffending, as Mathew had moved to Queensland to work as kitchen hand in an aged care facility.

He described Mathew as hard working in a sector where staff were hard to obtain and argued jail should be a last resort.

But Magistrate Thomas said, even if a community corrections order was available, he did not consider it an adequate sentence.

"Because of the serious nature of offending, the breach of trust involved and lack of remorse, no other disposition other than a term of imprisonment is appropriate," Magistrate Thomas said.

He sentenced Mathew to five months in jail.

World.title: Major aged care agency has licence suspended amid fears elderly at risk
World.content:
A staffing agency that has provided workers to aged care homes has had its licence suspended over findings it altered pay slips and deployed dozens of unqualified staff to care for the elderly.

The findings prompted Victoria's Labour Hire Authority (LHA) to take the "extraordinary" step of halting Barton Care Pty Ltd's ability to deploy staff due to safety concerns.

The ABC understands Barton Care Pty Ltd provided hundreds of workers to aged care homes across Victoria.

The LHA halted the company's operations on Friday, after finding nearly 70 per cent of the qualifications held by Barton Care workers were invalid.

The LHA said the qualifications had been issued by registered training organisations and cancelled by the Australian Skills Quality Authority due to non-compliance.

The authority also found a case in which one worker attained a qualification nine days after arriving in Australia, despite the course generally taking six to nine months to complete.

"We took the extraordinary step to suspend Barton Care's licence to put an immediate stop to their potentially dangerous conduct," acting labour hire licensing commissioner Michelle Osborne said in a statement.

According to its website, Barton Care has more than 600 healthcare professionals on its books, providing registered nurses, enrolled nurses, personal care assistants and facility support staff to aged care homes and hospitals across Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory.

The ABC understands Barton Care has provided staff to major aged care providers, including Jewish Care, Estia and Bass Care, while the company is also a registered NDIS provider.

The LHA said it also believed Barton Care Pty Ltd had been underpaying workers and enabled workers on student visas to work more than the maximum hours allowed by doctoring pay slips.

The LHA said it was looking to ultimately cancel Barton Care's licence, but needed to receive submissions from the company first.

Barton Care Pty Ltd has been contacted for comment.

World.title: 3.5m saltwater crocodile captured off Cable Beach
World.content:
A large saltwater crocodile that sparked periodic beach closures around Broome in recent weeks has been captured and relocated by authorities.

The 3.5-metre-long estuarine crocodile had been sighted in waters around the tourist town, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth in WA's Kimberley, multiple times in recent weeks.

But a sighting on Saturday, just north of Cable Beach and about 100 metres offshore, saw Yawuru and Parks and Wildlife rangers decide capture and relocation was the safest possible option.

This resulted in another beach closure, the third in recent weeks, as rangers began the "inherently risky" process of wrangling the reptile.

Loading...

Parks and Wildlife district officer Lyle Gilbert said the reptile, relatively large by Kimberley standards, was well within Broome's crocodile control zone, an area of ocean around the town where the animals were monitored and removed.

"The crocodiles we capture and relocate are ones occurring in the croc risk management area … where they're going to potentially run into people," Mr Gilbert said.

"And if they're causing problems, if they're threatening vessels or showing signs they could potentially attack people, we'll relocate them."

The crocodile was seen 100 metres offshore. (Supplied: Poppy Youdale)

How do you capture a crocodile?

Mr Gilbert said It took four rangers to capture the animal.

"[We] attach to the crocodile by either a grapple or a harpoon, which basically just sticks into the skin, which holds the animal in place," he said.

" Then it's a matter of actually securing its jaws to reduce the risk to people and cover its eyes. "

Mr Gilbert stressed the importance of managing the risks to both the people involved and the crocodile to ensure the process ran smoothly and safely.

He said people must remain vigilant and aware in "crocodile country".

Rare occurrence

Beach Hut Broome owner Angela Roberson was at Cable Beach on the weekend when the capture occurred.

Several beaches across Broome were periodically closed over recent weeks, as this crocodile lurked. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

She said there was lots of interest from locals and tourists, with people lining the stairs and looking out from the surf club to try to catch a glimpse.

"I have seen crocodiles, but not of that size and not right here in front of our business," she said.

"It does happen, but not too regularly; I think this one was a bit misplaced."

Ms Roberson, whose business rents sun chairs and beach equipment to beachgoers, said she was grateful to those involved with safely capturing the crocodile.

"They managed to capture it within an hour and a half, which is amazing. They really should get a lot of credit for responding so quickly," she said.

"I'm very thankful we're able to reopen the beach and we're able to continue to trade, which is great for Cable Beach and great for tourism in general."

Cable Beach is a tourist mecca for travellers from around the country. (ABC News)

Park crocodile's new home

The reptile was successfully transferred to Malcolm Douglas Crocodile Park, on the outskirts of Broome.

Mr Gilbert said it was fortunate the park was located so close because it led to better outcomes for the animal.

"Those guys look after the crocodiles really well and he'll get fed regularly and not have to work as hard for his food," he said.

"He should have a pretty good life out there."

World.title: SA man who wore Nazi uniform to McDonald's outlet avoids jail
World.content:
A young South Australian man who shared extreme right-wing, antisemitic material online and attended a McDonald's outlet dressed in a Nazi uniform has avoided jail time.

Heath Duke, 20, appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court on Monday after previously pleading guilty to 16 counts of using a Nazi symbol or salute.

The court heard police had identified 97 public posts containing Nazi symbols that Duke had shared on the messaging platform Telegram between February and April this year. ­­

It also heard on May 25 this year, Duke attended McDonald's at Collinswood — where he worked at the time — dressed in a Nazi uniform which featured swastikas.

The prosecutor told the court witnesses observed him speaking German and "rehearsing a speech".

"Members of the public appeared visibly concerned and one witness even reported to police that they were feeling that the defendant may harm somebody on the night," she said.

The court heard when police later went to his home they found the uniform, as well as a large Nazi flag which was visible from a shared driveway.

The prosecutor told the court Duke then breached a bail condition last month by accessing social media through a different account and posting content which "intended to glorify Hitler".

Police found a large Nazi flag at Heath Duke's home. (Supplied: TikTok)

The court heard Duke — who appeared via video link — had experienced a "very difficult time" in the 11 days he had been in custody.

The court heard he had a long-standing autism diagnosis, suffered significant loneliness and presented a fixation of extreme right-wing beliefs.

The defence lawyer told the court his client "identifies" with convicted criminal and leader of the neo-Nazi group National Socialist Network Thomas Sewell.

"He hasn't had any contact with Mr Sewell before, he does wish to advocate for Thomas Sewell politically," Duke's lawyer said.

"Moving forward, he wishes to continue advocating for his own interests but he'll project his beliefs in a different way.

" Prison has had the salutary effect of waking him up to be more mindful and careful of what he's sharing. "

While acknowledging Duke's behaviour was not acceptable in Australia, Magistrate Koula Kossiavelos also said she believed with the "right rehabilitation" the behaviour would not be repeated, noting he had no prior criminal history.

"For the Jewish community in Australia, this would be a very sad case to see a young man whose 20 years of age and is fixated on issues that have been deep-felt for them and continue to be," she said.

"You have political beliefs that are not shared in the community for good reason."

Heath Duke appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court for sentencing. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Magistrate Kossiavelos said there was a correlation between the defendant ceasing medication for his ADHD and the offending recurring, adding there was "good reason" for him to start taking it again.

"You are accepting that what you've done is outrageous right?" Magistrate Kossiavelos asked the defendant.

"Yeah, I don't want to break the law," Duke replied.

Magistrate Kossiavelos told the court she would "extend the maximum leniency" to Duke's sentence, handing him a two-year good behaviour bond and recording no conviction.

Duke was also banned from accessing social media platforms for two years.

World.title: Butcher backs meat producers as Woolworths to stop selling Tassie beef
World.content:
Tasmanian butchers have backed their local suppliers following Woolworths's decision to stop selling Tasmanian beef.

Suppliers say they were told last week that Woolworths would stop selling Tasmanian beef in stores due to rising costs of production and shipping across the Bass Strait.

Woolworths to stop selling Tasmanian beef from 2027 Woolworths confirms it will no longer sell Tasmanian beef in the state or the mainland from 2027, a move cattle farmers say is a "kick in the guts".

But one butcher is hopeful the move will lead to more Tasmanians buying Tasmanian produce.

Launceston butcher Rob Perry said that while he had never been "short of supply" of Tasmanian beef, his new-found focus was to buy and sell even more.

"I think other butchers and anyone in the meat game should be doing the same and promoting our local product," Mr Perry said.

"At the end of the day, we need to keep these producers alive."

Rob Perry says he will be promoting Tasmanian produce, and that "anyone in the meat game" should do the same. (ABC News: Rani Fletcher)

The Casalinga Gourmet Meats owner said he wanted to offer more choice to consumers off the back of Woolworths's exit.

"We're looking for the top end market and we're prepared to pay for that so we can get that product on a consistent basis," Mr Perry said.

"I've been in the game for 47 years and I believe a butcher is someone who gets carcass meat, makes his own sausages and value adds all the product.

"We need to think where we were 30 or 40 years ago … let's get some meat carters out there and get the abattoirs working so we can get some product out the door."

Rob Perry says he is willing to pay for premium Tasmanian produce for the sustainability of the industry. (ABC News: Rani Fletcher)

Lack of service kill processing facilities

Agricultural non-profit Sprout Tasmania CEO Jennifer Robinson said she was "gutted" to hear about Woolworths's decision.

"When we see corporates making decisions like this purely based on focusing on their profits, it's really disappointing," Ms Robinson said.

"Farmers are being squeezed by many things at the moment.

"We really just need to be making sure in our community here in Tassie that farmers have choices, farmers have access to markets."

Jennifer Robinson says Woolworths's decision is "really disappointing". (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

She said Tasmanian farmers who wanted to process their own animals to sell meat under their own brand could not, due to a lack of service kill processing facilities in the state.

She said if that were to change, local farmers would have "more choices and opportunities to diversify".

"There are not enough abattoirs out there of varying scales that enable farmers to take an animal to be processed and get their meat back," she said.

Much of the beef sold in Tasmania is processed on the mainland. (ABC News: Rani Fletcher)

The Bass Strait barrier

Liberal MP Nick Duigan said Bass Strait freight was a "substantial barrier" for businesses in Tasmania.

"Obviously, we're disappointed to hear that decision by one of our big supermarkets," Mr Duigan said.

"Freight is an issue and I understand that, but again, we'd call on the federal government to release its review of the Freight Equalisation Scheme."

Nick Duigan says the government will speak to TasFarmers about future conversations with Woolworths. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

An independent review into the scheme commenced in October last year and was expected to be handed down mid-2026, though a formal release date has not yet been announced.

"We will make the appropriate approaches to those businesses that have made those decisions about having Tasmanian produce on their shelves," Mr Duigan said.

"There will be conversations happening with TasFarmers and how we frame our conversations with Woolies going forward."

The ABC understands Woolworths does not access the Tasmanian Freight Equalisation Scheme.

The ABC understands Woolworths will continue to sell Tasmanian beef until the end of the year.

World.title: Cook dismisses One Nation's ambition to form government in WA as 'hubris'
World.content:
Fresh off winning One Nation's first lower house seat in Western Australia's parliament, MP Luke Herdegen says his populist party has now set its sights on forming government at the 2029 state election, banking on what he called the beginnings of a "huge shift" in voters in this Labor stronghold.

His claims were quickly shot down by WA Premier Roger Cook as "arrogance" and "hubris".

But on the back of a massive 18.6 per cent swing against the Australian Labor Party at the by-election in Secret Harbour, a seat Labor held onto for almost 20 years, Mr Cook also promised to renew efforts to listen to the community, denying his team had become complacent after more than 10 years in power.

Rod Caddies (left) and Luke Herdegen (right) have both claimed there was an actual shift among voters in Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

Mr Herdegen told 102.5 ABC Perth that preparations were already underway within his party to develop policies to stop Labor from winning a fourth term in the 2029 election.

"I think people are making smarter decisions now on who they do vote for," he said.

"We've seen the beginning now of a huge shift, and I expect that momentum to keep going.

One Nation is coming for the establishment and no-one is safe Pauline Hanson says she can smash Labor and, given the anger in the community, perhaps that messaging is resonating.

" And we're certainly going to push that [Labor government] out heading into the next election and we'll be looking to form a government in 2029. "

One Nation WA Leader Rod Caddies also told 102.5 ABC Perth the by-election results showed voters had had enough of Labor.

"This isn't just a protest vote. This is an actual shift," he said.

'Wake up' call

Labor still dominates the Legislative Assembly, known as the lower house, with 45 seats. The Liberals hold seven seats, the Nationals six and One Nation now one.

Mr Cook slapped down Mr Herdegen's projection for 2029.

"That's the sort of arrogance that trips you up in this game," he said.

"Hubris is usually served up with a double helping of humble pie when you go around with that sort of attitude."

Peter Malinauskas says it is time for Labor to "wake up". (ABC News)

But South Australian Labor Premier Peter Malinauskas said it was time for his party to "wake up".

"There is a movement here that has got momentum and we've got to make sure we're doing the right thing by whoever it is you're representing, in whatever state or whatever level of government," he said.

"You've got to have a policy conviction and get on and do things, otherwise people will make you down for it."

Cook doubles down

Mr Cook said Labor treated the community with respect and never took voters for granted.

Roger Cook says his party never takes voters for granted. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"There's no complacency in my team. None at all," he said.

Loading...

Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas maintained the Liberals could do better.

"Seventeen per cent [the Liberals' vote at the Secret Harbour by-election] is not at the numbers that we would want it to be at," he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"But we are very, very mindful that this is a by-election in a seat that we have never held and never done well in.

"But do we want to increase our primary, of course we do."

Basil Zempilas (left) denies the Liberals ran a weak campaign amid criticism within the party. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Zempilas again denied the Liberals had run dead in the campaign, as suggested by WA federal Liberal Andrew Hastie, whose seat of Canning overlaps Secret Harbour and who will be vulnerable to One Nation's growth at the next federal election.

Mr Herdegen easily won the by-election, with just over 57 per cent of the two-party preferred vote compared to almost 43 per cent for Labor candidate Georgia Tree, after 74.5 per cent of ballots were counted.

World.title: Charge upgraded to murder over shooting death of Melbourne father
World.content:
The charge against a man accused of shooting a Melbourne father has been upgraded to murder following the discovery of a body last week.

Mohammed Aboueid, 56, was initially charged with intentionally causing serious injury after an alleged dispute unfolded at a home in Wildwood, north-west of the city, on August 19.

During that dispute, police allege Mr Aboueid shot 37-year-old Khaled Malas, who was then reported missing.

The dog squad was involved in the search for Mr Malas near a Sunbury landfill site. (ABC News)

Police conducted a large-scale search for Mr Malas, which came to an end last Wednesday, when human remains were discovered.

Police said his body was found covered in grass on Havelock Road in Clarkefield, about 15 kilometres from Wildwood.

Mr Aboueid has been remanded in custody and will face the Melbourne Magistrates' Court in November.

Friends remembered Mr Malas as a "humble, hard-working man who loved his young family" and someone who was deeply respected by his community.

World.title: Danish giant steps in to help break Australia’s wind farm drought
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesEnergy Danish giant steps in to help break Australia’s wind farm drought Nick Toscano August 31, 2026 — 5:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A decision to greenlight the eastern seaboard’s largest wind farm in more than two years has provided a much-needed boost to Australia’s renewable energy ambitions, helping to break an investment drought that has stalled the rollout of wind turbines and threatened the nation’s 2030 climate targets. Danish investment giant Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners on Monday said it had acquired the Gawara Baya wind farm in North Queensland – a project combining up to 69 wind turbines with a battery storage system – and would begin constructing it imminently. An impression of the Gawara Baya wind farm, to be located on pastoral land 65 kilometres from Queensland’s Ingham. The $1.7 billion project, with 408 megawatts of wind power capacity, will be the biggest wind farm in eastern Australia to lock in financing since 2024. Only three other smaller wind projects across the grid gained the green light in the 2026 financial year, including the Delburn wind farm in Victoria, and the Palmer and Carmodys Hill projects in South Australia. Australia recently notched a milestone in its shift to cleaner electricity, as contributions from renewables and batteries supplied an average of more than 50 per cent of nation’s main grid for a three-month period. At the same time, more than half of the remaining coal-powered generators on the eastern seaboard are scheduled to be retired in the next decade, as their ageing, emissions-intensive equipment becomes less reliable and competitive.



However, the renewable rollout continues to lag the trajectory that experts say is needed to keep within striking distance of the Albanese government’s target for 82 per cent of the grid to be green by 2030. To hit that goal, roughly 8 to 9 gigawatts of utility-scale solar and wind projects would need to come online each year, according to David Dixon, a senior renewables analyst at research firm Rystad Energy. “The most we’ve ever started construction on in a single year is approximately 4 gigawatts – most years it’s closer to three,” Dixon said. “So the pace is a long way off where it needs to be.” The shortfall of wind generation is a particular concern. While solar farms have become cheaper as the cost of panels has fallen, major financial pressures loom over wind developers amid surging costs of steel, concrete, labour and financing, as well as heightened levels of community opposition in key regional areas and long connection delays due to a congested transmission network.



Origin Energy chief executive Frank Calabria earlier this year noted that building a wind farm today was 50 per cent more expensive than it was in 2020. “Every cost line is moving in the wrong direction,” he said. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last The Clean Energy Investor Group – representing developers holding a combined $41 billion in Australian renewables assets – said the government’s recent backdown from plans to extend 30 per cent capital gains tax to foreign investors in the industry would help “crowd in” more international capital like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ investment in Gawara Baya. “An Australian project is now actually going to have legs thanks to an international funder, and one of the major reasons why is that the government has set up the right framework on tax,” the investor group’s chief executive, Richie Merzian, said. Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen on Monday said the green light for Gawara Baya showed that the government’s flagship renewable energy underwriting program, the Capacity Investment Scheme, was working.



“Today’s announcement is further proof that the Capacity Investment Scheme is working – using Australia’s sun and wind to shield our grid from global energy volatility and put downward pressure on energy bills,” he said. Related Article Renewables Australia needs more renewables. This 900-kilometre cable will help Copenhagen Infrastructure partners bought Gawara Baya from Windlab, a wind developer previously majority-owned by billionaire Andrew Forrest’s Squadron Energy. Yi-Hua Lu, a partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said the project marked a significant addition to its Australia portfolio, which also includes the proposed Star of the South offshore wind farm, off Victoria’s Gippsland coast. “The Gawara Baya project represents a significant long-term investment in Queensland, supporting regional jobs, infrastructure development and the reliable energy supply needed to underpin the state’s continued economic growth,” he said. World.title: ‘A stonking gold result’: WA tops the nation in hunt for mineral riches
World.content:
NationalWAMining ‘A stonking gold result’: WA tops the nation in hunt for mineral riches Michael Philipps August 31, 2026 — 5:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Western Australia continues to top the nation in resources exploration, with new data revealing the state is spending more than all others combined – with a particular focus on gold and iron ore. However, the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies has warned the impact of capital gains tax changes, announced in the May federal budget, are yet to trickle down. Gold was the dominant mineral exploration companies searched for over the June quarter according to the ABS. Dominic Lorrimer Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released on Monday show explorers in WA spent $843.6 million in the search for mineral deposits throughout the June quarter, taking up more than 70 per cent of the nation’s total mineral exploration expenditure. The amount spent across the nation on mineral exploration jumped almost 25 per cent compared to the previous three-month period.



Australia-wide, a total of almost $1.19 billion was spent from April to the end of June on mineral exploration, with gold taking out the majority of the spend at $565.6 million, followed by iron ore with $234.7 million and selected base metals taking out $177.9 million. Locally, WA explorers spent more than $460 million in the search for gold – a record exploration investment in the precious yellow metal since the data became available in 1988. Iron ore continued to contribute strongly to the exploration budget, with more than $230 million invested in the June quarter – and the largest amount since the March quarter of 2013. Perth-based AMEC acting chief executive Neil van Drunen said he was particularly impressed with the latest figures in terms of the gold numbers. “It’s a stonking gold result,” he said.



“Costs are going up, but people are drilling. You can’t get a drill rig at the moment for love or money, at least not for the next month or so. Editor's pick Courts WA government appeals landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, seeking ‘clarity’ on law “People are people looking for gold everywhere, which is good.” Nickel has dipped to its lowest exploration spend since March 2017, although the combined base metals figures had climbed from an eight-year low during the March quarter. However, van Drunen said the organisation’s members had not given up on nickel.



“We’ve got members that are still holding nickel assets, but people can only explore for one thing at one time,” he said. “A lot of that money that would have chased nickel is chasing gold at the moment. “So they’re drilling for gold, and that maybe they’ll drill for nickel when the price continues to rise. “There will be nickel expiration in the future, but not this quarter, and it’s hard to blame companies for that – the gold price is astronomical.” While van Drunen said the latest figures spoke of confidence within the exploration sector, he warned that there would be a significant lag effect from the federal government’s changes to CGT.



“We don’t expect it’ll affect mineral exploration statistics in this quarter or next quarter, or maybe even the quarter after that,” he said. “But by the time it comes in, it will start affecting directly into how investors choose to invest, and as a consequence, there’s going to be less cash for explorers to spend on drilling.”

World.title: ‘Joint criminal enterprise?’ Charles Perrottet denies colluding with wife to hide payments
World.content:
One-time Liberal Party powerbroker Charles Perrottet has been accused of tailoring his evidence to a corruption inquiry and “tying himself in knots” after he had previously said under oath that he had not helped his political allies with their dealings with fugitive property developer Jean Nassif. Perrottet returned on Monday to give evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption, where he said he leveraged his good relationship with Nassif to help Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis pursue money owed to their company Beckington. Charles Perrottet appeared for a second day before the ICAC. Sitthixay Ditthavong Perrottet also told the inquiry that his wife, Anita, received ongoing payments through her business Macquarie Consulting as remuneration for advice he gave to Greenwood to help Nassif, which included telling Greenwood to join the Property Council and about ways to fast-track developments. However, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, presented the evidence Perrottet had given in 2025 during a private ICAC hearing, where he was asked if he provided any assistance to Beckington for the work they did for Nassif’s construction company Toplace.



“I didn’t assist them, I don’t believe I ever assisted them with the work, but I was certainly providing advice to Jean on how to proceed on certain things,” Perrottet said in 2025. He did not mention during that hearing that his wife received ongoing payments as a result of advice he had given to Greenwood for Toplace. Charles Perrottet’s wife, Anita, also gave evidence to the ICAC last week. Louie Douvis Dwyer suggested Perrottet created a story about the advice to Greenwood, and said his 2025 evidence “just doesn’t fit” with what he told the commission on Monday. “I suggest what you are doing at the moment is tailoring your evidence on the basis of what you are seeing being put to other witnesses, including Anita,” Dwyer said. Perrottet rejected this.



Perrottet was also pressed on why he was so involved with invoices sent out by his wife’s company, which “chopped and changed”, sometimes including large bonuses and often changed structure. Those payments were “holistic”, Perrottet told the commission, meaning they contained payments for both husband and wife. The invoices were structured the way Ellis wanted them, Perrottet said. Perrottet said he was happy for his wife to invoice for payments he had earned through advice he had given to Beckington, even though he did not pay income tax on the money and his name does not appear on the invoice. Dwyer asked: “Did it occur to you that Anita was in effect obtaining a benefit by deception in setting out the invoices in this way?” Perrottet responded: “No.” She then asked: “Did it occur to you that you might be participating in a joint criminal enterprise?”



Related Article Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Charles Perrottet accused of lying to commission over contact with Jean Nassif “No,” Perrottet said. Greenwood and Ellis, along with Perrottet, are persons of interest in this inquiry, which is investigating whether Nassif, who has fled to Lebanon and is wanted on serious fraud charges, gave illegal donations to the Liberal Party. Nassif will appear from Beirut via video link on Friday. Perrottet told the commission earlier on Monday that he was at the Longueville Hotel in January 2021 when Sharangan Maheswaran, a lawyer for Nassif, passed Greenwood or Ellis a cheque for Beckington. Maheswaran is also a person of interest. Perrottet said he did not ask his friends how much money was on the cheque. They met at the pub because it was close to home, Perrottet said, and he needed somewhere nearby as he was flying to Melbourne the next day. When asked if he had a memory of the cheque being handed over to Greenwood or Ellis, Perrottet said he believed that had happened.



Dwyer then showed Perrottet pictures taken on his phone the morning after the pub meeting. There was a photo of the envelope, addressed to Beckington, with the figure of $148,000 written on the front. “If the money was handed over ... as you just said on oath, at the Longueville Hotel, then there would be no reason for you to be taking a photograph of it the next morning, would there?” Dwyer asked. “No, you are correct. I’m obviously mistaken,” Perrottet said. Perrottet then provided evidence that perhaps Greenwood was not at the pub meeting after all, and that maybe Perrottet dropped off the cheque to Greenwood’s home. Earlier, Perrottet was shown a message he sent to Nassif asking if he could meet up to receive assistance from the property developer for a preselection.



Perrottet said he was chasing unpaid money for Beckington and mentioning preselections was a way to lead Nassif to believe his money was being used to support political work. “I think I was trying to describe, you know, how he could be supportive. Like I made it up,” Perrottet said. He said he provided political updates to encourage Nassif to pay his Beckington bills, Perrottet said, but told the commission the money was not actually used as political donations. “Mr Perrottet, you are tying yourself in knots to get around obvious messages about you picking up money from Mr Nassif, is that what’s happening?” Dwyer said. “I disagree,” Perrottet said.

World.title: Government has abandoned Oscar Jenkins in Russian prison: Australian interviewer
World.content:
An Australian teacher who travelled to Russian-controlled eastern Ukraine to interview jailed foreign fighter Oscar Jenkins has urged the federal government to do more to secure his release, saying the 34-year-old appeared to have been abandoned. Mark Lowe, an English teacher and amateur journalist who has lived in Vladivostok, a port city in Russia’s far east, for four years spent two days face-to-face with Jenkins earlier this month inside the eastern Ukrainian prison where he is serving a 13-year sentence. Australian Oscar Jenkins (right) has given his first interview since he was sentenced to 13 years’ imprisonment in Russia after being captured while fighting for Ukraine. Lowe, who runs a website that reports sympathetically on Russia and Vladimir Putin’s regime, said he had spent about a year seeking to interview Jenkins and used relationships with Russian government officials who had previously been his English-language students to secure access. He told this masthead on Monday that he wanted to give Australians a different perspective on the war in Ukraine, but also wanted to ensure Jenkins, a former Melbourne Grammar student, was not forgotten. Lowe said the access had come with no conditions or pressure from Russian authorities.



“I want to open debate around him,” he said. “He’s a young Australian who I felt had been abandoned. I wanted to make sure he was OK, and I would like to see him get home, and see him happy.” Mark Lowe, an English teacher and amateur journalist based in Vladivostock. “I understand the Australian government’s stance regarding Ukraine – I have no opinion on that. But I think the Australian government owes it to him, they need to open a dialogue and start talking about him with Russia.” Jenkins was captured by Russian forces in December 2024 after joining Ukrainian troops despite having no previous military background. He was sentenced in May last year to 13 years in a maximum-security penal colony after a court in the self-declared Luhansk People’s Republic convicted him of acting as a mercenary. Jenkins also extraordinarily told Lowe in the interview he had since offered to fight for Russia.



“I’ve written a statement saying that I’d be happy to fight as a soldier for Russia,” he said. “But if they don’t trust me or for whatever reason, don’t want that, then I can understand.” Lowe said Jenkins gave no indication that he’d met with Australian government officials since being imprisoned at the gulag about 45 minutes’ drive from Luhansk, in the Russian-controlled Donbas. In the video released to the ABC, he did not ask Jenkins directly. Jenkins when he was captured by Russain soldiers. It is also unclear whether the International Committee of the Red Cross has had any access to the prison. The federal government rejected the proceedings against Jenkins last year as a “sham trial”, while Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said Jenkins is a prisoner of war and must receive the protections afforded to him under international humanitarian law.



A spokesperson at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said diplomats had consistently sought welfare updates from Russia and urged them to grant the ICRC and Jenkins’ lawyers access to him. “We have made clear Australian’s expectations that Russia fully complies with its obligations under international law, including with respect to PoWs,” he said. “We continue to request Ukraine prioritise Mr Jenkins release in a future PoW swap with Russia.” Loading Ukrainian Ambassador to Australia Vasyl Myroshnychenko said he was pleased to see Jenkins was alive. He said the Ukrainian government had made efforts to ensure he was afforded the rights of a prisoner of war but that Russia had refused to do so, in breach of the Geneva Conventions.



Myroshnychenko said Russia has not put his name forward under a people-swap deal. The Russian branch of the International Committee for the Protection of Human Rights has previously said that Jenkins might be released as part of a swap involving alleged Russian spies Kira and Igor Korolev, whose case is next heard at Brisbane Magistrates’ Court at the end of September. In the interview, Jenkins appeared gaunt, with a shaved head and wearing a prison uniform, and maintained he had never killed anyone during his time on the front line. Lowe said Jenkins had told him he had spent much of his time digging trenches and was “happy to do my 13 years because of what I have done”. Lowe has been quoted by Russian media on a handful of occasions as an “Australian international relations expert” in relation to the Jenkins case. He said last year many Australians had adopted their government’s view that Russia “is bad”.



“You will never change their minds. They are what they are,” he told Russian newspaper Izvestia last year. Lowe said he found Jenkins likeable and intelligent. “He’s quite quirky and clearly very intelligent,” he said. “The translator heard him speaking fluent Russian to his guard and mentioned that he would not have known he wasn’t a local by listening to him.” “We had a lot of discussion, I think he enjoyed seeing another Australian.” Jenkins described a highly regimented daily routine in prison, telling Lowe he rose at 5.30am to brush his teeth before the Russian anthem was played at 6am. He said he worked in a garden during the day, with lights out at 10pm. He slept in a 40-man dormitory.



Jenkins told Lowe he had decided to join Ukrainian forces after watching videos while working in China as a biology teacher. He had initially considered fighting in Myanmar against the military junta or joining the Israeli Defence Force, but chose Ukraine because it was easier to enter. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Your typical Aussie cricket boy’: Why Oscar Jenkins went to fight in Ukraine “I’m a young guy. It’s not that my life doesn’t mean anything to me, but sacrifices might need to be made. That’s still the attitude I have,” he said. Jenkins’ family in Melbourne has not publicly spoken about his plight, on advice from the Department of Foreign Affairs. The interview, which Lowe is using as the basis for a documentary, is believed to be Jenkins’ first since his conviction.



The Russian embassy in Canberra was approached for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
