World.title: ‘You can’t just say we’re evil’: Joyce backs Hanson when she says PM is inciting violence
World.content:
Pauline Hanson’s personal protection detail has increased following threats against her, as the One Nation leader claimed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had incited violence by describing her as dangerous. This masthead can reveal that Hanson’s security detail has increased from the usual two or three federal police to include as many as a dozen officers, including some undercover. Deputy leader Barnaby Joyce also has an occasional security detail, as the party’s leadership has become the target of protests following surging popularity in the polls. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Farrer MP David Farley. Dominic Lorrimer Albanese used a speech on the weekend to attack One Nation and its leader for sowing division, but Hanson fired back on Monday, just days after her party’s first successful foray into Labor heartland outside Queensland – winning the West Australian state byelection in Secret Harbour – and a Victorian campaign event where she drove a nail into, and later buried, a coffin labelled “net zero”. “The incitement that is happening is through our educational system and a prime minister who should know better than that,” Hanson said on Monday at a press conference in Gippsland, east of Melbourne, before demanding Albanese take “full responsibility” for threats made against her.



“I think he’s a pathetic prime minister. He’s not the leader of this nation. You don’t go out saying those things, and they’re all scared. They’re scared because now we’ve won a safe Labor seat, and this is worrying them.” Speaking on Sunday at Labor’s Queensland state conference, Albanese said Hanson sought “to divide Australians” and “talks Australia down both here and overseas”. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson with her party’s state leader, Warren Pickering, at Loy Yang on Monday. Joe Armao “Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems,” Albanese said. “Their own divisions and disagreements are now showing through. They think Australians are lazy and overpaid. That people working from home are bludging. That domestic violence is sometimes a woman’s fault. That we should, somehow, become a monoculture.” Joyce told this masthead that “I think we have to go back to our primal nature as Australians – laconic, cheeky, but we don’t hurt people”.



Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition “Right now you have Albanese giving a speech not on policy, but on what he believes is a fundamental character malfeasance of One Nation. That’s the wrong approach, PM. You can fight us on policy, but you can’t just say we’re evil,” Joyce said. “Remember when Mr Albanese makes a judgment about One Nation, he’s made a judgment about 30 per cent of Australia. There are parties on the ballot paper who are nut jobs and people don’t vote for them. One Nation is the most conservative party in Australia, but it’s not an evil party, it’s not promulgating hate.” Hanson cited the death of conservative British politician Ann Widdecombe as a warning over the danger of violent political rhetoric. Widdecombe was found dead in her home in July, having suffered a serious injury to her head. A man has been charged with her murder and is expected to face trial next year. Threats against MPs have been steadily escalating recently. There are about 20 ongoing court matters across the country in which people are accused of making violent threats against Albanese. Nearly 40 people have been charged with Commonwealth crimes since September last year for threatening MPs and other high office holders.



Related Article Exclusive

Right-wing extremism Pauline Hanson interviewed by far-right influencer who is now a One Nation member One of the threatened MPs, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, has been afforded additional security. Sources told this masthead Hastie believed the decision was driven by an orchestrated campaign against him online that had been fuelled by One Nation and its supporters over the Ben Roberts-Smith saga. On August 20, Perth man Anton Raymond Illich, 47, appeared in court charged with threatening to kill Hanson. He is alleged to have threatened her on Facebook, including a claim he said he would “hunt her down”. He is scheduled to appear again in October. The prime minister is travelling to the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau and did not respond.



Assistant Minister Patrick Gorman said Hanson had also sought to fan outrage and dissent. “I have found some of the stunts Hanson has done over the years, including in the Senate chamber, to be not consistent with the effort to make sure we bring Australians together and do our politics respectfully,” he said on ABC News. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce. Alex Ellinghausen “I welcome Senator Hanson in joining the government in saying we can do politics in a more respectful way, and I hope that is a standard she sets for all her MPs and all the candidates she endorses.” One Nation won the West Australian state byelection in the previously safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour on Saturday, with an enormous swing towards new MP Luke Herdegen.



Related Article Investigation

Extremism Far-right threats to kidnap Albanese, post bombs to mosques, secret chats reveal However, the day’s success was hampered by a report in The Saturday Paper that new MP David Farley was “poised” to quit the party and sit as an independent. The One Nation MP was elected in May at the Farrer byelection, the first time the party had won a seat in the House of Representatives. Farley told this masthead that “speculation of my departure from One Nation are without fact or truth” and that he remained focused on the needs of people in his seat of Farrer. “One Nation is the only political party with the political courage and tenacity to address the critical issues important to Farrer. What’s good for Farrer is good for the nation,” he said. Hanson told radio station 2GB on Monday that she had spoken to Farley on Sunday, and that he had confirmed he wouldn’t be moving to the crossbench. “David’s not going anywhere,” Hanson said. “He’s a team player.”



During her Monday press conference, Hanson railed against Labor’s renewables rollout, saying it was hampering industry, and campaigned for the rollout of nuclear energy in Victoria. Hanson and her Victorian leader Warren Pickering did not reveal costs associated with their energy policy. Loading Victorian state Energy and Resources Minister Jaclyn Symes said the state had the cheapest power in Australia because Labor has invested in renewables, the cheapest form of energy. World.title: Rock legend Angry Anderson suffers a cardiac arrest
World.content:
Updated CultureMusicAustralian music Rock legend Angry Anderson suffers a cardiac arrest Nell Geraets Updated August 31, 2026 — 4:55pm ,first published 3:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian rock legend Angry Anderson has suffered a cardiac arrest, according to a statement shared by his bandmates on Monday. The musician, who recently turned 79, is one of Australia’s most influential rock stars. He founded the band, Rose Tattoo, in 1976 and has served as its lead vocalist since. Angry Anderson of Rose Tattoo on stage in Victoria in 2025. WireImage “Your thoughts, prayers and well wishes mean more to Angry and his family than we can express. We would like to let everyone know that Angry suffered a cardiac arrest and is currently in hospital receiving treatment and the care he needs,” the members of Anderson’s band Rose Tattoo wrote on Instagram. “On behalf of Angry and his family, we would like to sincerely thank everyone for the overwhelming messages of support, love and kind words.”



The band cancelled the European leg of its One Last Ride tour this month after Anderson was hospitalised. It was set to be the band’s final tour before stepping away after more than five decades of performing live. “Angry Anderson is currently in hospital due to a medical issue,” the band said on its website on August 10. “We are absolutely devastated that we cannot continue this tour and share these remaining shows with you ... We kindly ask everyone to respect Angry’s and his family’s privacy at this time.” The band had begun its European tour in July, and had nine more shows to go before announcing the cancellation.



Loading Rose Tattoo are scheduled to return to Australia in September to perform several farewell gigs across Melbourne, Sydney, Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane. The veteran rocker was born Gary Stephen Anderson in Melbourne in 1947. Beginning in the Australian pub circuit, his music career picked up major steam when Rose Tattoo released its debut self-titled album in 1978. The record was well-received both at home and abroad, climbing to the top of UK heavy metal charts. Anderson’s solo single, Suddenly, released in 1987, became a huge success after it was played during the wedding between Scott and Charlene (played by Jason Donovan and Kylie Minogue) on the TV soap, Neighbours. The track shot to No.2 on the Australian charts at the time, and No.3 on the UK Singles Chart. Rose Tattoo released a slew of other well-known tracks with Anderson as lead vocalist, including Bad Boy for Love (1977), Rock ‘N’ Roll Outlaw (1978) and We Can’t Be Beaten (1982). In 1978, the band released the song, Nice Boys, which American rockers Guns N’ Roses famously went on to cover on their 1986 EP, Live ?!*@ Like a Suicide (and again on their 1988 EP, G N’ R Lies).



Related Article Vale Actor Tim Curry, known for stage and screen villains, dies aged 80 Rose Tattoo disbanded in 1987, though briefly reassembled in 1993 to open for Guns N’ Roses. In 1998, they officially regrouped and began touring again. Rose Tattoo was later inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2006. Beyond his music career, Anderson has also appeared on screen, most notably as Ironbar in Mad Max: Beyond Thunderdome in (1985), and on stage as King Herod in the 1992 Australian arena concert, Jesus Christ Superstar. He also became a prominent advocate for prostate cancer research after some of his bandmates died from the disease, including the group’s founding guitarist, Pete Wells. And in 1993, Anderson was made a Member of the Order of Australia for his role as a youth advocate. In Rose Tattoo’s latest statement, Anderson’s bandmates asked for privacy while thanking the fans for their ongoing support.



“At this time, we kindly ask that you please respect the privacy of Angry and his family as they focus on Angry, his treatment and his recovery,” the statement read. “We appreciate everyone’s understanding and ask that you continue to keep Angry and his family in your thoughts and prayers during the days ahead.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. World.title: Maduro flashes peace sign in prison picture
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaVenezuela crisis Maduro flashes peace sign in prison picture Iona Cleave August 31, 2026 — 4:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nicolás Maduro held up the peace sign in new photographs of him posing inside a New York federal prison. The ousted Venezuelan president, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been detained in the US for seven months after US forces captured them in a raid in Caracas in January. In a post on his official X account, the autocratic former leader wrote that he and his wife “stand firm, with our hearts full of love” as they await trial on narco terrorism and drug-trafficking charges. The ousted Venezuelan president, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been detained in the US for seven months after US forces captured them in a raid in Caracas in January. Provided In the two pictures – dated June 25 – Maduro is seen grinning as he holds up his fingers in the “V” shape while wearing a grey prison-issued tracksuit.



The post said Maduro offered the pictures as a “small gift of hope and lift” to “all the noble people who love us”. After quoting a passage from the bible, the post added: “God will provide. Venezuela will be reborn.” Related Article Updated

Venezuela crisis Trump claims US carried out strikes on Venezuela and captured president They are the first known images of him inside the Metropolitan Detention Centre in Brooklyn. It is not clear who took the photographs or how they came to be posted on social media. Maduro served as president of Venezuela for more than 10 years until the January 3 raid on Caracas, which resulted in Maduro being detained and brought to the US to face drugs and weapons charges.



He has denied all the charges and declared himself a “prisoner of war”. In April, Washington allowed Venezuela to pay for the couple’s legal defence, something previously barred under US sanctions. During Maduro’s 2013-26 presidency, he was accused of carrying out political persecution, including ordering arbitrary detentions, torture and extra-judicial killings. Both of his re-elections, in 2018 and 2024, were widely rejected as fraudulent. Since Maduro’s capture, the Trump administration appointed Delcy Rodríguez, his former vice-president and close Maduro ally, to lead the country. The US now effectively controls Venezuela’s oil revenues and reserves, with proceeds going into special accounts overseen by Washington.

World.title: Danish giant steps in to help break Australia’s wind farm drought
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesEnergy Danish giant steps in to help break Australia’s wind farm drought Nick Toscano August 31, 2026 — 5:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A decision to greenlight the eastern seaboard’s largest wind farm in more than two years has provided a much-needed boost to Australia’s renewable energy ambitions, helping to break an investment drought that has stalled the rollout of wind turbines and threatened the nation’s 2030 climate targets. Danish investment giant Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners on Monday said it had acquired the Gawara Baya wind farm in North Queensland – a project combining up to 69 wind turbines with a battery storage system – and would begin constructing it imminently. An impression of the Gawara Baya wind farm, to be located on pastoral land 65 kilometres from Queensland’s Ingham. The $1.7 billion project, with 408 megawatts of wind power capacity, will be the biggest wind farm in eastern Australia to lock in financing since 2024. Only three other smaller wind projects across the grid gained the green light in the 2026 financial year, including the Delburn wind farm in Victoria, and the Palmer and Carmodys Hill projects in South Australia. Australia recently notched a milestone in its shift to cleaner electricity, as contributions from renewables and batteries supplied an average of more than 50 per cent of nation’s main grid for a three-month period. At the same time, more than half of the remaining coal-powered generators on the eastern seaboard are scheduled to be retired in the next decade, as their ageing, emissions-intensive equipment becomes less reliable and competitive.



However, the renewable rollout continues to lag the trajectory that experts say is needed to keep within striking distance of the Albanese government’s target for 82 per cent of the grid to be green by 2030. To hit that goal, roughly 8 to 9 gigawatts of utility-scale solar and wind projects would need to come online each year, according to David Dixon, a senior renewables analyst at research firm Rystad Energy. “The most we’ve ever started construction on in a single year is approximately 4 gigawatts – most years it’s closer to three,” Dixon said. “So the pace is a long way off where it needs to be.” The shortfall of wind generation is a particular concern. While solar farms have become cheaper as the cost of panels has fallen, major financial pressures loom over wind developers amid surging costs of steel, concrete, labour and financing, as well as heightened levels of community opposition in key regional areas and long connection delays due to a congested transmission network.



Origin Energy chief executive Frank Calabria earlier this year noted that building a wind farm today was 50 per cent more expensive than it was in 2020. “Every cost line is moving in the wrong direction,” he said. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last The Clean Energy Investor Group – representing developers holding a combined $41 billion in Australian renewables assets – said the government’s recent backdown from plans to extend 30 per cent capital gains tax to foreign investors in the industry would help “crowd in” more international capital like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ investment in Gawara Baya. “An Australian project is now actually going to have legs thanks to an international funder, and one of the major reasons why is that the government has set up the right framework on tax,” the investor group’s chief executive, Richie Merzian, said. Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen on Monday said the green light for Gawara Baya showed that the government’s flagship renewable energy underwriting program, the Capacity Investment Scheme, was working.



“Today’s announcement is further proof that the Capacity Investment Scheme is working – using Australia’s sun and wind to shield our grid from global energy volatility and put downward pressure on energy bills,” he said. Related Article Renewables Australia needs more renewables. This 900-kilometre cable will help Copenhagen Infrastructure partners bought Gawara Baya from Windlab, a wind developer previously majority-owned by billionaire Andrew Forrest’s Squadron Energy. Yi-Hua Lu, a partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said the project marked a significant addition to its Australia portfolio, which also includes the proposed Star of the South offshore wind farm, off Victoria’s Gippsland coast. “The Gawara Baya project represents a significant long-term investment in Queensland, supporting regional jobs, infrastructure development and the reliable energy supply needed to underpin the state’s continued economic growth,” he said. However, the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies has warned the impact of capital gains tax changes, announced in the May federal budget, are yet to trickle down. Gold was the dominant mineral exploration companies searched for over the June quarter according to the ABS. Dominic Lorrimer Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released on Monday show explorers in WA spent $843.6 million in the search for mineral deposits throughout the June quarter, taking up more than 70 per cent of the nation’s total mineral exploration expenditure. The amount spent across the nation on mineral exploration jumped almost 25 per cent compared to the previous three-month period.



Australia-wide, a total of almost $1.19 billion was spent from April to the end of June on mineral exploration, with gold taking out the majority of the spend at $565.6 million, followed by iron ore with $234.7 million and selected base metals taking out $177.9 million. Locally, WA explorers spent more than $460 million in the search for gold – a record exploration investment in the precious yellow metal since the data became available in 1988. Iron ore continued to contribute strongly to the exploration budget, with more than $230 million invested in the June quarter – and the largest amount since the March quarter of 2013. Perth-based AMEC acting chief executive Neil van Drunen said he was particularly impressed with the latest figures in terms of the gold numbers. “It’s a stonking gold result,” he said.



“Costs are going up, but people are drilling. You can’t get a drill rig at the moment for love or money, at least not for the next month or so. Editor's pick Courts WA government appeals landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, seeking ‘clarity’ on law “People are people looking for gold everywhere, which is good.” Nickel has dipped to its lowest exploration spend since March 2017, although the combined base metals figures had climbed from an eight-year low during the March quarter. However, van Drunen said the organisation’s members had not given up on nickel.



“We’ve got members that are still holding nickel assets, but people can only explore for one thing at one time,” he said. “A lot of that money that would have chased nickel is chasing gold at the moment. “So they’re drilling for gold, and that maybe they’ll drill for nickel when the price continues to rise. “There will be nickel expiration in the future, but not this quarter, and it’s hard to blame companies for that – the gold price is astronomical.” While van Drunen said the latest figures spoke of confidence within the exploration sector, he warned that there would be a significant lag effect from the federal government’s changes to CGT.



“We don’t expect it’ll affect mineral exploration statistics in this quarter or next quarter, or maybe even the quarter after that,” he said. “But by the time it comes in, it will start affecting directly into how investors choose to invest, and as a consequence, there’s going to be less cash for explorers to spend on drilling.”

World.title: ‘Joint criminal enterprise?’ Charles Perrottet denies colluding with wife to hide payments
World.content:
One-time Liberal Party powerbroker Charles Perrottet has been accused of tailoring his evidence to a corruption inquiry and “tying himself in knots” after he had previously said under oath that he had not helped his political allies with their dealings with fugitive property developer Jean Nassif. Perrottet returned on Monday to give evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption, where he said he leveraged his good relationship with Nassif to help Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis pursue money owed to their company Beckington. Charles Perrottet appeared for a second day before the ICAC. Sitthixay Ditthavong Perrottet also told the inquiry that his wife, Anita, received ongoing payments through her business Macquarie Consulting as remuneration for advice he gave to Greenwood to help Nassif, which included telling Greenwood to join the Property Council and about ways to fast-track developments. However, counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, presented the evidence Perrottet had given in 2025 during a private ICAC hearing, where he was asked if he provided any assistance to Beckington for the work they did for Nassif’s construction company Toplace.



“I didn’t assist them, I don’t believe I ever assisted them with the work, but I was certainly providing advice to Jean on how to proceed on certain things,” Perrottet said in 2025. He did not mention during that hearing that his wife received ongoing payments as a result of advice he had given to Greenwood for Toplace. Charles Perrottet’s wife, Anita, also gave evidence to the ICAC last week. Louie Douvis Dwyer suggested Perrottet created a story about the advice to Greenwood, and said his 2025 evidence “just doesn’t fit” with what he told the commission on Monday. “I suggest what you are doing at the moment is tailoring your evidence on the basis of what you are seeing being put to other witnesses, including Anita,” Dwyer said. Perrottet rejected this.



Perrottet was also pressed on why he was so involved with invoices sent out by his wife’s company, which “chopped and changed”, sometimes including large bonuses and often changed structure. Those payments were “holistic”, Perrottet told the commission, meaning they contained payments for both husband and wife. The invoices were structured the way Ellis wanted them, Perrottet said. Perrottet said he was happy for his wife to invoice for payments he had earned through advice he had given to Beckington, even though he did not pay income tax on the money and his name does not appear on the invoice. Dwyer asked: “Did it occur to you that Anita was in effect obtaining a benefit by deception in setting out the invoices in this way?” Perrottet responded: “No.” She then asked: “Did it occur to you that you might be participating in a joint criminal enterprise?”



Related Article Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Charles Perrottet accused of lying to commission over contact with Jean Nassif “No,” Perrottet said. Greenwood and Ellis, along with Perrottet, are persons of interest in this inquiry, which is investigating whether Nassif, who has fled to Lebanon and is wanted on serious fraud charges, gave illegal donations to the Liberal Party. Nassif will appear from Beirut via video link on Friday. Perrottet told the commission earlier on Monday that he was at the Longueville Hotel in January 2021 when Sharangan Maheswaran, a lawyer for Nassif, passed Greenwood or Ellis a cheque for Beckington. Maheswaran is also a person of interest. Perrottet said he did not ask his friends how much money was on the cheque. They met at the pub because it was close to home, Perrottet said, and he needed somewhere nearby as he was flying to Melbourne the next day. When asked if he had a memory of the cheque being handed over to Greenwood or Ellis, Perrottet said he believed that had happened.



Dwyer then showed Perrottet pictures taken on his phone the morning after the pub meeting. There was a photo of the envelope, addressed to Beckington, with the figure of $148,000 written on the front. “If the money was handed over ... as you just said on oath, at the Longueville Hotel, then there would be no reason for you to be taking a photograph of it the next morning, would there?” Dwyer asked. “No, you are correct. I’m obviously mistaken,” Perrottet said. Perrottet then provided evidence that perhaps Greenwood was not at the pub meeting after all, and that maybe Perrottet dropped off the cheque to Greenwood’s home. Earlier, Perrottet was shown a message he sent to Nassif asking if he could meet up to receive assistance from the property developer for a preselection.



Perrottet said he was chasing unpaid money for Beckington and mentioning preselections was a way to lead Nassif to believe his money was being used to support political work. “I think I was trying to describe, you know, how he could be supportive. Like I made it up,” Perrottet said. He said he provided political updates to encourage Nassif to pay his Beckington bills, Perrottet said, but told the commission the money was not actually used as political donations. “Mr Perrottet, you are tying yourself in knots to get around obvious messages about you picking up money from Mr Nassif, is that what’s happening?” Dwyer said. “I disagree,” Perrottet said.

World.title: Government has abandoned Oscar Jenkins in Russian prison: Australian interviewer
World.content:
An Australian teacher who travelled to Russian-controlled eastern Ukraine to interview jailed foreign fighter Oscar Jenkins has urged the federal government to do more to secure his release, saying the 34-year-old appeared to have been abandoned. Mark Lowe, an English teacher and amateur journalist who has lived in Vladivostok, a port city in Russia’s far east, for four years spent two days face-to-face with Jenkins earlier this month inside the eastern Ukrainian prison where he is serving a 13-year sentence. Australian Oscar Jenkins (right) has given his first interview since he was sentenced to 13 years’ imprisonment in Russia after being captured while fighting for Ukraine. Lowe, who runs a website that reports sympathetically on Russia and Vladimir Putin’s regime, said he had spent about a year seeking to interview Jenkins and used relationships with Russian government officials who had previously been his English-language students to secure access. He told this masthead on Monday that he wanted to give Australians a different perspective on the war in Ukraine, but also wanted to ensure Jenkins, a former Melbourne Grammar student, was not forgotten. Lowe said the access had come with no conditions or pressure from Russian authorities.



“I want to open debate around him,” he said. “He’s a young Australian who I felt had been abandoned. I wanted to make sure he was OK, and I would like to see him get home, and see him happy.” Mark Lowe, an English teacher and amateur journalist based in Vladivostock. “I understand the Australian government’s stance regarding Ukraine – I have no opinion on that. But I think the Australian government owes it to him, they need to open a dialogue and start talking about him with Russia.” Jenkins was captured by Russian forces in December 2024 after joining Ukrainian troops despite having no previous military background. He was sentenced in May last year to 13 years in a maximum-security penal colony after a court in the self-declared Luhansk People’s Republic convicted him of acting as a mercenary. Jenkins also extraordinarily told Lowe in the interview he had since offered to fight for Russia.



“I’ve written a statement saying that I’d be happy to fight as a soldier for Russia,” he said. “But if they don’t trust me or for whatever reason, don’t want that, then I can understand.” Lowe said Jenkins gave no indication that he’d met with Australian government officials since being imprisoned at the gulag about 45 minutes’ drive from Luhansk, in the Russian-controlled Donbas. In the video released to the ABC, he did not ask Jenkins directly. Jenkins when he was captured by Russain soldiers. It is also unclear whether the International Committee of the Red Cross has had any access to the prison. The federal government rejected the proceedings against Jenkins last year as a “sham trial”, while Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said Jenkins is a prisoner of war and must receive the protections afforded to him under international humanitarian law.



A spokesperson at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said diplomats had consistently sought welfare updates from Russia and urged them to grant the ICRC and Jenkins’ lawyers access to him. “We have made clear Australian’s expectations that Russia fully complies with its obligations under international law, including with respect to PoWs,” he said. “We continue to request Ukraine prioritise Mr Jenkins release in a future PoW swap with Russia.” Loading Ukrainian Ambassador to Australia Vasyl Myroshnychenko said he was pleased to see Jenkins was alive. He said the Ukrainian government had made efforts to ensure he was afforded the rights of a prisoner of war but that Russia had refused to do so, in breach of the Geneva Conventions.



Myroshnychenko said Russia has not put his name forward under a people-swap deal. The Russian branch of the International Committee for the Protection of Human Rights has previously said that Jenkins might be released as part of a swap involving alleged Russian spies Kira and Igor Korolev, whose case is next heard at Brisbane Magistrates’ Court at the end of September. In the interview, Jenkins appeared gaunt, with a shaved head and wearing a prison uniform, and maintained he had never killed anyone during his time on the front line. Lowe said Jenkins had told him he had spent much of his time digging trenches and was “happy to do my 13 years because of what I have done”. Lowe has been quoted by Russian media on a handful of occasions as an “Australian international relations expert” in relation to the Jenkins case. He said last year many Australians had adopted their government’s view that Russia “is bad”.



“You will never change their minds. They are what they are,” he told Russian newspaper Izvestia last year. Lowe said he found Jenkins likeable and intelligent. “He’s quite quirky and clearly very intelligent,” he said. “The translator heard him speaking fluent Russian to his guard and mentioned that he would not have known he wasn’t a local by listening to him.” “We had a lot of discussion, I think he enjoyed seeing another Australian.” Jenkins described a highly regimented daily routine in prison, telling Lowe he rose at 5.30am to brush his teeth before the Russian anthem was played at 6am. He said he worked in a garden during the day, with lights out at 10pm. He slept in a 40-man dormitory.



Jenkins told Lowe he had decided to join Ukrainian forces after watching videos while working in China as a biology teacher. He had initially considered fighting in Myanmar against the military junta or joining the Israeli Defence Force, but chose Ukraine because it was easier to enter. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Your typical Aussie cricket boy’: Why Oscar Jenkins went to fight in Ukraine “I’m a young guy. It’s not that my life doesn’t mean anything to me, but sacrifices might need to be made. That’s still the attitude I have,” he said. Jenkins’ family in Melbourne has not publicly spoken about his plight, on advice from the Department of Foreign Affairs. The interview, which Lowe is using as the basis for a documentary, is believed to be Jenkins’ first since his conviction.



The Russian embassy in Canberra was approached for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘You can’t just say we’re evil’: Joyce backs Hanson when she says PM is inciting violence
World.content:
Pauline Hanson’s personal protection detail has increased following threats against her, as the One Nation leader claimed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had incited violence by describing her as dangerous. This masthead can reveal that Hanson’s security detail has increased from the usual two or three federal police to include as many as a dozen officers, including some undercover. Deputy leader Barnaby Joyce also has an occasional security detail, as the party’s leadership has become the target of protests following surging popularity in the polls. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Farrer MP David Farley. Dominic Lorrimer Albanese used a speech on the weekend to attack One Nation and its leader for sowing division, but Hanson fired back on Monday, just days after her party’s first successful foray into Labor heartland outside Queensland – winning the West Australian state byelection in Secret Harbour – and a Victorian campaign event where she drove a nail into, and later buried, a coffin labelled “net zero”. “The incitement that is happening is through our educational system and a prime minister who should know better than that,” Hanson said on Monday at a press conference in Gippsland, east of Melbourne, before demanding Albanese take “full responsibility” for threats made against her.



“I think he’s a pathetic prime minister. He’s not the leader of this nation. You don’t go out saying those things, and they’re all scared. They’re scared because now we’ve won a safe Labor seat, and this is worrying them.” Speaking on Sunday at Labor’s Queensland state conference, Albanese said Hanson sought “to divide Australians” and “talks Australia down both here and overseas”. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson with her party’s state leader, Warren Pickering, at Loy Yang on Monday. Joe Armao “Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems,” Albanese said. “Their own divisions and disagreements are now showing through. They think Australians are lazy and overpaid. That people working from home are bludging. That domestic violence is sometimes a woman’s fault. That we should, somehow, become a monoculture.” Joyce told this masthead that “I think we have to go back to our primal nature as Australians – laconic, cheeky, but we don’t hurt people”.



Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition “Right now you have Albanese giving a speech not on policy, but on what he believes is a fundamental character malfeasance of One Nation. That’s the wrong approach, PM. You can fight us on policy, but you can’t just say we’re evil,” Joyce said. “Remember when Mr Albanese makes a judgment about One Nation, he’s made a judgment about 30 per cent of Australia. There are parties on the ballot paper who are nut jobs and people don’t vote for them. One Nation is the most conservative party in Australia, but it’s not an evil party, it’s not promulgating hate.” Hanson cited the death of conservative British politician Ann Widdecombe as a warning over the danger of violent political rhetoric. Widdecombe was found dead in her home in July, having suffered a serious injury to her head. A man has been charged with her murder and is expected to face trial next year. Threats against MPs have been steadily escalating recently. There are about 20 ongoing court matters across the country in which people are accused of making violent threats against Albanese. Nearly 40 people have been charged with Commonwealth crimes since September last year for threatening MPs and other high office holders.



Related Article Exclusive

Right-wing extremism Pauline Hanson interviewed by far-right influencer who is now a One Nation member One of the threatened MPs, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, has been afforded additional security. Sources told this masthead Hastie believed the decision was driven by an orchestrated campaign against him online that had been fuelled by One Nation and its supporters over the Ben Roberts-Smith saga. On August 20, Perth man Anton Raymond Illich, 47, appeared in court charged with threatening to kill Hanson. He is alleged to have threatened her on Facebook, including a claim he said he would “hunt her down”. He is scheduled to appear again in October. The prime minister is travelling to the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau and did not respond.



Assistant Minister Patrick Gorman said Hanson had also sought to fan outrage and dissent. “I have found some of the stunts Hanson has done over the years, including in the Senate chamber, to be not consistent with the effort to make sure we bring Australians together and do our politics respectfully,” he said on ABC News. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and MP Barnaby Joyce. Alex Ellinghausen “I welcome Senator Hanson in joining the government in saying we can do politics in a more respectful way, and I hope that is a standard she sets for all her MPs and all the candidates she endorses.” One Nation won the West Australian state byelection in the previously safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour on Saturday, with an enormous swing towards new MP Luke Herdegen.



Related Article Investigation

Extremism Far-right threats to kidnap Albanese, post bombs to mosques, secret chats reveal However, the day’s success was hampered by a report in The Saturday Paper that new MP David Farley was “poised” to quit the party and sit as an independent. The One Nation MP was elected in May at the Farrer byelection, the first time the party had won a seat in the House of Representatives. Farley told this masthead that “speculation of my departure from One Nation are without fact or truth” and that he remained focused on the needs of people in his seat of Farrer. “One Nation is the only political party with the political courage and tenacity to address the critical issues important to Farrer. What’s good for Farrer is good for the nation,” he said. Hanson told radio station 2GB on Monday that she had spoken to Farley on Sunday, and that he had confirmed he wouldn’t be moving to the crossbench. “David’s not going anywhere,” Hanson said. “He’s a team player.”



During her Monday press conference, Hanson railed against Labor’s renewables rollout, saying it was hampering industry, and campaigned for the rollout of nuclear energy in Victoria. Hanson and her Victorian leader Warren Pickering did not reveal costs associated with their energy policy. Loading Victorian state Energy and Resources Minister Jaclyn Symes said the state had the cheapest power in Australia because Labor has invested in renewables, the cheapest form of energy. World.title: Rock legend Angry Anderson suffers a cardiac arrest
World.content:
Updated CultureMusicAustralian music Rock legend Angry Anderson suffers a cardiac arrest Nell Geraets Updated August 31, 2026 — 4:55pm ,first published 3:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian rock legend Angry Anderson has suffered a cardiac arrest, according to a statement shared by his bandmates on Monday. The musician, who recently turned 79, is one of Australia’s most influential rock stars. He founded the band, Rose Tattoo, in 1976 and has served as its lead vocalist since. Angry Anderson of Rose Tattoo on stage in Victoria in 2025. WireImage “Your thoughts, prayers and well wishes mean more to Angry and his family than we can express. We would like to let everyone know that Angry suffered a cardiac arrest and is currently in hospital receiving treatment and the care he needs,” the members of Anderson’s band Rose Tattoo wrote on Instagram. “On behalf of Angry and his family, we would like to sincerely thank everyone for the overwhelming messages of support, love and kind words.”



The band cancelled the European leg of its One Last Ride tour this month after Anderson was hospitalised. It was set to be the band’s final tour before stepping away after more than five decades of performing live. “Angry Anderson is currently in hospital due to a medical issue,” the band said on its website on August 10. “We are absolutely devastated that we cannot continue this tour and share these remaining shows with you ... We kindly ask everyone to respect Angry’s and his family’s privacy at this time.” The band had begun its European tour in July, and had nine more shows to go before announcing the cancellation.



Loading Rose Tattoo are scheduled to return to Australia in September to perform several farewell gigs across Melbourne, Sydney, Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane. The veteran rocker was born Gary Stephen Anderson in Melbourne in 1947. Beginning in the Australian pub circuit, his music career picked up major steam when Rose Tattoo released its debut self-titled album in 1978. The record was well-received both at home and abroad, climbing to the top of UK heavy metal charts. Anderson’s solo single, Suddenly, released in 1987, became a huge success after it was played during the wedding between Scott and Charlene (played by Jason Donovan and Kylie Minogue) on the TV soap, Neighbours. The track shot to No.2 on the Australian charts at the time, and No.3 on the UK Singles Chart. Rose Tattoo released a slew of other well-known tracks with Anderson as lead vocalist, including Bad Boy for Love (1977), Rock ‘N’ Roll Outlaw (1978) and We Can’t Be Beaten (1982). In 1978, the band released the song, Nice Boys, which American rockers Guns N’ Roses famously went on to cover on their 1986 EP, Live ?!*@ Like a Suicide (and again on their 1988 EP, G N’ R Lies).



Related Article Vale Actor Tim Curry, known for stage and screen villains, dies aged 80 Rose Tattoo disbanded in 1987, though briefly reassembled in 1993 to open for Guns N’ Roses. In 1998, they officially regrouped and began touring again. Rose Tattoo was later inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2006. Beyond his music career, Anderson has also appeared on screen, most notably as Ironbar in Mad Max: Beyond Thunderdome in (1985), and on stage as King Herod in the 1992 Australian arena concert, Jesus Christ Superstar. He also became a prominent advocate for prostate cancer research after some of his bandmates died from the disease, including the group’s founding guitarist, Pete Wells. And in 1993, Anderson was made a Member of the Order of Australia for his role as a youth advocate. In Rose Tattoo’s latest statement, Anderson’s bandmates asked for privacy while thanking the fans for their ongoing support.



“At this time, we kindly ask that you please respect the privacy of Angry and his family as they focus on Angry, his treatment and his recovery,” the statement read. “We appreciate everyone’s understanding and ask that you continue to keep Angry and his family in your thoughts and prayers during the days ahead.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Maduro flashes peace sign in prison picture
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaVenezuela crisis Maduro flashes peace sign in prison picture Iona Cleave August 31, 2026 — 4:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nicolás Maduro held up the peace sign in new photographs of him posing inside a New York federal prison. The ousted Venezuelan president, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been detained in the US for seven months after US forces captured them in a raid in Caracas in January. In a post on his official X account, the autocratic former leader wrote that he and his wife “stand firm, with our hearts full of love” as they await trial on narco terrorism and drug-trafficking charges. The ousted Venezuelan president, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been detained in the US for seven months after US forces captured them in a raid in Caracas in January. Provided In the two pictures – dated June 25 – Maduro is seen grinning as he holds up his fingers in the “V” shape while wearing a grey prison-issued tracksuit.



The post said Maduro offered the pictures as a “small gift of hope and lift” to “all the noble people who love us”. After quoting a passage from the bible, the post added: “God will provide. Venezuela will be reborn.” Related Article Updated

Venezuela crisis Trump claims US carried out strikes on Venezuela and captured president They are the first known images of him inside the Metropolitan Detention Centre in Brooklyn. It is not clear who took the photographs or how they came to be posted on social media. Maduro served as president of Venezuela for more than 10 years until the January 3 raid on Caracas, which resulted in Maduro being detained and brought to the US to face drugs and weapons charges.



He has denied all the charges and declared himself a “prisoner of war”. In April, Washington allowed Venezuela to pay for the couple’s legal defence, something previously barred under US sanctions. During Maduro’s 2013-26 presidency, he was accused of carrying out political persecution, including ordering arbitrary detentions, torture and extra-judicial killings. Both of his re-elections, in 2018 and 2024, were widely rejected as fraudulent. Since Maduro’s capture, the Trump administration appointed Delcy Rodríguez, his former vice-president and close Maduro ally, to lead the country. The US now effectively controls Venezuela’s oil revenues and reserves, with proceeds going into special accounts overseen by Washington.

World.title: Sailors to make Cook Islands stopover after 53 years
World.content:
Veterans return to Pacific over 50 years after observing nuclear testing Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

It is a trip more than 50 years in the making.

Two New Zealand frigates were sent to the Pacific to observe and protest French nuclear testing at Mururoa Atoll in 1973, exposing 500 sailors to radiation.

One of the frigates - the HMNZS Canterbury - was invited to Rarotonga on the way back, but the ship's captain decided to head home.

Nineteen veterans who witnessed the tests are now finally heading to the Cook Islands for one last tour of duty together.

A nuclear explosion at Mururoa atoll in 1971, France stopped atmospheric testing in the Pacific in 1974. Photo credit:AFP AFP

'It was like a desert up there'

Prime Minister Norman Kirk farewelled HMNZS Otago before it headed to the Pacific to bear witness to the atmospheric testing.

HMNZS Canterbury was redirected from Honolulu for the same reason and in late July 1973 its crew saw a French test, from about 30 kilometres away.

Ant Kennedy - who turned 20 during the trip - remembers the sound.

Ant Kennedy got married before the Canterbury headed to the Pacific. Supplied

"I got up there just as the cloud was melting away, as it were, but apparently it wasn't quite as well formed as the Otago explosion," he told RNZ from his home in Whataroa on the West Coast.

"And I thought perhaps something might have gone wrong with the test.""

Like many, he did not appreciate the risks of what they were exposed to.

"At the time, the thing that stood out for me was it was a bit like a desert up there.

"There was no birds. Usually you'll see some sort of fish life, but there was none, so it was a really bleak place.

"I often thought afterwards, 'There's a reason for that. There's some reason for there being no bird life or sea life around it'."

Christchurch man Paddy Long - now known for his steel guitar playing - was also among the crew who viewed the test from the Canterbury's helicopter deck.

"We didn't actually have much in the way of protection at all for the whole trip, other than a little, what they called, a dosimeter,

"This was, in essence, a little blue plastic disk with a little litmus paper in it pinned to my shorts and, supposedly, if that was to change colour we should all get below deck fairly quickly."

Radiation alarm turned off

Radio mechanic Steve Aldridge was aware of the risks of radiation and said the Canterbury itself offered its crew protection, if warnings were acted on.

He remembers one occasion where they were not.

"We were having a BBQ on the flight deck - 44-gallon drums cut in half that they could BBQ on and a few beers, and a few rums.

"I got called to the bridge because an alarm was going off. It was a radiation alarm."

But there was no concern from his superiors, Aldridge said.

Paddy Long during the 1973 deployment. Supplied

"I said to the officer watch, 'I think you should clear the upper deck'. And he said, 'I'll make decisions like that. Just stop that noise. I can't hear myself think.'

"I said, 'Well, sir, to stop it, I'm going to have to disconnect the battery and disconnect the power supply to it. You'd better give me a direct order because I don't think I should do that'."

He received the order.

Aldridge - who lives in Auckland - thinks that given the timing, the Canterbury was sailing through fallout from the test the Otago witnessed.

The trip has had consequences for many down the years, including Long, who have battled cancers.

"I have had quite a long history with skin cancers. But, a lot of people have had a lot worse than that. So I can probably say I'm one of the lucky ones," Long said.

"I've just had another round of having a few bits and pieces surgically removed, but it's a constant maintenance thing with me. Other than that, I've been pretty good."

Aldridge said a high proportion of his children, with different partners, had autism or related conditions, leading him to think he was the common thread, and the reason was the radiation.

Veterans' health is covered by the government, but that was not the case for their children and grandchildren.

Kennedy is co-president of the Mururoa Nuclear Veterans Group, which is battling for change there.

Still going strong

For him, the trip away in 1973 has extra special memories from the Canterbury's time in Honolulu.

"Well, I got married. Yeah, against some advice, but we're still married today, so it was a good decision."

It was a whirlwind romance for Kennedy and his wife Stasia. Now, she will accompany him on the six-night visit to Rarotonga leaving on Tuesday.

Kennedy said that had come about because some former sailors have decided to take up the 1973 invitation to visit from then-Cook Islands Prime Minister Sir Albert Henry.

Although, Aldridge remembers the Canterbury maybe was not that welcome, saying while the trip was intended, the Cook Islands decided the vessel was radioactive.

"Otago came back and had a ticker-tape parade. We came back to some stale sandwiches the politicians were all eating in the overseas terminal."

This year's visit includes a presentation to the Cook Islands RSA as a thanks for the country's support in 1973.

It is a trip Long says he can not miss.

"Surprisingly, it'll be my first trip to Rarotonga. I've been to just about every other Pacific Island imaginable, so that'll be nice.

"It'll be all a new experience for me in the travelling department. We've got a bit of fishing organised and plus that night at the RSA will be quite memorable, I'm sure.

"Other than that, it'll be about enjoying some warm weather and having a few cold beers with my mates. It'll be great."

Long may also get a chance to reminisce on the time he appeared on Radio New Zealand back home, instead of government minister Fraser Colman.

Colman would spent a large part of his day giving interviews from around the world and it was Long's job to organise the connections.

One night Colman was not feeling great, so disappeared early, leaving Long to put on his best impression to unsuspecting listeners back home.

"I was pretty good at doing accents. Incidentally, when I got out of the navy, I ended up working for Radio New Zealand in Christchurch for about 16 years, but as a network engineer, rather than an announcing job."

France conducted almost 200 nuclear tests in the area between 1966 and 1996. About a quarter of these were atmospheric.

World.title: Emergency services battle Tauhara blaze in dry conditions
World.content:
Firefighters are still working to extinguish a large scrub fire in Tauhara near Taupō.

Fire and Emergency said it received multiple 111 calls reporting the blaze, which was about 150 metres in length, around 2.25pm on Monday.

Shift manager Lauren Sika told RNZ two helicopters were in the air at the peak of the blaze, which was threatening a nearby building.

She said the fire was esclated to second alarm, pulling in more crews, but has since been scaled back.

Sika said three ground crews were still in attendance and the fire was yet to be extinguished.

Police said the fire was first reported around 2.45pm.

World.title: Hawke's Bay community makes big effort to restore native A'Deane's Bush
World.content:
Rural Hawke's Bay community working hard to restore native bush Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A small community in rural Hawke's Bay is working hard to restore a large area of precious native bush that's home to one of New Zealand's largest Totara trees, a colony of threatened long tail bats and a rare native mistletoe.

A'Deane's Bush is the best remaining example of the original podocarp forest of the Ruataniwha Plains. Conservation powerhouse Kay Griffiths is the driving force behind the restoration project, which is funded by local landowners John and Jay Benton.

"The aim of 'Friends of A'Deane's Bush' has always been to have a bush where the fauna and flora that's characteristic of this kind of lowland podocarp forest that's acutely threatened - that those plants and animals that belong in there are flourishing," said Griffiths.

The Totara tree in A'Deanes Bush is one of New Zealand's largest and thought to be over 600 years old, standing at over 33 metres tall with a girth of 8.8 metres. Alexa Cook/RNZ

A'Deane's Bush was once part of the massive Ashcott Station and cattle grazed around the edges of the bush. In the 1980's the farm owner threatened to chop the bush down and convert it into more grazing, but was luckily persuaded to sell it to the Department of Conservation instead.

Then 18 years ago the Benton's and Kay Griffiths joined forces with DOC and signed a management agreement to restore the area.

"Ours was the very first one to go across the minister's desk, and now it's become the norm.

"It's successful because we have ongoing funding from John and Jay Benton. We don't have to go looking for extra funding every five minutes, which is very time consuming," said Griffiths.

A small community in rural Hawke's Bay is working hard to restore a large area of precious native bush. Alexa Cook/RNZ

Over the years the group, along with others in the community, have cleared large areas of blackberry and put thousands of plants in the ground.

At 40 hectares in size, A'Deane's is much larger than other pockets of protected bush in the area, and is a special habitat for various creatures and critters.

"It's only these big bits of bush that hold the key to biodiversity. So we've got a colony of long tailed bats that utilise this area for maternity roosting and breeding. 80 percent of their roosts are in this bit of bush and then 20 percent of them are in the 2000 hectares around.

"That just shows you why the 40 hectares is actually so important. It means that we can focus our pest control in this area knowing we are protecting about 80 percent of the roosts," said Griffiths.

The surrounding land is owned by the White family, and Larry White said protecting the bush is a priority.

"A lot of the pest control happens on our land around here, there are traps set everywhere. Without that buffer zone around it the pests are going to come up," he said.

Jane and Larry White own the surrounding land and are part of 'Friends of A'Deane's Bush'. Alexa Cook/RNZ

About 500 to 700 plants are planted each year during community planting days, and by students from Sherwood School.

"The idea is to just increase the habitat. The local school is heavily involved, they've got a shade house and they grow plants. The kids come down and do two or three plantings a year.

"Some of those kids are here today, they've grown up planting and know exactly what they are doing because they've been doing it since they were five - it's so cool," said Griffiths.

Seven-year-old Lottie White is an expert planter, having learnt through Sherwood School planting days since she was five. Alexa Cook/RNZ

This is something local DOC ranger Claire Grant is also thrilled about.

"These community days of bringing people together to do this mahi is really important to keep people engaged and interested and connected with their environments and with nature for the long term," said Grant.

Hawke's Bay DOC Ranger Claire Grant. Alexa Cook/RNZ

Others at the community planting day have travelled from further afield, such as 86-year-old Teresa Hurst from Hastings.

"I've worked on the land all my life. I've been at Forest and Bird for 26 years and I've been volunteering for DOC for 26 years.

"I just love nature and helping out," she said.

Teresa Hurst travelled nearly an hour to help with the A'Deane's Bush community planting day Alexa Cook/RNZ

The Flynn family from Maraekākaho were there too, making the most of the sunny Sunday weather.

"This is actually our first time doing this as a family so it's really exciting. Seersha is working towards her Duke of Edinburgh so this is what we're doing to tick away at our community hours for that," said Jayme Flynn.

Seersha, Brent and Jayme Flynn enjoying a family day out planting natives. Alexa Cook/RNZ

The group, 'Friends of A'Deane's Bush', has recently become an incorporated society to give the project longevity and the ability to source funding in future from other places.

"You just have to keep going and that can often be overlooked as well because it's very easy to start something, but to keep going for 18 years and keep having the enthusiasm and keep having this amazing number of people turning up to help us is pretty cool," said Griffiths.

A promising sign that the bush is flourishing, are the insects that Griffiths has found using 'insect tree wraps' to see what is living there.

Kay Griffiths from the Conservation Company is the powerhouse behind the A'Deane's Bush restoration project. Alexa Cook/RNZ

"We go around and check them and have a look at the different kinds of insects that are in them and we have things like peripatus that are in there, which is a velvet worm.. that's a sign that our pest control is working really well because they are very vulnerable to predation, particularly from rats."

Griffiths has also shown the Sherwood School students how to use light traps, which tells them what insects are in the middle of the forest versus out in the nearby farmland.

"Out in the open paddock you get thousands of the same kind because we've got a monoculture there, but in here you get lots and lots of different species, but not very many of them, that's the diversity.

"Then in the middle you get a real mix of the two. So we really are changing the diversity by doing these sorts of plantings... and that's all food that bats eat," she said.

World.title: Snow closes highway in South Island, power restored to most in Hawke's Bay
World.content:
Heavy snow closed roads and highways in the South Island on Monday while strong winds buffeted Hawke's Bay in the north, leaving hundreds without electricity and fire crews battling vegetation fires.

Dunedin hit with snow flurries and icy temperatures Checkpoint Download MP3 2m

State Highway 1 between Dunedin and Waitati (north of Dunedin) was closed due to snow on Tuesday morning but it had reopened by mid-afternoon with travellers still urged to take extra care on the route.

Earlier in the day roading crews were out helping people who were stuck in cars on SH1.

Driver Amy Turoa said she was heading south on State Highway 1 when traffic came to a standstill for about 30 minutes.

"It's probably the heaviest snow I've been in, it just came down so fast," she said.

Turoa said when things started slowly moving again she could see dozens of cars stuck in the opposite direction and a truck and trailer that had slid into a ditch.

"The snow plow came through maybe three times and now we're just following all the other trucks. We've probably passed maybe 40 cars waiting," she said.

Snow at Flagstaff, Dunedin. Tess Brunton / RNZ

Although SH1 has now reopened, SH87 from Outram to Middlemarch, in Otago, is set to remain closed overnight because of snow.

SH94 Te Anau to Milford Sound was expected to remain open overnight, but with snow forecast to continue throughout the day, disruptions and temporary closures were possible while snow clearing machinery is working.

The snow wasn't bad news for everyone though, one Dunedin dogwalker said his dogs loved a snow day.

In the South Island, MetService has issued road snowfall warnings for Lewis, Arthur's, Porters and Lindis Pass, as well as Crown Range Road, Milford Road and Dunedin to Waitati Highway and they are set to expire between 6pm and 11pm on Monday.

There is also a snowfall warning for the Desert Road in the North Island from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday and it says around 1cm could accumulate above 800 metres.

MetService forecasts that snow could lower to near sea level in Dunedin and Clutha on Monday night.

"Keep an eye on the snow level in your local forecast if you're planning to drive, especially in Dunedin and Clutha Monday evening, and keep up with any updates on road conditions from NZTA Waka Kotahi and local council or emergency management," MetService meteorologist Ethan Walton-Jones advised.

Snow in Dunedin's Halfway Bush. Vyshak Mohan / SUPPLIED

Strong winds cut power, fan fires in Hawke's Bay

Meteorologists said strong winds around Hawke's Bay were forecast to last until Monday evening.

An orange strong wind watch for for Hawke's Bay south of Hastings and the Tararua district is in place until 7pm.

Severe gale westerlies gusting 120km/h were expected in exposed places.

Firefighters tackle vegetation fires in Hawke's Bay. Hawke's Bay - Fire and Emergency

Earlier on Monday hundreds of homes in Hawke's Bay were without power due to the weather, but that had reduced to less than 100 Unison customers by Monday afternoon.

At one stage fire crews were struggling with four vegetation fires in the region that were being fanned by the high winds.

Twenty-two trucks were working across two of the fires earlier on Monday and then called in extra personnel and appliances to deal with another two fires.

By Monday afternoon, the service said two fires on Swamp Road in Ongaonga had been extinguished after tree stumps and slash caught fire.

Fires at Argyll Road and White Road have been extinguished except for one on Argyll Road that's still being monitored.

Fire crews have handed a fire at Maharakeke Road back to the landowner for monitoring.

World.title: Mike's Metres: Canterbury cancer survivor skiing to fundraise $58k for others in treatment
World.content:
Blood cancer suvivor raising money for other patients through skiing Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

A Canterbury based skier has only just recovered from his blood cancer but is already hitting the slopes to raise money for others travelling for treatment.

A few years ago Mike Wilwert was diagnosed with blood cancer and spent almost a year at Ranui House, which provides free and subsidised accommodation for families travelling to Christchurch for medical treatment.

Wilwert, who was living in Methven at the time, said Ranui House had become even more than a "home away from home".

"It gave me a chance to heal while I was going through my chemo treatments... but also it gave my wife a sense of calm and serenity in this maddening world of treatments and not being about to go home."

Having spent 17 seasons as a ski instructor at Mt Hutt and 30 more seasons in Utah's Park City, Wilwert decided to use his passion for skiing and raise donations for a place that helped him in a time of need.

Mike Wilwert spent 17 seasons as a ski instructor at Mt Hutt. SUPPLIED

So, he started Mike's Metres, were every metre he skis will benefit families staying at Ranui House.

His goal is to complete 100,000 vertical metres and raise $58,140, which is how much it would have cost to stay at Ranui House for the ten months he spent there.

He thinks it would take him about 20 more days to complete the challenge.

What makes Wilwert's goal even more impressive is that he's still undergoing treatment to keep the cancer in remission and his kidneys from failing.

"My health is doing quite well considering I have bone marrow cancer and kidney failure. I do my kidney treatment three to four times a week and I still take maintenance drugs to help keep the cancer in remission."

He said he was at about 80 percent of where he was before and felt that this was now the "new norm".

Mike Wilwert spent more than ten months at Ranui House with his wife Kate by his side. SUPPLIED

He still has to travel to Christchurch for dialysis treatment, but now that he lives in Rolleston the trip is easier.

Before being diagnosed and while living in Methven he was skiing five to seven times a week but now with his location and treatments he is on the slopes three or four times on a good week and about twice on a bad week.

"It's always great to give back ... its giving other families a chance to experience Ranui House if they go through these really bad, horrible situations."

World.title: Crown alleges minor traffic accident led to murder as Lok Fung Lorrence Li trial begins
World.content:
How does a minor traffic accident lead to double murder?

That is what Crown prosecutors have put forward as their version of events in the trial of Lok Fung Lorrence Li.

Li is accused of murdering Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong at their Ellerslie home in November 2023.

In the High Court at Auckland on Monday, Li entered guilty pleas through an interpreter to manslaughter, while pleading not guilty to murdering the couple.

Li also pleaded not guilty to a charge of conspiring to murder another person, who has name suppression.

He had been charged alongside another man, Shu Man Poon, who jurors were told earlier admitted to his role in the murder.

Poon was expected to give evidence later in Li's trial.

Prosecutor Harrison Bell gave jurors the Crown's account of the night of the murder.

Kwok, who was a theatre nurse at Auckland's North Shore Hospital, had arrived home from work late the night before the murder.

Two hours later, the Crown said Li along with Poon arrived in a car with a stolen license plate, went into the home, and attacked Kwok.

Kwok was shot an air gun, and stabbed four times in the chest and once in the neck, killing him, Bell said.

Mei Han Chong who was also in the home was killed by blunt force trauma to the head, before being taken out to Greenhithe on the city's North Shore, where her body was dumped, the Crown submitted.

"What possessed these men to act in such a violent way, killing two people?" Bell asked.

"The Crown says the answer begins with Mr Li."

Bell said about 11 months earlier, Li and Kwok had been involved in a traffic accident.

Li was told by Kwok's insurance that he was at fault, and the issue was taken to the Disputes Tribunal.

"The Crown says as a result of that grievance and having received the Kwok's home address from disclosure received from the Disputes Tribunal proceedings, Mr Li decided to go to the Kwok's address, intending to kill them, and he enlisted the assistance of Mr Poon in doing so," Bell said.

Bell explained that Kwok was found by his son, who was expecting a visit from his parents in Hamilton.

"He entered the house, saw his father lying on the floor with the smell of death, as he describes it," Bell said.

The trial was also expected to go through a conspiracy between Poon and Li to murder another person, going so far as to travel to her property and spray paint over the security cameras, before being interrupted by a vehicle on the street, Bell said.

Li had received an email from the Disputes Tribunal earlier that same day, with the Kwok's address attached, he said.

"Mr Li's murderous plan shifted at that point from [the person] to the Kwok's, or to Mr Kwok and anyone else they might encounter in his house," the Crown submitted.

It was the Crown's case that Li was not a bystander in the murder, but in fact the instigator of the murders.

"It might be suggested to you that this was all Mr Poon and that Mr Li did not knowingly participate in making the plan or assist in any way with the killings of the Kwoks as alleged by the Crown," Bell said.

"The evidence, once you've heard it all, you may agree, does not support that proposition."

The Crown could not say which of the two men dealt the fatal blows to the Kwok's, but did not need to, Bell said.

One of Li's defence lawyer, Rosemary Thomson, told jurors what happened to the Kwok's was a tragedy, that should never have happened.

"There is nothing that I'm going to say in my opening or indeed the defence is going to say throughout the trial which should in any way suggest otherwise," she said.

She pointed the jury to Li's guilty plea of manslaughter.

"Mr Li has taken responsibility for his actions and accepts that he played a role."

Thomson said Li did not have the necessary intention to commit the murders.

"The trial will therefore proceed on the basis that it will be a matter for you whether the Crown can establish a murderous intent."

Thomson urged jurors to keep an open mind.

"All trials have two sides," she said.

"As judges, you need to keep an open mind until you have heard all of the evidence and the legal directions from Her Honour.

"It is only then you can start reaching some conclusions."

The trial is set to hear from its first witnesses on Tuesday.

Manslaughter within murder

Li had entered guilty pleas on Monday morning to manslaughter for both of the victims, despite not having those charges read out in the courtroom.

Justice Jane Anderson explained to the jury that every murder charge included within it a charge of manslaughter.

She said murder had three elements, the killing of one person by another, that the killing was done by an unlawful act, and intent.

"Not all homicides are blame worthy," she said.

"However, the criminal law intervenes when a homicide is caused by an unlawful act."

World.title: Patients going blind, 36,000 overdue for tests amid high demand
World.content:
More than 20,000 people overdue for eye appointments Nine To Noon Download MP3 12m

*Correction: The number for outstanding follow ups has been updated as more accurate figures were provided.

Tens of thousands of people are overdue ophthalmology appointments in the public system and doctors are aware of patients going blind because of waiting too long.

Ophthalmology New Zealand chair Dr Sonya Bennett told Nine to Noon doctors were struggling with a "tsunami" of increased demand from an ageing population, poor IT systems, and staff shortages.

Bennett said as of February this year there were 125,105 outstanding Health New Zealand follow-ups in the ophthalmology service. Of those patients, 36,306 had been waiting 50 percent longer than the doctor recommended and 20,280 had been waiting 100 percent longer.

"We see, as hospital specialists, we see patients who haven't been seen in a timely fashion and they're losing vision, and it really concerns us."

Health New Zealand said it was working to improve access and cut waiting times, including by recuiting for vacancies and using community based models of care.

It acknowledged demand for eye health services continued to grow as the population aged and more people need treatment and monitoring for conditions.

Director national clinical networks Mary Cleary-Lyons said it did not keep figures on the number of people with deteriorating or lost vision as a result of long wait times.

"Clinical services routinely assess and prioritise patients based on urgency and risk, and patients whose condition changes are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider so that their clinical priority can be reviewed."

Bennett said these were often patients who had long term chronic diseases.

An ageing population meant there were many with age related issues such as cataracts, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration.

"So especially important for patients with glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration... these patients have recommended time frames to make it a safe estimate between when they're seeing the specialist.

"But if they're not being seen within that time frame, the risk of them having disease progression that goes on to lose vision that we can't bring back is very real."

Auckland and the Northern region were seeing some of the worst wait times with an increase of 4 percent in the last couple of years, with most other parts increasing by 2 percent, Bennett said.

"I was just having a chat with a colleague in Waikato, and he was saying that they have 3000 overdue follow-ups, that are over the 50 percent threshold.

"So it really is an indication of a system failure, which is multifactorial."

She said doctors were trying to use any recourses they have to reduce the wait times, including utilising allied health professionals.

This meant getting patients seen by optometrists, ophthalmic technicians or nurses, often in clinics called "imaging clinics".

"We have senior nurses who run age-related macular degeneration review clinics... However, we just don't have enough people that we're allowed to hire to get through the work."

She said aside from the ageing population there was a lack of investment in both person power and specialists.

Bennett said only 80 percent of specialist positions were filled in the country, with a lack of sufficient optometrists, nurses, technicians, and admin support staff within the departments.

"This is a tsunami. With a tsunami, you get ongoing, relentless increase in numbers, and you can't escape it."

"Apparently, the government says that we don't have a hiring freeze. However, the reality is that it's nigh impossible to employ new people. There's a lack of investment in the physical structures... We also have a lack of investment in our IT infrastructure."

She said patients who suffered the consequences of long wait times, such as vision loss, needed support systems which come can come at a high economic cost.

"In terms of the economic cost, it's much cheaper to actually put adequate funding into a public health system than have people end up with poor vision and try to look after them at the other end."

"We actually need cross-party support for a significant and sustained increase in funding for eye health care in the public sector."

Health New Zealand's Mary Cleary-Lyons said work was being done with the Eye Health National Clinical Network and local services as an attempt to improve access to and reduce waiting times.

"Work is underway to reduce variation in access across the country, strengthen clinical pathways, support greater integration between hospital and community-based services, and improve digital infrastructure."

"This includes expanding opportunities for shared care with community optometrists where clinically appropriate, reviewing follow-up pathways for lower-risk patients, and supporting nationally consistent approaches to triage and prioritisation."

World.title: Farmers to fund OSPRI's new NAIT software and $1.38m undercollection with levy hike
World.content:
Farmers are facing higher levies for a mandatory livestock tracing programme from Tuesday, despite most opposing cost increases.

OSPRI - funded by industry and government - runs the National Animal Identification and Tracing (NAIT) programme, tracking livestock movements for biosecurity and animal disease management.

Its board decided to raise prices for NAIT ear tags by 39 percent to $1.35 for deer and cattle, and slaughter fees up 28 percent to $1.91 per cattle beast, from 1 September.

During consultation in June and July, levy increase proposals were supported by industry groups like DairyNZ and Beef and Lamb New Zealand.

But 63 percent of 69 submitters - including farmers and meat processors - opposed them, due to concerns about affordability, governance and confidence in delivery.

Deputy chief executive Simon Andrew said it made the decision around levies carefully.

"There were mixed views on the levy increases itself, and that's understandable in terms of an added cost of their business," he said.

"So we had to balance those concerns around the affordability themselves with our responsibility to modernise the NAIT system and maintain a fit for purpose and reliable traceability system."

OSPRI deputy chief executive Simon Andrew. SUPPLIED/CATHERINE CATTANACH

Levies would help fund a new replacement software for the NAIT service.

Earlier reports cited concerns about the current platform's unsatisfactory farmer user experience, frustrating technological barriers to compliance and limited data access.

Andrew said it was working with an experienced New Zealand third party provider - which he did not name - to build and develop the new software.

"First and foremost, it's going to be modernised to the point that it's enhanced for modern-day applications, whether that's on your phone, a tablet or your desktop computer.

"The current system is not effective in terms of that particular situation. It's very clunky to use on your phone, for example."

Andrew said it would have guided workflows for required actions for its users, and link up with other third-party integrators, like the Livestock Improvement Corporation's MINDA herd management system, among others.

West Otago sheep farmer Mike McElrea of Tapanui agreed the NAIT software was hard to use for particular functions like downloading information, that he hoped would improve.

Farming an area once considered a bovine tuberculosis (TB) buffer zone in the 1990s, he said disease testing was most important.

However he said testing was not as frequent as it should be, which representatives told him were due to funding issues.
