OSPRI faced a $1.38 million funding shortfall due to historic undercollections of beef and dairy levies, that new levy revenue would address.

Levies would help fund a new replacement software for the NAIT service. SUPPLIED/OSPRI NZ

Andrew said levies were based on forecast slaughter numbers, which did not always line up.

"The levy increases are also on the basis of undercollection and recovering undercollection in terms of the levy previously," he said.

"It's important that we go through a reconciliation process and set the levies based on that moving forward as well."

The consultation document said it would contribute levies to the undercollections to "restore the intended funding contribution split between industry and government."

OSPRI also worked to tackle bovine tuberculosis in livestock herds by controlling possums, a common vector of the disease, in addition to Mycoplasma Bovis testing and surveillance.

Recently, OSPRI announced changes to its TB-Free programme, including carrying out less blanket testing across all farms in surveillance areas and doing more testing in higher risk areas it said would reinvest savings back into possum controls.

There were 17 herds infected with TB nation-wide, including five in Hawke's Bay, four in Waikato, three in Otago, and one herd each in Bay of Plenty, Canterbury, Manawatū-Whanganui, Marlborough and the West Coast.

World.title: Cats claim they are not distracted by concussion controversy
World.content:
Geelong midfielder Tom Atkins is adamant the club's concussion saga has not been a distraction for the players as they prepare for Friday night's elimination final against Carlton at the MCG.

The Cats were last week fined $140,000 for failing to officially inform the AFL about the concussion waiver in Jake Kolodjashnij's contract.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

The penalty is $100,000 plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

Asked on Monday whether he or another player had a discussion around a similar concussion agreement, Atkins said: "No."

"Our focus has been performing on the weekends and we just wanted to make sure Kola [Kolodjashnij] was all right as teammates and as friends," Atkins said.

Voss assesses Blues' finals hopes Michael Voss speaks about the Blues' chances in the finals following their stunning turnaround.

"That's probably the extent of the detail that we looked into it as players."

Atkins said it was "awesome" to have Kolodjashnij around the club, now the finals had arrived.

"Obviously we'd love him to be back playing and back in training, but hopefully that can get itself sorted soon," Atkins said.

"But just having him in the rooms and seeing him smiling again is good."

AAP

World.title: Ex-Carlton coach Voss gives assessment of Blues' finals hopes
World.content:
Michael Voss has stopped short of declaring Carlton a genuine premiership threat but sees no reason his former team cannot make a deep run in the finals.

The Blues are riding a wave of momentum under Josh Fraser, who has engineered a remarkable turnaround since taking the coaching reins when Voss stepped down in May.

Fraser has won 11 of 14 matches at the helm, capped off by the come-from-behind victory over Melbourne in last week's wildcard encounter.

The staggering run has optimistic Carlton fans daring to dream of a first premiership since 1995, ahead of an elimination final against Geelong at the MCG on Friday night.

But with another three wins required in sudden-death matches just to reach the grand final, Voss said a drought-breaking flag was most likely beyond the Blues this year.

"It's very hard, isn't it? Percentages say that's a tough gig," Voss said.

"But they're certainly playing a high level of football if you look over the course of the last 10 or 11 weeks.

"They're the equal-form team of the competition, so there should be no reason that they can't look at every game and say that it's winnable."

The Blues ended the Demons' season last Saturday night. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Voss fell on his sword at Carlton after a 1-8 (win-loss record) start to the season and is determined to look forward rather than back at what might have been.

He said Fraser was "doing a great job" as coach and results showed "the right decision has been made" in appointing the former Collingwood ruck as Blues coach.

Voss lauded captain Patrick Cripps and leaders of the playing group for their efforts in turning Carlton's season around.

"One of my last messages with the leaders was: 'It's over to you and how do you make this a really player-led group?'" Voss said.

"They've clearly done that and more numbers are coming with them, so the heavy lifting isn't just on a few.

"You've got a lot of people responding and there's some pretty incredible human beings amongst that group.

"I'm just really pleased that they're getting the rewards that they've obviously been working really hard for."

Voss says Carlton in a better place than when he took charge Michael Voss has struck a defiant tone after leaving Carlton, insistent the AFL club is in better shape than when he started as coach.

Carlton has won three of its past four meetings with Geelong, with Voss noting extra attention on key Cats duo Tom Stewart and Gryan Miers had served them well.

Voss said the Blues' work in the contested areas of the game would hold them in good stead.

"Where Geelong are underestimated quite a fair bit is their contested game," he said.

"They're not so much dominant when it comes to stoppages, but they are post-stoppage.

"Carlton can do that blindfolded and they showed that again on the weekend against Melbourne.

"When the whips were cracking they really ramped that part of the game up.

"Because they match up really well against that, they actually put themselves in a really good position to win games."

AAP

World.title: Knight's prop cops season-ending ban after send-off
World.content:
Jacob Saifiti's NRL season is all but over after the Newcastle prop was handed a four-game suspension for a high tackle on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii.

Saifiti was sent off in the first half of Sunday's 46-32 defeat in Auckland and was handed a grade two reckless high tackle charge by the NRL's match review committee on Monday morning.

The Knights have a bye for the final round of the regular season, meaning Saifiti's ban will only kick in for their first finals game.

Newcastle — currently sitting seventh — will play an elimination final in week one but even if they were to upset the odds and qualify for the grand final, the Fijian prop would still be on the sidelines.

Saifiti's only hope of playing in the NRL again this season hinges on the prop contesting the charge at the judiciary on Tuesday in a bid to reduce his punishment.

Should the front-rower fight the suspension and lose his appeal, he will have another week added to his four-game ban.

Elsewhere, Cronulla prop Tom Hazelton is set to miss Cronulla's final regular season game against Melbourne after being cited for a hip-drop tackle on Ronald Volkman.

Hazelton was sin-binned by referee Ashley Klein late in Sunday's loss to Parramatta but will serve a one-game ban with an early guilty plea and be free to return for week one of the finals series.

AAP

World.title: Indigenous numbers in the AFL are down, but there's talent in the Top End
World.content:
A couple of years ago Hawthorn's Kaitlyn Ashmore, a Dja Dja Wurrung woman, spent some time in Alice Springs.

She was immediately taken by the gift for footy so many kids had up there, but knew the pathways for development were limited.

"I've been out to the communities … the talent up there is incredible," Ashmore said on the eve of the AFLW's Indigenous Round.

"But it's just getting them down here, or getting them in a program, and then keeping them in there and making them feel culturally safe."

Loading Instagram content

She was in the Red Centre in support of the Dreamtime Academy, an initiative founded by AFLW player Lulu Pullar along with fellow First Nations players Courtney Hodder, a Badimaya and Whadjuk woman, and Ally Anderson, a Ghungalu and Wakka Wakka woman.

There are 22 Indigenous players listed across the AFLW competition, down from 26 in 2023. In the men's competition the number has dropped from 87 in 2020 to 62 this season.

Ashmore said that was why the Indigenous Round was so important.

"It's honestly representation," she said.

"If we keep doing that, and celebrating Indigenous people, culture and stories like that, then hopefully we can get some more girls that want to join us."

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

On Sunday night more than 4,000 people packed out the stands at Marrara Stadium to watch Richmond beat Essendon in the Dreamtime match.

Among the spectators were diehard Tigers and Bombers fans and some who had never seen an AFL game before.

Last year the marquee Indigenous Round match was on a Friday night in Darwin and attracted almost 6,000 people.

But the game was fixtured around the men's wildcard round on a day with six AFLW matches and many locals said Sunday's 6:50pm time slot may have led to lower attendance than last year.

Richmond beat Essendon in front of a 4,000-strong crowd in Darwin. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Match gets young fans dreaming

The elite game in the Top End was one part of nurturing football in the Northern Territory and helping to grow grassroots participation.

Top End Youth Academy head coach Ben White said just a couple of years ago most kids did not have an answer when he asked who their favourite AFLW player was.

He said now they were naming players such as Richmond's Monique Conti and Sydney's Zippy Fish.

"We've got those figureheads of the AFLW that girls can look up to and see that pathway. It's amazing," White said, crediting the Dreamtime match for bringing the game closer to community.

The crowd in Darwin for the Dreamtime game was a mix of diehard footy fans and new supporters. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

This has also been helped by the recent Northern Territory inclusions to the AFLW of Annabel Kievit, who plays for the Gold Coast Suns, and Dom Carbone, who was elevated to Collingwood's senior list for this season after playing for the Darwin Buffettes.

Essendon captain Bonnie Toogood said one of the most pleasing parts of coming up to the Top End with the Bombers was seeing the next generation of Indigenous kids in the stands.

Essendon has a strong connection with the Tiwi Islands. In April this year, AFLW players Mia Busch and Amy Gaylor, alongside The Long Walk's Jack Peris, ran footy clinics across the Tiwi Islands and West Arnhem Land.

Bonnie Toogood (right) says the Dreamtime game in Darwin is special for the players and competition. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

The Essendon players and staff will visit schools in Darwin on Monday.

Toogood said it was important to the team to connect with the community.

"It's the main reason as to why we want to come up here and celebrate Dreamtime," she said.

The Top End Youth Academy is fostering young talent and aiming to improve the standard of the game in the NT. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

AFLNT launched the Darwin-based Top End Youth Academy this year in response to years of community demand for development opportunities and to strengthen existing talent pathways.

In a matter of months more than 400 players attended academy trials and more than 270 participants were picked up.

Youth Academy manager Josh Kleine was not surprised by the interest.

"Where those numbers might be higher than we expected, it doesn't shock me because there is that love and passion for the game up here," he said.

The AFLW has shown young kids that there is a pathway to the elite level. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Kleine said there were a few times during the trials when he and White looked at each other and thought "we've got a fair bit of work to do here'".

But within a matter of months the skills of the kids, aged 10-15, improved out of sight.

"We were actually sitting here in this room and watching them do their warm up and they're just kicking in lanes, getting ready for the game, and nearly every target was being hit," Kleine said.

"We've done some work on things like leg drives and different things. And to see someone who was struggling to get the concept, panicked a little bit, and sort of rushed handballs out, to see that then translate into a game where they're actually taking the tackler on and driving through the contest, it's amazing to see.

"They're the moments that really get you. When you've had that time with the kids and you're coaching them, and you see those things where it's a kid who might have been struggling in this area, you put in the time on the track and then you see it translate on the field.

"It's those little moments that you find really touching."

There are more than 270 players in the Top End Youth Academy. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

Kleine said the Darwin kids had a bit more access to programs and competitions than those in other parts of the NT, but the plan was for the academy to expand to places such as Tiwi, Katherine and Alice Springs.

"One thing with our academy [that] we always talk about is, we've only got you for an hour and a half a week on the track with training … we're limited with the time we have," he said.

"So our encouragement is take the lessons we teach you and do the work away from on during the week as well.

"And the girls, the work they're putting in on the track, you're definitely seeing it. You can see when they come back the next week — they've gone away and they've worked on these things. They've done their extra 100 kicks or whatever it is."

Documentary follows young Indigenous women chasing AFLW dreams Arthurina Moreen's desire was so great to play footy, she'd practice kicking bottles with her bare foot. A new documentary has shone a light on her resilience, and that of three other Tiwi Islander women as they chase AFLW stardom.

Kleine said he hoped to see more local talent make it to the elite level, but the goal was also to strengthen the game in the NT.

"Ultimately, not everyone's going to make it, but we're creating stronger territory football off the back of it," he said.

"Half our kids, we hope they become the future captains, the future coaches, all those sorts of things, and that the local clubs are here in the next 15 years.

"It's a flow-and-effect to make Territory footy stronger in the long run … it is a tumbleweed-type thing, where it just flows on, and everyone's continually growing and improving.

"Hopefully it helps close those gaps."

World.title: Scheffler wins PGA Tour Championship, Min Woo Lee ties fourth
World.content:
Adam Scott has had to settle for yet another cool milestone as Scottie Scheffler surpassed Tiger Woods as the PGA Tour's all-time leading prize money earner with his second season-long FedEx Cup crown.

Scheffler once again underlined his undisputed status as the world number one with a decisive three-shot triumph at the $US40 million ($56 million) Tour Championship in Atlanta.

The 2024 champion fired a closing four-under-par 66 to reel in third-round leader Viktor Hovland and join grand slam greats Rory McIlroy (2016, 2019, 2022) and Woods (2007, 2009) as only the third player to win the showpiece finale multiple times.

In pocketing the monster $US10 million winner's cheque, Scheffler also surged past Woods ($US120,999,166) with a mind-blowing $US130,390,661 in career on-course earnings in only his seventh season on the PGA Tour.

After starting three shots behind Hovland and alongside Scott in joint third, Scheffler surged clear to finish at 16-under for the tournament.

Hovland, the 2023 winner, was the outright runner-up despite a Sunday slip-up, a 72 as the Norwegian fell short in his own bid to win a second FedEx Cup.

American Ryan Gerard was third at 12-under following his own faltering 72.

With a closing 68, Min Woo Lee wound up one shot ahead of Scott, finishing as Australia's top finisher in an impressive seven-way tie for fourth on his Tour Championship debut.

Lee finished at 11-under with England's Alex Fitzpatrick (66), Americans Jacob Bridgeman (68), Russell Henley (68) and Chris Gotterup (71), McIlroy (69) and Swede Ludvig Aberg (71).

At 46 years, one month and 14 days, Scott was striving to become the oldest FedEx Cup champion, with Vijay Singh more than a year younger when he won in 2008.

Alas, it was not the former world number one's day.

Scott was in third spot for much of the afternoon, even pulling to within two shots of the lead early on the back nine.

But, unable to buy a birdie putt, Scott's bold challenge ended with a bogey on the par-4 16th hole after he hooked his drive wildly off the tee and hit a sloppy drop shot on number 17.

He eventually signed for a 72 to finish at 10 under with England's 2025 champ Tommy Fleetwood (67) and American world number three Cameron Young (70).

Still, Scott's share of 11th, 20 years after winning the Tour Championship, earned the veteran a tidy $US660,000.

That was enough to push Australia's 2013 Masters champion one up to seventh, above Justin Thomas, on the PGA Tour's all-time money list with $US74,880,596 in prize money.

Only Scheffler, Woods, McIlroy, Phil Mickelson, Justin Rose and Dustin Johnson are now above Scott.

AAP

World.title: Tearful Djokovic makes shock US Open exit in first round
World.content:
An emotional Novak Djokovic has made his earliest exit at a major in 20 years following a shock five-set loss to Argentine Mariano Navone at the US Open.

Playing through tears in the final set, four-time champion Djokovic — who was in physical discomfort for much of the match — fell to 49th-ranked Navone in the first round, 7-6 (7/5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1.

The match lasted almost four hours and 36 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium and finished just before midnight, local time.

The last time Djokovic exited a major in the first round was at the 2006 Australian Open.

He had previously never lost in the opening round at Flushing Meadows.

Djokovic made 70 unforced errors during the match.

The 24-time major winner vomited at least once and later appeared to be cramping when he grabbed his left foot.

Novak Djokovic was in discomfort throughout the match. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

"I pretty much despised every moment ⁠I spent on the court for that," Djokovic told reporters.

"I didn't enjoy myself. I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me."

Djokovic added: "It's something that I've been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year: vomiting, throwing up. [It's a] serious issue there.

"Then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. The back just gave up in the end and shoulder, and I couldn't close it out."

The 39-year-old swallowed pills brought to him by a doctor and had his lower back massaged during a medical timeout between the fourth and fifth sets.

He also grimaced after several shots.

Throughout his time on court, it was clear Djokovic was not himself, as sickness and soreness took a toll.

"Five sets, against ‌the GOAT (greatest of all time), it's not something you ​do every day. I'm ‌very happy," Navone said in his on-court interview.

"It means a lot to me. It's a dream come true. Now I have to recover. It's almost 12 am. We have to go to sleep."

Mariano Navone (left) shakes hands with Novak Djokovic after his upset victory. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

Djokovic arrived for his 20th US Open appearance with questions ​over ‌his form and fitness after losing to Thiago Agustin Tirante in Cincinnati two weeks ago.

The match began in humid conditions but the roof of the main show court was soon closed when rain fell at Flushing Meadows.

Earlier, former champion Daniil Medvedev made light work of France's Hugo Gaston 6-4, 6-2, 6-4, exorcising the demons of his ill-fated campaign a year ago with an aggressive performance at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

A frequent — and gleeful — villain at the tournament he won in 2021, Medvedev crashed out in the opening round in 2025 but was all business on Sunday (local time), with 34 winners against just 11 from his opponent.

"You need to play your game. I knew he was going to do some drop shots, some underarm serves," Medvedev said.

"I needed to make some winners, put some pressure on him."

Russia's Daniil Medvedev celebrates after winning his first round match against France's Hugo Gaston. (Reuters: Mike Segar)

Gaston's creative shot-making had little impact on the nimble-footed, six-foot-six-inch Medvedev, and the Frenchman did himself no favours as he handed his opponent the break with a misplaced backhand in the seventh game.

The seventh seed upped his level in the second set, where the Frenchman gifted him the break in the third game when he whacked a forehand into the net.

Medvedev held the momentum from there, leaping into the air to hit a superbly placed backhand shot out of Gaston's reach on break point in the seventh.

Only days after publicly pondering a career in pickleball after his opening-match defeat at Winston-Salem, the mercurial Russian converted another break-point chance in the opening game of the third when he whipped a forehand past the Frenchman.

He closed it out with an unreturnable serve and will play the winner of a match later on Sunday between American wildcard Sebastian Gorzny and Belgian Raphael Collignon.

Cilic, Ruud pull out injured

Former champion Marin Cilic and 2022 runner-up Casper Ruud pulled out of the tournament due to injuries shortly after the tournament got underway on Sunday (local time).

Croatian Marin Cilic has pulled out of the US Open, a grand slam he won in 2014. (Reuters: Imagn Images/David Kirouac)

Cilic won the only major title of his career at Flushing Meadows 12 years ago, and the Croat will be replaced in the draw by lucky loser Otto Virtanen, who faces 23rd seed Andrey Rublev in the opening round.

Virtanen pulled out of his third-round qualifying match against Grigor Dimitrov with an injury.

Organisers did not specify what injured the 37-year-old Cilic. The veteran joins a growing list of withdrawals with the likes of Jannik Sinner, Jack Draper, Joao Fonseca and Holger Rune skipping the tournament this year.

Ruud, the runner-up to Carlos Alcaraz four years ago, was another high-profile player to pull out earlier, and lucky loser Arthur Gea will take his place in the opening round. The Frenchman meets Juan Manuel Cerundolo first up.

Loading Instagram content

The 27-year-old Ruud had retired during the second set of his Cincinnati Open meeting with Christopher O'Connell this month and said his back injury had not recovered in time.

"Unfortunately, my back hasn't healed as quickly as we had hoped," Ruud said on Instagram.

"We've been optimistic that I would recover in time, but my team and I have decided that we need to think long-term and give my body the time it needs. I'm very sad to announce that I have to withdraw from this year's U.S. Open singles event.

"It's never easy to miss a Grand Slam, but I know this is the right decision. I'll take the time I need to recover properly and come back stronger."

Ruud competed in the revamped mixed doubles tournament last week, partnering Diana Shnaider and the pair were beaten in the quarterfinals by Rublev and Mirra Andreeva.

Pegula shakes off nerves to win

Third-ranked Jessica Pegula shook off nerves that contributed to a slow start against Elena-Gabriela Ruse, winning her opening match in straight sets.

Leading off at Arthur Ashe Stadium, the 32-year-old American missed her first nine opportunities to break Ruse but found a rhythm and began dominating. Coming off a trip to the final at the Cincinnati Open, which she lost to Coco Gauff, Pegula won 92 per cent of her first-serve points on the way to a 6-3, 6-2 victory in 83 minutes.

"I was so nervous," Pegula said. "I was like sending GIFs of what I felt like. It was GIFs of people freaking out and stuff. … The first round of a slam, there's always a ton of nerves."

Maybe a little more this time, given what's at stake.

Pegula leads the women's tour with 46 wins this season. She has two titles and has reached three other finals. Pegula can become number one in the women's rankings if she wins her first major title and number two Elena Rybakina loses before the semifinals.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Rain forces Aussies off with US Open matches in the balance, Preston wins
World.content:
Kim Birrell and Aleksandar Vukic have been forced off the court due to rain, with their first-round US Open matches hanging in the balance.

Taylah Preston was the only victorious Australian on the first day at Flushing Meadows, with Birell and Vukic needing to wait until tomorrow to finish their tense matches.

Birrell, who lost the opening set to Croatia's Petra Marčinko, was locked in a tiebreaker in the second set when play was suspended.

The tiebreaker was locked at 3-3 when play was called off for the outside courts just after 8pm, local time, with Birrell needing to win to send the first-round match into a third and deciding set.

In the men's singles, fellow Australian Vukic was nearing the end of a five-set thriller when rain halted play.

Vukic, the world number 96, came from behind twice in the match to force a deciding set in New York against Japan's Rei Sakamoto.

Vukic is down a break in the fifth set, with Sakamoto, the world number 157, walking off the court with a 3-4 lead.

Wildcard Preston gets first grand slam win outside Australia

Taylah Preston is the first Australian into the second round of the US Open, claiming a straight-sets win over American Alycia Parks.

Taylah Preston has advanced to the second round of the US Open for the first time. (Reuters: Imagn Images/Mike Frey)

The 20-year-old from Western Australia, whose only previous second-round appearance at a grand slam was this year's Australian Open, produced a terrific performance to secure a 6-3, 6-3 victory.

"It's really special," the 20-year-old said after the straight-sets demolition job vindicated Tennis Australia's decision to award the tyro entry to the final major of 2026 under a reciprocal arrangement with the United States Tennis Association.

"Glad that my first grand slam win was in Australia, but hopefully I can keep winning rounds at all the slams, not just at home."

The Australian faced three break points in the fourth game of the opening set but was able to rally and level at 2-2. Preston then applied pressure to Parks's serve in the very next game, getting a 15-40 lead before winning the game on her second break point.

Preston broke Parks's serve in the ninth game to win the opening set.

Parks responded immediately by breaking Preston in the opening game of the second set.

Down 0-2 and facing, Preston roared back to win five games on the bounce, on her way to another 6-3 set win to close out the match.

Preston, world number 100, will either face Polish 20th seed Maja Chwalinska or American Taylor Townsend in the second round at Flushing Meadows.

Gibson, Hunter and Walton out in first round

A dejected Talia Gibson is doing her best to extract the positives after Donna Vekic crashed the rising star's US Open party in a rough start for the Australian contingent.

Talia Gibson went down in three sets to Donna Vekic of Croatia. (AP: Andres Kudacki)

Storm Hunter and Adam Walton also made early exits on day one at Flushing Meadows as Gibson was unable to disguise her anguish at an opportunity lost.

The 22-year-old rallied from a set and a service break down to look poised to claim her maiden grand slam victory outside Australia before Vekic steadied to post a 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 in two hours and 33 minutes.

The veteran Croat and 2024 Wimbledon semifinalist seemed to be unravelling after blowing a set and 4-1 lead, cursing herself and berating her box as Gibson roared back into the contest.

But Gibson was unable to wrestle back control after failing to convert any of four break-point chances in the second game of the deciding set.

She had Vekic down 0-40 serving at 4-2, only to miss five straight returns to ruefully let the Paris Olympics silver medallist off the hook.

"It's a hard one to swallow," Gibson said.

"Most of the time it's who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss, and today that was me, so it's just something to learn from."

But after starting the year well outside the world's top 100, Gibson has slashed her ranking in half after racking up some 30 match wins, including over former No.1 and dual Australian and US Open champion Naomi Osaka.

"Days like these are really tough. It's hard not to be disappointed. When it comes to the slams, every player wants to do well," said the world No.63.

"But if I'm looking at my entire year so far, I've been able to achieve some things that probably at the start of the year I probably wouldn't have thought I'd be able to do.

"So to still be in the position ranking that I currently have and moving forward to these next tournaments, I don't really have any points to defend, so it's kind of just no pressure and more opportunities."

Aussie qualifier Storm Hunter was defeated by 11th seed Marta Kostyuk in straight sets.

Storm Hunter was knocked out in the first round of the US Open after qualifying for the grand slam last week. (AP: Andres Kudacki)

After stumbling at this year's Australian Open, Kostyuk has been in sublime form at the grand slams, making the semifinals of the French Open and Wimbledon to arrive at Flushing Meadows as a genuine contender in the women's draw.

The 11th seed got down to business quickly once the match began, and powered to a 4-1 lead before overcoming a wobble to close out the first set when Hunter produced a double fault on set point.

Kostyuk tightened her grip on the clash in the second set, breaking early and never allowing Hunter a route back as she wrapped up a 6-4, 6-1 victory in 67 minutes.

"I'm very happy to be back to this amazing place," Kostyuk said on court.

"It's not easy to play a qualifier; they've played a whole tournament [already]. I'm very happy with my performance today. I try to keep myself grounded. There's still a long way to go; I'm enjoying my tennis."

Walton also bowed out early, missing two set points in the third set of a tight 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5 loss to China's Yibing Wu.

World number seven and three-time US Open quarterfinalist Alex de Minaur opens his title quest on Tuesday against Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

ABC/Reuters/AAP

World.title: 'I'm broken': Son confirms death of legendary Australian boxer
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name of a person who has died.

Australian boxer Tony Mundine has died aged 75.

One of the country's most accomplished Indigenous fighters, Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally in four weight divisions.

He held the Australian titles at middleweight, light-heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight.

His death was confirmed by his son, former world champion boxer Anthony Mundine.

"I don't know what to say, I'm broken," Anthony Mundine wrote on Instagram.

"Dad I love you man, may Allah bless your soul," he wrote.

"I'm on my way home to say goodbye one last time till we meet again.

"Thanks for doing all you did for me and supporting me in every moment, showing love and strength, gonna miss you Tonza, there's only one Tony Mundine."

Tony's son, Anthony (left) has led tributes to his late father. (Getty Images: Allsport/RobertLaberge)

Tony Mundine was born in Baryulgil, New South Wales, where he took part in a number of tent boxing shows as a teenager.

His career peaked with a world title challenge in October 1974 against Argentina's Carlos Monzon.

Despite losing via a seventh-round knockout, Tony Mundine said he had fulfilled a childhood dream.

"I was just a little chocolate boy from Baryulgil, and here I was travelling the world, you know," he said.

Tributes from the boxing world flowed in for Mundine after the news of his death.

Former Australian professional boxer Danny Green paid tribute to Mundine, saying he was a "gentleman I had a tonne of respect for."

"Grew up watching him on TV ringside. Drew a great deal of inspiration from watching him, one of my late father's favourite fighters," Green wrote.

Australian professional boxer Billy Dib said Mundine was "widely recognised as one of Australia's greatest fighters".

"Uncle Tony was a beautiful human being and a genuinely good man who always showed me love and respect."

Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984.

He was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1986 for his services to sport and Aboriginal youth.

He is survived by his son Anthony, his grandson — professional boxer Rahim Mundine — and his cousin — businessman and Indigenous rights advocate Warren Mundine.

ABC

Tech.title: Professor Murder Rides the Subway is a forgotten slice of dance punk perfection
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I recently dug out my CDs and started reripping them all. I’ve found a few forgotten gems in there, but few hit harder for me than the beautifully concise Professor Murder Rides the Subway EP. There was a period of time in the mid-aughts in NYC where it seemed like every indie band wanted you to let loose, dance like no one was watching, and just have some damn fun. Few embodied that as much as New York dance punk band Professor Murder.

LCD Soundsystem and The Rapture were the biggest names of the dance punk revival. But there were also bands like Rahim, Liars, Dan Deacon, and countless lesser-known acts on DFA that you could see on any given weekend around NYC. And I spent a lot of time in those venues, shamelessly dancing my ass off to all of them.

There’s something about Professor Murder’s specific blend of cheap synth blasts, shouted vocal chants, busy syncopated percussion, and throbbing bass that perfectly captures the vibe of the NYC music scene circa 2006. At their heart, the tracks on the 16-minute EP are built around a simple disco stomp (save for the brief a cappella of “Pedigree”). They’re dressed up with cowbell and other tuned percussion elements to add complexity. But they’re never allowed to disrupt the groove.

While some of their contemporaries like LCD Soundsystem were chasing bigger, more melodic textures, Professor Murder trafficked in stripped-back arrangements where, arguably, the drums are the lead instrument. While there are hooks and melodies to grab on to, like the fuzzy bass on “Camron’s New Color (Part 3)”, they’re always a little quieter in the mix.

The EP is bookended with two songs that are basically the Platonic ideal of 2000’s dance punk: “Champion” and “Free Stress Test.” If there was any justice in the world, the latter would have catapulted the band to at least Rapture levels of success. I dare you to not at least nod your head along to the beat.

Professor Murder Rides the Subway is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, YouTube Music, Spotify, Deezer, and Qobuz.

Tech.title: Enormous 12TB Steam leak includes abandoned Half-Life 2: Episode 3 assets
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Over 12 terabytes of data, containing builds of every game uploaded to Steam between 2003 and 2013, has been leaked. We don’t know everything in the archives yet because of its massive size. But people have already dug up assets related to the canceled Half-Life 2: Episode 3, content cut from Portal 2, and a build of a game called F-Stop that’s set in the Portal universe but is built around a camera mechanic.

The leak also includes titles from third-party developers. Early versions of Call of Duty and Resident Evil installments have been dug up, as have builds of Mirror’s Edge, Batman: Arkham Asylum, and Dragon Age: Origins. And more is likely to come to light as people dig through the trove. But arguably the most interesting discoveries are related to Valve’s Portal 2. Sleuths have dug up deleted dialog that completely changes how you’ll look at Companion Cubes, alternative intro and GlaDOS sequences, as well as a version of the Weaponizer intended for Half-Life 2: Episode 3.

Tech.title: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches to study dark matter and dark energy
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After funding struggles and a name change, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has been successfully launched. It will now make a three-month, one-million-mile journey to its orbit at the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2) beyond the Moon.

From this vantage point, Roman will conduct an unprecedented survey of the universe. Its field of view is 100 times larger than Hubble’s and, according to NASA, it can survey the sky 1,000 times faster using its 300-megapixel infrared camera. Roman also has a Coronagraph system that can block and mask glare from stars, allowing it to directly image exoplanets, even smaller, older, and colder planets orbiting close to their stars.

Roman will also conduct detailed 3D scans to help map the distribution of dark matter and narrow down the potential candidates for its makeup. Using the same 3D scans and gravitational lensing measurements, Roman will attempt to map how dark energy shaped the evolution of the universe.

Nicky Fox, associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate at NASA, said in a press release that “Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”

Tech.title: Texas Governor Abbott blocks funding for more Flock cameras
Tech.content:
As backlash grows over Flock’s AI surveillance cameras, Texas Governor Greg Abbott has frozen state spending on them. The move came just ahead of the publication of a Texas Tribune investigation that revealed the state spent over $30 million on Flock cameras. That money was primarily raised by tacking a $1 fee onto insurance policies, allegedly to help fight catalytic converter theft.

In recent months, cities around the country have been canceling their contracts with Flock, including many in Texas. Abbott’s Democratic opponent in the race for governor, Gina Hinojosa, has criticized him for expanding use of the cameras in the state. And Republican representative Keith Self recently posted on Instagram that, “From Flock cameras to kill switches, we will NOT surrender our Fourth Amendment rights to the growing surveillance state.” Cheering on the destruction of Flock cameras has even become a unifying pastime on the internet.

Tech.title: Chess.com launched a poker site and is planning even more classic games
Tech.content:
Chess.com has done one thing, and one thing very well, for almost 20 years, but now it’s going beyond its domain name. The biggest name in online chess quietly launched its first companion site in beta back in May: Gambit, a free online poker website where players can learn the game without risking any real money. Now Gambit’s ready to really get the ball rolling with its first livestreamed event and collaborations with content creators, and Chess.com is planning to branch out into even more games from here.

Chess.com’s chief growth officer, Albert Cheng, told The Verge the company chose poker for its first companion site because, like chess, it has learning and social elements on top of just playing the game. He also promised there will never be real-money gambling on Gambit, saying, “Real money is the problem we built Gambit to get away from, the whole industry makes money when beginners lose. We’d rather build a place where people can actually learn.”

Gambit will look familiar to anyone who’s used Chess.com. It borrows the same design style and includes similar play modes, like bot matches, games with friends, tournaments, a review mode for studying your past games, and a learning mode. Gambit even includes Chess.com’s bot characters, with matching skill levels — I immediately recognized “Martin,” the lowest skill level bot from Chess.com, who is also the lowest skill level bot on Gambit.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Gambit includes interactive lessons to learn poker. Image: Gambit

Chess.com also developed its own Elo-style rating system for Gambit. Cheng explained in an interview with The Verge that the rating system serves as the main motivator for players to improve: “You’re not gambling your own hard-earned money necessarily, so the stakes are lower from that standpoint, but you need something to counterbalance it that you care about, and that keeps the ecosystem in play, and keeps the poker that’s on Gambit reasonably high-quality.”

The rating system is also the backbone of Gambit’s paid subscription for access to premium learning features, following the same model Chess.com uses. “Our primary business model of Chess.com is a subscription, but most people play Chess.com for free,” Cheng said. “They subscribe to get unlimited access to review their games and to get unlimited puzzles, lessons, et cetera.” A reliable rating system allows players to track their improvement, potentially motivating them to pay for those premium features.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Players can study their past games in Gambit’s review mode. Image: Gambit

Rating systems are also at the heart of Chess’s next move. Chess.com is now looking to expand into even more classic games, including go, backgammon, and mahjong. Like Gambit, Chess.com is developing Elo-style rating systems for these games, as well. Cheng didn’t say when the new sites will launch but that “development is moving quite rapidly” on them, using the same playbook he used for Gambit.

AI is a key reason Chess.com was finally able to expand into other games after nearly 20 years, according to Cheng. He and one other employee took Gambit from prototype to launch within a year, partly with help from AI, mainly for coding tasks. “I think the biggest advantage that it’s provided is essentially being able to read our existing codebase and our design system and apply consistent patterns to how we develop Chess.com over to a different platform and do so quickly,” Cheng said.

He went on to add that there were also a lot of areas where AI struggles, such as brand and feature design. “I think that’s the best ultimate use of AI is that ultimately it’s going to be a blend, right?” Cheng said, adding, “Just because code is easier to write doesn’t mean that you just let it run on its own, but it certainly is a superpower in getting things off the ground.” Cheng also said the version of Gambit that’s live at the time of writing has “zero or close to zero” AI-created assets, which were used in early prototypes.

According to Cheng, without help from AI, getting another site up and running would have required a bigger team or “would have been a lot more disruptive to the status quo of building and growing Chess.” Now that a “small, scrappy” team can get a new platform off the ground much faster, it’s opened the door for Chess.com to dip into more games, starting with poker.

As Chess.com plans its next move, Cheng says they’re focusing on games with “both that classic durability plus the community around it,” like chess. Now that Gambit has launched, Cheng’s leaning into the community and social side of the platform more, following Chess.com’s lead, and getting content creators more involved. On August 31st at 12PM ET / 9AM PT, Gambit’s livestreaming its Gambit Cup for the first time on Twitch and YouTube with Chess.com co-founder Danny Rensch and chess content creator Alexandra Botez.

Tech.title: China’s robots race ahead
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on falling robots and the US-China AI race, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

I’ve admitted my fondness for robot fail videos on Stepback before, and let me tell you the World Humanoid Robot Games did not disappoint.

The five-day event, which wrapped this week in Beijing, brought high drama, and brought it well. One robot, made by smartphone maker Honor, lost a leg mid-sprint, while others tripped in a flurry of sparks. Another finisher ran straight into a crash mat, bounced off it, and promptly burst into flames. In the weightlifting, one robot lost its balance beneath a modest barbell and toppled inexorably into the judges’ table, arms cartoonishly aloft. Robotic cheerleaders tumbled and stumbled through routines, while a separate bot fell off a platform in circumstances that, had it been human, might have looked suspiciously like it was gawking at the performers.

This was only the second World Humanoid Robot Games, though it was already far bigger than the inaugural event last year. Unlike this year, last year’s records were paltry. The winning 100-meter sprint was a glacial 21.50 seconds and the highest standing high jump was just 0.95 meters. In keeping with China’s habit of turning robots into public spectacle — from intricate dances at a Spring Festival Gala to demos at major tech events — both this and last year’s games were staged in Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, a former Olympic venue.

And a spectacle it was. At most sporting events, contestants losing limbs, careening into walls, catching fire, and regularly being carried away on stretchers — oh, and did I mention catching fire?! — would probably be grounds to stop proceedings. At the Humanoid Robot Games, it was par for the course.

Fire aside, the games were unusual in other ways too. Alongside familiar events like sprinting, football, boxing, and weightlifting were more unusual competitions in bed-making, parcel delivery, shelf stacking, clothes folding, and hammering nails. Aptly, there was a firefighting contest too.

These less standard offerings spoke to the real purpose of the games: getting robots out of the lab and into the messy real-world environments their makers hope they will ultimately work in. And China is making no secret of wanting to lead the way.

How it’s going

For all the spectacle and drama, the games show there has been massive progress in robotics in recent years. Records fell, with one humanoid running the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds, beating Usain Bolt’s 2009 world record. Another bot reached 2.88 meters in a standing high jump, nearly half a meter above the human high-jump record that has stood since 1993. Those performances are almost unrecognizable compared to robotics competitions a decade ago, when even the most advanced machines struggled to stay upright.

While many events required robots to operate autonomously — including gymnastics, football, tug of war, table tennis, and some track events — others allowed for human assistance via teleoperation, albeit with a scoring penalty. The dexterity being displayed certainly points to genuine and impressive hardware improvements, but seems like there is still a long way to go before these machines can operate reliably on their own in places like factories or homes.

What happens next

Beijing has not yet confirmed a third Humanoid Robot Games, but given the government’s enthusiasm for the industry, it would be surprising to not get another installment. The city has already confirmed another humanoid half-marathon for April, and the country plans to open its first robot-run hotel next year.

China was the undisputed champion of the games, and the country looks well placed to stay in top position moving forward — both at future competitions and in the humanoid robot industry as a whole. The medal table was almost entirely a Chinese affair, dominated in particular by AgiBot and Tien Kung, each scooping up more medals than nearly every other competitor combined, excluding the other.

In part, that asymmetry reflected the lack of international competition. Although the games were framed as a global affair, 641 of 666 teams were Chinese, domestically representing 157 companies and 200 universities, according to state-run China Daily. While there doesn’t seem to be a public breakdown of entrants, the biggest US humanoid players like Tesla, Boston Dynamics, and Figure were conspicuous by their absence.

Nevertheless, the sheer diversity of Chinese institutions represented in Beijing was a show of force, and a sign of how quickly the country’s robotics sector is maturing, even amid growing concerns about circular investment, thriving companies that lack viable products, and a possible humanoid bubble.

It’s not clear a stronger US showing at the games would’ve changed much. The US still has an edge in frontier AI and advanced chips, but China has been rapidly closing parts of that gap, while also making embodied AI a strategic national priority. The same cannot be said of Washington, which has for years paid much less attention to robotics and now trails China in nearly every regard, including manufacturing, deployment, and hardware. Some reports even suggest that recent efforts to ban foreign robots, a general policy squarely aimed at China, could backfire, given how dependent domestic firms are on Chinese components.

Catching up to China will take serious and concerted effort, but given how quickly the technology is moving, there’s still time to make up ground. Washington is already treating other areas of AI as strategic priorities in its competition with Beijing; robotics could be one of them. There will be plenty of stumbling along the way, and, hopefully, plenty more robot fail videos too.

Tech.title: Two new small, powerful Macs
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 142, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, how is it almost September already, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)

This week, I also have for you new Macs, a Nokia phone that can charge your phone, a Wyze cam with a great privacy feature, and more.

Programming note: Installer is off next week. I’ll be on vacation. See you next month for Techtember!

(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What do you want to know more about? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / listened to / eaten recently? Drop a line to installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)

The Drop

Screen Share

Today I’m featuring John Gruber of Daring Fireball. If you follow Apple and are a regular Verge reader (which, as an Installer subscriber, I assume you are), you’re probably well aware of Gruber and his work as a writer, podcaster, friend of the site, and as a general tech person on the internet.

Ahead of Apple’s big launch event coming up on September 9th, I thought it would be fun to feature the homescreen of one of the most well-known people in the Apple universe.

Image: John Gruber

The phone: iPhone 17 Pro, deep blue, 1 TB (of which only 200 GB is used, but that won’t stop me from wasting money on a 1 TB model this year too).

The wallpaper: My wallpaper is a subtle gradient from very dark gray to black. For years I just stuck with a flat black wallpaper, as god and Steve Jobs intended. (You couldn’t change your homescreen wallpaper until iOS 4, and I remain unconvinced that was a good idea.) I like the subtle gradient now because it lets the dynamic island have a little visual contrast from the wallpaper background.

The apps: I’ve currently got three todo/task apps on the homescreen, which I can’t recommend, but it’s currently working for me: Unforgetful, Finalist, and Due. (The red “1” badge on Unforgetful is for a reminder to send you this email and the screenshot of my homescreen.) I’ve also arguably got three notes apps, if you count Journal (in addition to Tot and Apple Notes). Mosaic is a TestFlight-only alternative to the official MLB app, which has a great story behind it. Rather than shutting it down, MLB hired its developer, Jason Weingardt, because Mosaic is so awesome. If I took the screenshot later tonight, you’d see a Live Activity from Mosaic of the Yankees game in the Dynamic Island.

Kotoba is also TestFlight-only. It is, in my humble opinion, the best dictionary app for iOS, but because it uses the system-provided dictionaries and thesauruses to act as a dictionary app, it’s not permitted in the App Store. I look up words with it almost every single day. I wrote about it on Daring Fireball a while ago.

The Siri app shows that I’m testing the iOS 27 betas. It’s good. I tend to use it side by side with ChatGPT for now, to compare responses, but going forward, I’ll use both. So having that alongside ChatGPT is in line with my having multiple todo apps and multiple note apps (and multiple messaging apps).

I keep the badge on Mail counting my unread messages to remind myself that the heat death of the universe is inevitable.

Oh, and my App Store app icon isn’t the actual App Store app, but instead a shortcut that jumps me right to the list of apps with pending updates to install.

I also asked John to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

One show whose second season just finished: The Agency , on Paramount+. I think it’s probably the best spy series ever made.

One show whose sixth season is about to begin: Slow Horses , on Apple TV. I think it’s probably the most amusing spy series ever made.

Third, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia , whose 18th season just started; it’s the best and most realistic show set in Philadelphia ever made.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Bluesky.

“Feels like this week is all Dolly Parton, Tim Curry, and now Transformers for Peter Cullen in terms of what people are watching and listening to!” — Carli

“I’ve been playing A la Card and REALLY enjoying my time with it. It’s an indie roguelike deck builder game that feels like Slay the Spire and Balatro said ‘Let’s go out for food from a food truck.’ All cards can be mutated and changed via the events — their values, their effect, what triggers them. Great art and music, solid design, and it’s scratching an itch I didn’t know I had. Awesome game from a 2-person indie dev team.” — Tom

“My preorder shipped early so I’ve been reading Emo Revival by Andrew Sacher and it’s a 10/10 so far.” — @thoughtlesskyle.bsky.social

“Empire of AI, Karen Hao. Recently translated to PT-BR :)” — Milena

“Tonight I’m going to finish House of Guinness. It’s a fine show but even better if you drink when watching it.” — Nick

“I’ve been on a kick reading older sci-fi novels recently and came across Berserker by Fred Saberhagen (1967). Fantastic book but surprisingly hard to find a physical copy. Ended up purchasing an ePub. Highly recommend!” — Nathan

Signing off

I got a few good screentime reduction tips following last week’s issue. One person said they don’t install apps with an infinite scroll, which I thought was a good idea. They also have Screen Time enabled to block various things, but their partner holds the password to unlock Screen Time if needed. Clever! Another reader suggested zipping up their phone in a phone pocket.

On my vacation next week, to make sure I actually unplug, I plan to deploy my favorite hack: hiding every gadget with a browser in my daughter’s closet. My only free time where I could potentially slip into mindless scrolling would be when she’s sleeping, but there’s no way I’m risking waking her up just to get out the laptop. More time for the important stuff — like playing Switch 2.

See you in two weeks!

Tech.title: Vicariously hike the Appalachian in the gorgeous A Trail Tale
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I used to be an avid hiker and would try to go backpacking a few times a year. I always dreamed of thru-hiking the Appalachian Trail, but life kind of got in the way. (Turns out jobs, wives, and children aren’t thrilled with the idea of you disappearing for three months.) But I’ve been longing to reconnect with my love of the outdoors and just recently took my kids on their first camping trip. So I discovered A Trail Tale at a really opportune time. It’s an interactive trail journal created by Andy Moliski with help from his brothers Adam and Alex.

The various segments of the trail are rendered in beautiful pixel art reminiscent of a ‘90s Sierra point-and-click adventure. Alex recorded an equally gorgeous original score that combines nature sounds, acoustic guitar, strings, and even what sounds like clarinet.

As you click through each day, you’re greeted with information about landmarks and a game-like UI that is partially inspired by titles like Oregon Trail. (Spoiler: nobody dies of dysentery in this one.) Clicking on Andy unfurls a menu of icons that offer details about the journey, his mental state, and even bits of poetry. There are even little icons for things that impact his fortitude and morale meters, like inclement weather or picturesque scenery.

It’s insanely easy to just get lost in Andy’s journey for hours. And it’s making me wonder if I should get back out there and start tackling some more of the AT myself.

Tech.title: The U.S. is building barriers around drones and robots, but China has scale to get around them
Tech.content:
In July and August, Washington tightened restrictions on foreign-made advanced robotic systems and imposed steep tariffs on imported drones and their components, both moves citing national-security concerns. The drone tariffs take effect in September, with additional component tariffs following in 2027.

These moves are part of a broader U.S. effort to restrict foreign technology in strategically important industries. The FCC’s Covered List, established in 2021, initially targeted telecommunications and surveillance equipment from companies including Huawei, ZTE and Hikvision before expanding to foreign-made drones and, most recently, to advanced robotic devices.

The latest move comes as Chinese manufacturers have built commanding positions in both drones and humanoid robots, often competing at prices U.S. and European rivals struggle to match.

Taken together, the restrictions are raising a bigger question for the global robotics industry: If Chinese drones and humanoids are increasingly shut out of the U.S., where does the competition move next?

The restrictions may protect parts of the American market, but they don’t directly address China’s global manufacturing scale and cost advantages.

Industry analysts and executives who spoke with TechCrunch said the result may be less a clean U.S.-China split than a more fragmented global market, with Chinese companies expanding elsewhere while U.S. and allied manufacturers compete in markets where security requirements matter more.

The Scale Gap

The U.S. and Chinese robotics industries remain deeply connected, but the two countries enter the competition with very different advantages. Unlike semiconductors, robotics does not hinge on a single technology that one country can easily control, said Ankur Saxena, an investment director at TDK Ventures.

China dominates global humanoid robot manufacturing, with global shipments hitting 22,000 units in the first half of this year — the vast majority from Chinese manufacturers — according to a report by Counterpoint. U.S. companies, by contrast, are operating at a far smaller scale, said Soumen Mandal, a principal analyst at Counterpoint Research.

The world’s five largest humanoid robot makers by shipments — AgiBot, Unitree, Galbot, UBTECH and Leju Robotics — were all Chinese and together accounted for 86% of global shipments in the first half of 2026, according to Counterpoint.

That advantage could compound. Lower prices allow Chinese manufacturers to put more robots into use, generating real-world data that can improve their technology. Higher production volumes, in turn, can drive costs down further, Saxena said.

Mandal said Chinese humanoid makers are also pushing costs down by bringing more of the technology stack in-house and drawing on China’s existing manufacturing base. Unitree, for example, is developing more components internally, while automakers such as XPeng can draw on their experience in chips and vehicle manufacturing as they move into robotics.

“The United States leads in frontier AI, software and semiconductor innovation,” Saxena told TechCrunch. “China leads in manufacturing scale, supply-chain depth and cost.”

That manufacturing edge has let Chinese companies cut humanoid prices faster than most U.S. competitors can match.

“You cannot sanction your way around a cost curve. You can only out-build it, and America has yet to begin making the decade-long investment that will require,” Saxena said.

Where Does China Go Next?

The answer may increasingly be outside the U.S. Even if Chinese robotics companies lose access to the American market, they still have a large domestic market and room to expand elsewhere, particularly in regions where demand for affordable automation is growing, Saxena said.

Chinese robotics companies are already targeting price-sensitive markets with severe labor shortages across Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America and the Middle East, said Mandal.

Mandal expects humanoid makers to follow a path similar to Chinese electric-vehicle companies: build scale at home, expand into overseas markets, and eventually establish local production. Countries facing labor shortages and demographic decline could become early markets for humanoids, particularly in manufacturing, where robots can take on repetitive work.

The drone market offers an early glimpse of what that more fragmented robotics landscape could look like. The industry is increasingly splitting into two ecosystems: a U.S.-led market built around American-made, NDAA-compliant systems, and a China-led market focused on low-cost, high-volume production, said Bentzion Levinson, founder and CEO of Virginia-based drone maker Heven AeroTech.

Levinson said Western manufacturers are unlikely to beat Chinese companies in the low-end consumer drone market, where cost remains a major advantage. Instead, U.S. and allied companies could increasingly compete in long-range autonomous systems for defense and critical infrastructure, where security requirements carry more weight.

Levinson sees the next competitive frontier shifting from the drones themselves to the technology that powers them and the equipment they carry. “The next battleground is over who owns the next-gen energy and payload architecture,” he said, pointing to battery constraints in particular. As drones become more capable, he added, battery limitations could make power systems an increasingly important point of competition.

Agility Robotics welcomed the FCC’s decision in July, saying it could address security concerns around foreign-made advanced robots before they become deeply embedded in the U.S. market, as has happened in the drone industry. The company pointed to its Digit humanoid, which is designed and assembled in the U.S., while also calling for continued access to the tools and technologies needed to advance robotics research.

A More Regional Robotics Market

“The alternative to China isn’t a purely domestic U.S. supply chain; it’s a diversified allied one,” Saxena said.

That could create opportunities elsewhere in Asia. Japan has decades of experience in industrial robotics and precision manufacturing, South Korea brings strengths in electronics, batteries and automobiles, and Taiwan is a major player in semiconductors. But none can simply replace China, Saxena said, given how deeply Chinese components remain embedded across the global robotics industry.

Asian manufacturers could emerge as a middle ground between lower-cost Chinese robots and more expensive U.S. offerings, Mandal said. South Korea’s Hyundai, which owns Boston Dynamics, and Japan’s Toyota are among the automakers investing in robotics, drawing on their expertise in vehicles, manufacturing and autonomous systems as they move into humanoid robots.

Yang Fang of Beagle Technology, a California-based agtech startup that uses AI and robotics software to turn conventional farm equipment into autonomous machines, told TechCrunch that robotics is likely to become more regional as companies design machines for the labor needs, working conditions and customers in their home markets. Chinese robotics companies, for example, may focus on products suited to China and nearby markets, while U.S. companies are more likely to build for industries across North America, he said.

The result may not be two neatly separated U.S.- and China-led robotics industries. Instead, the restrictions could accelerate the emergence of regional markets: Chinese companies competing on cost and scale across much of the world, U.S. and allied manufacturers gaining ground where security requirements matter most, and manufacturers in Japan, Taiwan and South Korea trying to carve out space between the two.

Tech.title: Grindr wants to be the everything app for gay men; investors are still deciding whether it can pull it off
Tech.content:
When George Arison took over Grindr in 2022, he inherited a company that had been bounced from Chinese ownership to a forced divestiture to a private-equity rescue — a business that was printing money but also had no real product or business strategy. Four years, a SPAC listing, and a controversial return-to-office mandate later, Grindr has become convincing as a growth story. Revenue is on pace to roughly triple, from $195 million in 2022 to a guided $540 million-plus this year, with adjusted EBITDA margins holding above 40%.

That growth has come almost entirely from getting existing customers to pay more versus dramatically growing its user base. In the second quarter of this year, it had 1.4 million paying users, or 9% of its user base, but average revenue per user has risen considerably since 2022, and Arison is very focused on where the next leg of growth comes from. Part of that plan includes turning Grindr into a “gayborhood in your pocket” — a platform that handles not just dating and hookups but healthcare (from ED medication to HIV prevention to, eventually, connecting users with gay doctors) and travel (helping users find community wherever they land). It’s the same “everything app” instinct driving much of consumer tech right now.

But that’s not the only thing Arison is throwing against the wall; later this year, Grindr is rolling out a subscription that it’s betting the market will support, a far pricier “EDGE” tier that has already raised hackles from some on the internet (“literally who’s paying for this,” and “we need 2012 grindr back”).

Arison, who previously founded and ran Shift Technologies, the online used-car marketplace he also took public via a SPAC, in 2020, is also aggressively seeking out press to argue that institutional investors continue discounting Grindr’s stock simply because it’s a gay dating app. In a Zoom call with TechCrunch on Thursday, he cited an investor who once showed him a financial model with a literal “Grindr discount” line item, knocking 25% off a fair-value estimate.

Not everyone thinks the discount is justified. Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and Raymond James have all raised their price targets on the stock this year, and Morgan Stanley upgraded it to “overweight” in July, citing the EDGE tier and Grindr’s telehealth push — part of a run-up that’s seen the stock climb roughly a third over the past six months. Still, that discount isn’t Arison’s imagination — the stock trades at roughly 11 times 2027 EBITDA, about a 35% discount to peers — even if it’s not clear why.

Arison — amiable, with a hint of his native Georgia still in his voice — was game to talk about all of it in a Q&A that has been edited for clarity and length.

You came in to run Grindr in 2022 when it was pretty adrift. What was the first thing you wanted to prioritize?

Three things, really. First, company building. A lot of people had been hired during the peak-COVID era when expectations for in-office productivity were low, and average output was maybe three to four hours of real work a day. We brought people back to the office two days a week in the summer of 2023 — a decision that got a lot of press and a lot of anger. We went down to about 70 employees as a result. Today only around 25 people who were here before I arrived still work at Grindr, and we run lean: 175 U.S. employees plus a team in Colombia, doing $540 million in guided revenue this year.

Second was driving revenue growth by shipping product people would actually pay for — that’s how pay conversion went from under 6% to over 9%, and ARPU nearly doubled. Third was setting a long-term vision: the “gayborhood in your pocket” idea, and everything else — healthcare, travel — that flows from it.

You’ve said Grindr’s engineering culture is underrated. How small is the team actually running this?

About 94 or 95 people across all technical roles. A large-tech-company CEO once told me AI would let me do with far fewer people what I thought I’d need 300 to 350 for — he was right. We’re doing roughly 350 people’s worth of work with about 100. Something like 80% of our code is now AI-written, and we’ve seen a 2.5x increase in engineering productivity over the past year.

Grindr tested an AI-powered premium tier, EDGE, at a price that in Canada worked out to roughly $350–375 a month in U.S. dollars — a number that got mocked online as more expensive than just dating someone. What actually happened there?

We haven’t released EDGE — we’re testing it, and some people have access as part of that test. It sits above our existing XTRA ($23.99) and Unlimited ($44.99) tiers. We’re not selling AI itself; we’re selling features derived from it — using what we know about a user’s behavior and intent, with consent, to make much better matches than a sparse profile ever could. Retention on these features so far is higher than anything we’ve had before.

The pricing people quoted was one test point among several — we ran a range to understand elasticity, not a final price. EDGE goes live toward the end of this year or early next, and we’ll know where it lands by then. We think of it like a Tesla Model X or S: a premium flagship now, with the underlying capability rolling down to the broader product over time.

On the matching itself — you’ve described using AI to suggest partners outside someone’s home city, because gay-dating pools even in places like San Francisco are small. What evidence do you have that those long-distance matches lead anywhere?

Even in San Francisco, where the share of the gay population is higher than almost anywhere else in the country, you’re talking about maybe 50,000 to 60,000 gay people total. That’s not a big pool to be fishing in if you’re trying to find a partner, and it’s a big reason dating is so hard for gay men generally. So yes — what if AI could break down the geographic constraint entirely, and surface someone in St. Louis who actually matches what you want, based on real behavior rather than what people say in a profile?

As for whether it leads anywhere real: we don’t track people’s relationships after the fact — that’s going too far. What we do know is that Grindr is where most gay men say they meet each other for relationships, and that younger cohorts want something different than older ones did: about 50% of gay men under 35 say they want a long-term monogamous relationship, and 25% say they want children — numbers that would have been unthinkable for my own generation. When you ask people why they’re not in a relationship, the answer is usually that they have a hard time finding a partner. I can’t promise this solves that. But it’s worth trying something new, because what’s been done so far clearly hasn’t solved it.

There are so many ways to expand your addressable market beyond the dating app itself. The healthcare stuff is really interesting — can you tell us more about what you’re doing there, and whether you’re building these products yourselves or acting as the interface to outside providers?

We started with cash-pay products through a line we call Woodwork — ED medications, GLP-1s, peptides, and so on — because cash-pay was the simplest place to get going, and we just launched an AI bot that handles the whole transaction inside the app rather than sending people out to Woodwork.com. The second bucket is HIV prevention and treatment: we’ve committed to giving 10 million people direct access to information on where to get PrEP, both in the U.S., where we already offer that in our in-app health center, and internationally.

The third bucket — actual clinical care, like connecting people to a gay doctor through telehealth — is very much long-term. That’s not something we’re building today, but I do think there’s a world, a decade out, where healthcare is a bigger revenue stream for Grindr than what we do today.

Right now, though, non-subscription revenue — ads and everything else, including healthcare — is a small fraction of the business.

Subscriptions are about 83% of revenue today, down from around 86% in 2022, even though subscription revenue itself has grown enormously — that tells you how much bigger the base is overall. The newer businesses are genuinely small right now. What I want is a company that, 10 years from now, has a strong subscription business, a strong advertising business, a real healthcare business, and a real travel business alongside it. Today those last two are early.

You’ve said investors still apply what one called a “Grindr discount” to the stock because of what the company is. But the stock is up sharply over the past six months, Morgan Stanley just upgraded it, and it trades at a premium multiple to Match Group. Isn’t the market telling you the discount is gone?

I hope we’re being treated as a growth company at this point — we’ve grown revenue more than 25% for 16 straight quarters as CEO, so there’s reason to expect that. The stigma conversation is a real one; we’ve had a consulting firm decline to work with us over reputational concerns, and a bank refuse our money during the Silicon Valley Bank crisis, even as other major banks like Goldman and Morgan Stanley have been strong partners. I think a lot of that is really about Grindr being a gay dating product rather than dating being controversial per se — nobody says that about Tinder, which literally has a “free tonight” button on its homepage. But I’d agree the market’s read on us has clearly improved.

Tech.title: Liux’s Big microcar bets on sustainability to take on Chinese rivals
Tech.content:
Cars in European cities are smaller than ever. But as Europe’s appetite for microcars has grown, the cute Italian ‘yoghurt pots’ have largely given way to small Chinese EVs. Even Smart, the the iconic ultracompact car brand, has moved manufacturing to China.

Spanish startup Liux thinks it can compete in a crowded market with a tiny electric car built around sustainability.

Following the tracks of the Microlino out of Switzerland, Liux is trying to carve out a place in the market with its upcoming microcar, the Liux Big. The “Big” name is a joke. It is small enough to park at a right angle to the curb; but the name also reflects the oversized ambitions of a team that rarely takes the expected route.

“The idea of ​​a European car does not exist,” Liux co-founder Antonio Espinosa de los Monteros told TechCrunch. Coming from the CEO of a startup whose cars are already making headlines for being “made in Spain,” it was a surprising take — and one that reveals a lot about the company’s priorities.

It is true that Liux opened Spain’s first new car plant in more than 30 years. But as we sat down in its elegant showroom, Espinosa and his co-founder David Sancho said they had concluded that a fully sovereign supply chain is unattainable. Instead, Liux is trying to navigate that reality while keeping sustainability as its north star.

Image Credits:Liux /

Liux’s batteries are not made in Europe, but they are rechargeable at home, including with power generated from solar panels. The car is also meant to be easy to maintain and avoid the faster obsolescence cycles of modern cars. Perhaps most notably, its fiber body is made from a novel linen-based biocomposite designed so the material can later be extracted and recycled.

“One thing that’s very clear for David and me is that recycling isn’t just a lab concept. You can recycle almost anything in a lab. What makes something recyclable has to do with how it’s built,” Espinosa said. “When you build something, you have to try to preserve the integrity of the material and the components so that a second life is possible.”

“Real circularity” is where Espinosa comes from; he previously cofounded Auara, a Spanish B Corp selling natural mineral water in bottles that are both recycled and recyclable. But after a larger player acquired this successful brand, he embarked on a new chapter with Sancho as his co-driver.

When it comes to cars, Sancho is in the driver’s seat, with low emissions on the radar. His specialty is engineering electric vehicles that can rival gas-powered ones. Before Liux, his most impressive feat was the Bóreas, a hybrid supercar unveiled at the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2017. But after a fallout with his former partners, he and Espinosa teamed up to found Liux.

Liux’s first prototype, the Animal, combined their expertise: The fully electric five-seater was made almost entirely from recycled or plant-based materials.
